entries.title: Course sources and scope
entries.text: Course sources and scope Course index Confirmed course identity ADS205 — Decision, Computation and Language , confirmed on the lecture title pages and tutorial first pages. Lecturers named in the source: Dr Chunchuan Lyu and Dr Xinhong Chen. The current material studies formal languages, finite automata, regular expressions and proofs of nonregularity. Lecture 1 pp. 2–9 motivates precisely specified models of computation and mathematical argument; pp. 10–13 emphasize independent understanding, attending lectures/tutorials and asking questions. Page 15's wider model hierarchy is a roadmap, not enough material for future chapters. Introductory images (programming example, physical computation/perception illustrations, AI-study screenshots) serve motivation and are not assigned coding exercises. Original sources The five PDFs below were copied byte-for-byte from /Users/muxnoz/Downloads/ADS205 into Original Sources . SHA-256 checks confirmed identity. No byte-identical duplicates were found among the supplied files; no distinct versions were discarded. Tutorials include their supplied solutions and optional Python code. No separate assignments, code files, datasets or lab sheets were supplied. Unit boundaries 1. Strings, Languages and Proofs: Lecture 1 p.19, p.30 and set operations on p.33; Lecture 2 pp.3–7; Tutorial 1 Problems 1–8, Extra and Python activity. 2. Finite Automata and Closure: Lecture 1 pp.20–29, 32–37; Lecture 2 pp.8–29; Tutorial 1 p.2 Q&A and all of Tutorial 2. Repeated source question occurrences are retained in the map even when they share one exercise. 3. Regular Expressions and Automata Conversion: Lecture 1 p.31; Lecture 3 pp.3–24. Conversion examples are also available as exercises. 4. The Pumping Lemma: Lecture 3 pp.25–41, both proof examples and all four closing questions. Administrative, recap, title and closing pages are accounted for as context or repeated material. No future chapters on context-free languages, pushdown automata or Turing machines have been inferred from the roadmap. Lecture 1 p.14 recommends additional videos, a code repository, MIT material and a textbook; these were not supplied or fetched, and they do not expand the present scope. Course conventions and tools - Alphabets are finite and nonempty; strings are finite; languages may be infinite. The tutorial identifies a symbol with its one-symbol string. Epsilon is not an alphabet symbol. - Use the tutorial tuple order (Q, Σ, δ, q0, F) . Some lecture slides reorder the same named components. Complement is relative to the stated alphabet's full string set. - DFA transitions are total. NFAs include epsilon transitions and set-valued successors. Missing NFA transitions are empty sets. Acceptance requires consuming all input. - Regular expressions are the mathematical union/concatenation/star formalism. No programming regex engine is a confirmed course requirement. - Python is explicitly used in both optional tutorial activities, with standard-library sets, strings and (Tutorial 2) collections.deque . Required Python version: UNCONFIRMED . Generated lab scripts were executed here with Python 3.14.6; that is local verification, not a lecturer-mandated version. - Learning Mall is named for in-class tests. Its version and any required IDE or automata package are UNCONFIRMED . The introductory mention of Lean is a comparison about formality, not a required tool. Assessment and teaching information in the supplied source Lecture 1 p.16 announces two in-class tests worth 20% each and one exam worth 60%, with weekly lectures/tutorials except consolidation Week 7. Pages 10 and 12 say there is no marked/take-home homework in this offering. These are statements in the supplied slides, not a separate verification of current institutional policy. Specific test/exam dates and question formats are UNCONFIRMED . Office-hour/contact details are retained in the original Lecture 1 pp.17–18; consult those original pages for the announcement. They are not prerequisites for studying these units. entries.title: ADS205 Tutor Mode
entries.text: ADS205 Tutor Mode This is the guided companion to the unchanged ordinary ADS205 reference edition. Preview cards orient you; recall cards require retrieval. Reading does not establish mastery, so every unit remains study_status: untested until actual attempts provide evidence. The study cycle 1. Read In 60 Seconds and the concept preview. 2. Work through the motivating question before opening the detailed explanation. 3. Close the reference and attempt recall/practice. 4. Open a hint only when needed; then compare your full reasoning with the collapsed solution. 5. Record a specific demonstrated gap, revisit its explanation, and try a transfer problem. Optional chat conventions are /teach , /quiz , /grade , /weak and /cram ; they are not installed slash commands. To resume document study, return to the first unattempted problem rather than treating reading as completion. Units 1. Strings, Languages and Proofs — Tutor Notes · Recall and Practice · Reference · Lab 2. Finite Automata and Closure — Tutor Notes · Recall and Practice · Reference · Lab 3. Regular Expressions and Automata Conversion — Tutor Notes · Recall and Practice · Reference 4. The Pumping Lemma — Tutor Notes · Recall and Practice · Reference If You Are Short on Time [!warning] LIMITED EXAM EVIDENCE The supplied corpus has zero complete papers, two distinct partial INT201 administrations, same-session variants, no marking scheme and an unconfirmed INT201→ADS205 code relationship. This guide describes the supplied sample; it is not a forecast of the next exam. Priority 1 — High Exam Relevance No HIGH tier is justified. The installed evidence gate requires stronger complete-paper recurrence or explicit official emphasis. Consequently no red HIGH marker is applied to a question. Priority 2 — Medium Exam Relevance - First preserve the Unit 01 definitions needed by every later unit. - Study NFA semantics and subset construction, positively observed in both partial administrations. - Study closure constructions, observed in the 2024–25 partial paper and prerequisite to regex construction. - Study regex design and conversion, positively observed in both partial administrations. - Review equal-count nonregularity; the equal-count distinction appeared once, but a direct regular pumping proof was not observed. Priority 3 — Remaining Source-Supported Material Complete Unit 01 proof methods, all original tutorial tasks, Unit 02 closure proofs, Unit 03 state-elimination reasoning, and Unit 04 square-length transfer. “Not observed” never means unimportant or non-examinable. If You Have Only 30 Minutes - 5 min: distinguish symbol/string/language, ε / ∅ / {ε} , and finite/regular. - 10 min: reconstruct DFA versus NFA acceptance and one subset-construction step. - 8 min: translate a language description to a regex and explain one state-elimination update. - 7 min: state pumping-lemma quantifiers and outline the 0^p1^p contradiction. This sacrifices most original exercises, detailed proofs, GNFA algebra, closure edge cases, transfer practice and all lab work. It is a last-pass orientation, not full coverage or a measured learning guarantee.

entries.title: In 60 Seconds
entries.text: This unit supplies the language needed by everything that follows. A computation problem becomes a membership question: is a finite string inside a specified set of strings? You will learn to keep symbols, strings and languages separate; manipulate concatenation and Kleene star; handle the empty string and empty language correctly; and write proofs whose quantifiers match the claim. After study, you should be able to decide membership from definitions, expose witnesses for prefix/substring claims, and prove a language identity in both directions.[^t1-1][^l1-19]

entries.title: Concept Preview
entries.text: [!note] Concept — Type discipline Plain-language meaning: A symbol, a string, and a set of strings are different kinds of object. ε , ∅ , and {ε} therefore behave differently. Why it matters: Many false proofs perform an operation on the wrong type. Connects to: automata inputs, regex languages, pumping witnesses. Source: Tutorial 1, PDF p.1. [!note] Concept — Concatenation and star Plain-language meaning: Concatenation joins chosen strings in order. L allows any finite number of L -blocks, including zero. Why it matters: It describes infinitely many strings with a finite rule. Connects to: regex and NFA composition. Source: Tutorial 1, PDF pp.1–4; Lecture 2, PDF pp.4–5. [!note] Concept — Witnesses and quantifiers Plain-language meaning: “There exists” requires one verified witness; “for every” requires an arbitrary case or a valid general argument. Why it matters: Examples can refute a universal claim but cannot prove one. Connects to: closure proofs and pumping-lemma quantifiers. Source: Tutorial 1, PDF pp.4–7. [!note] Concept — Finite versus cofinite Plain-language meaning: A finite language lists its members; a cofinite language lists finitely many exclusions relative to a fixed Σ . Why it matters: “Infinite” does not mean “cannot have a finite description.” Connects to: complement and decidable membership procedures. Source: Tutorial 1, PDF pp.7–8; Lecture 2, PDF pp.6–7.

entries.title: Before You Start
entries.text: You need only basic set membership and equality. Test yourself: [!question] What must be checked for two finite strings to be equal? [!success]- Check your answer They must have the same length and the same symbol at each position. Source: Tutorial 1, PDF pp.1–3.

entries.title: A motivating question
entries.text: Synthetic case using Tutorial 1 P5. A validator accepts zero or more blocks from L={ac,bd} . A colleague says every even-length input is valid and stores only ac , bd , acac , and bdbd . Decide whether ε , acbd , aaaa , and acbdac are accepted. Then explain why a finite stored list cannot be complete, while the rule L can still be a complete specification. Question Knowledge needed --- --- What is a valid factorization? Concatenation and star Why is even length insufficient? Necessary versus sufficient conditions Why is the language infinite? A family of pairwise distinct witnesses Why is the rule complete? Definition and a terminating membership procedure Success means every decision has a witness or impossibility argument; checking a few examples is insufficient.

entries.title: Learn the mechanism
entries.text: Types first: ε , ∅ , and {ε} An alphabet Σ is a nonempty finite set of symbols. A string is a finite ordered sequence of symbols, and Σ is the set of all strings over Σ . A language is a subset of Σ and may be finite or infinite.[^t1-1] Object Type Key fact --- --- --- ε string length 0 ∅ language/set contains no strings {ε} language/set contains exactly one string The course identifies a symbol with its one-symbol string, so Σ ⊆ Σ ; it does not make ε a symbol. Consequently ε∈Σ but ε∉Σ .[^t1-1] [!warning] Common confusion ∅ ={ε} , not ∅ . Star permits zero factors even when no positive-factor choice exists. This is a definition-based fact, not a special exception. Concatenation preserves order For strings x,y , xy appends y to x , so xy = x + y . It is associative but generally not commutative. For languages A,B , $$AB=\{xy\mid x\in A,\ y\in B\}.$$ To prove w∈AB , exhibit both factors. To prove nonmembership, rule out every possible factorization compatible with the sets. The same witness habit appears in prefix and substring definitions: v is a substring of w exactly when w=xvz for some x,z .[^t1-1] mermaid flowchart LR W["w = x · v · z"] -- X["prefix x"] W -- V["contiguous substring v"] W -- Z["suffix z"] Figure 1 — A substring needs two witnesses Read it: The whole string is decomposed into the material before, the contiguous target, and the material after. Key takeaway: Deleting an arbitrary middle part does not preserve contiguity; the equality must literally be w=xvz . Provenance: Pedagogical diagram derived from Tutorial 1, PDF pp.1–3. Star is a finite-list constructor The definition $$L^ =\{w_1\cdots w_k\mid k\ge0,\ w_i\in L\}$$ allows a different L -string at every position and permits repetition. Each output uses finitely many factors, but no common upper bound on k is imposed.[^t1-1] Worked example. Let L={ac,bd} and ask for members of length at most four. 1. Every factor has length 2, so a product of k factors has length 2k . 2. 2k≤4 implies k∈{0,1,2} . 3. For k=0 , obtain ε ; for k=1 , obtain ac,bd ; for k=2 , take all four ordered pairs. 4. Therefore the complete list is ε, ac, bd, acac, acbd, bdac, bdbd . Even length is necessary because all blocks have length two. It is not sufficient: aaaa splits into aa·aa , and aa∉L . [!question] Explain it yourself Why can different factor choices produce the same output for A={a,aa} , even though there are A ^k ordered choices for fixed k ? [!success]- Check your explanation Concatenation may erase factor boundaries: (a,aa) and (aa,a) both yield aaa . The power counts choices, not necessarily distinct outputs. Source: Lecture 2, PDF p.5, qualified by the definitions. Finite description is not finite membership The family (ac)^k , for every integer k≥0 , consists of accepted strings with distinct lengths. This proves L infinite. Yet the rule “split into pairs and require every pair to be ac or bd ” is finite and terminates on each finite input. A language can therefore be infinite and finitely specified.[^t1-78] For complement, fix Σ : L̄=Σ \L . A finite language can store all members. A cofinite language can store its finite complement. Neither category contains all finitely describable languages; the even-length language and its complement are both infinite over {a,b} .[^l2-67][^t1-78] Match the proof to the claim Claim form Correct burden --- --- ∃x P(x) Give one witness and verify it ∀x P(x) Start with arbitrary x and derive P(x) ¬∀x P(x) Give one counterexample A=B Prove A⊆B and B⊆A Worked identity: L ={ε}∪LL . For w∈L , either it uses zero factors and equals ε , or it uses at least one factor; separate the first factor to place it in LL . Conversely, ε uses zero factors, while a word in LL has one L -factor followed by a finite list of L -factors, so it is in L . This covers L=∅ and languages containing ε ; examples alone would not.[^t1-67]

entries.title: Return to the motivating question
entries.text: - ε is accepted using zero blocks. - acbd is accepted with witness ac·bd . - aaaa is rejected: its only two-symbol blocks are not in L . - acbdac is accepted with witness ac·bd·ac . The colleague's even-length rule is only necessary, and the four-entry list misses acbd , bdac , every valid length-six input, and infinitely many later inputs. The finite specification L is complete because it characterizes every accepted input by a finite factorization. Pairwise scanning decides membership. [!warning] Source discrepancy Tutorial 1 P5 uses L={ac,bd} , but its supplied P5.3 answer and Python activity use aa/bb blocks. For the stated exercise, aaaa is rejected; for the activity's different language {aa,bb} , it is accepted. Source: Tutorial 1, PDF pp.4, 8–9.

entries.title: 5-Minute Review
entries.text: - Type-check every expression before calculating. - Concatenation needs ordered factor witnesses; substring needs w=xvz . - L always contains ε and permits any finite factor count. - A length condition may be necessary without identifying valid factors. - Infinite languages may have finite rules and terminating membership procedures. - Universal claims need arbitrary-case reasoning; language equality needs both inclusions.

entries.title: Strings, Languages and Proofs
entries.text: Strings, Languages and Proofs Course index · Exercises · Lab Opening case — A validator built from blocks Synthetic teaching case using Tutorial 1's exact block language. A small input validator allows any finite sequence of blocks from $L=\{ac,bd\}$, including no blocks. The input is a finite string over $\Sigma=\{a,b,c,d\}$. A colleague proposes storing all valid inputs in a list and reports that aaaa is valid because its length is even. Your tasks are to specify the accepted language, list all accepted inputs of length at most four, decide whether a and aaaa belong, and justify whether a finite list can represent every accepted string explicitly. Success means a definition-based argument that covers arbitrarily long inputs and the empty input. What We Need to Learn Case question Required concepts --- --- What counts as an input? Alphabet, string, length, empty string How do blocks combine? Concatenation, language operations, Kleene star Does even length suffice? Necessary versus sufficient conditions; counterexamples Can a list contain every input? Finite and infinite languages; representation How can the answer be justified? Quantifiers, witnesses, two-inclusion proofs 1. From a decision problem to a language A decision problem asks for a yes/no answer. Once each candidate is encoded as a string, the language is precisely the set of inputs whose correct answer is yes. An algorithm for membership decides whether $w\in L$. Defining a set and giving a method to decide membership are separate achievements. This distinction motivates the module's study of simplified computation models; the later models mentioned in the introductory roadmap are outside these supplied chapters. Source: Lecture 1, PDF pp. 2–9, 15, 19. [!note] Alphabet, string and language An alphabet $\Sigma$ is a nonempty finite set of symbols. A string over $\Sigma$ is a finite ordered sequence of its symbols. $\Sigma^ $ denotes all such strings. A language over $\Sigma$ is any subset of $\Sigma^ $. A language may be finite or infinite. Source: Tutorial 1, PDF p. 1; Lecture 1, PDF p. 19. For $w=w_1\cdots w_n$, $ w =n$ counts symbols; $w_i$ is the symbol in position $i$, counting from one. Length is a count, with no physical units. String equality requires the same length and the same symbol in every position. Thus ab differs from ba , and a differs from aa . The course identifies a symbol with its corresponding one-symbol string, so $\Sigma\subseteq\Sigma^ $. This convention does not make the empty string a symbol. Object Type Size or length --- --- --- $\varepsilon$ Empty string $\vert \varepsilon\vert =0$ $\varnothing$ Empty language Zero elements $\{\varepsilon\}$ Language containing one string One element, whose length is zero In particular, $\varepsilon\notin\Sigma$ and $\varepsilon\in\Sigma^ $. It need not belong to an arbitrary language: $\varepsilon\notin\{abc\}$. Checkpoint. Before reading on, explain why “an infinite set of finite strings” is consistent, while an infinite string is excluded by the course definition. A length can be finite for every individual member without one upper bound applying to all members. 2. Concatenation and contiguous pieces Why we need it. A block validator combines entire strings, not unordered collections of letters. For strings $x$ and $y$, their concatenation $xy$ writes $x$ followed by $y$. Therefore $ xy = x + y $ and $x\varepsilon=\varepsilon x=x$. Concatenation is associative: $(xy)z=x(yz)$. It is generally not commutative: ab and ba demonstrate the difference. Source: Tutorial 1, PDF pp. 1, 3. A prefix $x$ of $w$ satisfies $w=xy$ for some string $y$; that $y$ is a suffix. A substring $v$ satisfies $w=xvz$ for some strings $x,z$. The existential words for some tell you exactly what witnesses a proof must supply. Substrings are contiguous. Removing the middle of abc produces ac , which is not a substring of abc . Both $\varepsilon$ and the entire string count as prefixes, suffixes and substrings. The prefixes of abc are $\varepsilon,a,ab,abc$. string-decomposition.svg Figure 1 — Regrouping proves nested substring containment Read it: Read the five blocks from left to right. The teal bracket identifies y; the central block is v. Key takeaway: If s = xyz and y = uvw, then s = (xu)v(wz). Associativity supplies the witnesses required by the definition. Provenance: Original teaching diagram derived from the cited concepts. Worked example. Suppose $s=abcab$, $y=bca$ and $v=c$. Then $x=a$, $z=b$, $u=b$, $w=a$ give $s=(ab)c(ab)$. The general proof uses these roles as arbitrary strings, not these particular letters. The formal proof conversion appears in Exercise T1 P6. 3. Operations on languages Union, concatenation and star are the three regular operations named by the lectures. Other set operations are meaningful too; “regular operation” here is a specific course term. Source: Lecture 1, PDF p. 30; Lecture 2, PDF pp. 4–6. For languages $A,B\subseteq\Sigma^ $: $$A\cup B=\{w\mid w\in A\text{ or }w\in B\},$$ $$AB=A\circ B=\{xy\mid x\in A,\ y\in B\}.$$ Union selects a whole string from either set; concatenation selects a pair and joins it in order. For $A=\{good,bad\}$ and $B=\{boy,girl\}$, union contains four separate words, whereas $AB=\{goodboy,goodgirl,badboy,badgirl\}$. These are the lecture's examples, not a rule about grammatical English. [!note] Kleene star $L^ =\{w_1\cdots w_k\mid k\geq0,\ w_i\in L\text{ for }1\leq i\leq k\}$. The factors $w_i$ are strings , and may repeat. The empty product ($k=0$) is $\varepsilon$. Consequently ==every star contains the empty string==, including $\varnothing^ $. Source: Tutorial 1, PDF pp. 1–4. star-factors.svg Figure 2 — Enumerating by number of factors Read it: Start with zero blocks, then one block, then every ordered pair. Key takeaway: A length bound can become a factor bound when all allowed blocks have the same positive length. Provenance: Original teaching diagram derived from the cited concepts. Edge cases derived from the definitions. There is no pair with first component in $\varnothing$, so $\varnothing A=\varnothing$. Similarly $A\varnothing=\varnothing$. By contrast, the pair $(\varepsilon,x)$ gives $\{\varepsilon\}A=A$. No positive number of factors can be chosen from $\varnothing$, but zero factors remain possible: $\varnothing^ =\{\varepsilon\}$. Repeating $\varepsilon$ any number of times still gives $\varepsilon$, so $\{\varepsilon\}^ =\{\varepsilon\}$. [!warning] Factor choices are not always distinct output strings Lecture 2, PDF p. 5 says the number of strings for fixed $k$ is $ A ^k$. For finite $A$, this always counts ordered choices of factors , but different choices may concatenate to the same string. For $A=\{a,aa\}$ and $k=2$, (a,aa) and (aa,a) both produce aaa ; the four choices give only three strings. Equality holds for the case language's distinct equal-length blocks, because the block boundaries are recoverable. This is a definition-based qualification of the source claim. Reversal writes a string backwards: $(abc)^R=cba$, and $L^R=\{w^R\mid w\in L\}$. For two strings, $(xy)^R=y^Rx^R$: reversing changes both internal order and block order. Tutorial 1's optional Python activity computes this operation (PDF pp. 1, 8–9). 4. Complements, finiteness and representation Fix the alphabet before taking a complement: $\overline L=\Sigma^ \setminus L$. If $L$ contains the even-length strings over $\{a,b\}$, its complement contains the odd-length strings. Also $K\setminus L=K\cap\overline L$, because membership requires being in $K$ and not in $L$. Source: Lecture 2, PDF pp. 6–7. FINITE is the collection of all finite languages over the fixed alphabet. coFINITE consists of languages whose complements are finite. The prefix “co” here concerns complementing a language, not taking the complement of the collection FINITE. A finite language can be represented by listing all its strings. Test membership by comparing the candidate with each entry; the list is finite and each comparison is finite, so the procedure terminates. For a cofinite language, list its finite complement, reject listed candidates, and accept the rest. Neither method says every infinite language lacks a finite description: a rule such as “even length” is itself finite. Source: Tutorial 1, PDF pp. 7–8. Worked proof. No language is both finite and cofinite over $\Sigma=\{a,b\}$. If $L$ and $\overline L$ were finite, then $L\cup\overline L=\Sigma^ $ would be finite. But $\varepsilon,a,aa,aaa,\ldots$ are pairwise different by length. This contradiction proves $\mathrm{FINITE}\cap\mathrm{coFINITE}=\varnothing$. The even-length language is neither finite nor cofinite: $a^{2k}$ supplies infinitely many members and $a^{2k+1}$ infinitely many nonmembers, for integers $k\geq0$. This is an existence argument, not a counting proof about how many languages fall in each class. 5. Writing proofs that cover every input Source: Tutorial 1, PDF pp. 4–7. First restate the givens and the goal; then unpack definitions; choose a proof structure that matches the logical claim. Examples test an intuition but do not prove a universal assertion about infinitely many inputs. Claim Sufficient proof structure --- --- There exists an object with property P Construct one witness and verify P Every object has P Start with an arbitrary object and derive P A universal assertion is false Supply one counterexample $X=Y$ for sets Prove $X\subseteq Y$ and $Y\subseteq X$ A proposed assumption is impossible Derive a contradiction from that assumption A statement–reason proof makes each dependency explicit. A paragraph proof joins the same valid steps into readable prose. Planning backwards from a goal may help you find a proof, but the written implication must be justified from the givens; assuming the goal proves nothing. Worked general identity. To prove $\{\varepsilon\}L=L$, let $w\in\{\varepsilon\}L$. Then $w=uv$ for $u=\varepsilon$ and $v\in L$, so $w=v\in L$. Conversely, if $w\in L$, write $w=\varepsilon w$ to obtain $w\in\{\varepsilon\}L$. Both inclusions apply even when $L=\varnothing$. The harder recursive identity $L^ =\{\varepsilon\}\cup LL^ $ needs a split between zero and positive numbers of factors. Work through T1 P7 and its Extra before consulting their local solutions. Solve the opening case Decision. The accepted language is $L^ $ for $L=\{ac,bd\}$, because the specification permits zero or more complete blocks. Justification and operation. Every block has length two. A product of $k$ blocks has length $2k$, so $2k\leq4$ forces $k\in\{0,1,2\}$. Enumerating each permitted value gives: $k$ Result --- --- 0 $\varepsilon$ 1 ac , bd 2 acac , acbd , bdac , bdbd Membership decisions. a has odd length, so it cannot be a product of length-two blocks. aaaa has even length, but its first block would have to be aa , which is not allowed. Hence both are rejected. Even length is necessary, not sufficient. Representation. The strings $(ac)^k$, for integers $k\geq0$, are all accepted and have distinct lengths $2k$. Thus the language is infinite and no finite list explicitly enumerates it. Its finite block rule still describes it. Reading the string in pairs and checking each pair against $L$ gives a terminating membership procedure for every finite input. Success check. The result includes the empty input, accounts for every factor count under the requested bound, rejects both specified bad candidates, and proves infinitude without relying on a finite sample. [!warning] Source discrepancy — Tutorial 1 P5 The statement and enumeration on PDF p. 4 use $L=\{ac,bd\}$, but the supplied P5.3 solution accepts aaaa using aa factors. Those factors are not in the stated language. The Python activity on PDF p. 9 explicitly uses the different language $\{aa,bb\}$, for which aaaa is accepted. Both versions are preserved and compared in the lab; the original exercise is solved using its actual stated inputs. Exam-style answer and reusable method “Membership in $L^ $ requires a decomposition into finitely many factors from $L$, allowing zero factors. Length conditions can rule inputs out, but membership requires valid factors. For $L=\{ac,bd\}$, aaaa fails because its two-symbol factors are aa . The family $(ac)^k$ proves $L^ $ infinite.” For a new problem: identify each object's type; expand the operation's definition; treat empty cases; give witnesses for membership; rule out all possible witnesses for nonmembership; choose proof quantifiers to match the question. Enumeration proves completeness only when you justify a finite bound on all possibilities. Misconceptions and quick review - $\varepsilon$, $\varnothing$ and $\{\varepsilon\}$ have different types. Check type before calculating. - A substring must be contiguous; a subsequence-like deletion is insufficient. - Infinite languages can contain only finite strings and can have finite descriptions. - $\varepsilon\in L^ $ does not imply $\varepsilon\in L$. - A few successful cases cannot establish a universal identity. [!summary] Retrieval targets Define string, language, concatenation and star without examples. Reconstruct the two empty-star calculations. Explain finite versus cofinite representation. Prove one set equality in both directions, then tackle the original exercises without opening their help panels.

entries.title: Exercises
entries.text:
Exercises Notes · Lab Attempt each problem without help. Open its hint only when stuck, then compare your reasoning with the adjacent solution. Original tasks retain their source IDs; supplementary practice is labelled. T1 P1 — Symbols and languages Source: ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE — Tutorial 1 - Strings, Languages and Proofs.pdf, PDF pp. 2–3. Assume $\Sigma=\{a,b,c\}$. Determine true or false and justify each statement. 1. $\Sigma\subseteq\Sigma^ $. 2. $\varepsilon\in\Sigma$. 3. $\varepsilon\in\Sigma^ $. 4. $a=aa$. 5. $ab=ba$. 6. $\varepsilon\in\{abc\}$. 7. $\{abc\}\cup\varnothing=\{abc\}$. 8. $\{abc\}\cup\{\varepsilon\}=\{abc\}$. 9. $\Sigma^ =\Sigma^ \cup\{\varepsilon\}$. [!tip]- Hint Separate symbols, strings and sets of strings. A union adds elements only when they were absent. [!success]- Solution 1. True: the course identifies each symbol with its one-symbol string. 2. False: $\varepsilon$ has zero symbols; it is not an alphabet symbol. 3. True: length zero is finite, so the empty sequence belongs to $\Sigma^ $. 4. False: the lengths are 1 and 2. 5. False: the first positions differ. 6. False: the only element is abc , not $\varepsilon$. 7. True: the empty set adds no elements. 8. False: the left side is $\{abc,\varepsilon\}$, with two elements. 9. True: $\varepsilon$ is already in $\Sigma^ $. Interpretation: the same union with $\{\varepsilon\}$ changes one language and leaves another unchanged; inspect actual membership. T1 P2 — Contiguous pieces Source: ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE — Tutorial 1 - Strings, Languages and Proofs.pdf, PDF p. 3. 1. List all prefixes of abc . 2. What is $ \varepsilon\varepsilon\varepsilon $? 3. Give an example where $xz$ is not a substring of $xyz$, then one where it is. [!tip]- Hint Include empty and whole-string prefixes. A substring requires one contiguous occurrence. [!success]- Solution 1. Cut after zero, one, two and three symbols: $\varepsilon,a,ab,abc$. 2. Concatenating empty strings leaves $\varepsilon$, so the length is 0 . 3. Choose $x=a,y=b,z=c$: ac is not contiguous in abc . For a positive example choose $x=a,y=\varepsilon,z=c$: $xz=xyz=ac$, and every string is a substring of itself (empty surrounding witnesses). T1 P3 — What may be infinite Source: ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE — Tutorial 1 - Strings, Languages and Proofs.pdf, PDF p. 3. Under the stated definitions, can there be (1) an infinite alphabet, (2) an infinite string, or (3) an infinite language? Justify from definitions. [!tip]- Hint Distinguish the size of the collection from the length of its members. [!success]- Solution 1. No: alphabets in this course are finite by definition. 2. No: strings are finite sequences by definition. 3. Yes: over an alphabet containing $a$, the set $\{a^n\mid n\geq0\}$ contains infinitely many different finite strings. Their lengths distinguish them. These answers concern the course's definitions, not alternative theories with infinite words. T1 P4 — Empty objects Source: ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE — Tutorial 1 - Strings, Languages and Proofs.pdf, PDF pp. 3–4. Compute (1) $\varnothing\circ\{a\}$, (2) $\{\varepsilon\}\circ\{a\}$, (3) $\varnothing^ $, and (4) $\{\varepsilon\}^ $. Then decide whether $L\circ\varnothing=\varnothing$ holds for every $L$, and whether $L^ =\varnothing$ is ever possible. [!tip]- Hint Unfold the pair definition for concatenation and include k = 0 in star. [!success]- Solution 1. No first component exists in $\varnothing$, so the result is $\varnothing$. 2. The sole pair is $(\varepsilon,a)$; its concatenation is $a$, so the result is $\{a\}$. 3. Zero factors produce $\varepsilon$; no positive-factor choice exists. Thus $\varnothing^ =\{\varepsilon\}$. 4. Every permitted product is $\varepsilon$, so $\{\varepsilon\}^ =\{\varepsilon\}$. 5. Always true: the second factor of a pair cannot come from $\varnothing$. 6. Impossible: the zero-factor case puts $\varepsilon$ in every $L^ $. T1 P5 — Concrete language operations Source: ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE — Tutorial 1 - Strings, Languages and Proofs.pdf, PDF p. 4. Let $A=\{c,d\}$, $B=\{at,og\}$ and $L=\{ac,bd\}$. 1. Compute $A\circ B$. 2. List every string in $L^ $ of length at most 4, recording its factor count $k$. 3. Is $a\in L^ $? Is $aaaa\in L^ $? [!tip]- Hint Every L-block has length two. Check the identity of each block as well as the total length. [!success]- Solution Step 1 — Form every ordered pair. $AB=\{cat,cog,dat,dog\}$. Step 2 — Bound the factors. Length $2k\leq4$ gives $k=0,1,2$. For $k=0$: $\varepsilon$. For $k=1$: ac , bd . For $k=2$: acac , acbd , bdac , bdbd . Larger $k$ exceeds the bound, so the list is complete. Step 3 — Membership. $a
otin L^ $ because its length is odd. $aaaa
otin L^ $ because neither two-symbol block aa is in $L$. Source correction: the printed P5.3 solution instead uses aa factors and says yes. That solves the Python activity's different $L=\{aa,bb\}$, not this statement. No inputs have been changed here. T1 P6 — Translate proof formats Source: ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE — Tutorial 1 - Strings, Languages and Proofs.pdf, PDF pp. 5–6. (a) Convert the following paragraph proof into a statement–reason proof, identifying dependencies: if $s$ is a string, every substring of a substring of $s$ is a substring of $s$. Let $y$ be a substring of $s$, so $s=xyz$ for some $x,z$; let $v$ be a substring of $y$, so $y=uvw$ for some $u,w$. Then $s=xuvwz$, so $v$ is a substring of $s$. (b) Convert this statement–reason proof into a paragraph proof of “every prefix of a suffix of $w$ is a suffix of a prefix of $w$”: Statement Source reason --- --- --- 1 $v$ is a suffix of $w$ Given 2 $y$ is a prefix of $v$ Given 3 There is $x$ with $xv=w$ 1, suffix definition 4 There is $z$ with $yz=v$ 2, prefix definition 5 $xyz=w$ 3, 4, substitution 6 $xy$ is a prefix of $w$ 5, prefix definition 7 $y$ is a suffix of $xy$ 6, suffix definition [!tip]- Hint Expose the witnesses and the regrouping step. In (b), distinguish why xy is a prefix from why y is its suffix. [!success]- Solution (a) Statement–reason version Statement Reason --- --- --- 1 $y$ is a substring of $s$ Given 2 $v$ is a substring of $y$ Given 3 $s=xyz$ for some $x,z$ 1, substring definition 4 $y=uvw$ for some $u,w$ 2, substring definition 5 $s=x(uvw)z$ 3 and 4, substitution 6 $s=(xu)v(wz)$ 5, associativity 7 $v$ is a substring of $s$ 6, witnesses $xu,wz$ (b) Paragraph version. Let $v$ be any suffix of $w$ and $y$ any prefix of $v$. Choose $x,z$ such that $w=xv$ and $v=yz$. Substitution and associativity give $w=x(yz)=(xy)z$. Thus $xy$ is a prefix of $w$. Since $xy=x\cdot y$, $y$ is a suffix of $xy$. Therefore the arbitrary prefix of a suffix is a suffix of a prefix. The source table's last dependency is abbreviated: $xy=x\cdot y$ directly witnesses the suffix relation; line 6 establishes that this containing string is a prefix of $w$. T1 P7 — A recursive identity for star Source: ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE — Tutorial 1 - Strings, Languages and Proofs.pdf, PDF pp. 6–7. For every language $L$, prove $L^ =\{\varepsilon\}\cup LL^ $. Before the paragraph proof: state the requirements, test $L=\{a\}$, $L=\{\varepsilon\}$ and $L=\varnothing$, and split the equality into both inclusions. [!tip]- Hint For a positive number of factors, remove the first factor. Treat the empty product separately. [!success]- Solution Requirements. An element of $L^ $ is a finite concatenation of $L$-factors. An element of $LL^ $ has one $L$-factor followed by a finite concatenation of them. Intuition checks. For $L=\{a\}$, both sides contain exactly $a^k$ for $k\geq0$. For $L=\{\varepsilon\}$ both are $\{\varepsilon\}$. For $L=\varnothing$, the right side is $\{\varepsilon\}\cup\varnothing$, again equal to the left. These checks are not the general proof. Paragraph proof. Let $w\in L^ $. Then $w=w_1\cdots w_k$ with $k\geq0$ and each factor in $L$. If $k=0$, $w=\varepsilon\in\{\varepsilon\}$. If $k 0$, take $u=w_1\in L$ and $v=w_2\cdots w_k\in L^ $, where $v=\varepsilon$ is allowed when $k=1$. Hence $w=uv\in LL^ $. This proves the first inclusion. Conversely, take $w\in\{\varepsilon\}\cup LL^ $. If $w=\varepsilon$, use zero factors to get $w\in L^ $. Otherwise $w=uv$ with $u\in L$ and $v=v_1\cdots v_k\in L^ $. Then $w=uv_1\cdots v_k$ is a product of $k+1$ factors from $L$, so $w\in L^ $. Both inclusions establish equality. The argument includes languages containing $\varepsilon$ and the empty language. T1 P7 Extra — Star of a star Source: ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE — Tutorial 1 - Strings, Languages and Proofs.pdf, PDF p. 7. Prove $(L^ )^ =L^ $ in the same two-inclusion style. [!tip]- Hint A factor from L is itself a finite list of L-factors. Flatten all lists. [!success]- Solution First inclusion. Let $w\in(L^ )^ $. Write $w=u_1\cdots u_m$ with $m\geq0$ and each $u_j\in L^ $. Write each $u_j$ as a product of $k_j\geq0$ factors from $L$. Concatenating these finite lists writes $w$ as a product of $k_1+\cdots+k_m$ factors from $L$, so $w\in L^ $. If there are no factors, the same argument gives $w=\varepsilon$. Reverse inclusion. For $w\in L^ $, use the single factor $u_1=w$ in the outer star, so $w\in(L^ )^ $. Therefore equality holds, including $L=\varnothing$. T1 P8 — Finite and cofinite representation Source: ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE — Tutorial 1 - Strings, Languages and Proofs.pdf, PDF pp. 7–8. Fix $\Sigma=\{a,b\}$. FINITE contains all finite languages over $\Sigma$, and $\mathrm{coFINITE}=\{L\subseteq\Sigma^ \mid\overline L\in\mathrm{FINITE}\}$, with $\overline L=\Sigma^ \setminus L$. You may assume the union of two finite sets is finite. 1. For finite $L$, give a data structure and membership procedure. 2. For cofinite $L$, do the same. 3. Is any language in $\mathrm{FINITE}\cap\mathrm{coFINITE}$? Prove your answer. 4. Is any language outside $\mathrm{FINITE}\cup\mathrm{coFINITE}$? Prove your answer. [!tip]- Hint For (2), store excluded strings. For (3), inspect the union with the complement. For (4), make both sides infinite. [!success]- Solution 1. Store the strings of $L$ in a finite list (or set). Compare the input with each entry; accept a match and reject after exhaustion. Finitely many finite comparisons ensure termination. 2. Store the finite complement. Reject when the input matches an excluded string; accept after no match. This also terminates. 3. No. If $L$ and $\overline L$ were both finite, $\Sigma^ =L\cup\overline L$ would be finite. But all $a^n$, $n\geq0$, belong to $\Sigma^ $ and have distinct lengths. Contradiction. 4. Yes. Let $E=\{w\in\{a,b\}^ \mid w 	ext{ is even}\}$. Its members $a^{2k}$ are infinitely many distinct strings, so $E$ is not finite. The nonmembers $a^{2k+1}$ show $\overline E$ infinite, so $E$ is not cofinite. The source solution's cross-reference to Problem 5 for the even-length language is inaccurate: P5 uses $\{ac,bd\}$. The witness in part 4 is defined explicitly here and needs no such reference. L2 recap — Language difference Source: ORIGINAL COURSE QUESTION — Lecture 2 DFA and NFA.pdf, PDF p. 6. How do we compute $K\setminus L$ using complement and intersection? [!tip]- Hint Translate set difference into two membership conditions. [!success]- Solution $w\in K\setminus L$ exactly when $w\in K$ and $w
otin L$, equivalently $w\in K$ and $w\in\overline L$. Thus $K\setminus L=K\cap\overline L$, with complement taken in the same $\Sigma^ $. L1 introduction — A membership decision Source: ORIGINAL COURSE QUESTION — Lecture 1 Intro and Regular Language.pdf, PDF p. 2. Is $0\in\{0,11,01\}$ true? [!tip]- Hint Compare the whole input with the listed elements. [!success]- Solution Yes. The one-symbol string $0$ is explicitly an element. Membership does not ask whether 0 merely occurs inside 01; it asks whether the entire string equals one listed member.

entries.title: Testing language operations with finite sets
entries.text: Testing language operations with finite sets Notes · Exercises Purpose and setup Original optional activity: Tutorial 1 - Strings, Languages and Proofs.pdf, PDF pp. 8–9, section 7.2. Run the cell and compare its outputs with Problems 4 and 5, especially star(set()) against P4.3. The PDF remains the original source. The accompanying script transcribes its three functions, normalizes PDF wrapping, and labels a second run using P5's actual inputs. Use Python 3 with its standard library; the lecturer's required version is UNCONFIRMED . This run was executed with Python 3.14.6. Open a terminal in this unit folder and run: sh python3 Attachments/language_operations.py Open the script '' represents $\varepsilon$, set() represents $\varnothing$, and {''} represents $\{\varepsilon\}$. concat enumerates pairs and the set removes duplicates. In star , frontier holds products of exactly the current number of factors, while out accumulates products of zero through that number. rev uses Python's reverse slice [::-1] ; this syntax implements string reversal. Procedure and expected results First predict the results by hand. Run the original activity's $L=\{aa,bb\}$, then compare it with the statement's $L=\{ac,bd\}$. Treat this as a controlled change of the block set. [!tip]- Hint For the length-four comparison, zero, one and two factors suffice. The function's default limit of four factors therefore includes every relevant product for these two equal-length block sets. [!success]- Solution and observed results Execution returned the following values (strings sorted where order matters for display): Computation Observed result --- --- $AB$ cat , cog , dat , dog $(AB)^R$ goc , god , tac , tad $\{aa,bb\}^ $ through length 4 $\varepsilon$, aa , aaaa , aabb , bb , bbaa , bbbb $\{ac,bd\}^ $ through length 4 $\varepsilon$, ac , acac , acbd , bd , bdac , bdbd Membership of a False in both cases Membership of aaaa True for {aa,bb} ; False for {ac,bd} $\varnothing\{a\}$ set() $\{\varepsilon\}\{a\}$ {'a'} $\varnothing^ $ and $\{\varepsilon\}^ $ {''} in both cases These results agree with the definition-based solutions. The source code comment linking reversal to P5.3 is a stale cross-reference: P5.3 asks membership questions. Reversal is nevertheless an actual computation in the supplied activity and is retained here. Limitations and troubleshooting star(A, max_factors=4) computes a ==finite approximation==, not an arbitrary infinite star. A positive result supplies a witness; a negative result may merely mean that more factors are needed. Completeness under a length bound needs its own argument, as above. Set display order is not semantic. If Python is unavailable, the hand derivation remains valid; no installation is required to study the topic. Changing the script does not modify the original PDF.

entries.title: In 60 Seconds
entries.text: A finite automaton replaces an unbounded input history with one of finitely many summaries called states. A DFA has exactly one next state for every state-symbol pair; an NFA tracks a set of possible states and accepts when at least one complete path succeeds. Subset construction turns that set into an ordinary DFA state. Product states track two machines at once, while epsilon links implement union, concatenation and star. After study, you should be able to design state meanings, trace both models, determinize an epsilon-NFA, and justify closure constructions.[^l2][^t2]

entries.title: Concept Preview
entries.text: [!note] Concept — State invariant Plain-language meaning: A state says exactly what relevant fact about the consumed prefix is currently true. Why it matters: A labelled diagram becomes a proof when every transition preserves the stated meaning. Connects to: suffix detectors, product states, pumping loops. Source: Lecture 1, PDF pp.20–28. [!note] Concept — Nondeterministic acceptance Plain-language meaning: An NFA follows all permitted paths conceptually and accepts if one consumes the entire input and finishes accepting. Why it matters: Dead branches do not veto a successful one. Connects to: regex construction and closure. Source: Lecture 2, PDF pp.11–14; Tutorial 2, PDF p.1. [!note] Concept — Subset construction Plain-language meaning: One DFA state records the whole set of NFA states reachable after the same prefix. Why it matters: It proves NFAs and DFAs recognize the same languages. Connects to: complement and implementation. Source: Lecture 2, PDF pp.16–18; Tutorial 2, PDF pp.3–4. [!note] Concept — Closure construction Plain-language meaning: New finite machines can combine old machines while preserving union, intersection, concatenation, star or complement semantics. Why it matters: It proves results for every pair of regular languages, not only examples. Connects to: regular-expression syntax. Source: Lecture 1, PDF pp.32–35; Lecture 2, PDF pp.19–27.

entries.title: Before You Start
entries.text: Recall that a language is a set of strings and that acceptance is decided after the whole string is consumed. [!question] If an accepting state is visited before the input ends, is the input already accepted? [!success]- Check your answer No. Continue every transition; acceptance depends on the state after all symbols are consumed. Source: Lecture 1, PDF pp.22–28.

entries.title: A motivating question
entries.text: Synthetic monitoring case based on Tutorial 2 P2. Design a streaming checker over {a,b} that accepts exactly strings ending in ab . It cannot store the whole input. It must define a transition for every state and symbol, correctly reject ε and aba , and accept ab , aab , and bbab . Question Knowledge needed --- --- What must be remembered? Equivalence classes of useful suffix information How is a run computed? DFA tuple and total transition function How is the design proved? Initialization, transition preservation, final equivalence How can choices be simulated? NFA set semantics and subset construction

entries.title: Build a DFA from state meanings
entries.text: Use three meanings: q0 means the prefix ends in neither a nor ab ; q1 means it ends in a ; q2 means it ends in ab . They are mutually exclusive and cover every prefix. Empty input begins at q0 ; only q2 is accepting.[^t2] State on a on b --- --- --- q0 q1 q0 q1 q1 q2 q2 q1 q0 Appending a always creates suffix a . Appending b creates suffix ab exactly when the previous prefix ended in a . These two observations derive the table. mermaid stateDiagram-v2 [ ] -- q0 q0 -- q1: a q0 -- q0: b q1 -- q1: a q1 -- q2: b q2 -- q1: a q2 -- q0: b state q2 Figure 1 — State meaning drives every arrow Read it: Follow exactly one edge per input symbol; the double-role accepting state is reached only when the current entire prefix ends in ab . Key takeaway: Visiting q2 early is irrelevant if later symbols leave it. Provenance: Tutorial 2, PDF pp.2–3, redrawn as Mermaid. [!note] DFA A DFA is (Q,Σ,δ,q0,F) with total δ:Q×Σ→Q . Starting at q0 , apply one transition per symbol and accept iff the final state is in F .[^l2] The invariant proof is an induction on prefix length. The empty prefix satisfies q0 's meaning. The table preserves the meanings for either next symbol. Therefore the final state is q2 exactly when the full input ends in ab .

entries.title: From one path to a set of paths
entries.text: An NFA has δ:Q×(Σ∪{ε})→P(Q) . A missing transition yields no successor for that branch. An epsilon transition changes state without consuming input. Acceptance is existential: at least one path must consume every symbol and finish in F .[^l2][^t2] For a set S , its epsilon closure E(S) contains every state reachable through zero or more epsilon edges. One symbol step is: $$S' = E\left(\bigcup_{q\in S}\delta(q,a)\right).$$ The initial set is E({q0}) , not merely {q0} . The empty set is a legitimate rejecting subset and becomes a sink under the construction. Worked subset construction. The 2024–25 partial paper's displayed NFA has transitions: - 1 --a,ε→ 2 ; 2 --b→2 ; 2 --b→3 ; - 3 --a→2 ; 3 --b→1 ; accepting state 3 . Name reachable subsets A={1,2} , B={2} , C={2,3} , D=∅ , E={1,2,3} . The initial epsilon closure is A . DFA subset a b Accepting? --- --- --- --- A={1,2} B C No B={2} D C No C={2,3} B E Yes D=∅ D D No E={1,2,3} B E Yes For example, C on b reaches {2,3} from state 2 and {1} from state 3; epsilon closure of {1,2,3} changes nothing, giving E . Subsets containing 3 accept. This is a teaching solution; no official scheme is supplied.[^exam11] [!question] Explain it yourself Why can subset construction stop after reachable subsets instead of drawing all 2^ Q subsets? [!success]- Check your explanation An input run starts at one subset and follows transitions; an unreachable subset can never affect any input's acceptance. Source: Lecture 2, PDF pp.16–18.

entries.title: Closure constructions
entries.text: For DFAs MA,MB over the same alphabet, product state (q,r) tracks both component states after the same prefix. Accept pairs by OR for union, AND for intersection, and “A final, B nonfinal” for difference. The invariant proves the construction for all words.[^l1closure] Complement requires a complete DFA : replace F by Q\F . Flipping an arbitrary NFA is wrong because it changes “some accepting path exists” into “some formerly rejecting path exists,” not “no accepting path exists.” Determinize and complete first.[^t2] For NFA composition: Operation Construction Why it works --- --- --- Union Fresh start epsilon-branches to both old starts Choose either machine Concatenation Epsilon-link every A-final to B's start; only B-finals accept Choose a split into A-prefix and B-suffix Star Fresh accepting start, epsilon to old start, epsilon returns after old finals Accept zero or finitely many complete factors A fresh star start matters. Merely making an old start accepting can accept a nonempty path returning there even when that path is not one whole language factor.[^l2]

entries.title: Return to the motivating question
entries.text: Using the table above: Input Trace Result --- --- --- ε q0 reject ab q0,q1,q2 accept aab q0,q1,q1,q2 accept aba q0,q1,q2,q1 reject bbab q0,q0,q0,q1,q2 accept The state invariant proves correctness beyond these tests. An NFA alternative can guess where a useful suffix begins; subset construction then records every guess deterministically. Product and epsilon constructions reuse complete machines without changing their internal meaning.

entries.title: Definitions and distinctions
entries.text: Term A Term B Decisive distinction Source --- --- --- --- DFA transition NFA transition One required state versus a set of zero or more states L2 pp.9–14 Epsilon move Self-loop Consumes no symbol versus consumes its labelled symbol T2 p.1 Accepting branch Accepting NFA One path versus existence of at least one complete accepting path T2 p.1 Complete DFA Shorthand partial drawing Every state-symbol pair defined versus omitted sink edges L2 pp.9–10 Reachable subset Powerset upper bound Actually encountered state-set versus any of 2^n subsets L2 pp.16–18

entries.title: Review
entries.text: Full Understanding Revisit the mechanisms above and the ordinary reference for the full lecture NFA, closure diagrams and edge cases.

entries.title: 5-Minute Review
entries.text: - Give every DFA state a prefix invariant and every symbol a transition. - DFA: one run; NFA: a set of possible runs and existential acceptance. - Epsilon closure is applied initially and after every consumed symbol. - DFA subsets accept exactly when they intersect the NFA final set. - Product states combine simultaneous facts; epsilon links compose sequential choices. - Complement by flipping finals only after determinizing/completing.
