entries.title: Finite Automata and Closure
entries.text: Finite Automata and Closure Course index · Exercises · Lab Opening case — A streaming suffix detector Synthetic engineering context for Tutorial 2 P2. A stream contains symbols from $\Sigma=\{a,b\}$. At end of input, a checker must accept exactly when the stream ends in ab . It may use only finitely many states and must define what happens for every next symbol. Design the states and transitions, test $\varepsilon$, ab , aab , aba , and bbab , and justify the design for every input, not just those tests. A second requirement is reusable design: explain how finite machines can combine conditions and why nondeterministic designs can still be implemented deterministically. What We Need to Learn Question Concepts --- --- What must the checker remember? States as invariants about the prefix read When is acceptance decided? Complete input, transition function, final states Can there be several possible next states? NFAs and existential path acceptance How can those choices be simulated? Epsilon closure and subset construction How can conditions be combined? Product construction, union, concatenation, star Prerequisite: Unit 01's language operations and proof methods. The alphabet is fixed for each construction; machines combined here share it. State sets of component machines are renamed to be disjoint when necessary. 1. A state is a finite summary of the past A machine need not store the whole prefix if future decisions depend only on some finite summary. For “ends in 1”, the summary is whether the last symbol was 1. A start arrow has no input label and marks initialization; double circles mark accepting states; labelled arrows consume input symbols. A self-loop is a transition, even though the state name does not change. Source: Lecture 1, PDF pp. 20–27. [!note] Deterministic finite automaton A DFA is $M=(Q,\Sigma,\delta,q_0,F)$, where $Q$ is a finite state set, $\Sigma$ the alphabet, $q_0\in Q$ the start state, $F\subseteq Q$ the accepting set, and $\delta:Q\times\Sigma\to Q$ a total function . Every pair of state and symbol has exactly one successor. The lectures sometimes list the same named components in a different tuple order; these notes use the tutorials' order. Sources: Lecture 1, PDF p. 22; Lecture 2, PDF pp. 9–10; Tutorial 2, PDF p. 1. For input $w=w_1\cdots w_n$, define $r_0=q_0$ and $r_i=\delta(r_{i-1},w_i)$ for $1\leq i\leq n$. Accept exactly when $r_n\in F$. This formal trace separates states visited from symbols consumed : a length-$n$ input has $n$ transitions and $n+1$ entries in the trace, which may repeat. For $\varepsilon$, no transition is taken; acceptance depends on whether $q_0\in F$. Lecture example. Let $Q=\{q_0,q_1\}$, start $q_0$, finals $\{q_1\}$, and set $\delta(q,0)=q_0$, $\delta(q,1)=q_1$ for either state $q$. The traces are: Input State sequence Result --- --- --- 0100 $q_0,q_0,q_1,q_0,q_0$ Reject 011 $q_0,q_0,q_1,q_1$ Accept 0110 $q_0,q_0,q_1,q_1,q_0$ Reject The invariant is “$q_1$ exactly when the prefix ends in 1.” Empty input is in $q_0$, each new symbol restores the invariant, and final acceptance therefore recognizes exactly the language ending in 1. Source: Lecture 1, PDF pp. 23–28. A machine accepts a string ; it recognizes a language when it accepts all and only its members. $L(M)=\{w\mid M\text{ accepts }w\}$. A language is regular if some DFA recognizes it. Finite states can recognize an infinite language because loops reuse the same finite memory. 2. Design by state meanings Before drawing arrows, decide which distinctions about the prefix could change the outcome of a future continuation. For a suffix target, remember the longest useful matching suffix. This is a design explanation for the tutorial example, not a general minimization algorithm supplied by the course. For the opening case use $q_0$ when the prefix ends in neither a nor ab ; $q_1$ when it ends in a ; $q_2$ when it ends in ab . These cases are mutually exclusive and cover every prefix, including the empty one. Adding a symbol updates its suffix, so the meanings determine the transitions. ends-ab.svg Figure 1 — A three-state suffix detector Read it: Start at q0; follow exactly one labelled arrow per symbol. Only q2 has a double circle. Key takeaway: States summarize relevant suffix information. Reaching q2 early does not guarantee final acceptance. Provenance: Original teaching diagram derived from the cited concepts. Limitation. A machine that accepts immediately on first seeing ab would recognize “contains ab ”, a different language. aba separates the two requirements. A missing DFA transition is a malformed total-function specification; an omitted rejecting transition in a shorthand diagram must be completed with a rejecting sink before using DFA theorems. 3. Nondeterminism means possible paths An NFA may have zero, one or several successors for a symbol. It may also change state on an $\varepsilon$-transition without moving the input position. The empty string is not a wildcard and does not skip an unread symbol. Source: Lecture 2, PDF pp. 11–14. [!note] NFA transition function and acceptance An NFA uses $\delta:Q\times(\Sigma\cup\{\varepsilon\})\to\mathcal P(Q)$, where $\mathcal P(Q)$ is the set of all subsets of $Q$. Missing arrows mean the empty set of successors. An input is accepted if ==at least one finite path consumes all input and ends in F==. Other dead or nonaccepting branches do not veto that path. Source: Tutorial 2, PDF p. 1. The outcome is existential, not probabilistic. No guessing probability is involved. A DFA is represented as an NFA by replacing each successor with its singleton set and giving no epsilon moves. Worked example: contains 01 . Start in $q_0$, loop there on both symbols, and additionally go to $q_1$ on 0 . From $q_1$, go to accepting $q_2$ on 1 ; loop on both symbols at $q_2$. The extra branch guesses which 0 begins an occurrence. A failed guess can die while the scanning branch continues. Source: Tutorial 2, PDF p. 3, P3. After reading 10010 , the possible sets are: Consumed prefix Current possibilities --- --- $\varepsilon$ $\{q_0\}$ 1 $\{q_0\}$ 10 $\{q_0,q_1\}$ 100 $\{q_0,q_1\}$ 1001 $\{q_0,q_2\}$ 10010 $\{q_0,q_1,q_2\}$ A single branch reads one symbol per labelled step; the set simulation records all branches after that same prefix. Its final set contains $q_2$, so the word is accepted. lecture-nfa.svg Figure 2 — The lecture NFA used again in state elimination Read it: The diagonal 0 arrow goes from q2 to q0. The only accepting state is q3; unshown transitions are absent. Key takeaway: Arrow direction changes the language. Epsilon moves change the state without consuming symbols. Provenance: Original teaching diagram derived from the cited concepts. The figure faithfully redraws Lecture 2, PDF p. 14. Its transition table is: State $0$ $1$ $\varepsilon$ --- --- --- --- $q_0$ $\varnothing$ $\varnothing$ $\{q_1\}$ $q_1$ $\varnothing$ $\{q_2,q_3\}$ $\varnothing$ $q_2$ $\{q_0,q_2\}$ $\varnothing$ $\{q_3\}$ $q_3$ $\varnothing$ $\varnothing$ $\varnothing$ 4. Epsilon closure and subset construction For $S\subseteq Q$, $E(S)$ (epsilon closure) is every state reachable from a member of $S$ by zero or more epsilon moves. Zero moves include $S$ itself. Compute it with a worklist: begin with all states in $S$, repeatedly add unseen epsilon successors, and stop when none remain. A finite state can be newly added only once, so even epsilon cycles terminate in this algorithm. If $S$ already includes its epsilon closure, consuming symbol $a$ gives: $$\operatorname{move}(S,a)=\bigcup_{q\in S}\delta(q,a),\qquad S'=E(\operatorname{move}(S,a)).$$ Take $S_0=E(\{q_0\})$ before any input. After all symbols, accept precisely if $S_n\cap F\ne\varnothing$. epsilon-steps.svg Figure 3 — One input step, all possible paths Read it: Compute the initial closure once. Repeat the lower two steps for each symbol. Key takeaway: Forgetting closure after a symbol loses valid computations, even if the initial closure was correct. Provenance: Original teaching diagram derived from the cited concepts. Determinization. Make each subset of $Q$ a possible DFA state. Its start is $E(\{q_0\})$, transition is the formula above, and accepting subsets are those meeting $F$. Construct only reachable subsets with a queue. If the empty subset is reached, retain it as a rejecting sink: it transitions to itself on every symbol. Source: Lecture 2, PDF pp. 16–18; Tutorial 2, PDF pp. 3–4. Why it works. Induct on prefix length. Initially the subset includes exactly the NFA states reachable without consuming input. If the invariant holds after a prefix, every path for the next symbol consists of a labelled successor followed by zero or more epsilon moves; taking their union and closure includes exactly all such possibilities. Thus after the full input, the subset meets $F$ exactly when some NFA path accepts. The constructed DFA recognizes the same language. For $n$ NFA states, there are $2^n$ subsets: each of the $n$ states is either present or absent. This is an upper bound; not all subsets need be reachable. Equivalent machines need not have the same number of states. Worked conversion. For Figure 2 let $A=\{q_0,q_1\}$, $B=\{q_2,q_3\}$, $C=\{q_0,q_1,q_2,q_3\}$ and $D=\varnothing$. Then: DFA subset On 0 On 1 Accepting? --- --- --- --- $A$ (start) $D$ $B$ No $B$ $C$ $D$ Yes $C$ $C$ $B$ Yes $D$ $D$ $D$ No For instance, $B$ on 0 first gives $\{q_0,q_2\}$; closure adds $q_1$ from $q_0$ and $q_3$ from $q_2$, yielding $C$. This reproduces the lecture's reachable subsets, with the sink explicit. 5. Product states combine two facts A class of languages is closed under an operation if applying that operation to languages in the class gives a language still in the class. This is a universal assertion; one successful example is only a warm-up. Source: Lecture 1, PDF pp. 32–35. Given DFAs $M_A=(Q_A,\Sigma,\delta_A,s_A,F_A)$ and $M_B=(Q_B,\Sigma,\delta_B,s_B,F_B)$, build a DFA with state set $Q_A\times Q_B$, start $(s_A,s_B)$, and $$\delta((q,r),a)=(\delta_A(q,a),\delta_B(r,a)).$$ The invariant is that the pair records both component states after the same prefix. It holds at initialization and is preserved by each transition, so changing only the final-state rule gives: Wanted language Accept a pair when --- --- $A\cup B$ $q\in F_A$ or $r\in F_B$ $A\cap B$ $q\in F_A$ and $r\in F_B$ $A\setminus B$ $q\in F_A$ and $r\notin F_B$ For union, $F=(F_A\times Q_B)\cup(Q_A\times F_B)$. For intersection, $F=F_A\times F_B$. Source: Lecture 1, PDF p. 35; Tutorial 2, PDF p. 4, P5. Difference follows from the Unit 01 identity and these constructions. Lecture union example. Let $A$ be binary strings ending in 0 and $B$ those ending in 1. The union contains exactly the nonempty binary strings, not $\varepsilon$. After a nonempty input the pair says either “ends 0, not ends 1” or “not ends 0, ends 1”; both are accepting under the OR rule. The “both end conditions true” pair exists in the full Cartesian product but is unreachable. Source: Lecture 1, PDF pp. 34–35. For complement of a complete DFA , replace $F$ by $Q\setminus F$. Every string has one complete run, so its acceptance flips. Flipping an NFA's finals instead asks whether some formerly nonaccepting path exists, not whether no formerly accepting path exists. Determinize first. This distinction is tested with a counterexample in P5. 6. NFA constructions for the regular operations closure-patterns.svg Figure 4 — Choose, bridge, repeat Read it: Each box stands for a disjoint copy of a whole component machine. Arrows between boxes consume no symbols. Key takeaway: The placement of new start states, epsilon bridges and accepting states encodes the language operation. Provenance: Original teaching diagram derived from the cited concepts. Union. Add a fresh nonaccepting start with epsilon moves to both old starts. Keep both sets of finals. An accepting run chooses a component and then accepts exactly a word in that component's language; conversely every component accepting run is available. This proves both directions. Source: Lecture 2, PDF pp. 20–21. Concatenation. Start in $M_A$. Add epsilon moves from every old $A$ final to the start of $M_B$. Only $B$ finals remain accepting. An accepting run consumes some prefix $x$ in $A$, crosses a bridge, then consumes a suffix $y$ in $B$, so its input is $xy\in AB$. Conversely any such decomposition yields an accepting path. Epsilon factors are handled without consuming input. A branch may choose when to cross; it is not forced to cross at the first accepting prefix. Source: Lecture 2, PDF pp. 22–23. Star. Add a fresh accepting start $r$, epsilon-connect it to the old start, retain old finals, and add epsilon moves from each old final back to $r$. Remaining at $r$ accepts zero factors. An accepting path through the old machine consumes one or more accepted factors, possibly empty; conversely every finite sequence of factors can be followed using the return edges. Source: Lecture 2, PDF pp. 24–27. Counterexample to a tempting shortcut. Merely marking the old start accepting can admit nonempty paths returning there that are not complete allowed factors. For the lecture's $A=$ “ends in 0”, that shortcut accepts 1 at the old start; yet $A^ =A\cup\{\varepsilon\}$ excludes 1 . A fresh accepting start prevents this error. Since every resulting NFA has an equivalent DFA, these constructions prove regular languages closed under union, concatenation and star. They also explain the composition machinery used by regular expressions in Unit 03. Solve the opening case Decision and justification. Use Figure 1's three suffix categories. $q_0$ is the start because the empty prefix ends in neither target suffix. Only $q_2$ is accepting. State meaning On a On b --- --- --- $q_0$: neither a nor ab suffix $q_1$ $q_0$ $q_1$: ends a $q_1$ $q_2$ $q_2$: ends ab $q_1$ $q_0$ Operation and intermediate states. On bbab , begin $q_0$, read b to $q_0$, another b to $q_0$, a to $q_1$, then b to $q_2$. Accept after the final symbol. Input Trace Interpretation --- --- --- $\varepsilon$ $q_0$ Reject: no ab suffix ab $q_0,q_1,q_2$ Accept aab $q_0,q_1,q_1,q_2$ Accept aba $q_0,q_1,q_2,q_1$ Reject: final suffix is a bbab $q_0,q_0,q_0,q_1,q_2$ Accept Proof for all inputs. The three meanings hold for the empty prefix. Appending a always gives suffix a , so every row goes to $q_1$. Appending b gives suffix ab exactly when the old prefix ended in a , so only the $q_1$ row goes to $q_2$; all other rows go to $q_0$. Induction preserves the meanings. Thus the final state is $q_2$ exactly when the complete input ends in ab . This meets all case constraints. Reusable design requirement. Product states combine this suffix checker with a second DFA; epsilon constructions combine accepted blocks or alternatives; subset construction implements the resulting NFA as a DFA without changing its language. These are justified constructions, not assumptions that sample tests establish equivalence. Exam-style answer and reusable method To prove regularity, give a complete machine and a state invariant, then prove initialization, preservation and acceptance equivalence. For an NFA, explain both why every desired word has an accepting path and why no undesired word can acquire one. For subset construction: close the start, move on one symbol, close again, enqueue unseen subsets, and mark every subset intersecting the old finals. Misconceptions and quick review - An accepting state visited before the end does not decide the word. - Missing transitions kill an NFA branch; they do not keep it in place. - “Same state after several steps” can occur through a cycle without a self-loop; a single consuming step that leaves the state unchanged needs a self-loop. Waiting between input events consumes nothing. - Nondeterminism is existential choice, not random choice or a requirement that all branches accept. - A powerset upper bound is not a claim that all subsets are reachable. - Complement flipping requires a complete DFA. [!summary] Reconstruct before checking State both transition-function types, trace the lecture NFA on 101 , explain why the empty subset is a sink, derive each product final-state rule, and explain why star needs a fresh start in the general construction. The exercise solutions give the exact traces and proofs.

entries.title: Exercises
entries.text: Exercises Notes · Lab Attempt each problem without help. Open its hint only when stuck, then compare your reasoning with the adjacent solution. Original tasks retain their source IDs; supplementary practice is labelled. T1 Q&A — Basic finite automata Source: ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE — Tutorial 1 - Strings, Languages and Proofs.pdf, PDF p. 2. 1. Does a finite automaton need at least one state? 2. What if a character has no corresponding transition? 3. Can a character be read without conducting a transition? 4. Can the empty string be accepted? 5. Is the empty language regular? These are also Lecture 1's five questions on PDF p. 37; their original occurrences are mapped separately. [!tip]- Hint Use the required start state, total DFA transitions, and end-of-input acceptance. [!success]- Solution 1. Yes. A start state must be an element of $Q$, so $Q$ cannot be empty. 2. In a complete DFA this cannot happen for a symbol in $\Sigma$. In an NFA the affected branch dies, while other branches may still succeed. A partial DFA drawing may use omission as rejection shorthand, completed formally with a rejecting sink. A symbol outside $\Sigma$ is outside the declared input domain. 3. No successful consuming step occurs without a transition. A self-loop is a transition. If no NFA move is available, the branch dies; it does not silently consume and remain. An epsilon move does not consume a character. 4. Yes. A DFA accepts $\varepsilon$ exactly when its start is final. An epsilon-NFA accepts it when the epsilon closure of its start meets $F$, even if its start itself is not final. This qualifies the tutorial's abbreviated answer. 5. Yes. A one-state DFA with self-loops on every symbol and no accepting states rejects every word, including $\varepsilon$, and recognizes $\varnothing$. T2 P1 — Quick diagnostic Source: ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE — Tutorial 2 - DFAs and NFAs.pdf, PDF p. 2. Answer true/false with a justification. 1. A DFA must have exactly one accepting state. 2. A DFA has exactly one computation path per input string. 3. An NFA without a transition on the next symbol stays in the same state. 4. An NFA accepts only when every path accepts. 5. Two different DFAs can recognize the same language. 6. An epsilon transition consumes the empty string, so the input position does not change. [!tip]- Hint Check whether the claim concerns a single branch, the whole machine, or a DFA total function. [!success]- Solution 1. False: $F$ may be empty, singleton, or larger. 2. True: the fixed start and total single-valued transition function determine every next state. 3. False: that branch has no successor on the symbol and dies. 4. False: one fully consuming accepting path is enough. 5. True: add an unreachable state with defined transitions to any DFA, retaining the old start and old final states. Its language stays unchanged although the machine differs. 6. True: an epsilon move changes state but reads no symbol; the same next input symbol remains to be processed. T2 P2 — A DFA for a final ab Source: ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE — Tutorial 2 - DFAs and NFAs.pdf, PDF pp. 2–3. For $\Sigma=\{a,b\}$ construct a DFA for $L=\{w\in\Sigma^ \mid w\text{ ends with }ab\}$. Give every state's meaning and a complete transition table. Test $\varepsilon$, ab , aab , aba , bbab . [!tip]- Hint Remember whether the prefix ends in a, ends in ab, or neither. Test only after all input. [!success]- Solution Step 1 — States. Let $q_0$ mean neither a nor ab suffix, $q_1$ mean a suffix, $q_2$ mean ab suffix. Start at $q_0$ and let $F=\{q_2\}$. Step 2 — Complete table. State a b --- --- --- $q_0$ $q_1$ $q_0$ $q_1$ $q_1$ $q_2$ $q_2$ $q_1$ $q_0$ Every appended a creates suffix a. An appended b creates suffix ab only if the previous prefix ended in a. This proves preservation of the stated meanings, which hold initially. Thus the machine recognizes exactly $L$. Step 3 — Tests. $\varepsilon$: $q_0$ (reject). ab : $q_0,q_1,q_2$ (accept). aab : $q_0,q_1,q_1,q_2$ (accept). aba : $q_0,q_1,q_2,q_1$ (reject). bbab : $q_0,q_0,q_0,q_1,q_2$ (accept). T2 P3 — An NFA for contains 01 Source: ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE — Tutorial 2 - DFAs and NFAs.pdf, PDF p. 3. For $\Sigma=\{0,1\}$ construct an NFA for $L=\{u01v\mid u,v\in\Sigma^ \}$. Explain where nondeterminism occurs and why one successful branch suffices. [!tip]- Hint Keep a scanning branch alive and branch when a zero might begin the occurrence. [!success]- Solution Start $q_0$; finals $F=\{q_2\}$; no epsilon moves. State 0 1 --- --- --- $q_0$ $\{q_0,q_1\}$ $\{q_0\}$ $q_1$ $\varnothing$ $\{q_2\}$ $q_2$ $\{q_2\}$ $\{q_2\}$ On a zero at $q_0$, one branch keeps searching and another guesses the start of 01. The guessed branch must immediately read 1 to reach $q_2$, after which all suffixes are allowed. For any word $u01v$, stay at $q_0$ through $u$, take the guessing transition on the chosen 0, reach $q_2$ on 1 and loop through $v$. Conversely, any accepting path must enter $q_2$ via $q_1$ on 1 after entering $q_1$ on 0, so it witnesses a contiguous 01. Acceptance is existential, so dead wrong guesses do not matter. The printed table omits some singleton braces and uses a typographic $q_o$ in one entry. The states here are consistently $q_0,q_1,q_2$, and every entry is a set as required by the NFA definition. T2 P4 — Subset construction with epsilon moves Source: ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE — Tutorial 2 - DFAs and NFAs.pdf, PDF pp. 3–4. Let $N$ have states $\{s,p,f\}$, alphabet $\{0,1\}$, start $s$, accepting state $f$, and transitions: State $\varepsilon$ 0 1 --- --- --- --- $s$ $\{p\}$ $\{s\}$ $\varnothing$ $p$ $\varnothing$ $\varnothing$ $\{f\}$ $f$ $\varnothing$ $\{f\}$ $\{f\}$ 1. Compute $\varepsilon$-closure$(\{s\})$. 2. Apply subset construction to show the DFA states. 3. Identify accepting state-sets. 4. Describe the language. [!tip]- Hint Close the initial set and each symbol result; discover only reachable subsets. [!success]- Solution 1. Zero epsilon moves retain $s$; its epsilon edge adds $p$. Thus $E(\{s\})=\{s,p\}$. 2. From $\{s,p\}$ on 0, the union of successors is $\{s\}$ and closure restores $\{s,p\}$. On 1 the union is $\{f\}$, whose closure is itself. From $\{f\}$, either symbol returns to $\{f\}$. No other subsets are reachable. DFA state 0 1 --- --- --- $\{s,p\}$ (start) $\{s,p\}$ $\{f\}$ $\{f\}$ $\{f\}$ $\{f\}$ 3. A subset is final iff it contains $f$, so the only reachable final subset is $\{f\}$. 4. Exactly the binary strings containing at least one 1: before the first 1 stay in the first subset, and after it stay in the second. Empty and all-zero strings reject. The full powerset has eight subsets, but only these two are reachable. T2 P5 — Intersection and complement Source: ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE — Tutorial 2 - DFAs and NFAs.pdf, PDF p. 4. 1. Given DFAs for regular languages $A,B$, construct a DFA for $A\cap B$. 2. Given a ==complete DFA== for $A$, construct one for $\overline A$. 3. Explain why flipping accepting states of an arbitrary NFA is incorrect. [!tip]- Hint Track two states simultaneously for intersection. Compare negating “there exists” with “there exists a negation”. [!success]- Solution 1. Assume the same alphabet (complete over a common alphabet if needed). Use $Q_A\times Q_B$, start $(s_A,s_B)$, and transition $\delta((q,r),a)=(\delta_A(q,a),\delta_B(r,a))$. Set finals to $F_A\times F_B$. By induction on prefix length the pair tracks the two original runs. It is final exactly when both accept, proving recognition of the intersection. 2. Keep $Q,\Sigma,\delta,s$ and replace $F$ by $Q\setminus F$. Every input has one complete run; its final state belongs to exactly one of those two sets. Thus acceptance reverses for every word, including $\varepsilon$. 3. Concrete counterexample: an NFA starts at $s$, has $\delta(s,a)=\{f,r\}$ and $F=\{f\}$. It accepts a along the branch to $f$. Flipping finals to $\{s,r\}$ still accepts a , now along $r$. The complement should reject it. Determinize and complete first, then flip finals. T2 P6 — STRETCH and CHOP Source: ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE — Tutorial 2 - DFAs and NFAs.pdf, PDF pp. 4–5. For $w=w_1\cdots w_n$, define $\operatorname{STRETCH}(w)=w_1w_1w_2w_2\cdots w_nw_n$. For $ w \geq2$, define CHOP$(w)$ by deleting its first and last symbols. For a language, apply each operation to all strings in its domain. Prove (1) STRETCH$(L)$ regular if $L$ is regular; (2) CHOP$(L)$ regular if $L$ is regular. [!tip]- Hint Modify a DFA for L. Doubling requires fresh intermediate states; chopping requires guessing the two deleted symbols without reading them from the new input. [!success]- Solution Let $M=(Q,\Sigma,\delta,s,F)$ recognize $L$. 1 — STRETCH. For each transition $p\xrightarrow{a}q$ of $M$, introduce a fresh state $r_{p,a}$ and replace the edge by $p\xrightarrow{a}r_{p,a}\xrightarrow{a}q$. Keep start $s$ and finals $F$; no fresh intermediate is final and no other edges leave it. Any old accepting run becomes a run consuming two copies of every symbol, so every stretched member is accepted. Conversely, an accepting new run alternates old states and intermediates and consumes equal-symbol pairs; contracting those pairs gives an old accepting run. Thus exactly STRETCH$(L)$ is recognized by this NFA. The empty string is preserved precisely if the old machine accepts it. 2 — CHOP. Add a fresh nonfinal start $t$ with epsilon moves to every $\delta(s,a)$ for $a\in\Sigma$. Keep all old labelled transitions. Make exactly the old states $G=\{q\in Q\mid\exists b\in\Sigma,\ \delta(q,b)\in F\}$ accepting. Do not apply this rule to fresh $t$. If $aub\in L$ with $a,b\in\Sigma$, the new machine can epsilon-enter $\delta(s,a)$, simulate the middle $u$, and finish in $G$ because the guessed final $b$ reaches $F$. Conversely, any new accepting run chooses an initial $a$ via its epsilon entry, reads some middle $u$, and ends in a state with a final-symbol witness $b$. Therefore $aub\in L$ and $u=\operatorname{CHOP}(aub)$. The old word has length $ u +2\geq2$, as required. Empty $u$ is accepted exactly when $L$ contains a two-symbol word. NFA–DFA equivalence proves both languages regular. L2 p14 — Trace the lecture NFA Source: ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE — Lecture 2 DFA and NFA.pdf, PDF p. 14. For the four-state diagram in the notes (Lecture 2 p. 14), decide acceptance of 10 , 101 , 01 and 10101 . Its transitions are $q_0\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}q_1$, $q_1\xrightarrow{1}q_2,q_3$, $q_2\xrightarrow{0}q_0,q_2$, and $q_2\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}q_3$. Start $q_0$; only $q_3$ final; all unlisted moves absent. [!tip]- Hint Use A = {q0,q1}, B = {q2,q3}, C = all four states, D = empty. [!success]- Solution Start with $A=\{q_0,q_1\}$. Its 1 successor is $B=\{q_2,q_3\}$, its 0 successor is $D=\varnothing$. From $B$, 0 gives $C=\{q_0,q_1,q_2,q_3\}$ and 1 gives $D$. From $C$, 0 stays $C$ and 1 gives $B$. Both $B$ and $C$ contain the final $q_3$. - 10 : $A\to B\to C$, accept . - 101 : $A\to B\to C\to B$, accept . - 01 : $A\to D\to D$, reject . - 10101 : $A\to B\to C\to B\to C\to B$, accept . The return edge on 0 goes from $q_2$ to $q_0$, not the other way round. L2 p18 — How many subset states? Source: ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE — Lecture 2 DFA and NFA.pdf, PDF p. 18. If an NFA has $n$ states, how many states can its subset-construction DFA have at most? [!tip]- Hint Count independent inclusion/exclusion choices. [!success]- Solution Each of the $n$ states has two membership choices in a subset, so there are $2^n$ subsets. The full construction can use that many; the reachable construction may use fewer. For the four-state lecture example, the theoretical bound is 16 and only four subsets are reachable. L2 Q&A — Path semantics Source: ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE — Lecture 2 DFA and NFA.pdf, PDF p. 29. 1. Must a DFA have exactly one accepting state? 2. What happens to an NFA computation with no next-symbol transition? 3. Can an NFA accept even if some paths reject? 4. Can a computation stay in a state without a self-loop? 5. Can different DFAs recognize the same language? [!tip]- Hint For question 4, distinguish one consuming step from a longer cycle or no input step. [!success]- Solution 1. No: $F$ is any subset of $Q$. 2. That branch dies; it does not consume the symbol while remaining still. 3. Yes, provided another path consumes the entire input and ends in $F$. 4. A single step consuming a symbol that leaves the state unchanged requires a self-loop on that symbol. A multi-step cycle can return to the same state without a direct self-loop, and taking no step consumes no symbol. This makes the scope of the source question precise. 5. Yes. Adding unreachable states to a complete DFA gives a different complete DFA with the same language, since no input from the start reaches the additions. L2 p11-p12 — Effect of an epsilon option Source: ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE — Lecture 2 DFA and NFA.pdf, PDF pp. 11–12. The p. 11 NFA has start $q_0$, final $q_1$, a 0-loop at $q_0$, a 1-loop at $q_1$, $q_0\xrightarrow{0}q_1$, and $q_1\xrightarrow{1}q_0$. Page 12 adds $q_0\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}q_1$. Trace the source's example inputs 00 and 11 on both machines. [!tip]- Hint Close the start before processing page 12 inputs. [!success]- Solution Page 11: 00 has sets $\{q_0\}\to\{q_0,q_1\}\to\{q_0,q_1\}$, so it accepts. 11 immediately reaches $\varnothing$ and rejects. Page 12: initial closure is $\{q_0,q_1\}$. On 0 the moved set is $\{q_0,q_1\}$, already closed; on 1 the moved set is also $\{q_0,q_1\}$. Thus both 00 and 11 remain in that set and accept. The epsilon edge creates access to the 1-reading branch without consuming the first 1. L2 closure-challenges — Build machines for the operations Source: ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE — Lecture 2 DFA and NFA.pdf, PDF pp. 19–27. Explain how to use NFAs for union, concatenation and star of regular languages. For $A=$ binary strings ending in 0, explain why making the old start final is an incorrect general star construction. [!tip]- Hint Use disjoint component copies and distinguish new versus old final states. [!success]- Solution Union: fresh start, epsilon edges to each component start, retain both final sets. A run chooses one component; acceptance means membership in either language. Concatenation: start in A, epsilon-link every A final to B's start, and mark only B finals. A successful run consumes an A-prefix then a B-suffix; every valid split is possible. Star: fresh accepting start r, epsilon edge to A's start, retain A finals, and epsilon-link every A final back to r. This accepts zero factors and arbitrary finite sequences of completed A-runs; every accepting run has such a factorization. Counterexample: the old start of the ends-in-0 DFA has a 1-loop. Making it final accepts 1 , but every nonempty string in $A^ $ ends in 0. The fresh start fixes empty-input acceptance without changing old nonempty-prefix meanings.

entries.title: Compare one run with a set of possible runs
entries.text: Compare one run with a set of possible runs Notes · Exercises Purpose and environment Original optional activity: Tutorial 2 - DFAs and NFAs.pdf, PDF pp. 5–7, Part E. The source demonstrates the P2 DFA on five words and the P3 NFA on 10010 , and supplies determinize . This lab preserves those function identifiers and demonstrations, adding labelled bounded checks and the lecture/P4 machines. The original code remains in the unmodified PDF; the runnable transcription is: automata_simulation.py Python 3 standard library only; no third-party package. Lecturer version: UNCONFIRMED . Observed runtime for this run: Python 3.14.6. From the unit folder: sh python3 Attachments/automata_simulation.py How the code represents the concepts run_dfa stores one state , reads each symbol , looks up the next state, and appends it to trace . run_nfa stores a set instead. It unions successors and then applies epsilon_closure . The empty dictionary key '' represents an epsilon edge, not an alphabet character. epsilon_closure uses an agenda worklist and a closure set; it enqueues only unseen states, preventing epsilon cycles from causing an infinite loop. determinize uses frozenset because a mutable set cannot serve as a dictionary key. Its queue explores reachable subsets; dfa_accepting filters those intersecting the old final set. deque is a queue implementation detail, not part of the mathematical definition. Procedure — Original demonstrations Predict the P2 traces for $\varepsilon$, ab , aab , aba , bbab , then run them. Predict all P3 reachable sets for 10010 and compare the program output. [!tip]- Hint The trace includes the initial state or initial epsilon-closed set. A five-symbol input therefore has six trace entries. [!success]- Solution and observed results The executed P2 demonstrations returned reject, accept, accept, reject, accept, with exactly the traces in P2's local solution. For 10010 , the executed P3 trace was {q0} → {q0} → {q0,q1} → {q0,q1} → {q0,q2} → {q0,q1,q2} , with acceptance True. The final accepting branch witnesses the occurrence of 01 in positions 3–4. Sorted state names are used only for stable display; sets are unordered. Supplementary verification and controlled change The script also compares the DFA against endswith('ab') , the P3 NFA against substring membership, and the P4 NFA against the predicate “contains 1”. It checks each of those three NFAs against its determinized DFA for all 511 binary words of lengths zero through eight. The six comparisons total 3,066 cases. These are SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE / verification , not additional source assessment questions. Observed results: all 3,066 comparisons passed. The P3, lecture and P4 machines produced 4, 4 and 2 reachable subsets respectively. Lecture inputs 10 , 101 , 01 , 10101 returned True, True, False, True. For a controlled change, copy the script outside the original source folder, remove the initial call to epsilon_closure in run_nfa , and predict the effect on the lecture machine before running it. [!tip]- Hint At q0 the lecture machine has only an epsilon edge. What would happen if the first input symbol were processed before following it? [!success]- Solution Without the initial closure, the initial set would be {q0} . On the first 1, there is no labelled successor, so the set becomes empty and all the sample words starting with 1 are wrongly rejected. Expected result of this intentional mutation: the equivalence assertions detect disagreement. This mutation was not executed ; it is a prediction justified by the transition table. Limits and troubleshooting Bounded tests are useful for detecting errors; equivalence for all inputs follows from the invariant proof, not 511 samples. Missing NFA entries mean an empty set; missing DFA entries cause a KeyError , exposing an incomplete table. Input symbols must belong to the declared alphabet. Membership computations use no probability. The lab checks recognition, not state minimality or performance.

entries.title: In 60 Seconds
entries.text: A regular expression is finite syntax denoting a language, not a single input string. Atomic languages are combined by union, concatenation and star. Those same operations build an NFA from an expression. In reverse, a generalized NFA labels edges with expressions and removes states while preserving every path language. After study, you should be able to interpret parentheses precisely, design expressions from language conditions, build an NFA recursively, and apply the state-elimination update without losing direct routes.[^l3]

entries.title: Concept Preview
entries.text: [!note] Concept — Recursive semantics Plain-language meaning: Every regex node denotes a language; parent nodes combine child languages by one regular operation. Why it matters: Parentheses and operation scope determine which strings exist. Connects to: syntax trees and NFA composition. Source: Lecture 3, PDF pp.4–9. [!note] Concept — Expression-to-NFA construction Plain-language meaning: Build atomic machines, then compose them with epsilon edges for union, concatenation and star. Why it matters: It proves every regex language is regular. Connects to: Unit 02 closure constructions. Source: Lecture 3, PDF pp.6–9. [!note] Concept — Generalized NFA Plain-language meaning: A single edge can consume any word denoted by its regex label. Why it matters: Whole path families can be compressed while states are removed. Connects to: state elimination. Source: Lecture 3, PDF pp.11–17. [!note] Concept — Direct-or-bypass update Plain-language meaning: After removing state k , preserve the direct route and add every route entering, looping at, and leaving k . Why it matters: Omitting either alternative changes the language. Connects to: Rij ∪ Rik(Rkk) Rkj . Source: Lecture 3, PDF pp.15–22.

entries.title: Before You Start
entries.text: You need Unit 01's language operations and Unit 02's NFA closure constructions. [!question] What is the language of ∅ ? [!success]- Check your answer {ε} : zero factors are possible, but no positive-factor choice exists. Source: Lecture 3, PDF pp.6–7; Tutorial 1, PDF pp.3–4.

entries.title: A motivating question
entries.text: Synthetic specification task based on the partial papers. Over {a,b} , write a regular expression for strings with an odd number of a s. It must allow any number of b s anywhere, reject ε and all even- a strings, and accept a , ba , abbababa exactly when their a count is odd. Then explain how your expression could be compiled to an NFA and how an arbitrary finite automaton could, in principle, be converted back to an expression. Question Knowledge needed --- --- How do we enforce odd parity? One a plus pairs of later a s Where can b s occur? b gaps around every a Why is the expression correct? Both-direction factorization argument Why are machines equivalent? Recursive construction and state elimination

entries.title: Expressions denote languages
entries.text: Atomic expressions a , ε , and ∅ denote {a} , {ε} , and ∅ . If R,S are expressions, then R∪S , RS , and R denote language union, concatenation, and star. Σ is used as shorthand for the finite union of its symbols.[^l3] Star binds to its preceding expression; concatenation joins factors; union selects alternatives. Compare: - (a∪ab) : any finite sequence of blocks a or ab ; - a∪ab : either the single word a , or a followed by zero or more b s. The word aa separates them: it belongs to the first but not the second. The word abb belongs to the second but not the first. Parentheses are semantic, not decorative. mermaid flowchart TD S["(a ∪ ab) "] -- STAR["star"] STAR -- UNION["union"] UNION -- A1["a"] UNION -- CONCAT["concatenation"] CONCAT -- A2["a"] CONCAT -- B["b"] Figure 1 — Read a regex as a language-construction tree Read it: Start at the leaves, build ab , union it with a , then apply star to the entire union. Key takeaway: Moving one parenthesis changes the root operation and therefore the language. Provenance: Pedagogical Mermaid derived from Lecture 3, PDF pp.4–9. [!warning] Expression versus input Lecture 3 p.10 calls (a∪ab)(a∪ab) an input string. It is an expression denoting four inputs: aa , aab , aba , abab . The distinction is necessary for type-correct reasoning.

entries.title: Design by blocks and boundaries
entries.text: To obtain an odd number of a s, choose one initial a , then add zero or more pairs of a s. Allow arbitrary b s before, between and after them: $$R=b^ ab^ (ab^ ab^ )^ .$$ Why every generated word is valid. The prefix contributes one a ; every repeated group contributes two. Total a count is 1+2k , odd. Every other consumed symbol comes from a b gap. Why every valid word is generated. Take any word with 2k+1 occurrences of a . Its b s form a prefix, gaps between consecutive a s, and a suffix. Assign the first a to the prefix factor and pair the remaining 2k a s in order. The corresponding b factors absorb exactly the gaps. This provides the required factorization. Boundary tests are part of the argument: ε has zero a s and is excluded; a uses every star zero times; arbitrary b s alone are excluded because the required a is absent.

entries.title: From expressions to machines and back
entries.text: For ∅ , use a nonaccepting start with no transitions. For ε , use an accepting start. For symbol a , use one a edge from start to final. Compose recursively with Unit 02's epsilon constructions. Structural induction says the atomic machines are correct and each composition preserves exactly its language operation, so every regex has an equivalent NFA.[^l3] For the reverse direction, a GNFA edge label is a regex. Normalize with a fresh start s and fresh sole final f ; combine parallel edges by union and treat missing edges as ∅ . When removing internal state k , update every remaining pair: $$R'_{ij}=R_{ij}\cup R_{ik}(R_{kk})^ R_{kj}.$$ The direct term preserves paths avoiding k . The bypass term enters k , repeats its loop zero or more times, then exits. Every old path expands to one alternative, and every new-label word expands back to an old path, so the language is preserved.[^l3] Worked local update. Suppose i→j is labelled b , i→k is a , k→k is b , and k→j is a . Removing k gives b∪ab a . Writing only ab a loses the direct word b . [!question] Explain it yourself Why does an absent k -loop contribute ε rather than making every bypass impossible? [!success]- Check your explanation Its label is ∅ ; ∅ ={ε} represents taking the loop zero times, so entry can connect directly to exit. Source: Lecture 3, PDF pp.15–17. Source-faithful state-elimination result For the lecture's four-state NFA (Lecture 2 p.14; Lecture 3 pp.14–22), eliminating q3,q1,q2,q0 yields $$\varepsilon(10^ 0)^ (1\cup10^ )=(10^ 0)^ (1\cup10^ )=(10^ 0)^ 10^ .$$ The final equivalence uses {1}⊆L(10 ) . It accepts 10 , 101 , and 10101 , and rejects 01 , agreeing with direct NFA traces. [!warning] Source grouping correction Lecture 3 p.22 prints (10 0) 1 ∪ 10 without the grouping required by the preceding graph. The graph gives (10 0) (1∪10 ) . The word 1010 is accepted by the graph and grouped expression but excluded by the ordinarily parsed ungrouped one. Different elimination orders may produce different equivalent expressions. The method proves existence, not shortest syntax.

entries.title: Return to the motivating question
entries.text: For R=b ab (ab ab ) : - ε rejects because one explicit a is required. - a accepts with every b and the pair-star empty. - ba accepts with prefix b and no pairs. - abbababa has four a s, so it rejects; no factorization can change the explicit count 1+2k into four. The correctness proof covers every word through counting and ordered gaps. Atomic machines plus closure compile the expression to an NFA. GNFA normalization and repeated direct-or-bypass updates convert any finite automaton back. Together with subset construction, DFA, NFA and classical regexes characterize the same regular languages.

entries.text: - Interpret every subexpression as a language. - Build specifications from required blocks, parity and boundary cases. - Prove a regex in both directions: generated implies property; property implies factorization. - Expression→NFA follows the expression tree. - GNFA elimination keeps direct routes and adds entry(loop) exit routes. - Parenthesize every union used as a concatenation factor.

entries.title: Regular Expressions and Automata Conversion
entries.text: Regular Expressions and Automata Conversion Course index · Exercises Opening case — Recover a checkable specification Source-derived mechanism, synthetic review scenario. A colleague gives you the four-state NFA from Lecture 2 p. 14 (reused in Lecture 3 pp. 14–22). You must replace it with one ordinary regular expression, while preserving its accepted language. The machine starts at $q_0$, accepts only at $q_3$, and has: From Label To --- --- --- $q_0$ $\varepsilon$ $q_1$ $q_1$ $1$ $q_2$ and $q_3$ $q_2$ $0$ $q_0$ and $q_2$ $q_2$ $\varepsilon$ $q_3$ Unlisted transitions are absent. Derive the expression step by step, explain the grouping, and use it to decide membership of 10 , 101 , 01 , and 10101 . Success means a language-preserving derivation, not guessing from these four inputs. Unit 02 supplies the machine diagram and NFA semantics. What We Need to Learn Case question Concepts --- --- What does an expression denote? Recursive syntax and language semantics Why do parentheses matter? Operation scope and precedence Why can expressions build automata? Atomic machines and closure composition How can a machine yield an expression? Generalized NFA and state elimination How do we justify every elimination? Direct route versus entry, loop, exit 1. Expressions denote languages A regular expression is finite syntax that describes a language using the regular operations. It is not itself a language member unless one separately encodes the expression as input. Source: Lecture 1, PDF p. 31; Lecture 3, PDF pp. 4–6. [!note] Recursive definition and meaning Atomic expressions are $a$ for $a\in\Sigma$, $\varepsilon$ and $\varnothing$, denoting $\{a\}$, $\{\varepsilon\}$ and $\varnothing$. The lectures also use $\Sigma$ as shorthand for the finite union of its symbols. If $R,S$ are regular expressions, so are $(R\cup S)$, $(RS)$ and $R^ $, denoting $L(R)\cup L(S)$, $L(R)L(S)$ and $L(R)^ $. Every expression is built by finitely many applications of these rules. Use parentheses to make scope explicit. Star binds to its preceding expression, concatenation combines factors, and union selects alternatives. Thus $(a\cup ab)^ $ allows any finite sequence of a or ab blocks. It differs from $a\cup ab^ $, which allows either a or a followed by any number of b s. The word aa is in the first language but not the second; abb is in the second but not the first. regex-structure.svg Figure 1 — A construction tree for the lecture expression Read it: The leaves are atomic symbols; build concatenation, then union, then the outer star. Key takeaway: The expression tree fixes which operation applies to which language. Provenance: Original teaching diagram derived from the cited concepts. Worked language descriptions. Over $\Sigma=\{0,1\}$, $(0\cup1)^ =\Sigma^ $ gives all binary strings. $\Sigma^ 1$ gives strings ending in 1, and $\Sigma^ 11\Sigma^ $ gives strings containing 11: the prefix and suffix may be empty. These examples are from Lecture 1 p. 31. $\Sigma^ 0$ similarly gives the Lecture 3 p. 4 language ending in 0. The empty-language and empty-string expressions must remain distinct. Concatenating with $\varnothing$ destroys all possible strings; concatenating with $\varepsilon$ leaves them unchanged. Therefore $R\varnothing=\varnothing$, $R\varepsilon=R$, $R\cup\varnothing=R$, and $\varnothing^ =\varepsilon$ are language-equivalence simplifications. They do not assert that the written syntax is identical. 2. From a regular expression to an NFA Source: Lecture 3, PDF pp. 6–9. For $\varnothing$, use a start state with no finals and no transitions. For $\varepsilon$, use one accepting start and no transitions. For $a$, use a nonfinal start with one $a$-edge to an accepting state. Unshown NFA edges are absent; these machines therefore recognize exactly their atomic languages. Build a compound expression recursively using Unit 02's epsilon constructions: choose a branch for union, bridge accepting states to the next start for concatenation, and add a fresh accepting start plus restart edges for star. The construction argument is structural: the atomic cases work, and each composition preserves the intended language operation, so every finite regular expression has an equivalent NFA and hence DFA. Worked example — $(a\cup ab)^ $. First build a two-state a machine with edge $p_1\xrightarrow{a}f_1$. For ab , build $p_2\xrightarrow{a}c\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}d\xrightarrow{b}f_2$. Add union start $u$ with epsilon edges to $p_1,p_2$. For star add accepting start $r$ with an epsilon edge to $u$ and add epsilon edges from $f_1,f_2$ back to $r$. Keep $f_1,f_2$ accepting. This is the source's construction pattern with explicit state names. To accept aab , take the a branch once, return to $r$ by epsilon, then take the ab branch. The trace consumes a , then a , then b ; all bridges consume nothing. Empty input is accepted by staying at $r$. No accepting run can consume a standalone b block because every nonempty component begins with a . Source clarification. Lecture 3 p. 10 calls $(a\cup ab)\circ(a\cup ab)$ an “input string”. It is an expression denoting four strings: aa , aab , aba , abab . Each is a concatenation of two allowed blocks and is accepted by $(a\cup ab)^ $. Treat the expression as a description of a set, not as a literal string over $\{a,b\}$. 3. Generalized NFAs compress paths A generalized NFA (GNFA) allows an edge label to be a regular expression. Traversing such an edge consumes some whole substring in that expression's language. A label $\varepsilon$ consumes no symbols; $\varnothing$ permits no traversal. Source: Lecture 3, PDF pp. 11–17. Normalize the original machine with a fresh start $s$ (epsilon to the old start) and a fresh sole final $f$ (epsilon from every old final); unmark the old finals. Give $s$ no incoming edges and $f$ no outgoing edges. Combine parallel edges by union and regard absent edges as $\varnothing$. This is a language-preserving transformation , not a claim that every NFA already has that shape. A path label describes all words consumed along that path: successive edges concatenate; choosing parallel routes takes union; repeating a loop takes star. For instance, entering on $A$, looping on $B$ exactly $m$ times and exiting on $C$ gives $AB^mC$. Allowing any $m\geq0$ gives $AB^ C$. state-elimination.svg Figure 2 — The local elimination rule Read it: Compare the direct i-to-j edge with a path through k. Removing k must preserve both possibilities. Key takeaway: The bypass label is D ∪ AB C; a missing loop has label ∅, and ∅ = ε allows zero visits to that loop. Provenance: Original teaching diagram derived from the cited concepts. 4. Derive the elimination formula Let $R_{ij}$ denote the current label from state $i$ to state $j$. Remove internal state $k$ and update every pair of remaining states , including $i=j$, by: $$R'_{ij}=R_{ij}\cup R_{ik}(R_{kk})^ R_{kj}.$$ All right-hand labels come from the graph before eliminating $k$. The first term accounts for routes not using $k$; the second accounts for entering $k$, making zero or more loops there, and exiting to $j$. This derives the formula from the three regular operations taught on Lecture 3 pp. 15–17; the single formula is a pedagogical consolidation. Why language is preserved. Each old path segment through $k$ can be replaced by a new bypass edge with the same consumed word. Conversely, a word selected from a bypass label decomposes into an entry word, a finite sequence of loop words and an exit word, so it can be expanded back into a path through $k$. Other edges are preserved by the union. Repeating this argument until only $s,f$ remain makes their edge label denote precisely the original language. Limitation. Different elimination orders can yield different, sometimes much larger, equivalent expressions. The procedure proves existence; it does not guarantee the shortest expression. Always retain an existing direct route and always parenthesize unions used as concatenation factors. [!warning] A nonstandard label in the source Lecture 3 p. 13 includes $0^ \cap10^ $ as a GNFA edge label, although intersection is not a primitive in the course's regex grammar. Over the displayed binary alphabet that intersection is empty: one language has only zeros, the other begins with 1. Replace this particular label by $\varnothing$ when applying the stated grammar. This is a documented simplification of that source diagram, not an extra syntax rule. Solve the opening case Follow Lecture 3 pp. 14–22, using explicit grouping where the final slide omits it. Step 1 — Normalize. Add $s\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}q_0$ and $q_3\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}f$, with only $f$ final. All other old edges stay as in the opening table. Step 2 — Eliminate $q_3$. It has no self-loop, so the loop factor is $\varnothing^ =\varepsilon$. Replace $q_1\xrightarrow{1}q_3\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}f$ by $q_1\xrightarrow{1}f$, and $q_2\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}q_3\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}f$ by $q_2\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}f$. Step 3 — Eliminate $q_1$. Its incoming label from $q_0$ is $\varepsilon$; it has no loop; its outgoing labels to $q_2$ and $f$ are both 1. Thus add $q_0\xrightarrow{1}q_2$ and $q_0\xrightarrow{1}f$. Step 4 — Eliminate $q_2$. Its self-loop is 0. Enter from $q_0$ on 1 and exit back to $q_0$ on 0, giving the new loop $10^ 0$. Enter on 1 and exit to $f$ on $\varepsilon$, giving $10^ $. Union this with the existing direct label 1: Remaining edge Label --- --- $s\to q_0$ $\varepsilon$ $q_0\to q_0$ $10^ 0$ $q_0\to f$ $1\cup10^ $ Step 5 — Eliminate $q_0$. The start-to-final label becomes $$\varepsilon(10^ 0)^ (1\cup10^ )=(10^ 0)^ (1\cup10^ )=(10^ 0)^ 10^ .$$ The first simplification removes the empty-string prefix. The second uses $\{1\}\subseteq L(10^ )$, since the star may supply zero zeros. Every repeat block is a 1 followed by at least one 0; the final block is 1 followed by zero or more zeros. Step 6 — Interpret and check the requested words. 10 uses zero repeat blocks and final block 10 ; 101 uses repeat 10 and final 1 ; 01 fails because every accepted word begins in 1; 10101 uses repeats 10 , 10 and final 1 . Hence accept, accept, reject, accept, agreeing with the independently traced NFA. The path-preservation derivation proves more than these examples. [!warning] Source correction — missing grouping on PDF p. 22 The slide's final label is written $(10^ 0)^ 1\cup10^ $. The preceding graph requires $(10^ 0)^ (1\cup10^ )$. Under ordinary precedence, the written label excludes 1010 , whereas the graph accepts it (repeat block 10 , final block 10 ). Keep the grouped expression or the equivalent simplified $(10^ 0)^ 10^ $. Page 21 also shows a duplicated/overlaid union label; the direct and bypass routes above determine the correct union explicitly. Exam-style answer and reusable method “Normalize the NFA, then eliminate internal states while preserving the direct label and adding the entry–loop–exit language. The update $R_{ij}\cup R_{ik}R_{kk}^ R_{kj}$ preserves exactly all path words. For the supplied machine it yields $(10^ 0)^ (1\cup10^ )$, equivalently $(10^ 0)^ 10^ $.” For a new conversion, write the transition table first, normalize endpoints, select a state, list its incoming/outgoing pairs, update with old labels, remove it, and repeat. Check empty strings, zero loops, and grouping at each step. A failed attempt to find an expression does not establish nonregularity; that requires the next unit's proof method. Misconceptions and quick review - Regex syntax describes a language; an expression containing union is not a single input over the base alphabet. - $\varnothing$ and $\varepsilon$ are different edge labels, but $\varnothing^ =\varepsilon$. - Removing a state without its bypass paths loses words; omitting the direct route can also lose words. - State elimination may create a self-loop on another state; update pairs with $i=j$ too. - Classical regexes here use only union, concatenation and star plus atomic expressions. No programming regex engine or version is assumed. [!summary] Equivalence chain Every regular expression builds an NFA, every NFA has an equivalent DFA, and every finite automaton can be converted back to a regular expression. These representations characterize the same class of languages. Reconstruct one conversion in each direction without opening the exercise solutions.

entries.title: Exercises
entries.text: Exercises Notes Attempt each problem without help. Open its hint only when stuck, then compare your reasoning with the adjacent solution. Original tasks retain their source IDs; supplementary practice is labelled. L3 conversion — Build the lecture regex machine Source: ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE — Lecture 3 Regular Expression and Pumping Lemma.pdf, PDF pp. 7–9. Convert $(a\cup ab)^ $ to an equivalent NFA, showing atomic and composite stages. [!tip]- Hint Build a and ab, union them, and then add the outer-star start and return edges. [!success]- Solution Atomic/concatenation stage: $p_1\xrightarrow{a}f_1$ represents a; $p_2\xrightarrow{a}c\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}d\xrightarrow{b}f_2$ represents ab. Union stage: fresh $u$ epsilon-connects to $p_1,p_2$. Star stage: fresh accepting start $r$ epsilon-connects to $u$; $f_1,f_2$ remain accepting and epsilon-connect back to $r$. Here is the complete list of nonempty transition sets; every unlisted entry is $\varnothing$: State a b $\varepsilon$ --- --- --- --- $r$ $\varnothing$ $\varnothing$ $\{u\}$ $u$ $\varnothing$ $\varnothing$ $\{p_1,p_2\}$ $p_1$ $\{f_1\}$ $\varnothing$ $\varnothing$ $f_1$ $\varnothing$ $\varnothing$ $\{r\}$ $p_2$ $\{c\}$ $\varnothing$ $\varnothing$ $c$ $\varnothing$ $\varnothing$ $\{d\}$ $d$ $\varnothing$ $\{f_2\}$ $\varnothing$ $f_2$ $\varnothing$ $\varnothing$ $\{r\}$ Finals are $\{r,f_1,f_2\}$. Each completed component consumes a or ab; restart edges join any finite number of such components. Conversely each sequence of permitted blocks has that path. Staying at r supplies the zero-block case, so the recognized language is exactly $(a\cup ab)^ $. L3 expression input — Interpret a language-valued input Source: ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE — Lecture 3 Regular Expression and Pumping Lemma.pdf, PDF p. 10. The slide describes $(a\cup ab)\circ(a\cup ab)$ as an input. Explain what it denotes and whether its represented strings are accepted by $(a\cup ab)^ $. [!tip]- Hint Enumerate the two independent block choices and distinguish expression from string. [!success]- Solution It denotes $\{aa,aab,aba,abab\}$, from choices $(a,a),(a,ab),(ab,a),(ab,ab)$. All four are accepted because the outer star allows exactly two blocks among its possibilities. The written expression itself is not a single word over $\{a,b\}$. L3 elimination — Eliminate the lecture states Source: ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE — Lecture 3 Regular Expression and Pumping Lemma.pdf, PDF pp. 14–22. Convert the four-state lecture NFA from the opening table to a regular expression by adding fresh start/final states, then removing $q_3,q_1,q_2,q_0$ in that order. Explain every new edge label. [!tip]- Hint For each incoming/outgoing pair, account for zero or more loops on the removed state and retain any direct edge. [!success]- Solution 1. Add $s\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}q_0$ and $q_3\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}f$; only f is final. 2. Remove $q_3$: add $q_1\to f$ labelled 1 and $q_2\to f$ labelled $\varepsilon$. The missing q3-loop contributes $\varnothing^ =\varepsilon$. 3. Remove $q_1$: $q_0\to q_2$ becomes 1 and $q_0\to f$ becomes 1. 4. Remove $q_2$: the q0-loop becomes $10^ 0$, and the q0-to-f label becomes $1\cup10^ $, combining its direct route with the route through q2. 5. Remove $q_0$: obtain $\varepsilon(10^ 0)^ (1\cup10^ )=(10^ 0)^ 10^ $. 6. The union factor needs parentheses in the unsimplified expression. The ungrouped final expression printed on p.22 misses words such as 1010 . The grouped derivation preserves every original path by the entry–loop–exit rule. Practice — Diagnose a missing direct route Source: SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE — synthetic application of the cited conversion rules. A GNFA has an i-to-j edge labelled b, i-to-k labelled a, a k-loop labelled b, and k-to-j labelled a. A student removes k and labels i-to-j only $ab^ a$. Give the correct label and a lost word. [!tip]- Hint The old direct route survives even when k is never visited. [!success]- Solution The correct label is $b\cup ab^ a$. The first alternative preserves the direct edge, while the second preserves paths through k. The student loses the word b : it follows the old direct route and cannot have the required first and last a of $ab^ a$.

entries.title: In 60 Seconds
entries.text: Every sufficiently long accepted run of a finite automaton repeats a state. The input consumed around that loop can be repeated or omitted while the remaining suffix follows the same path. The regular pumping lemma formalizes this as a necessary property of regular languages. To prove nonregularity, assume a pumping length, choose a long language member depending on it, defeat every permitted split, and choose a pumping exponent that leaves the language. After study, you should be able to state the quantifiers, derive the lemma from a DFA run, and write complete equal-count and square-length contradictions.[^l3pump]

entries.title: Concept Preview
entries.text: [!note] Concept — Repeated state Plain-language meaning: p transitions create p+1 state visits in a p -state DFA, so two visits name the same state. Why it matters: The intervening input labels a loop. Connects to: finite memory and pumpable substrings. Source: Lecture 3, PDF pp.26–34. [!note] Concept — Pumping conditions Plain-language meaning: The loop is nonempty, lies within the first p input symbols, and can be repeated any nonnegative number of times. Why it matters: These bounds let a proof locate what changes. Connects to: block languages and length gaps. Source: Lecture 3, PDF p.32. [!note] Concept — Quantifier game Plain-language meaning: The assumed regular language supplies p and a potentially helpful split; the contradiction chooses the witness and a failing exponent. Why it matters: Refuting only one convenient split proves nothing. Connects to: adversarial proof structure. Source: Lecture 3, PDF pp.35–40. [!note] Concept — Necessary, not sufficient Plain-language meaning: Every regular language pumps, but finding a pumpable example does not prove a language regular. Why it matters: The lemma is mainly a nonregularity tool here. Connects to: construction proofs for regularity. Source: Lecture 3, PDF pp.24–32, 41.

entries.title: Before You Start
entries.text: You need DFA runs, contradiction, and quantifier discipline. [!question] Does failing to find a DFA prove that no DFA exists? [!success]- Check your answer No. It reports a failed search, not a proof covering every possible finite automaton. Source: Lecture 3, PDF pp.24–30.

entries.title: A motivating question
entries.text: Can any DFA recognize exactly $$L=\{0^n1^n\mid n\ge0\}?$$ A proposed checker may have as many states as its designer wants, but the number is fixed before the input arrives. Testing many strings or rejecting one candidate machine does not settle the question. Success requires a proof applying to every finite automaton. Challenge Needed idea --- --- Cover every possible state count Use an arbitrary pumping length p Force a loop into the zero block Choose 0^p1^p and use xy ≤p Cover every legal split Write y=0^b with 1≤b≤p Break equality Pump to change zeros while ones remain fixed

entries.title: Why a long run contains a loop
entries.text: Assume DFA M has p= Q ≥1 states and accepts a word w of length at least p . During the first p transitions it visits positions r0,r1,…,rp : p+1 visits but only p possible state identities. Therefore ra=rb for some 0≤a x R["repeated state r"] R -- y, nonempty loop R R -- z F["accept"] Figure 1 — The suffix cannot detect how often the loop ran Read it: x reaches state r ; each copy of y returns to r ; z therefore begins from the same state. Key takeaway: Pumping changes the string without changing the state from which the accepted suffix runs. Provenance: Pedagogical Mermaid derived from Lecture 3, PDF pp.26–34. [!note] Regular pumping lemma If L is regular, some integer p≥1 exists such that every w∈L with w ≥p has a split w=xyz satisfying y ≥1 , xy ≤p , and xy^iz∈L for every integer i≥0 .[^l3pump]

entries.title: Read the quantifiers as a proof protocol
entries.text: $$\exists p\;\forall w\;\exists(x,y,z)\;\forall i.$$ The split is also constrained by the three conditions above. For contradiction, negate the operational order: 1. Assume regularity and accept an arbitrary promised p . 2. Choose a long w∈L , allowed to depend on p . 3. Consider an arbitrary legal split, not your favourite split. 4. Choose an i that may depend on that split. 5. Prove the pumped word is outside L . mermaid flowchart TD A["Assumption supplies p"] -- W["You choose long w in L"] W -- D["Lemma may choose any legal split"] D -- I["You choose a failing i"] I -- C["Contradiction: pumped word not in L"] Figure 2 — Who controls each choice Read it: Alternate between the assumption/lemma and the contradiction proof. Key takeaway: A proof that selects one convenient split skips the lemma's existential choice. Provenance: Pedagogical quantifier diagram derived from Lecture 3, PDF pp.35–40. [!warning] Source shorthand “For any i ” on Lecture 3 p.35 should be read through the exact quantifiers: for each legal split, finding one failing exponent is enough. “One example” on p.40 means a witness family depending on arbitrary p , with every legal split covered.

entries.title: Return to the motivating question
entries.text: Assume L={0^n1^n} is regular and let p be a pumping length. Choose w=0^p1^p , which belongs to L and has length 2p≥p . For an arbitrary legal split, x and y lie within the first p symbols, all zeros. Therefore $$x=0^a,\quad y=0^b,\quad z=0^{p-a-b}1^p$$ for integers a≥0 , b≥1 , a+b≤p . The residual zeros in z matter: the lemma does not require a+b=p . Pump with i=2 : $$xy^2z=0^a0^{2b}0^{p-a-b}1^p=0^{p+b}1^p.$$ Because b≥1 , zeros outnumber ones. The pumped word is not in L . This defeats every legal split, contradicting the lemma. Thus L is not regular, so no DFA, NFA, or classical regex recognizes it. [!warning] Source proof repair Lecture 3 pp.36–37 display only splits with a+b=p . Including 0^(p-a-b) in z covers all permitted splits while preserving the same contradiction.

entries.title: 5-Minute Review
entries.text: - p+1 visits among p states force a repeated state. - The loop y is nonempty and ends within the first p symbols. - To disprove regularity: arbitrary p , chosen w , arbitrary legal split, chosen failing i . - Equal-count proof changes only the initial zero block. - Square-length proof traps the new length between consecutive squares. - Passing one pumping attempt never proves regularity.
