entries.title: The Pumping Lemma
entries.text: The Pumping Lemma Course index · Exercises Opening case — Can finite memory compare unbounded counts? Synthetic checker scenario using the lecture's language. A checker reads a block of zeros followed by a block of ones. It should accept exactly $L=\{0^n1^n\mid n\geq0\}$: the two blocks have equal length, including the empty input. A proposed design may use any finite number of states, but that number is fixed independently of input length. Decide whether any DFA, NFA or classical regular expression can recognize exactly this language. If the answer is no, provide a proof covering every possible finite-state design. Finite testing or failure to draw a machine does not meet the success criterion. What We Need to Learn Question Concepts --- --- Why does any sufficiently long run repeat a state? State visits, finite memory, pigeonhole reasoning What does a repeated state allow? A nonempty loop and pumping Who chooses the long word and its split? Quantifier order How can the loop violate equal counts? Bound the split, then pump Why is one lucky sample insufficient? Necessary condition versus a regularity proof Prerequisites: DFA run traces, the equivalence of DFA/NFA/regex, and contradiction proofs. Source scope: Lecture 3, PDF pp. 25–41. 1. Failure to find a machine is not impossibility A construction proves regularity when it recognizes all and only the desired strings. If we cannot find one, we have only learned about our search, not all possible machines. We need a necessary property of every regular language and then a contradiction. This is the motivation on Lecture 3 pp. 24–30. The useful intuition is finite memory: a long enough run revisits some state. Once it reaches the same state again, its later behavior has no record of how many times that intervening path was followed. The argument below makes this precise without treating “cannot count” as a proof. 2. Derive the pumping lemma from a run Suppose $L$ is recognized by a DFA with $p= Q \geq1$ states. Take any $w\in L$ with $ w \geq p$. During its first $p$ transitions it visits $p+1$ state positions $r_0,r_1,\ldots,r_p$. Since there are only $p$ state identities, two positions have the same state: $r_a=r_b$ for some $0\leq a [!note] Regular pumping lemma If $L$ is regular, there is an integer $p\geq1$ such that every $w\in L$ with $ w \geq p$ has some split $w=xyz$ satisfying $ y \geq1$, $ xy \leq p$, and $xy^iz\in L$ for every integer $i\geq0$. Here $p$ is a pumping length, $x,y,z$ are strings and $i$ counts copies of $y$. All lengths are symbol counts; no rounding or physical units apply. Source: Lecture 3, PDF p. 32. The bound is $ w \geq p$, not strictly greater. There are $p+1$ visits , not necessarily $p+1$ distinct states. The word need not end just after the repeated state; $z$ can be long or empty. Different DFAs can give different valid pumping lengths, and the proof never needs the smallest one. Worked positive example. For the regular language of binary strings ending in 1, use its two-state DFA, so $p=2$ is valid. For 001 , choose $x=\varepsilon$, $y=0$, $z=01$. Then $xy^iz=0^{i+1}1$ ends in 1 for every $i\geq0$. This is an illustration of a valid split; it is not a proof that checking one word establishes regularity. 3. Quantifiers determine the proof strategy The lemma says: $$\exists p\geq1\;\forall w\in L\text{ with } w \geq p\;\exists x,y,z\;\forall i\geq0.$$ The split in this shorthand must satisfy the three displayed structural conditions. To contradict the lemma, the nonregularity argument must defeat every candidate pumping length : Stage Proof obligation --- --- Assume regularity Receive an unknown $p\geq1$ promised by the lemma Choose $w$ It may depend on $p$; prove $w\in L$ and $\vert w\vert \geq p$ Consider the split Cover all $xyz$ with $\vert y\vert \geq1$ and $\vert xy\vert \leq p$ Choose $i$ It may depend on the split; show $xy^iz\notin L$ Conclude No promised split works, contradicting regularity You control the witness $w$ and pumping exponent $i$, but you do not get to choose just the easiest split. A symbolic description of all legal splits often makes the proof short. One exponent such as $i=0$ or $i=2$ may defeat them all; the proof needs one failing exponent for each split , not every exponent failing. In fact $i=1$ always restores the original $w\in L$. [!warning] Qualifying the lecture shorthand Page 35's “for any i” should be read through the lemma's quantifiers: find an exponent that breaks each permitted split. Page 40's “only needs one example” means one witness family depending on arbitrary p , with all legal splits covered. One fixed word or one chosen split does not prove nonregularity. 4. Bound the movable part before changing it For a block-structured word, $ xy \leq p$ locates $y$ in the first $p$ symbols. If those symbols are all 0, every valid $y$ consists only of 0s, even though you do not know its exact length. This is how a local loop changes one block's count without changing the other. pumping-split.svg Figure 2 — All legal splits of the equal-count witness Read it: The first p positions are zeros. Both x and y lie inside that region; z includes the remaining zeros and all the ones. Key takeaway: Do not assume x and y consume every zero. The condition is a + b ≤ p, not a + b = p. Provenance: Original teaching diagram derived from the cited concepts. Counterexample to a proof shortcut. If a proposed proof examines only $x=\varepsilon,y=0$, it may show that this particular split fails but leave all other splits untouched. The lemma needs only one successful split; a contradiction must rule out every permitted one. Using a variable $b$ with $1\leq b\leq p$ handles all loop lengths at once. Solve the opening case Decision. No DFA, NFA or ordinary regular expression recognizes $L=\{0^n1^n\mid n\geq0\}$. Justification. Assume, for contradiction, that $L$ is regular. Let $p\geq1$ be a pumping length. Choose $w=0^p1^p$. It belongs to $L$ and has length $2p\geq p$. Operation — characterize every split. For any permitted $w=xyz$, the first $p$ symbols are zeros and $ xy \leq p$. Write $$x=0^a,\quad y=0^b,\quad z=0^{p-a-b}1^p,$$ where $a\geq0$, $b\geq1$ and $a+b\leq p$. The nonnegative exponent $p-a-b$ accounts for any zeros remaining in $z$. Intermediate result — pump twice. Choose $i=2$. Then $$xy^2z=0^a0^{2b}0^{p-a-b}1^p=0^{p+b}1^p.$$ There are $p+b$ zeros but only $p$ ones. Since $b\geq1$, the counts differ, so $xy^2z\notin L$. Interpretation and conclusion. This argument applies to every valid split. No split promised by the lemma can survive all pumping exponents, contradicting regularity. Therefore $L$ is not regular. Unit 03's equivalence means NFAs and classical regexes cannot evade this limitation. The proof allows any fixed finite state count; it does not merely refute one candidate design. It says nothing here about more powerful computational models. [!warning] Source proof repair Lecture 3 pp. 36–37 display $z=1^p$ and $a+b=p$, covering splits at the end of the zero block. The lemma also permits $a+b 0$. No integer square lies strictly between the consecutive squares $p^2$ and $(p+1)^2$. Thus the pumped word is not in $S$, for every permitted split, contradicting regularity. square-gap.svg Figure 3 — Trap the new length between consecutive squares Read it: The pumped length increases by b, but b is at most p. The next square is 2p + 1 beyond p². Key takeaway: Being larger than one square is insufficient; the upper bound rules out reaching the next square. Provenance: Original teaching diagram derived from the cited concepts. For a numerical illustration only, take $p=3$. The original length is 9 and possible added lengths are 1, 2 or 3, producing 10, 11 or 12; the next square is 16. The symbolic inequalities establish the result for arbitrary $p$, including $p=1$, where the new length is 2 between 1 and 4. [!warning] Source proof repair Page 39 states that $p^2+b p^2$ makes the pumped word leave the square-length language. That lower bound alone is insufficient: a larger number can be another square. The necessary upper bound is $p^2+b [!summary] Retrieval targets State the lemma with its quantifiers. Derive it from $p+1$ visits among $p$ states. Reconstruct both source proofs with all legal splits and both square-gap bounds. Explain exactly what your chosen witness and exponent depend on.

entries.title: Exercises
entries.text: Exercises Notes Attempt each problem without help. Open its hint only when stuck, then compare your reasoning with the adjacent solution. Original tasks retain their source IDs; supplementary practice is labelled. L3 equal counts — Unbounded matching blocks Source: ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE — Lecture 3 Regular Expression and Pumping Lemma.pdf, PDF pp. 36–37. Prove $L=\{0^n1^n\mid n\geq0\}$ is not regular. [!tip]- Hint Choose a word whose first p symbols are all zero. Describe every possible legal y, rather than choosing one. [!success]- Solution Step 1 — Assumption and witness. Assume regularity and let $p\geq1$ be its pumping length. Choose $w=0^p1^p\in L$, of length $2p\geq p$. Step 2 — All legal splits. Any $w=xyz$ with $ xy \leq p$ and $ y \geq1$ has $x=0^a$, $y=0^b$ and $z=0^{p-a-b}1^p$, where $a\geq0$, $b\geq1$, $a+b\leq p$. Step 3 — Contradiction. Pump twice: $xy^2z=0^{p+b}1^p$. Since $b 0$, the zero count exceeds the one count, so the word is outside $L$. This defeats every valid split and contradicts the lemma. Hence $L$ is not regular. The remaining zeros in z repair the source's restricted displayed split. L3 square lengths — Unary squares Source: ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE — Lecture 3 Regular Expression and Pumping Lemma.pdf, PDF pp. 38–39. Prove $S=\{0^{n^2}\mid n\geq0\}$ is not regular. [!tip]- Hint The pumped length must lie strictly between two consecutive squares. Bound the increase using the split conditions. [!success]- Solution Assume $S$ regular and let $p\geq1$ be a pumping length. Choose $w=0^{p^2}\in S$, with $ w =p^2\geq p$. For any permitted split, write $y=0^b$ with $1\leq b\leq p$. Pump to $xy^2z$, whose length is $p^2+b$. Because $1\leq b\leq p$, $$p^2 The last inequality follows from $(p+1)^2-(p^2+p)=p+1 0$. Consecutive integer squares leave no other square between them, so the new length is not a square. Every split fails for $i=2$, contradicting the lemma. Thus S is not regular. The upper bound supplies the missing part of the printed argument. L3 Q&A — What does the lemma establish? Source: ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE — Lecture 3 Regular Expression and Pumping Lemma.pdf, PDF p. 41. 1. If you cannot find a regex for a language, have you proved it nonregular? 2. Why do we pump long strings? 3. If all pumped versions of one string stay in L, is L regular? 4. Is $0^n1^n$ a regular expression? [!tip]- Hint Separate an existence claim about all machines from your search, and a theorem about every long word from one example. [!success]- Solution 1. No. Failure to construct one does not rule out every possible expression or machine. Supply a nonregularity proof. 2. A length of at least $p$ forces $p+1$ visits among $p$ DFA states, so a nonempty loop exists within the first $p$ transitions. Short words lack this guarantee. 3. No conclusion of regularity follows. One successful word and split do not meet the lemma's requirements for every sufficiently long member. Moreover the lemma is a necessary condition, not a provided converse regularity criterion. 4. If $n$ is fixed, the specific finite word can be written as a regex by concatenating n zeros and n ones. If $n$ ranges over all nonnegative integers with the two counts constrained equal, $0^n1^n$ is not an ordinary regex in the course's grammar; the language it describes is nonregular by the first proof. Practice — Find the unjustified choice Source: SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE — proof diagnosis based on the supplied lemma. A student says: “Assume a pumping length p for the equal-count language. Choose $w=0^p1^p$, split $x=\varepsilon,y=0,z=0^{p-1}1^p$, and pump down. The new word is outside the language, so the language is not regular.” Identify the logical gap and repair it. [!tip]- Hint The chosen split is legal, but the theorem says some split can pump. What about the others? [!success]- Solution The student refutes only one split; another could satisfy the lemma. Repair by taking an arbitrary legal split, writing $y=0^b$ with $1\leq b\leq p$, and observing that pumping down produces $0^{p-b}1^p$. Since $b\geq1$, this leaves the language for every split. The same witness now supports a valid contradiction. Practice transfer — Repair a square-length inference Source: SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE — proof diagnosis based on the supplied lemma. A proof says “the new length is greater than $p^2$, so it is not a square.” Explain why this is invalid and provide the missing inequality for the lecture witness. [!tip]- Hint A number larger than p² might equal (p+1)². Show why the permitted increment cannot reach it. [!success]- Solution The lower bound does not rule out later squares; for example $(p+1)^2 p^2$ is itself a square. Here the loop length b obeys $b\leq p$, so $p^2+b\leq p^2+p<(p+1)^2$. Together with $b\geq1$, this traps the length strictly between consecutive squares. Both bounds are essential.

entries.title: What is an alphabet?
entries.text: A nonempty finite set of symbols.

entries.title: What is Σ ?
entries.text: The set of all finite strings over Σ , including ε .

entries.title: Distinguish ε and ∅ .
entries.text: ε is a length-zero string; ∅ is a language containing no strings.

entries.title: Why is ε∈L for every language L ?
entries.text: Star permits k=0 ; the empty product is ε .

entries.title: What witnesses that v is a substring of w ?
entries.text: Strings x,z satisfying w=xvz .

entries.title: What proves a universal assertion false?
entries.text: One valid counterexample within its stated domain.

entries.title: What must a set-equality proof contain?
entries.text: Both inclusions: every left member is right, and every right member is left.

entries.title: What is a cofinite language?
entries.text: A language whose complement relative to the fixed Σ is finite.

entries.title: Does an infinite language require infinite strings?
entries.text: No. It may contain infinitely many distinct finite strings.

entries.title: For a language A, why can $ A ^k$ exceed the number of distinct strings in $A^k$?
entries.text: Different ordered factor tuples can concatenate to the same string.

entries.title: What makes a DFA deterministic?
entries.text: Every state-symbol pair has exactly one defined next state.

entries.title: When does a DFA accept ε ?
entries.text: Exactly when its start state is accepting.

entries.title: What does a missing NFA transition do?
entries.text: It kills that branch; it does not keep the state unchanged.

entries.title: What is NFA acceptance?
entries.text: Some path consumes all input and finishes in an accepting state.

entries.title: What does an epsilon transition consume?
entries.text: Nothing; the next unread input symbol remains unchanged.

entries.title: What is epsilon closure?
entries.text: States reachable from a set using zero or more epsilon moves.

entries.title: When is a subset-construction state accepting?
entries.text: When the subset contains at least one old accepting state.

entries.title: When must the empty subset appear in a reachable-state DFA construction from an NFA?
entries.text: If reachable, it represents that no NFA path survives the consumed prefix. Every symbol keeps it empty, so it is a rejecting sink. An unreachable empty subset need not be drawn.

entries.title: How does a DFA product recognize intersection?
entries.text: Track both states and accept only pairs where both components accept.

entries.title: Why can an NFA's finals not simply be flipped?
entries.text: Existential acceptance may retain a formerly rejecting branch even when an accepting branch exists.

entries.title: How do you construct an NFA for $A^ $ from an arbitrary NFA for A, including acceptance of ε?
entries.text: Add a fresh accepting start r and an epsilon edge r→q0. Keep all old transitions and accepting states, and add an epsilon edge from each old accepting state back to r. Staying at r accepts zero factors; repeated complete old runs accept more factors.

entries.title: What does atomic regex a denote?
entries.text: The one-word language {a} .

entries.title: What does regex ε denote?
entries.text: The language {ε} , containing one empty string.

entries.title: What does regex ∅ denote?
entries.text: The empty language, containing no strings.

entries.title: What does regex union express?
entries.text: A word may come from either operand language.

entries.title: What does concatenation require?
entries.text: A split into a first-language word followed by a second-language word.

entries.title: Why is a regex not normally an input word?
entries.text: It is syntax denoting a set of base-alphabet words.

entries.title: Why add a fresh start and a fresh sole accepting state before GNFA state elimination?
entries.text: To obtain one start with no incoming and one final with no outgoing edges.

entries.title: When eliminating GNFA state k, what label replaces the edge from i to j, and what does each term mean?
entries.text: $R_{ij} \cup R_{ik}(R_{kk})^ R_{kj}$. Keep the direct route i→j, or enter k, traverse its loop zero or more times, then exit to j. Omitting the direct term can lose accepted words.

entries.title: What does an absent GNFA edge mean?
entries.text: Its label is ∅ , permitting no traversal.

entries.title: Does elimination order change the language?
entries.text: No, but it can change expression syntax and size.

entries.title: Why must a DFA with p states repeat a state within the first p transitions of a sufficiently long run?
entries.text: p+1 visits among only p state identities.

entries.title: In the pumping lemma for regular languages, why must the loop substring y be nonempty?
entries.text: The repeated visits occur at different input positions, so b-a≥1 .

entries.title: Which pumping-lemma bound ensures that the loop substring y ends within the first p symbols?
entries.text: The condition xy ≤p .

entries.title: Who chooses the pumping length?
entries.text: The assumed regularity claim supplies some valid p .

entries.title: In a nonregularity proof using the pumping lemma, who chooses the witness word, and when?
entries.text: The contradiction proof, after seeing p .

entries.title: Must a contradiction cover every legal split?
entries.text: Yes; the lemma needs only one surviving split.

entries.title: In a pumping-lemma contradiction, may the failing exponent i depend on the chosen legal split?
entries.text: Yes; each split needs at least one failing exponent.

entries.title: What does i=0 do?
entries.text: It removes the loop substring y .

entries.title: Does successful pumping prove regularity?
entries.text: No. The lemma supplies a necessary condition, not a converse proof here.

entries.title: For $L=\{0^{n^2}:n\ge0\}$, why is $p^2+b p^2$ alone insufficient when pumping a loop with $1\le b\le p$?
entries.text: An upper bound below (p+1)^2 , not merely a length above p^2 .

This guide records the supplied material; it does not establish a current timetable or assessment update. The separate Prompts_Advanced_Database_Development_Obsidian.md is a working-instructions file, not a course-content source. Conventions to carry into your answers Convention Consequence --- --- Unspanned records and entries; maximum packing Floor capacity before taking the ceiling of page demand No invented tutorial overhead Add headers or slots only where explicitly supplied Sparse means one representative per data block by default Count data blocks before sparse entries Primary index follows file order It need not use the logical primary key Dense coverage must reach every match Duplicates may use runs or buckets; Q4 specifically uses one entry per student Q4 keeps the student and five modules together Pack 1300-byte groups, not a pooled stream of record bytes Q2 transfers four 4096-byte sectors Its 16 384-byte transfer block differs from the file questions' 4096-byte blocks Q2 averages seek as half the maximum Keep full transfer time; state that this is the course approximation Each tutorial retains its own identifiers: student , students , student_ID , studentID , sID , module , product , and productID . They describe different cases, not a normalised shared schema. Clarifications that affect Unit 01 - Track distance: the Q1 answer uses 16 384 as the distance, giving 17.384 ms. There are 16 383 gaps between 16 384 track centres, giving 17.383 ms. Notes retain both conventions. - Rounding: Q2's printed totals use rounded intermediate values. The notes also show totals calculated with precision retained until the end. - Sparse equality boundary: the unique block-minimum example uses ≤ to select the candidate block directly. The slide's strict predecessor rule includes a forward scan and needs first-key handling. - Q6 compares access methods: simple sparse sampling of unordered IDs is incomplete. This does not imply that a name index answers an ID predicate better or that primary indexes are always faster. - NAND erasure: the textbook distinguishes page programming from erasing groups of pages, and explains remapping. - SQL in the slides: schematic b-index syntax is not presented as an executable portable command. The separate lab supplies unchanged SQLite scripts. Environment and scope The course-wide relational DBMS, version, and SQL dialect remain unconfirmed. The newly released Lab 2 explicitly uses MySQL with MySQL Connector/J and driver class com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver ; that is a lab-specific confirmation, not evidence that every SOE201 topic or assessment uses MySQL. The existing supplementary lab ran on SQLite 3.53.1 ; its teaching purpose and observed results are in 03 Lab. Unit 01 covers physical storage, record and file organisation, and the introductory indexing required for Tutorial 1. Units 02–04 now cover B+ tree balancing, hashing algorithms, and advanced indexes from the remaining supplied lectures. Lecture1b recommends textbook chapters 12 and 13, but only the passages needed for this scope are used. The supplied introduction announces later work on query processing and optimisation; transactions, concurrency, and recovery; web and distributed data; and analytics. Its laboratory list includes JDBC, Java transactions, XML, RDF, ontologies, linked data, and MongoDB. Big-data and blockchain sessions are marked tentative. These announcements do not substitute for missing later lectures or a practical setup guide. Assessment recorded in the supplied introduction: indexing test 15%, laboratory reports 25%, final examination 60% ( Lecture1a - Module Introduction.pdf , PDF p. 4). The FAQ points to the final lecture for precise exam scope; that lecture and the module handbook are not supplied. Treat this as source context, not a verified current schedule. The legacy _AI Staging archive remains unchanged. Compact review evidence for Units 02–04 is stored in _AI Staging/Production 2026-09-20 ; Lab 02 ingestion evidence is in _AI Staging/Production 2026-09-21 , and local runtime/Task 2 timing evidence is in _AI Staging/Production 2026-09-24 . Study from the course index rather than staging. Official Lab 02 — JDBC and Index The canonical course-level lab is Lab 2 — JDBC and Index. Its byte-preserved originals are in Labs/Lab 02 - JDBC and Index/Sources/ ; the external download copies remain untouched. Official item Released scope Status --- --- --- Task 1.1 Set up the environment; understand and test JDBC.java on a basic JDBC query Released and mapped; remote runtime not performed during ingestion Task 1.2 Understand and test JDBCandIndex.java on a basic JDBC query with an index Released and mapped; remote runtime not performed during ingestion Task 2 Print the time for the Task 1 query without and with an index; time only rs = stmt.executeQuery(sql); Released, implemented, compiled, and locally executed Lab-specific configuration is MySQL with MySQL Connector/J. The PDF states Connector/J 9.4.0 as current on PDF p. 10, but gives no MySQL server/JDK/storage-engine version. The supplied Java uses com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver , searchKey = "num" , and searchKeyValue = "7" . Lab 02 discrepancies and import cautions - Server host: PDF p. 6 gives 10.7.1.127 ; PDF p. 11 gives 10.7.1.36/[DATABASE_NAME] ; both supplied Java files use 10.7.1.127/[DATABASE NAME] . A 24 September 2026 reachability probe connected to 10.7.1.127:3306 , while .36:3306 did not respond within three seconds; no university authentication or SQL was attempted. - Java filename: PDF p. 11 names JDBCIndex.java , while the supplied official files are JDBC.java and JDBCandIndex.java . - SQL width: yeast_prosite.sql declares mmatch varchar(12) , but static inspection finds 771 supplied non- NULL values longer than 12 characters, with a maximum of 89. The original is preserved; import errors/warnings depend on the actual server mode and must be inspected. - SQL bootstrap: the dataset begins with unconditional drop table Orf_Motif; , which can report a missing-table error in a fresh schema. - Date mapping wording: PDF p. 24 says java.Date ; the mapping table on p. 25 specifies java.sql.Date . The lab note preserves the discrepancy and uses the fully qualified JDBC type shown in the table. - Performance: the two official Task 1 Java files do not time the query or inspect a plan. The separate Task 2 solution times only executeQuery , compares logical results, and verifies key=numIndex ; its one local timing pair is not a universal speedup, I/O, or physical B+ tree claim. The two official Java files compile together with JDK 17 without Connector/J on the compile classpath. A separate reference solution was compiled with JDK 17.0.18 and Connector/J 9.4.0 and executed against isolated local MySQL instances. Tasks 1.1 and 1.2 returned the same 607 final rows, and the indexed plan named numIndex . The released Task 2 run then measured 8.723 ms without the index and 2.083 ms with it, again returned the same 607 logical rows, and confirmed EXPLAIN key=numIndex . This did not authenticate to or execute SQL on the university server. The SQL contains one table definition with columns orf , acc_num , num , pos , len , and mmatch ; 285 inserts use NULL for both pos and mmatch . Static parsing finds 614 INSERT statements with num=7 , while later deletions produced 607 final matches in that controlled local import. [!note]- SOE201 Presentation Standard Use Unit 01 as the approved presentation reference. The current production request authorised all remaining supplied lecture units; do not rewrite Unit 01. - Structure: Unit NN - Topic/ contains 01 Notes.md , 02 Exercises.md , an optional useful 03 Lab.md , and Attachments/ . Keep operational evidence in the archive. - Hierarchy: begin with a compact roadmap and observable abilities; use short contextual openers, concept headings, named formula sections, and occasional checkpoints. Finish with a checklist, a 60-second recap, and practice links. - Callouts: abstract = roadmap; info = key idea or interpretation; note = definition; example = worked example; tip = study/exam guidance; warning = misconception or implementation-specific caveat; question = retrieval; summary = takeaway; success = hidden solution/check. Use them selectively. - Exercises: organise A–E as Quick Retrieval, Guided Problems, Independent Problems, Error Diagnosis, and Exam-Style Problems. Every question is immediately followed by [!tip]- Hint and [!success]- Solution ; both are collapsed. Keep solutions local, with no duplicate answer appendix. Use difficulty labels mainly for reasoning problems. - Figures: retain consistent SVG typography, spacing, teal/blue/amber roles, and arrowheads; use Mermaid for clear relationships and sequences. Number educational figures consistently and place a bold caption, Read it , and Key takeaway beneath each. A compact navigation roadmap is separate from figure numbering. - Calculations: introduce the model before the formula; explain symbols once nearby. Worked examples show Given, Find, Method, Calculation/Answer, and Interpretation where useful. Preserve validated assumptions, formulas, source quotations, and results. - Navigation: use vault-relative wiki links and descriptive aliases. Link Notes ↔ Exercises ↔ Lab, resolve heading targets and attachment embeds, and show only Notes, Exercises, and Lab in the course index. Keep SQL and original source filenames unchanged. - Readability: use ==highlight== sparingly for method-changing assumptions, selected inputs, key distinctions, and final outputs. Keep mathematical expressions, source quotations, and identifiers intact. Separate dense exercise inputs into Key Data and tasks into What You Need to Find only when helpful; use short bullet hints and stepwise solutions ending in a key idea. Keep short recall questions compact. Newly completed lecture coverage Unit Primary course source Coverage and practice --- --- --- 02 — B+ Tree Indexing Lecture2b - B+Tree Indexing (1).pdf , PDF pp. 2–37 Structure, lookup, capacity, insertion, deletion; all original lookup/construction/update tasks and their intermediate states 03 — Hash Indexing Lecture3a - Hash Indexing.pdf , PDF pp. 2–43 Static hashing, extendable hashing, lookup, splitting, overflow, coalescing and workload choice; all embedded worked tasks including the two-split Taiyuan case 04 — Advanced Indexing Lecture3b - Advanced Indexing.pdf , PDF pp. 2–22 LSM/buffer, bitmap/Bloom, spatial and temporal mechanisms; original bitmap outputs and temporal table, plus explicitly supplementary exercises and a Python lab Each lecture's cover, learning outcomes and final reading page are accounted for as context. Lecture 2a's pp. 3–4 provide retrieval motivation and illustrative indexes, pp. 5–18 are already in the approved Unit 01 boundary, and p. 19 is a reading reference: no additional unfinished unit is implied by this file. The original Tutorial 1 Q1–Q6 remain in their approved Unit 01 locations; they were not re-audited or relocated in this run. Textbook availability does not extend the production scope to every textbook chapter or exercise. During the Units 02–04 production run, the earlier 12 PDFs were rechecked unchanged, and the same two duplicate pairs yielded 10 distinct documents. Lab 2 was ingested afterward as an additional official PDF plus Java/SQL sources; all 26 PDF pages were inspected visually as well as through extracted text. Conventions and clarifications for Units 02–04 - B+ tree order: maximum internal child pointers; leaf capacity is one fewer key. Lecture 2b p. 4's leaf-root “children” wording is clarified as key entries. The root has its own minimum-occupancy exception. - B+ tree deletion: follow the source's merge-first rule. Retained internal separators may be absent from leaves while still defining valid ranges (Lecture 2b pp. 9, 27, 32–33). The source does not prescribe a universal sibling preference when both are valid. - Height calculation: the million-key, order-100 example has at most four visited index nodes under the course occupancy model. The displayed logarithm on Lecture 2b p. 11 is rounded; the chapter derives the bound and separates edges, node visits, cache effects and data-page reads. - Hash bit direction: Lecture 3a reads high-order bits from the left; preserve leading zeros in fixed-width hashes. Directory size is $2^i$ pointers and physical buckets number at most $2^i$ (p. 13 uses a strict inequality that excludes the equality case). - Failed hash splits: retain the course's rollback-before-overflow convention. The city case permits exactly two unsuccessful splits (pp. 32–40). Its initial Taiyuan is a real existing record; the new Taiyuan is another record with the same city name. - Hash-source ambiguities: p. 5 repeats G in the J position and gives X as 25; punctuation/spacing encoding is unspecified. Page 11 shows index ID 33456 but a Gold row labelled 33465. Preserve source-local IDs; do not silently equate them. The department overflow example supplies no numeric hash or exact trial limit, so only its supported duplicate-key overflow result is claimed. - Vendor correction: Lecture 3a p. 42's PostgreSQL statement is contradicted by [PostgreSQL 18's official on-disk hash-index documentation]( The correction is supplementary; it does not identify the course DBMS. Other vendor mentions remain lecture context, not a verified current support matrix. - LSM deletion: the slide's matching deletion/record removal is a simplified merge model. The new chapter explains why older unmerged versions must not be resurrected by prematurely discarding a tombstone. - Bloom estimates: Lecture 3b p. 12's 10% and 1% are rounded estimates; the chapter derives approximately 9.52% and 0.819% under its stated model. The tiny lab deliberately uses different, correlated functions and reports its actual finite-domain result. - Time endpoints: the slides do not fully specify interval inclusion. Unit 04 declares half-open intervals [start,end) for its worked queries; this remains an instructor-convention uncertainty rather than an asserted source rule. Lecture 3b p. 6 names BigTable, Cassandra, MongoDB, SQLite4, LevelDB and MyRocks in its discussion of LSM-related systems. Those names are preserved here as source examples only; the supplied material does not establish a specific installed engine, version, or configuration. The new material teaches the depicted abstract mechanism rather than inferring identical current behaviour across those products. Validation and learning status Units 02–04 passed technical/pedagogical review, source/task mapping, deterministic calculation or invariant checks, and Markdown/YAML/link/SVG checks. All 41 new SVGs and 231 MathJax expressions were rendered in a standalone Chromium harness. Its dark and narrow layouts and expanded-help A4 PDFs were inspected; these are standalone checks , not native Obsidian tests. Some standalone page breaks separate captions or callout titles from their following content, so native pagination still needs review; no approved CSS was changed to impose a different print policy. The new Python 3.14.6 lab executed 98 bitmap predicate comparisons and 4356 spatial rectangle comparisons against direct predicates. Its observed output and limits are recorded with the unchanged script hash in staging. It makes no DBMS, disk-I/O or latency claim. Native Obsidian Reading View/Live Preview and native PDF export for all new units remain pending , including whether the selected exporter includes expanded or collapsed help. Unit 01's user-reported approval does not transfer to the new units. All new material has study_status: untested . No study completion is inferred. No remaining supplied lecture supports another new theory unit. Lab 2 is a course-level practical rather than “Unit 2”; its released Tasks 1.1, 1.2, and 2 are now covered. Announced later topics still need their own released original material, so the entire SOE201 course is not declared complete.

entries.title: SOE201 Tutor Mode
entries.text: SOE201 Tutor Mode This is a guided companion to the ordinary SOE201 reference edition. It covers every unit currently supported by supplied teaching materials: physical storage/index foundations, B+ trees, hash indexing, advanced indexes and the released JDBC/index lab. How to use it 1. Orient: read a unit's In 60 Seconds and Concept Preview. 2. Learn: work through the motivating problem, explanation, visual and worked example. 3. Retrieve: close references and answer the atomic cards. 4. Practise: attempt a question before opening its collapsed hint. 5. Compare: open the complete solution and compare method, assumptions and intermediate steps. 6. Record real gaps: only an actual attempt can establish a learning weakness. 7. Transfer: finish with a changed surface problem that requires choosing the method. Preview cards support recognition; recall cards require retrieval. Reading does not establish mastery, and the time labels are navigation aids rather than measured learning guarantees. Tutor units Tutor route Ordinary reference Main capability --- --- --- Unit 01 · Tutor Notes · Practice Notes · Exercises · Lab calculate storage/index blocks and justify access paths Unit 02 · Tutor Notes · Practice Notes · Exercises trace and validate lookup, insertion and deletion Unit 03 · Tutor Notes · Practice Notes · Exercises route fixed-width hashes and manage split/overflow states Unit 04 · Tutor Notes · Practice Notes · Exercises · Lab choose and reason about write, set, membership, spatial and temporal indexes Lab 02 · Tutor Notes · Practice Reference Lab 02 distinguish JDBC execution, index creation, plan evidence and performance evidence Assessment evidence The supplied image-only pack contains four distinct official logical papers: 2023/24 Final and Resit, and 2024/25 Final and Resit. Every rendered question page was inspected. Each paper's cover/administrative page 1 is absent, but its complete question pages are present. See Past-paper intelligence. This is a study-priority guide based on the supplied historical assessment sample, not a forecast of the next exam. No official marking schemes were supplied. If You Are Short on Time Prerequisites come first: Unit 01's packing/index language supports the later index units. Priority 1 — High Exam Relevance - Unit 01 record/block packing and introductory index sizing/selection — observed in 4/4 papers, 20 known marks. Study whole-record capacity and attempt Tutorial Q3 practice. - B+ tree deletion/repair — observed in 3/4 papers, 6 known marks. Study deletion repair and attempt independent deletion. - Spatial-index identification/selection — observed in 3/4 papers, 6 known marks. Study spatial distinctions and attempt selection practice. Priority 2 — Medium Exam Relevance - Hash-index trade-offs — observed in 2/4 papers, 4 known marks: comparative explanation. - B+ lookup trace — observed in 1/4 papers, 2 known marks: guided lookup. Priority 3 — Remaining Source-Supported Material Do not omit source-supported topics merely because they were not observed in four papers: - HDD timing, variable records, slotted pages and file maintenance; - B+ insertion, capacity/height and range access; - hash calculations, directory aliases, coalescing and full-hash overflow; - LSM/buffer trees, bitmaps, Bloom filters and temporal indexing; - released JDBC Tasks 1.1–1.2 and their evidence limits. Later exam topics such as query optimisation and transactions are repeatedly visible in the papers but their teaching lectures are NOT IN MATERIALS . Tutor Mode does not invent those missing units. If You Have Only 30 Minutes Suggested schedule—not a measured guarantee: 1. 8 minutes: Unit 01 floor→ceiling packing method and dense/sparse/primary/secondary distinctions. 2. 8 minutes: B+ lookup plus merge-first deletion decision. 3. 5 minutes: k-d versus quadtree versus R-tree selection. 4. 4 minutes: static versus extendable hashing trade-offs. 5. 5 minutes: attempt one Unit 01 packing problem without notes, then compare the solution. Sacrificed coverage: detailed HDD modelling, B+ insertion sequences, extendable-hash multi-split traces, LSM/bitmap/Bloom/temporal mechanisms and JDBC practice. This is not full course coverage and does not make the omitted topics unimportant or non-examinable. Optional interactive conventions /teach , /quiz , /grade , /weak , and /cram can be used in conversation. They are not native commands. Document answers are collapsed locally; chat quiz answers remain withheld until an attempt or explicit reveal request. Status and limitations - All generated material has study_status: untested . - Structural and standalone-render checks are recorded separately from native Obsidian and native PDF checks. - Tutor Mode does not modify or replace ordinary SOE201 material.

entries.title: In 60 Seconds
entries.text: This unit explains how logical rows become physical records, how whole records fit into fixed-size blocks, and how file order and index density change the route to a record. The central ideas are: 1. a query ultimately needs pages, not isolated bytes; 2. unspanned capacity uses floor(block size / item size) before counting blocks; 3. clustered groups must be packed as groups when the question says they stay together; 4. a primary index follows physical file order, while dense/sparse describes coverage; 5. an index is useful only if its entries can lead to every required match. After study, you should be able to calculate record and index blocks, trace a disk-read model, and justify an access path without inventing overhead or performance results.

entries.title: Concept Preview
entries.text: [!note] Page and buffer Plain-language meaning: the DBMS transfers a page/block and then reads records from the in-memory copy. A buffer hit avoids that data-page fetch. Why it matters: row count alone does not determine physical I/O. Connects to: record packing, file organisation and indexes. Source: Lecture1b - Data Storage Structures.pdf , PDF pp. 3–10. [!note] Blocking factor Plain-language meaning: the maximum number of whole, unspanned records that fit in one block. Why it matters: rounding in the wrong order changes every later result. Connects to: dense and sparse index sizing. Source: Lecture1b - Data Storage Structures.pdf , PDF pp. 16–18; Tutorial Q3–Q6. [!note] File organisation Plain-language meaning: the physical rule used to place records—heap, sequential, hashed or clustered. Why it matters: the same logical table can support very different access and maintenance costs. Connects to: primary indexes and range access. Source: Lecture1b - Data Storage Structures.pdf , PDF pp. 24–29. [!note] Dense and sparse indexes Plain-language meaning: dense coverage normally has an entry for every search-key occurrence/record; sparse coverage samples ordered data blocks. Why it matters: a sparse entry is safe only when the file order lets the search continue to every match. Connects to: primary versus secondary access paths. Source: Lecture2a - Indexing Techniques (1).pdf , PDF pp. 5–18.

entries.title: Before You Start
entries.text: You need integer division, ceilings and the distinction between a logical tuple and a physical record. [!question] Prerequisite check A 4096-byte block stores unspanned 350-byte records. Which operation determines records per block: floor or ceiling? [!success]- Check your answer Floor: $\lfloor4096/350\rfloor=11$. A twelfth record would cross the block boundary. Source: Tutorial Q3, Lab1-Tutorial (1).pdf , PDF p. 4.

entries.title: A motivating question
entries.text: Synthetic case using Tutorial Q3's physical model. A registry has 25,000 fixed 350-byte records in 4096-byte blocks. Records are ordered by a 10-byte student_ID . A sparse primary-index entry is the 10-byte key plus a 10-byte pointer. 1. How many data blocks are required? 2. How many sparse entries and index blocks are required? 3. Why is the index sparse only because the file is ordered on the same search key? Success criteria: keep records and entries unspanned, show both floor and ceiling steps, and explain the access invariant rather than reporting numbers alone. Question Knowledge needed --- --- Data blocks blocking factor, ceiling of record demand Index blocks one sparse entry per data block, entry capacity Correctness physical order and candidate-block selection

entries.title: Learn the mechanism
entries.text: From tuple to page fetch A tuple is a logical row. Its encoded record lives inside a page/block. The buffer holds page copies in memory. On a buffer miss, the page is fetched; on a hit, the record can be read from the resident page. Index pages and data pages are separate costs unless a problem explicitly combines them. mermaid flowchart LR Q["Row predicate"] -- A["Choose access path"] A -- I["Read index page(s), if used"] I -- D["Locate data block"] A -- D D -- B{"Data block buffered?"} B -- no F["Fetch block"] B -- yes R["Read record"] F -- R Figure 1 — A logical lookup becomes page work Read it: follow either the index route or direct file route; both converge on a data block. Key takeaway: a short index does not prove a query is cheap when qualifying records occupy many scattered data pages. Provenance: teaching construction from Lecture1b , PDF pp. 3–10, and Lecture2a , PDF pp. 5–18. Whole-record capacity For block size $B$, record size $R$, and $N$ records: $$bfr=\left\lfloor\frac{B}{R}\right\rfloor, \qquad b=\left\lceil\frac{N}{bfr}\right\rceil.$$ bfr is the blocking factor. Floor first because only whole records fit; ceiling second because a partially filled final block still occupies a block. [!warning] Pedagogical trap — dividing total bytes directly $\lceil NR/B\rceil$ permits unused bytes from one block to combine with another. That contradicts the unspanned-record condition whenever the remainder cannot hold another complete record. Groups that must stay together Tutorial Q4 requires one 300-byte student and five 200-byte module records in the same block. The indivisible group is $$G=300+5(200)=1300\text{ bytes}.$$ Then $\lfloor4096/1300\rfloor=3$ groups fit per block and $\lceil1000/3\rceil=334$ blocks are needed. Pooling all student and module bytes would violate the clustering constraint. Dense, sparse, primary and secondary are different axes Term Decisive question --- --- Primary index Is the data file physically ordered by this search key? Secondary index Is the index on a different order from the data file? Dense index Is every search-key value represented, with a route to all records having that value? Sparse index Can representative entries select a block/range because the file order completes the search? A logical primary key need not be the primary index key. In Tutorial Q6 the file is ordered by the non-key name ; an index following that physical order is primary in the lecture terminology. Index capacity For key length $K$, pointer length $P$, and $E$ entries: $$e=K+P,\qquad bfr_I=\left\lfloor\frac{B}{e}\right\rfloor,\qquad b_I=\left\lceil\frac{E}{bfr_I}\right\rceil.$$ For a sparse primary index in this course, $E$ is normally the number of data blocks. For a dense index, read the question: Tutorial Q4 explicitly requires one entry per student tuple. HDD read phases The source model separates seek, rotational waiting and transfer: $$T_{read}=T_{seek}+T_{rotation}+T_{transfer}.$$ Minimum, maximum and average cases choose different seek/rotation assumptions. Tutorial Q2 averages seek as half the stated maximum and rotation as half a revolution, while retaining the full transfer time. This is the course approximation, not a universal disk benchmark. [!question] Explain it yourself Why can a sparse index on unordered IDs miss a matching record even if every index entry is correct? [!success]- Check your explanation Sampling blocks works only when file order makes the selected block/range contain every possible match. Unordered IDs can occur outside that range. Source: Lecture2a - Indexing Techniques (1).pdf , PDF pp. 8–18; Tutorial Q6.

entries.title: Worked example — solve the motivating question
entries.text: Step 1 — Data records per block $$bfr=\lfloor4096/350\rfloor=11.$$ Step 2 — Data blocks $$b=\lceil25000/11\rceil=\lceil2272.727\ldots\rceil=2273.$$ Step 3 — Sparse entries One entry per data block gives $E=2273$ entries. Each entry is $10+10=20$ bytes. Step 4 — Index entries per block and index blocks $$bfr_I=\lfloor4096/20\rfloor=204,$$ $$b_I=\lceil2273/204\rceil=\lceil11.142\ldots\rceil=12.$$ Interpretation: the sparse index occupies 12 blocks and selects among 2273 ordered data blocks. A lookup still needs its index traversal and at least the candidate data block; cache state is unspecified. Source: Tutorial Q3, Lab1-Tutorial (1).pdf , PDF p. 4; supplied answer, Lab1-Tutorial_Answers.pdf , PDF p. 8.

entries.title: Return to the motivating question
entries.text: The answers are 2273 data blocks , 2273 sparse entries , and 12 index blocks . The sparse design is correct because data blocks are sequentially ordered by student_ID ; an entry representing a block identifies the candidate range, and the search continues within that block. Remove the order assumption and the same sampling no longer guarantees complete lookup.

entries.title: Definitions and distinctions
entries.text: Term A Term B Decisive distinction Source --- --- --- --- Tuple Record logical row versus encoded physical representation Lecture1b, pp. 3–4 Page/block Record transfer/container unit versus one stored item Lecture1b, pp. 7–10 Primary key Search key logical uniqueness constraint versus lookup attribute(s) that may repeat Lecture2a, pp. 5–7 Dense index Sparse index direct complete coverage versus representative coverage relying on order Lecture2a, pp. 8–18 Primary index Secondary index follows physical file order versus indexes another order Lecture2a, pp. 8–18

entries.title: Common confusions
entries.text: - Ceiling too early: records per block uses floor; required blocks uses ceiling. - Invented overhead: add page headers or slots only when supplied. - Logical key = physical order: not necessarily. - Fewer index blocks = faster: retrieval may still touch many data blocks. - Sparse = one entry per arbitrary block: only safe with an ordering/routing invariant.

entries.text: Full Understanding Return to Learn the mechanism and Worked example — solve the motivating question.

entries.title: 5-Minute Review
entries.text: 1. Identify the indivisible item: record, clustered group or index entry. 2. Compute whole items per block with floor. 3. Compute blocks with ceiling. 4. Decide entry count from dense/sparse coverage. 5. Verify that physical order makes the access path complete. 6. Keep index-node, data-page and buffer assumptions separate.

entries.title: 60-Second Recall
entries.text: - tuple → record → page → file - buffer hit versus miss - floor(B/R) then ceil(N/bfr) - clustered group as indivisible item - primary versus secondary - dense versus sparse - key bytes + pointer bytes - seek + rotation + transfer
