entries.title: Physical Storage & File Organisation
entries.text: Physical Storage & File Organisation SOE201 · Unit 01 From logical rows to physical pages—and the cost of finding them. Course home · Practise · Try the lab Unit Roadmap mermaid flowchart TD A["Pages and buffers"] -- B["Storage and I/O"] B -- C["Record layouts"] C -- D["Page updates"] D -- E["File organisation"] E -- F["Index access"] classDef default fill: E6F3F1,stroke: 117D83,color: 172B42,stroke-width:1.5px; [!abstract] What You Will Be Able to Do - Explain when a logical lookup causes a physical page fetch. - Separate seek, rotational wait, and transfer costs. - Calculate space for whole records, related groups, and index entries. - Trace deletion, insertion, and compaction while preserving valid references. - Justify file organisation and index coverage for a stated workload. - Interpret the SQLite lab's results without inferring unmeasured performance. Topic overview A database stores records in pages , arranges those pages into files, and uses access structures to find the right data. This unit connects the layout of bytes with space, reads, insertions, and deletions. Learn to… Start here --- --- Explain where a lookup's cost comes from From rows to pages and the buffer · HDD geometry and read phases Calculate storage without losing whole-record constraints Fixed-length records and blocking factor Trace records as they grow, move, or disappear Variable-length records · Slotted pages and stable references Choose an organisation for a workload File organisations Size an index and explain how it finds a record Introductory indexes Revise the tutorial calculations Worked examples · Exam-style summary Scope: Lecture1b, PDF pp. 2–29; introductory indexing from Lecture2a, PDF pp. 5–18; Tutorial 1, Q1–Q6. B+ tree balancing and hashing algorithms are outside this unit. You need rows, attributes, keys, basic SQL, and integer division. [!info] Key Idea — Keep the model explicit Tutorial records and index entries are ==unspanned==, with maximum packing and no invented overhead. Count overhead when a question explicitly supplies it. The HDD question transfers ==16 384 bytes== per block; the file-sizing questions use ==4096-byte blocks==. These are separate cases. The course DBMS and dialect are unconfirmed. The optional SQLite lab demonstrates logical behaviour; it does not reproduce the tutorial's physical layout. Why this matters Imagine a university registry during registration week. Staff need quick student lookups, address updates, ordered reports, and student-plus-module information. Each task favours different properties: Task Storage question --- --- Find one student How many pages must be located and fetched? Store new registrations Where can new records fit, and what must be maintained? Change a long address Can the record grow without invalidating references? Read a student and five modules Would keeping related records together save data-page fetches? Produce an ordered report Does logical order also provide physical locality? A good design explains space, access, and maintenance together . Fewer index pages alone do not prove faster queries. Key concepts Follow the storage path from a logical row to its page, then examine how records and access structures change. From rows to pages and the buffer A query asks for rows; storage retrieves the pages that contain them. A schema defines attributes and constraints; a tuple is a logical row. A physical record contains the encoded fields, and a ==page/block== holds records. A file groups pages. Databases also need metadata, statistics, indexes, and logs, which are outside a tutorial count of data blocks.[^logical][^architecture] Aspect Logical view Physical view --- --- --- Unit of data Tuple and attribute Record and encoded field Grouping Relation File and pages Lookup A requested row An access path plus buffer state A ==primary key== is a logical unique, non-null identifier; a search key is an attribute set used for lookup and may repeat. A foreign key connects a child value to a referenced key. DDL declares structures; DML reads or changes their contents. [!note] Definition A ==buffer== holds page copies in memory. A hit uses a resident page; a miss requires fetching it. A dirty page has changes not yet reflected in its persistent copy.[^buffer] mermaid flowchart TD A["Locate required page"] -- B{"In buffer?"} B -- "Hit" C["Read record in memory"] B -- "Miss" D["Fetch page into a frame"] D -- C C -- E{"Changed?"} E -- "Yes" F["Mark dirty; later writeback"] E -- "No" G["Read complete"] classDef default fill: E6F3F1,stroke: 117D83,color: 172B42,stroke-width:1.5px; Figure 1 — A logical request meets the buffer Read it: choose the hit or miss branch before reading the record. Key takeaway: two row requests can require only one data-page fetch if both rows share a retained page; eviction can change that. Index and metadata fetches need separate accounting. A memory write alone does not establish durability. Storage hierarchy and units Before comparing costs, identify both the storage layer and the unit being transferred. Layer in the course model Examples Role --- --- --- Primary Cache, main memory Fast working copies; volatile in this model Secondary Flash, magnetic disk Persistent database storage Tertiary Optical storage, tape Archival storage The course hierarchy describes roles, not current hardware prices or a rule covering every memory technology.[^media] 1 byte = 8 bits; 1 KiB = 1024 bytes. Thus 4096 bytes = 4 KiB, while four 4096-byte sectors = 16 KiB. A disk transfer block, a DBMS page, a NAND page, and a NAND erase block are different objects.[^blocks] Larger pages may reduce transfer counts but also bring unwanted data into memory or waste space. Keep the ==unit and storage layer== explicit. HDD geometry and read phases Reaching the right track and reaching the right sector are separate operations. A platter is a disk with recording surfaces. Each surface has circular tracks , divided into sectors . A ==cylinder== groups tracks of equal radius across surfaces.[^hdd] figure-02-hdd-geometry.svg Figure 2 — Platter, track, sector, cylinder Read it: follow the highlighted ring; the highlighted arcs across the stack share its radius. Key takeaway: moving to a track is radial positioning; reaching a sector also depends on angular position. The geometry is schematic. Phase What happens Symbol --- --- --- ==Seek time== Move the head to the required track $T_s$ ==Rotational wait== (latency) Wait for the starting sector $T_w$ ==Transfer time== Read all requested sectors $T_t$ Formula — Read time For $r$ revolutions/minute, $S$ sectors/track, and $q$ contiguous sectors/block: $$ T_r=\frac{60\,000}{r}\text{ ms},\qquad T_t=\frac{q}{S}T_r,\qquad T_{\text{read}}=T_s+T_w+T_t. $$ Symbol Meaning Unit --- --- --- $T_r$ Time for one revolution ms $T_s$, $T_w$, $T_t$ Seek, rotational wait, transfer ms [!info] Interpretation Transfer occupies the fraction $q/S$ of one revolution. Faster rotation reduces the rotation and transfer terms in this model; seek remains a separate input. figure-03-read-phases.svg Figure 3 — Position first, then transfer the complete block Read it: compare the worst-case and course-average bars; transfer has the same duration. Key takeaway: averaging the positioning costs does not halve the number of sectors read. Segment widths are schematic; the labels give the times. We use total read time , including transfer. The textbook's “access time” ends when transfer begins; the lecture also allows a definition including transfer.[^timing] Uniform angular arrival gives half a revolution on average. The tutorial additionally approximates average seek as ==half the maximum==; that is a course convention, not a universal probability law.[^q2-answers] [!info]- Optional depth — why an average needs a model For independent continuous uniform positions $X,Y$ across a span of $L$ tracks, $$\mathbb{E} X-Y =\frac{2}{L^2}\int_0^L\int_0^x(x-y)\,dy\,dx=\frac{L}{3}.$$ A positive-distance seek model $1+d/1000$ ms would then give approximately $1+L/3000$ ms. This alternative is not substituted for the tutorial's half-maximum convention. Elevator scheduling. The lecture's policy serves pending requests in one direction, then reverses when none remain in that direction.[^elevator] Starting at 40, moving upwards: Current head Next request Movement Pending after service ---: ---: ---: --- 40 45 5 tracks 10, 20, 70 45 70 25 tracks 10, 20 70 20 50 tracks 10 20 10 10 tracks None The path is 40 → 45 → 70 → 20 → 10 , totalling 90 tracks . Under $1+d/1000$ ms per positive seek, its seek component is $4+90/1000=4.09$ ms. Rotation and transfer are additional. Some scheduling variants travel to the physical disk end before reversing; they require a different trace. Sequential reads can exploit proximity, but this is not a measured timing guarantee.[^sequential-book] SSDs, mirroring, and striping Different mechanisms change access costs, placement, and protection against failure. NAND flash has no mechanical seek or rotation. It still has read, program, transfer, controller, and reclamation costs. Programming and erasing operate at different granularities: pages are programmed, while groups of pages form ==erase blocks==. A translation layer may remap logical addresses.[^ssd][^flash-book] mermaid flowchart TD A["Logical page L maps to X"] -- B["Program new content into erased Y"] B -- C["Remap L to Y; X becomes obsolete"] C -- D["Later: move live pages, erase old block"] classDef default fill: E6F3F1,stroke: 117D83,color: 172B42,stroke-width:1.5px; Figure 4 — A logical overwrite can change physical location Read it: L keeps its logical identity while X and Y are physical locations. Key takeaway: deleting a row need not immediately erase a NAND page. This diagram does not prescribe crash-safe ordering. figure-05-mirroring-striping.svg Figure 5 — Copies versus distribution Read it: identical page labels denote copies; different labels denote different data. Key takeaway: a mirror can retain data after one device fails under the shown assumptions; striping alone cannot.[^raid] Mechanism What it provides Limit to remember --- --- --- Striping Independent devices may work concurrently No exact speedup is guaranteed Mirroring Redundancy against some failures A mistaken deletion can propagate to every mirror; no exact speedup is guaranteed Key distinction: ==redundancy== is not historical recovery or backup. [!question] Before continuing Can two row requests cause just one data-page fetch? Would replacing the HDD with an SSD make every remaining access cost disappear? [!success]- Check Yes, if both rows share a page that remains buffered. An SSD removes mechanical seek and rotation, but electronic access, controller work, transfer, and possible reclamation remain. Fixed-length records and blocking factor The first question is how many complete records fit in one page. In ==fixed-length== storage, every record in the model occupies $R$ bytes. Unspanned means each record stays within one page; spanned storage permits a record to continue across pages and needs an appropriate continuation representation.[^records] Aspect ==Unspanned== ==Spanned== --- --- --- Page boundary A record stays within one page A record may continue across pages Leftover tail Cannot complete a record on another page May hold a fragment under the chosen representation Model used here Tutorial capacity calculations Contrast only; continuation overhead is unspecified figure-06-blocking-and-spanning.svg Figure 6 — Why leftover bytes do not combine across unspanned pages Read it: the twelfth record needs 350 bytes but the tail has only 246. Key takeaway: calculate whole records per page before counting pages. The spanned alternative illustrates a different model; its continuation overhead is not specified. Formula — Whole-record capacity Let $N$ be records, $B$ bytes/page, $H$ fixed overhead/page, and $U=B-H$ usable bytes: $$ \boxed{f=\left\lfloor\frac{U}{R}\right\rfloor} \qquad \boxed{b=\left\lceil\frac{N}{f}\right\rceil} \qquad w=U-fR. $$ [!info] Interpretation Capacity changes in whole-record steps. More usable space helps only when another complete record fits; any remaining records still need another page. - $f$: ==blocking factor== — whole records/page, because $fR\leq U$. - $b$: required data pages, because $bf\geq N$. - $w$: residual bytes in a maximally packed page. Check the model before calculating: - Use $H=0$ for the tutorial unless overhead is supplied. Do not count a record header twice if already included in $R$. - The formula assumes $N\geq0$ and $0 U$, the unspanned representation cannot store even one record; do not divide by $f=0$. - Zero records imply zero data pages in this model, not a zero-byte database. [!tip] Exam Tip — Round according to the constraint ==Floor== capacity; ==ceiling== demand. First find how many complete objects fit. Then allocate enough complete pages for all objects. The object might be a record, a whole related group, or an index entry. Deletion and free lists Deleting a record is useful only if its space can be found and reused. A ==free list== links reusable fixed-size record positions from a header pointer. Each free position stores the next link.[^free-list] In this teaching example, deletion adds a slot at the front. figure-07-free-list.svg Figure 7 — Delete slot 3, then reuse it Read it: follow the header through free slots; occupied slots are outside the chain. Key takeaway: ==save a free slot's successor== before overwriting its bytes. Other occupied records need not move. A deleted flag marks a hole but does not efficiently locate it. A free list helps discover space; it does not preserve a sequential file's key order or guarantee that a variable-length record fits. Affected indexes still need maintenance. The sequence shown is a logical trace, not a concurrent or crash-recovery protocol. Variable-length records When a field grows, the record must still describe where its fields begin and end. [!note] Definition If field lengths vary, a fixed prefix can store ==(offset, length)== pairs. A field offset is relative to the record start . A ==null bitmap== distinguishes a missing value from a present empty string.[^variable][^variable-book] Aspect Fixed-length records ==Variable-length records== --- --- --- Size in the model Every record occupies $R$ bytes Field values can change the record length Finding fields Predetermined boundaries Offset/length descriptors in the illustrated layout Growth Must fit the chosen representation May require new space and updated offsets Question Metadata to consult --- --- Where are the field's bytes, and how long are they? The field's (offset, length) descriptor Is the value missing rather than a present empty string? The null bitmap figure-08-record-layouts.svg Figure 8 — Fixed fields and variable-field descriptors Read it: follow each descriptor to its bytes. Key takeaway: an unchanged offset can still need a new length; growth must also fit in the containing page. Widths are schematic; the variable example assumes a 16-byte prefix and one byte per character. In the example, Ana occupies bytes 16–18. Changing Hall to Hall-B changes the address pair from (19,4) to (19,6) and the total record length from 23 to 25 bytes. If the name instead grows by two bytes, the following address begins at 21. Character count is not generally byte count. The lecture's instructor example uses three 4-byte pairs at bytes 0–11: ID (21,5) , name (26,10) , and department (36,10) . salary uses bytes 12–19, and the null bitmap is at 20. The last field ends at byte 45, so the total is 46 bytes . These are that figure's encoding assumptions, not a universal format.[^variable][^variable-book] Slotted pages and stable references A small directory lets record bytes move without rewriting every surviving reference. [!note] Definition A ==slotted page== has a header, a directory of record locations and lengths, free space, and record bytes. Referencing a record through (page, slot) lets its bytes move within the page while its slot stays stable.[^slotted][^slotted-book] Formula — Page free space For $n$ allocated slots of $s$ bytes each—including ==retained deleted slots==—the free space after compaction is: $$ F=B-H-ns-\sum_{i\in\mathrm{live}}R_i. $$ [!info] Interpretation Both live records and allocated slots consume page space. Deleting a record releases its payload bytes; retaining its slot keeps the directory cost. Insertion situation Free bytes required --- ---: Allocate a new slot $R_{\mathrm{new}}+s$ Reuse a retained slot $R_{\mathrm{new}}$ figure-09-slotted-page.svg Figure 9 — Delete, compact, reuse Read it: left-to-right bars show byte order; track record C and slot 2 through compaction. Key takeaway: contiguous free space grows when C moves, while updating slot 2 keeps surviving references valid. Intervals are half-open: [start,end) has length end − start ; directory widths are enlarged for readability. [!warning] Common Mistake — Counting only record bytes Wrong: If the page has enough free bytes for the record, insertion must fit. Why it fails: Total free bytes may be fragmented; contiguous free bytes may be smaller. A new slot also consumes space, and a retained deleted slot still occupies directory bytes. Correct idea: Check a ==usable extent== and include any directory growth. Reference limits: - Compaction does not preserve the identity of a deleted record when its slot is reused. - Moving a record to another page needs additional reference handling. - A raw byte pointer becomes stale when its record moves. Immediate compaction is the course's explanatory model, not every DBMS's deletion policy. [!question] Before continuing When C moves during compaction, what must change so that (page, slot 2) still finds it? Why does a deleted-but-retained slot still count toward page occupancy? [!success]- Check Update slot 2 to C's new offset. The directory entry remains allocated even when its record is deleted, so its bytes remain part of the page's occupied space. File organisations Choose what should stay together: free space, nearby keys, or related records. Organisation Layout and access Update cost or trade-off --- --- --- ==Heap== No record ordering; use free space where available Easy placement; searches need a scan or suitable complete index ==Sequential / ordered== Records follow a search-key order Good ordered locality; insertion may need movement or overflow ==Multitable clustering== Related records from different relations share pages Helps grouped access; single-relation scans fetch other relation bytes B+ tree / hashing Named alternatives in the lecture taxonomy Their algorithms are deferred beyond this unit These are the course's layout concepts.[^file-organisations] Choose using query frequency, ranges, joins, insertions, memory, and maintenance—not a universal ranking. Heap free-space map A map advertises approximate available space per page; a higher level can summarise groups with their maximum.[^heap] With illustrative buckets [1,4,0,2] , a group maximum of 4 directs a request needing 3/8 of a page toward the page with bucket 4. The actual page must still be checked. For the teaching rule $v=\min(7,\lfloor8F/B\rfloor)$, a 4096-byte page with 2100 free bytes has bucket 4. Inserting 1536 bytes, including any slot cost, leaves 564 bytes and bucket 1; the group maximum becomes 2. Stale maps or fragmentation may require retrying or compaction. This rounding rule is illustrative, not a specified course implementation. figure-10-file-organisations.svg Figure 10 — Three ways to organise records Read it: distinguish physical boxes from the logical chain in the ordered example. Key takeaway: order, free-space discovery, and locality solve different problems. The small page capacities are teaching assumptions. Sequential insertion and reorganisation Into full pages [10,14,19] and [23,28,35] , insert 16 by allocating an overflow record, setting its successor to 19, then redirecting 14 to 16. The logical sequence is now 10 → 14 → 16 → 19 → 23 → 28 → 35 . An ordered scan must include ==overflow==.[^sequential] Reorganisation rewrites the sequence into [10,14,16] , [19,23,28] , [35] , with affected references and indexes repaired. It restores locality at the cost of reads and writes. On a separate branch from the post-insertion state , delete 19 by saving successor 23, redirecting 16.next to 23, and reclaiming 19 under the free-space policy. Do not mix this branch with the seven-record reorganisation result. Multitable clustering Keep one student(sID, ...) record with its five related module(sID, ...) records. module.sID references the student's key; the module record's own key is unspecified. Tutorial Q4 requires all six records in the same block, so pack ==whole groups==.[^clustering][^q4] Formula — Whole-group capacity $G$ is bytes/group, $R_s$ and $R_m$ are bytes/student and bytes/module, $m$ is modules/student, and $N_s$ is the number of student groups. $$ G=R_s+mR_m,\qquad f_G=\lfloor B/G\rfloor,\qquad b_G=\lceil N_s/f_G\rceil. $$ [!info] Interpretation More child records make each group larger. The packing unit is the entire related group, so leftover bytes cannot be pooled across pages to complete it. With variable child counts, group lengths vary even if each record type has fixed length. A student with 25 modules would need $300+25(200)=5300$ bytes, violating a 4096-byte one-page requirement. Per-relation pointer chains can skip module records logically during a student-only scan, but fetched pages still contain their bytes. Introductory indexes An index must provide a complete route from the requested value to every matching record. An ==index entry== stores a search-key value and a pointer. Ordered indexes sort search values; hash indexes map them to buckets without preserving key order.[^index-key][^ordered-hash] File-order category Meaning in this course Distinction --- --- --- ==Primary index== Index on the file's ordering key Different from the relational primary-key constraint Secondary index Index on a different key Sorting its directory does not make unordered data suitable for simple sparse lookup Aspect ==Dense index== ==Sparse index== --- --- --- Coverage Every search-key value; all matching records must be reachable Selected representatives; default here is one per data block Entry count Depends on the duplicate representation Depends on the representative rule Absence reasoning No matching entry can establish absence when coverage is complete No matching representative does not establish absence from the data The slides also use clustering/clustered and non-clustering/non-clustered as aliases for primary and secondary. Product terminology can differ. Multitable clustering is a related-record layout, not the same definition.[^index-types] figure-11-index-coverage.svg Figure 11 — When sparse lookup works, and when sampling fails Read it: for target 28 choose the largest block minimum ≤ 28; compare the missing route to ID 20 below. Key takeaway: sparse lookup needs a valid continuation rule in the underlying file, not merely sorted sampled index entries.[^sparse] For ==unique keys== and block-minimum representatives , choose the largest representative ≤ K and inspect that block. With representatives 10, 23, 40: Target Candidate and result ---: --- 23 Choose D1 directly; equality matters 9 Below the first minimum: absent 39 Search D1; absent before next minimum 40 99 Search D2 to its end; absent The slide uses [!info] Interpretation Decide what one entry represents before counting entries. A sparse directory may use fewer entries, but that space saving is useful only if the access path remains complete. Index maintenance - Changed indexed value: remove its old entry/pointer and add its new one consistently with the data change. - Insertion or deletion: index entries and page allocation can change. - Deleted block minimum: its sparse representative can change; deleting a non-minimum may leave it unchanged. - Empty page: remove or redirect its entry. - Unindexed field update without record movement: an index may remain unchanged.[^index-metrics] Multilevel directories A small outer index can describe the pages of an inner ordered index.[^multilevel] mermaid flowchart TD A["Outer index: 1 page, 12 entries"] -- "Choose one inner page" B["Inner sparse index: 12 pages"] B -- "Choose one data page" C["Registry: 2273 data pages"] classDef default fill: E6F3F1,stroke: 117D83,color: 172B42,stroke-width:1.5px; Figure 12 — A directory over a directory Read it: follow one selected page at each level. Key takeaway: a cold lookup on this path uses three fetches; with the outer page resident it needs two more. This extension has 13 index pages , while Q3's requested single-level index has 12 . A secondary-index scan may jump among scattered data pages while a primary-index scan follows nearby ones. This locality argument depends on the access pattern and buffer; neither index size nor correct results alone establishes a speedup. The supplementary lab demonstrates index maintenance and result preservation without claiming a physical footprint or timing result. [!question] Before continuing Why can a value be absent from a sparse directory but present in the file? What makes its candidate page discoverable? [!success]- Check Sparse entries represent selected values. Compatible file order and a valid representative/continuation rule lead to the candidate data page; sorting samples alone cannot create that property. Worked examples The cases below are separate tutorial datasets , not a single shared schema. All use unspanned, maximally packed records and entries. The page-update example is a labelled teaching construction. Example 1 — Registry storage and its index · Q3 [!example] Worked Example — Registry storage and its index · Q3 Given - student(student_ID, address, ...) : 25 000 records , 350 bytes each. - Ordered by unique 10-byte student_ID ; 4096-byte blocks , 10-byte pointers . - The 50-byte address is already included in 350 bytes.[^q3] Find · Calculate data pages, sparse and dense index alternatives, and packing slack. Method · Records → records/block → data blocks → index entries → index blocks. Calculation and answer Step Calculation Result --- --- ---: Records/block $\lfloor4096/350\rfloor$ 11 Data blocks $\lceil25\,000/11\rceil$ 2273 Last block $25\,000-2272(11)$ 8 records Index entry $10+10$ 20 bytes Entries/block $\lfloor4096/20\rfloor$ 204 Sparse index $\lceil2273/204\rceil$ 12 blocks Dense unique-ID alternative $\lceil25\,000/204\rceil$ 123 blocks Interpretation The requested single-level sparse design uses ==2273 data + 12 index = 2285 blocks==.[^q3-answer] Its last index block holds $2273-11(204)=29$ entries. A full data block leaves $4096-11(350)=246$ bytes. Payload is 8 750 000 bytes ; allocated data space is 9 310 208 bytes ; slack is 560 208 bytes . Check it independently: $2272(246)+1296=560\,208$. Pooling all row bytes gives 2137 blocks, but that answer illegally combines tails across unspanned pages. Example 2 — HDD timing · Q1–Q2 [!example] Worked Example — HDD timing · Q1–Q2 Given - 16 384 tracks/surface ; 128 sectors/track ; 4096 bytes/sector . - 7200 rpm ; four contiguous sectors per transfer block; no gaps . - For positive distance $d$, seek time is $1+d/1000$ ms; no movement costs zero seek time in the best case.[^q1][^q2] Find · Calculate the seek cases and the best, approximate worst, and course-average read times. Method · Keep seek, rotational wait, and full-block transfer separate; state the distance convention. Calculation and answer One-track seek: $1+1/1000=1.001$ ms. The answer sheet uses 16 384 as the end-to-end distance, yielding 17.384 ms . Literally, 16 384 track centres have 16 383 gaps, yielding 17.383 ms . State which convention you use.[^q1-answer] $$ T_r=60\,000/7200=8.333333\ldots\text{ ms},\qquad T_t=(4/128)T_r=0.2604167\text{ ms}. $$ Read case Seek + wait + full transfer Total --- --- ---: Best $0+0+0.2604167$ 0.2604 ms Approximate worst $17.384+8.3333333+0.2604167$ 25.9778 ms Course average $17.384/2+8.3333333/2+0.2604167$ ==13.1191 ms== A near-full revolution is the worst rotational bound. The published answer rounds intermediate values to 17.38, 8.33, and 0.2603, producing about 25.9703 and 13.1153 ms . Retaining precision until the end explains the difference; it does not change the model.[^q2-answers] Example 3 — Page insertion and compaction [!example] Worked Example — Page insertion and compaction Given — teaching assumptions - 4096-byte page ; 64-byte header ; three 8-byte slots . - Records: A = 600 bytes , B = 800 , C = 1000 . - Records are packed from the end downwards . Find · Decide what fits, then track deletion, compaction, and slot reuse. Method · Account for the header, all allocated slots, live records, and free bytes on each independent branch. Calculation and answer $$F=4096-64-3(8)-(600+800+1000)=1608\text{ bytes}.$$ A new 1600-byte record plus an 8-byte slot fits exactly; 1601 bytes plus its slot does not. These are ==independent tests== from the original page. Now restart from that original page, delete B, compact, and insert D = 1600 using B's retained slot: State Slot 0 → A Slot 1 Slot 2 → C Free space --- --- --- --- --- Initial (3496,600) B (2696,800) (1696,1000) 1608 contiguous bytes Delete B Unchanged Retained, marked free Unchanged 2408 total, split into two gaps Compact Unchanged Still free (2496,1000) 2408 contiguous bytes Insert D Unchanged D (896,1600) (2496,1000) ==808 contiguous bytes== The final check is $64+24+600+1600+1000+808=4096$. Slot count remains three; surviving C is still reachable through slot 2 after its offset changes. Use Figure 9 to connect the arithmetic with the byte movement. Example 4 — Student and module groups · Q4 [!example] Worked Example — Student and module groups · Q4 Given - 1000 student records , 300 bytes each; 5000 module records , 200 bytes each. - Exactly five modules per student ; each whole group must share a 4096-byte block . - Groups are ordered by 20-byte sID . - A 10-byte pointer contains an 8-byte block ID and a 2-byte offset .[^q4] Find · Calculate combined data blocks and the two alternative index sizes. Method · Pack a whole student-plus-five-module group before counting data blocks; count each index alternative separately. Calculation and answer $$G=300+5(200)=1300,\qquad f_G=\lfloor4096/1300\rfloor=3,\qquad b_G=\lceil1000/3\rceil=\mathbf{334}.$$ Three groups leave 196 bytes per full block. The last block holds one group. Entries are $20+10=30$ bytes, so each index block holds $\lfloor4096/30\rfloor=136$ entries. Index alternative What one entry represents Required index blocks --- --- ---: Dense, as Q4 defines it One student tuple: 1000 entries 8 Sparse primary One combined data block: 334 entries 3 These are alternatives, not two indexes to add together by default.[^q4-answer] After locating a group, one data block contains all six records; locating it may still require index reads. Separate files would use $\lceil1000/13\rceil=77$ student blocks and $\lceil5000/20\rceil=250$ module blocks: 327 total . Clustering spends ==7 extra blocks== for guaranteed group locality. A student-only scan must fetch pages containing module bytes. Example 5 — Product file · Q5 [!example] Worked Example — Product file · Q5 Given - 10 000 product records , 50 bytes each. - Ordered by unique 2-byte productID . - 4096-byte blocks ; 10-byte pointers ; sparse primary index .[^q5] Find · Calculate data blocks and a single-level sparse primary index. Method · Find whole-record capacity, then count one sparse entry per data block. Calculation and answer $$ f=\lfloor4096/50\rfloor=81,\quad b=\lceil10\,000/81\rceil=124, \quad E=2+10=12,\quad f_I=341,\quad b_I=\lceil124/341\rceil=1. $$ Answer: ==124 data blocks + 1 index block==. The last data block contains $10\,000-123(81)=37$ products. There are 124 sparse entries, not 10 000.[^q5-answer] Example 6 — A file ordered by a non-key name · Q6 [!example] Worked Example — A file ordered by a non-key name · Q6 Given - 30 000 students records , 30 bytes each; ordered by non-key name (4 bytes) . - studentID is the 2-byte primary key . - Blocks are 4096 bytes ; index pointers are 6 bytes .[^q6] Find · Identify the primary-index key, calculate its maximum compact dense size, and assess ID sampling. Method · Use the file ordering to classify the index, then state how dense entries cover duplicates. Calculation and answer The primary-index key is name , because it determines file order. $$ f=\lfloor4096/30\rfloor=136,\quad b=\lceil30\,000/136\rceil=221, \quad E=4+6=10,\quad f_I=409. $$ The last data block holds 80 records . If $D$ is the number of distinct names, a compact dense-by-value directory has $D\leq30\,000$ entries, giving a maximum of $\lceil30\,000/409\rceil=74$ index blocks . Non-key status permits duplicates; it does not require them in every dataset. Unspecified duplicate buckets, headers, and spare space are excluded. A one-entry-per-tuple format also yields 74, so that total alone does not establish the representation. A simple sparse secondary index on unordered studentID cannot locate all omitted IDs (Figure 11). A dense secondary ID index would provide complete coverage while preserving name order. The valid primary index supports ==name searches==; it does not automatically answer an ID predicate better.[^q6-answer] Visual revision The figures are placed beside the concepts they explain. Use this visual revision route to reconstruct the unit without rereading every paragraph. Figures Reconstruct from the visual --- --- 1 · Buffer path Explain why a logical request need not cause a physical read 2–3 · Disk geometry and phases Point to the radial, angular, and transfer operations 4–5 · Flash and RAID Distinguish remapping, redundancy, and parallelism 6–8 · Records and free lists Explain unused tails, reuse, and variable-field descriptors 9 · Slotted page Track C's movement and its stable slot reference 10 · File layouts Compare placement, logical order, and related-record locality 11–12 · Indexes Prove complete access, then count the selected page fetches All figures are original teaching diagrams. Numeric assumptions come from the identified tutorial case or are explicitly labelled as teaching constructions. SVG figures remain sharp when zoomed. Common mistakes Use the left column to spot a tempting shortcut and the right column to repair the model behind it. Tempting shortcut Better reasoning --- --- Divide total row bytes by block bytes once Unspanned packing requires the per-block floor first Add the registry's 50-byte address again It is already inside the 350-byte record Primary key = primary-index key The course's primary index follows file order Sorting sampled IDs makes a valid sparse secondary index The underlying records still need a complete continuation path Dense always means one entry per tuple State how duplicates are reached; obey explicit local definitions Average read = half worst read All requested sectors still transfer 90 tracks = 90 ms Apply the seek model, then include wait and transfer A 1600-byte gap always fits a 1600-byte record A new slot can require additional bytes (page, slot) is permanent object identity It protects surviving within-page moves under this model Free bytes are always one usable gap Distinguish total space from contiguous space A smaller index is always faster Account for coverage, cache, selectivity, locality, and maintenance SSD writes are cost-free overwrites Programming, remapping, and erasure still cost work Mirroring is a backup Logical mistakes can propagate to every current copy Expected output is observed output Only an actual run establishes an observation Exam-style summary Use these relationships to build a justified answer to the tutorial problem types. [!summary] Takeaway — Six relationships to remember Packing: $f=\lfloor(B-H)/R\rfloor$, then $b=\lceil N/f\rceil$. Indexing: count what an entry represents; then $E=K_b+P_b$, $f_I=\lfloor B/E\rfloor$, $b_I=\lceil n_I/f_I\rceil$. Timing: total read = seek + rotational wait + full transfer. Page updates: header + allocated directory + live records + free space = page size. Sparse access: representatives need compatible file order and boundary handling. Design: space savings, locality, update cost, and reliability answer different questions. Tutorial Key result under the stated model --- --- Q1 1-track seek 1.001 ms ; published maximum 17.384 ms ; centre-gap alternative 17.383 ms Q2 Best / worst / course-average reads 0.2604 / 25.9778 / 13.1191 ms with full intermediate precision Q3 2273 data + 12 sparse index blocks ; dense alternative 123 index blocks Q4 334 combined data blocks ; 8 dense or 3 sparse index blocks Q5 124 data + 1 sparse index block Q6 Primary-index key name ; 221 data blocks ; maximum compact dense index 74 blocks Build an exam answer in this order: state the model → choose the indivisible unit → calculate capacity → calculate pages → check the remainder → explain the access path or update invariant → qualify any performance claim. For a design question, tie the layout to the workload and name what measurements could change your choice. The generated block-minimum example uses ≤ ; the slide uses [!summary] Takeaway Physical layout determines what fits and what must be fetched. Buffers may avoid a fetch. HDD positioning and transfer have distinct costs. Fixed records favour simple packing; variable records need descriptors and indirection. Heap, sequential, and clustered layouts serve different workloads. An index helps only if its coverage and continuation rules can find all required records, and every update must preserve that property. entries.text: Unit 1 Exercises Notes · Lab [!abstract] Practice Map A · Retrieve → B · Build the method → C · Apply it → D · Repair reasoning → E · Integrate Work with the notes closed. Show units, state assumptions, and explain every rounding decision. All datasets in these exercises are teaching constructions. Use ==unspanned records and entries==, maximum packing, and only the overhead explicitly stated . Attempt → reveal a hint if needed → check your solution. Both help panels sit directly below their question and stay collapsed until opened. Difficulty labels describe the amount of reasoning required, not predicted exam difficulty. A. Quick Retrieval Explain each distinction in a few sentences before revealing help. Exercise A1 — Explain an access path Draw fields → record → page → file, and show where memory enters a lookup. Why can two row requests cause ==one data-page fetch==? [!tip]- Hint - Separate row requests from page fetches . - Check whether the same page remains in the buffer for the second request. [!success]- Solution Step 1 — Follow the storage hierarchy Fields form records, records occupy pages, and pages form a file. A requested page is fetched into a buffer on a miss. Step 2 — Apply buffer state If it remains resident and contains both rows, the second request hits that same buffer page. Index and metadata access require separate accounting. Key idea: A ==buffer hit== can satisfy a second row request without another data-page fetch. Exercise A2 — Derive rather than memorise Why does records-per-block use ==floor== while required block count uses ==ceiling==? What happens if one record is larger than the usable block? [!tip]- Hint - Ask how many complete records can fit inside one block. - Then ask how many complete blocks are needed for all records. - Check whether even one record fits before dividing. [!success]- Solution Step 1 — Enforce whole-record capacity Only whole unspanned records fit, so fractional capacity is discarded. Step 2 — Allocate enough blocks Any remaining records still need a whole additional block. Step 3 — Check the domain If a record exceeds usable capacity, the assumed unspanned layout is impossible; a zero blocking factor cannot be used as a divisor. Key idea: ==Whole objects== determine both rounding decisions. Exercise A3 — Predict a boundary lookup [!info] Key Data - The file is ==ordered by a unique key==. - Pages: D0 [10,14,19] ; D1 [23,28,35] ; D2 [40,47] . - Index representatives are the ==block minima==: 10, 23, and 40. For a lookup of key 23 : - Which block should be chosen? - What extra rule is needed if the implementation uses a strict predecessor ? [!tip]- Hint - Test equality with a block minimum . - For a strict predecessor, identify what must happen after reading the preceding block. - Consider the first representative as a boundary case. [!success]- Solution Step 1 — Choose the direct candidate Choose D1 through representative 23. Step 2 — Handle a strict predecessor A strict-predecessor rule chooses the preceding representative and must explicitly continue forward and handle the first-key boundary. It cannot simply inspect only the predecessor block and stop. Key idea: The ==equality boundary== and continuation rule determine whether lookup is complete. Exercise A4 — Interpret a diagram During ==compaction==, C moves from offset 1696 to 2496 . - Which pointer remains useful? - What must be changed? [!tip]- Hint - Compare a raw byte offset with a reference through a slot . - Identify which directory value must follow the moved record. [!success]- Solution Step 1 — Maintain indirection (page, slot 2) remains useful if slot 2's directory offset is changed to ==2496==. Step 2 — State the limit A raw pointer to offset 1696 does not follow C. Slot identity is not a guarantee for deleted records or movement between pages. Key idea: Stable slots protect surviving ==within-page references== under the stated model. Exercise A5 — Compare mechanisms [!info] Key Data - The students file is ==ordered by name ==; its logical primary key is studentID . - A separate advising layout groups students with module records. Distinguish primary key , primary index , and multitable clustering using these two cases. [!tip]- Hint - Identify the logical row identifier. - Identify the actual file-ordering attribute. - For advising, ask which related records occupy the same page. [!success]- Solution Step 1 — Identify the logical key studentID is a logical unique identifier in the legacy relation. Step 2 — Identify file order Its primary index follows the actual ordering attribute name . Step 3 — Identify co-location Advising multitable clustering instead co-locates a student's record with five records from another relation. These answer different questions. Key idea: Logical identity, file order, and co-location are ==different properties==. Exercise A6 — Explain a timing model Which HDD terms disappear as ==mechanical mechanisms== on an SSD? Does that leave exactly the old transfer time? [!tip]- Hint - First identify the delays that require moving parts . - Then list the work still needed to deliver the data. [!success]- Solution - ==Arm seek and rotational waiting== disappear. - Electronic access, controller processing, data transfer, and possible reclamation remain; the HDD transfer formula does not specify those costs. Key idea: Removing moving parts does not remove every access cost. Exercise A7 — Reason about SQL and NULL A table has ==250 missing addresses==. Why do address = NULL and address IS NULL produce different counts? [!tip]- Hint - Determine the truth value of equality with NULL. - Recall which truth value WHERE retains. - Compare that with an explicit missing-value test. [!success]- Solution - Equality with NULL is unknown, which WHERE does not retain; IS NULL directly tests missingness. - The counts are ==0 and 250== respectively. - This is not evidence of an index losing the missing-address rows. Key idea: ==Missingness== is not tested by ordinary equality. Exercise A8 — Compare reliability claims Why does ==mirroring== not provide the same protection as restoring an ==older backup== after an accidental deletion? [!tip]- Hint - Follow the same logical deletion on both live copies. - Ask whether either copy still retains the earlier state. [!success]- Solution - A mirror can preserve service after some device failures while also applying the same logical deletion to every current copy. - Recovering a former state requires suitable historical recovery or backup facilities. Key idea: Device redundancy does not by itself preserve an earlier logical state. Exercise A9 — Interpret dense duplicates [!info] Key Data - name has ==5000 distinct values==. - The file contains 30 000 rows . Must every dense index have exactly 30 000 search-value entries? [!tip]- Hint - Count distinct values separately from rows . - Explain how a lookup reaches the second and later matches. [!success]- Solution Step 1 — Count value entries No. A dense-by-value representation can have ==5000 value entries== plus a way to reach all matching records, such as contiguous runs or pointer buckets. Step 2 — Compare the tuple representation One-entry-per-tuple representations have ==30 000 entries==. State the representation and include additional storage before counting physical blocks. Key idea: State the ==duplicate representation== before counting blocks. Exercise A10 — Transfer beyond the model What additional evidence is needed to replace the registry's academic block count with a ==real DBMS file-size estimate==? [!tip]- Hint - Separate record/page format details from additional storage . - Identify what the ideal packing model omits. [!success]- Solution Step 1 — Specify the implementation Confirm the engine/version, page and record formats, headers, alignment, variable representations, compression, indexes and their levels, free-space policy, overflow, metadata, and any other files being counted. Step 2 — Obtain implementation evidence Inspect or measure that implementation; do not label the tutorial's ideal packing as a real footprint. Key idea: An ideal packing count is not an implementation measurement. B. Guided Problems Use the supplied structure; justify the rounding and the timing model. Exercise B1 — Complete the missing steps Difficulty: ★★☆ [!info] Key Data - Records: 12 000 records; ==180 bytes== per record. - Block size: ==4096 bytes==; no extra header . - Organisation: ==ordered by a unique key==; records are unspanned . - Index fields: key 8 bytes ; pointer 8 bytes . Complete the missing steps and justify each rounding decision . [!question] What You Need to Find - Records/block: $f=\lfloor4096/180\rfloor=\square$. - Data blocks: $b=\lceil12\,000/f\rceil=\square$. The last block holds $\square$ records. - A full block leaves $4096-f(180)=\square$ bytes. - Index entry length is $8+8=16$ bytes; capacity is $\square$ entries/block. - ==Sparse== entries = $\square$, hence sparse index blocks = $\square$. - ==Dense== entries = $\square$, hence dense index blocks = $\square$. - Which quantity changes between the indexes, and what property makes the sparse index valid? [!tip]- Hint - Find whole-record capacity with ==floor==, then required blocks with ==ceiling==. - Do not size the index until you know what one entry represents . - For the last data block, subtract the records in all preceding full blocks. [!success]- Solution Step 1 — Pack the data file $f=22$; $b=546$. The first 545 blocks hold $545(22)=11\,990$ records, leaving ==10==. A full block leaves $4096-22(180)=136$ bytes. Step 2 — Size one index block Entries occupy 16 bytes, so $f_I=256$. Step 3 — Count the two alternatives Sparse: 546 entries and $\lceil546/256\rceil=3$ blocks. Dense: 12 000 entries and $\lceil12\,000/256\rceil=47$ blocks. Step 4 — Explain the rounding and coverage The entry count changes, not entry length. Sparse representatives work because the data are ==ordered by the represented unique key==. Floor prevents partial records/entries; ceiling reserves space for remainders. Answer: ==546 data blocks==; 3 sparse or 47 dense index blocks . Key idea: The ==entry count== changes; the ==entry length== does not. Exercise B2 — Transfer the timing model Difficulty: ★★☆ [!info] Key Data - Rotation: ==6000 rpm==. - Track: 200 sectors. - Transfer block: ==five contiguous sectors==. - Maximum seek time: 12 ms . [!question] What You Need to Find - Revolution time and transfer time. - Best, approximate worst, and ==course-average read time==. - Why the average is not half the worst total . [!tip]- Hint - Convert minutes to milliseconds once. - Use the fraction of a revolution occupied by the block. - Apply the course's half-maximum approximation to seek and rotational wait only. [!success]- Solution Step 1 — Separate revolution and transfer Revolution: $60\,000/6000=10$ ms. Transfer: $(5/200)(10)=0.25$ ms. Step 2 — Combine the three costs Best: ==0.25 ms==. Approximate worst: $12+10+0.25=\mathbf{22.25}$ ms. Course average: $12/2+10/2+0.25=\mathbf{11.25}$ ms. Step 3 — Interpret the average Half of the worst total, 11.125 ms, incorrectly halves the transfer. All calculations assume no queue or controller overhead and contiguous sectors without gaps. Answer: best 0.25 ms ; worst 22.25 ms ; course average ==11.25 ms==. Key idea: The average still includes the ==full transfer==. C. Independent Problems Choose the method yourself and state the assumptions that make it valid. Exercise C1 — Calculate a new case Difficulty: ★★☆ [!info] Key Data - Records: 18 000; ==150 bytes== each. - Block size: ==4096 bytes==. - Ordering key: unique; 6 bytes . - Pointer: 10 bytes . [!question] What You Need to Find - Data blocks and ==sparse-index blocks==. - The number of records in the last data block. [!tip]- Hint - Determine the object stored in one data page. - Determine what one sparse entry represents. - Use the last-block remainder as a separate check. [!success]- Solution Step 1 — Pack and check the data file $f=27$, $b=667$; 666 blocks hold 17 982 records, leaving 18. Step 2 — Count the sparse index Index entries are 16 bytes, capacity 256; one entry per data block gives 667 entries and ==3 index blocks==. Answer: ==667 data blocks== and 3 sparse index blocks ; last data block 18 records . Key idea: A ==sparse entry== represents a data block in this model. Exercise C2 — Transfer to a changed workload Difficulty: ★★☆ Compare advising clustering under two workloads: - Why might it help a ==join== but hurt a ==student-only scan==? - What happens if a group grows beyond one page ? [!tip]- Hint - Compare the bytes needed by a grouped lookup with those needed by a student-only scan . - Test whether one whole group still fits in a page. [!success]- Solution Step 1 — Compare the workloads Related records share one page for the group lookup, but a student-only scan reads pages full of module bytes. Step 2 — Check the group-size limit If a group exceeds usable page capacity, the one-page requirement becomes impossible; change the layout or the constraint rather than applying the same floor formula blindly. Key idea: A one-page group is a constraint, not an automatic guarantee. D. Error Diagnosis Identify the first faulty assumption, then repair the reasoning. Exercise D1 — Diagnose a wrong solution Difficulty: ★★☆ The file is ==ordered by surname ==; personID is its primary key . A classmate writes: “The primary key is personID , so a primary index must use personID . Store only the first ID in each block, sort those IDs in the index, and use the greatest stored ID no greater than the query. Every record will then be found.” [!question] What You Need to Find - Identify the first incorrect assumption and the later error. - Give a concrete failure . - Propose a correction that ==preserves the current file order==. [!tip]- Hint - Try surname-ordered pages containing IDs 90, 20 and then 70, 10 . - Identify the sampled IDs. - Ask how the proposed access path would find an omitted ID. [!success]- Solution Step 1 — Find the two assumptions The first error equates the relational primary key with the course's file-order primary index. Here the primary index follows surname . The second error assumes sorting sampled personID values creates ordering in the underlying records. Step 2 — Construct a failure Counterexample: surname-ordered block A contains (Adams,90),(Brown,20) and block B contains (Clark,70),(Davis,10) . Sampling 90 and 70 gives no complete path for ID 20. Sorting the two entries still cannot reveal the omitted identifier's location. Step 3 — Repair the proposal Retain surname order and use a ==dense secondary index== with a reference for every personID . Reordering the entire file by personID could enable a sparse primary alternative, but would change the stated condition. Key idea: Sorting sampled values does not sort the underlying file. Exercise D2 — Debug a free-list update Difficulty: ★☆☆ An insertion overwrites the head slot ==before reading== its next field. What information can be lost? [!tip]- Hint - Locate the free slot's successor pointer . - Identify which write destroys that value. [!success]- Solution - The pointer to the remainder of the free list. - Save that pointer first, update the header, and only then overwrite the slot's bytes, within the assumed single-operation model. Key idea: ==Save the successor== before overwriting the free slot. Exercise D3 — Predict an overflow scan Difficulty: ★☆☆ [!info] Key Data - The ==ordered file== has full pages D0 [10,14,19] and D1 [23,28,35] . - Record 16 is inserted into an ==overflow page== linked between 14 and 19. - The later scan reads only D0 and D1 . What is wrong with the scan's result? [!tip]- Hint - List the physical pages the scan visits. - Compare them with the full live logical sequence. [!success]- Solution - It omits the overflow record 16. - Until reorganisation or another complete access method incorporates it, traversal must follow the structure containing the overflow record. Key idea: A complete scan must include ==overflow==. Exercise D4 — Diagnose an unjustified measurement claim Difficulty: ★★☆ A report says “2273 blocks means 2273 physical reads at 13 ms each.” Give ==at least three missing assumptions==. [!tip]- Hint - Separate file capacity from the pages visited by this query. - Check buffer state , access pattern, and the device model. [!success]- Solution Step 1 — Identify missing access assumptions The query may not scan all blocks; some may be buffered; reads may be sequential or prefetched; index pages may add work; the actual device and transfer block size may differ; contention may matter. Step 2 — Interpret the timing claim The 13 ms figure is an approximate tutorial model, not a measured latency for this file. Key idea: ==Stored blocks== and ==physical reads== are different quantities. Exercise D5 — Debug an index experiment Difficulty: ★★☆ The row sequence changed after CREATE INDEX , but the query had ==no ORDER BY ==. [!question] What You Need to Find - What should you compare? - Which claim remains unsupported? [!tip]- Hint - Separate row membership from requested output order . - Ask what evidence establishes correctness, index use, or speed. [!success]- Solution Step 1 — Make the results comparable Compare the same multiset of rows, or add a deterministic ordering before comparing sequences. Step 2 — State what the evidence proves Equivalent results establish correctness for those tests. Unforced comparisons do not establish that the optimiser used the new index or that execution became faster. The lab’s separately required index probes verify a named access path, not its unforced selection or speed. Key idea: ==Correctness==, index selection, and speed require different evidence. E. Exam-Style Problems Combine calculation, interpretation, and limitations in one defensible answer. Exercise E1 — Choose and justify a file organisation Difficulty: ★★★ [!info] Key Data - Workload: many new registrations; frequent ==unique-identifier lookups==; occasional name-ordered reports. - Records: 18 000 , each 150 bytes ; blocks contain 4096 bytes . - Index fields: identifier 6 bytes ; pointer 10 bytes . - Storage contract: ==unspanned records and entries==; ignore other overhead . - You may choose the file organisation . [!question] What You Need to Find - Propose a layout and access structure; justify them against the workload. - Calculate ==data and index blocks== under your chosen model. - State what evidence could reverse your decision. - Compare a file ordered by the identifier , using one representative per block . [!tip]- Hint - Start with the frequent operations . - Explain how the chosen access structure finds every identifier . - Compare the cost of maintaining order with the saving in index entries; fewer entries alone do not settle the choice. [!success]- Solution Step 1 — Choose a complete access structure A defensible provisional choice is a ==heap with a dense secondary index== on the unique identifier. It avoids maintaining a name-ordered sequential layout for frequent arrivals and gives complete identifier coverage; name reports can sort explicitly. Step 2 — Size the data file With maximal packing, $f=\lfloor4096/150\rfloor=27$, $b=\lceil18\,000/27\rceil=667$. The first 666 blocks hold 17 982 records, leaving 18. Step 3 — Size the dense index Entry length is $6+10=16$ bytes, so 256 entries/block. Dense entries = 18 000, requiring $\lceil18\,000/256\rceil=71$ blocks. This includes no spare capacity or extra index levels. Step 4 — Compare an ordered alternative If identifier order were maintained, a sparse primary index would have 667 entries and need $\lceil667/256\rceil=3$ blocks. Step 5 — Revisit the workload That saving must be weighed against maintaining order and the actual search path. High report/range frequency, expensive sorting, or different insertion patterns could change the decision. Frequencies, memory, actual implementation, and measurements are needed for a performance conclusion; a justified alternative can be correct. Answer under the stated models: 667 data blocks ; ==71 dense index blocks== for the heap choice, or 3 sparse index blocks if identifier order is maintained. Key idea: Choose ==complete coverage== first, then compare space and maintenance costs. Exercise E2 — Track page capacity through two branches Difficulty: ★★★ [!info] Key Data - Page size: ==4096 bytes==. - Overhead: 96-byte header plus three 8-byte slots . - Existing records: 500, 900, and 700 bytes . - Initially, the free region is ==contiguous== and no slot is reusable . [!question] What You Need to Find - Branch A: find the ==largest new record== that fits. - Branch B: restart from the initial state; delete the 900-byte record , compact, retain and reuse its slot , and find the largest replacement. - State the reference guarantee . [!tip]- Hint - Treat the two branches independently . - Branch A needs a new directory slot . - Branch B reuses a retained slot ; deleting payload bytes does not delete the slot entry. [!success]- Solution Step 1 — Account for initial occupancy Initial occupancy is $96+3(8)+500+900+700=2220$ bytes, leaving 1876. Step 2 — Branch A: allocate a new slot A new slot costs 8, so the maximum new record is ==1868 bytes==. Step 3 — Branch B: restart and reuse On the restarted deletion branch, free bytes become $1876+900=2776$. After compaction and slot reuse, a ==2776-byte replacement== fits because no new slot is needed. Step 4 — State the reference guarantee Both branches exactly fill 4096 bytes. Surviving records can retain (page, slot) references if their directory offsets are updated; the deleted record's identity is not preserved, and movement between pages needs additional mechanisms. Key idea: A ==new slot== costs bytes; a ==reused slot== is already counted. Choose Your Next Review If you missed… Revisit in Notes --- --- Capacity or remainders Blocking factor Page growth or surviving references Slotted pages Lookup completeness or key terminology Indexes Timing units or averages Read costs Claims about plans or speed Lab interpretation - [ ] I attempted the questions before opening solutions. - [ ] I corrected the reasoning behind each error. - [ ] I can solve a changed-number version without copying the method.

entries.title: What changes when we add an index?
entries.text: What changes when we add an index? Notes · Exercises Purpose See how an additional index preserves logical query results and remains consistent when records change. The lab connects the unit's index-maintenance ideas to an executable example using ==synthetic student data==. [!info] General database concept Adding a non-unique index changes an access structure. It should preserve the tested answers, including duplicate addresses and NULL values. Updates and deletions must remain visible through that index. [!warning] SQLite-specific behaviour This is a supplementary SQLite experiment. It does not reproduce 350-byte physical records, measure query speed, or identify the course DBMS. Environment used The existing recorded run used SQLite 3.53.1 , through Python's standard-library sqlite3 module, on 20 September 2026 at 12:42:10 UTC . It used one connection and an isolated temporary on-disk database, configured with PRAGMA page_size = 4096 before table creation. No server or additional Python packages are needed. Your Python installation may bundle a different SQLite version. The runner prints its actual version and flags a difference from the recorded environment. The previous observed results are summarised below; this presentation refactor did not rerun the experiment.[^sqlite-release][^sqlite-pragma] Files and how to run All six executable source files are in this unit's Attachments folder, with their original filenames and contents. File What to inspect --- --- schema.sql Table, explicit NOT NULL , primary key, length constraint seed.sql Deterministic generation of 25 000 rows queries.sql Fourteen named queries, including duplicates, NULLs, ranges, and ordered results indexes.sql Non-unique idx_student_address experiment.sql Address update and record deletion run_lab.py Controlled sequence, comparisons, and reversible edge cases Open a terminal in the SOE201 course folder and run: sh python3 "Unit 01 - Physical Storage/Attachments/run_lab.py" The runner creates a temporary database beside the scripts, closes and removes it afterwards, and prints a concise result. It needs no report option for studying. A failed assertion stops the run instead of reporting success. The scripts use their own folder to locate one another, so relocating them together preserves how they work. Follow the experiment Track the baseline, the changed state, and the restored state as separate observations. mermaid flowchart TD A["Create schema and synthetic rows"] -- B["Record baseline answers"] B -- C["Add idx_student_address; compare answers"] C -- D["Savepoint: update ID 1, delete ID 2"] D -- E["Check counts and required-index ID sets"] E -- F["Roll back; baseline returns"] F -- G["Reversible branches: constraints, empty table, BLOB ID"] G -- H["Drop added index; compare again; clean up"] classDef default fill: E6F3F1,stroke: 117D83,color: 172B42,stroke-width:1.5px; Figure 13 — Change one part, compare with a known state Read it: each reversible branch returns to the baseline before continuing. Key takeaway: these comparisons test correctness and index consistency; they do not measure an unforced optimiser plan or latency. 1. Understand the schema. student_ID TEXT NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY supplies explicit uniqueness and non-nullness. name is non-null; address permits NULL. CHECK(length(student_ID) = 10) tests reported length, not a complete ==ten-digit text domain==.[^sqlite-table] 2. Read the seed. WITH RECURSIVE numbers(n) generates 1–25 000; UNION ALL keeps those generated rows. printf('%010d', n) makes padded IDs. n % 100 produces 100 names; multiples of 100 get NULL addresses, while other rows get hall values.[^sqlite-with][^sqlite-functions] 3. Predict the baseline. Multiples of 100 give 250 missing addresses. Hall-01 and Hall-02 each contain 2500 rows. The padded text-ID range 100–110 contains 11 rows because BETWEEN includes both ends.[^sqlite-expr][^sqlite-aggregate] 4. Add the address index. The table already has SQLite's primary-key support. “Before the index” means before the ==additional address index==, not before all indexes. Duplicate addresses remain allowed.[^sqlite-index] 5. Change data under a savepoint. ID 0000000001 moves from Hall-01 to Hall-02 ; ID 0000000002 is then deleted. ROLLBACK TO restores the saved state; RELEASE closes the savepoint. The runner checks complete expected ID sets using separate INDEXED BY diagnostics.[^sqlite-savepoint][^sqlite-indexedby] 6. Inspect edge cases. Duplicate, NULL, and wrong-length IDs are rejected. Separate branches empty the table and probe a ten-byte BLOB ID; each is rolled back. Finally, drop only idx_student_address and compare the original queries again. Observed results summary [!summary] Takeaway These values come from the existing recorded execution , which passed 45 of 45 checks . Adding the address index preserved all 14 tested query results; the update and deletion changed the expected memberships, and rollback restored the ==baseline==. Stage Observed result Interpretation --- --- --- Baseline 25 000 rows; 250 NULL addresses; 100 distinct names Seed matches its construction Duplicate name N001 matches 250 rows A search value need not be unique Address queries Hall-01 2500; Hall-02 2500; Hall-00 2250 The NULL rule removes 250 would-be Hall-00 values NULL comparison IS NULL → 250; = NULL → 0 Equality with NULL is unknown, so WHERE does not retain it Point / range / missing key ID 1 returns its row; range 100–110 returns 11; absent ID returns none Lookup boundaries agree with expectations Add index All 14 query results unchanged The additional index preserves tested answers Update ID 1 Hall-01 2499; Hall-02 2501; total 25 000 Both the record and indexed memberships reflect the change Delete ID 2 Hall-02 2500; total 24 999 Deleted membership disappears Rollback Baseline restored The reversible branch returns to its starting state Invalid values Duplicate / NULL / short IDs, NULL name, and short-ID update rejected Explicit constraints take effect for these cases Empty-table branch Count 0; no point or indexed results Empty-state behaviour is consistent Ten-byte BLOB ID Accepted; reported storage class blob , length 10 The ordinary non-STRICT table does not enforce a text-only ID domain Drop index / integrity Baseline answers unchanged; integrity check ok Removing the added structure preserves tested data General ideas and SQLite-specific details Use the distinction below when transferring the lesson to another database engine. General idea illustrated SQLite detail used here --- --- Indexes must preserve logical answers CREATE INDEX idx_student_address ON student(address) Results need a requested order for sequence comparison ORDER BY student_ID in full-result queries Missing values differ from ordinary values IS NULL versus = NULL Changes must maintain access structures Diagnostic INDEXED BY idx_student_address requires that named index A reversible experiment needs a known earlier state SAVEPOINT , ROLLBACK TO , RELEASE Declared types and constraints need precise interpretation Explicit text-key NOT NULL ; ordinary SQLite affinity can still accept BLOBs Storage configuration belongs to an implementation PRAGMA page_size , sqlite_master , sqlite_source_id() , and integrity checks Explicit ORDER BY defines output order; a changed sequence without it is not by itself an incorrect result.[^sqlite-select] For seeded text without embedded NUL characters, SQLite's length counts Unicode code points; for BLOB values, it counts bytes. Ten ASCII digits happen to be ten UTF-8 bytes, but that does not make the full stored record ten bytes or reproduce the tutorial's fixed-size layout. printf , recursive seed syntax, transaction interfaces, and typing behaviour should not be assumed portable to an unidentified course engine. [!warning] SQLite-specific behaviour — Required-index probes ==Equal results== do not prove that an unforced query used the new index or became faster. The separate INDEXED BY probes require the named index for those probes; they are not an optimiser hint or a benchmark. No full plans, timings, concurrency conflicts, or crash-recovery behaviour were measured. The detailed execution tables, source identity, fingerprints, and earlier review evidence remain in the unchanged _AI Staging archive. They are not required for this study workflow. [^sqlite-release]: External official documentation: [SQLite 3.53.1 release log, release identity and hashes]( consulted 20 September 2026. The installed sqlite_source_id() matches the published identifier; the course engine remains unconfirmed. [^sqlite-pragma]: External official documentation: [SQLite PRAGMA page_size]( consulted 20 September 2026; actual configured value queried and verified in the SQLite 3.53.1 lab. [^sqlite-table]: External official documentation: [SQLite CREATE TABLE, §3.1 typing and §§3.5–3.8 constraints]( consulted 20 September 2026; the relevant behaviour was tested on SQLite 3.53.1. [^sqlite-with]: External official documentation: [SQLite WITH Clause, §3 Recursive Common Table Expressions]( consulted 20 September 2026; deterministic seed executed on SQLite 3.53.1. [^sqlite-functions]: External official documentation: [SQLite Built-In Scalar SQL Functions, length and printf]( consulted 20 September 2026; used by the SQLite 3.53.1 schema and seed. [^sqlite-expr]: External official documentation: [SQLite SQL Language Expressions, §2 operators and §6 BETWEEN]( consulted 20 September 2026; NULL and range cases tested on SQLite 3.53.1. [^sqlite-aggregate]: External official documentation: [SQLite Built-In Aggregate Functions, DISTINCT and count]( consulted 20 September 2026. Supports row counts and distinct-value aggregation in the supplementary SQLite lab. [^sqlite-index]: External official documentation: [SQLite CREATE INDEX, introductory semantics and §1.1]( consulted 20 September 2026; the lab's non-unique index was tested on SQLite 3.53.1. [^sqlite-savepoint]: External official documentation: [SQLite Savepoints, §2]( consulted 20 September 2026; update/deletion rollback tested on SQLite 3.53.1. [^sqlite-indexedby]: External official documentation: [SQLite INDEXED BY, §1]( consulted 20 September 2026. This SQLite-only clause requires the specified index; its diagnostic use here is not a recommendation to tune queries by forcing indexes. entries.title: In 60 Seconds
entries.text: A B+ tree is a balanced ordered index. Internal nodes route by separator ranges; leaves hold the searchable key entries and are linked for range scans. In this course, order $n$ means at most $n$ child pointers in an internal node and therefore at most $n-1$ leaf keys. Lookup follows boundaries to a leaf. Insertion splits overflowing nodes. Deletion repairs underflow using the lecture's merge-first, otherwise redistribute rule. The root has special occupancy rules. After study, you should be able to trace lookup/range access, apply insertion and deletion one state at a time, and validate occupancy, order, routing, leaf links and equal depth.

entries.title: Concept Preview
entries.text: [!note] Separator boundary Plain-language meaning: an internal key divides child ranges; it is not itself proof that a record exists. Why it matters: membership is confirmed only at a leaf. Connects to: lookup and separator maintenance. Source: Lecture2b - B+Tree Indexing (1).pdf , PDF pp. 4–9. [!note] Occupancy Plain-language meaning: non-root nodes have minimum and maximum capacities; the root is allowed to be smaller. Why it matters: overflow triggers splitting and underflow triggers repair. Connects to: insertion, deletion and height. Source: Lecture2b, PDF pp. 4–6, 12–27. [!note] Copy versus promote Plain-language meaning: a leaf split copies a boundary upward while retaining data keys in leaves; an internal split promotes a separator. Why it matters: treating both splits identically loses a searchable leaf key or duplicates routing incorrectly. Connects to: cascading splits. Source: Lecture2b, PDF pp. 12–18. [!note] Merge-first deletion Plain-language meaning: when a node underflows, the supplied algorithm first merges with an eligible sibling if the combined content fits; otherwise it redistributes. Why it matters: it determines the exact intermediate tree expected by the source examples. Connects to: parent deletion and root contraction. Source: Lecture2b, PDF pp. 19–27.

entries.title: Before You Start
entries.text: Recall ordered keys, pointers and the distinction between an index block and a data block. [!question] Prerequisite check If an internal node has separators [10, 20] , how many child ranges does it have? [!success]- Check your answer Three: values below 10, values from 10 to below 20, and values at least 20. Source principle: Lecture2b, PDF pp. 4–9.

entries.title: A motivating question
entries.text: Use the exact order-4 initial tree from Lecture2b, PDF p. 34: text [7 13 19] / \ [4,5] [7,9] [13,17] [19,25,31] Apply insert 33, insert 11, delete 25 in that order. How can the tree remain balanced while only local nodes change? What evidence proves the final tree is valid? Question Knowledge needed --- --- Insert 33 and 11 leaf overflow, split, copied separator, parent capacity Delete 25 underflow test, merge-first repair, parent/root repair Validate sorted leaves, range boundaries, occupancy, equal depth

entries.title: Learn the mechanism
entries.text: Course order and occupancy For order $n$: Node Minimum Maximum --- ---: ---: non-root internal $\lceil n/2\rceil$ child pointers $n$ pointers non-root leaf $\lceil(n-1)/2\rceil$ keys $n-1$ keys internal root 2 child pointers $n$ pointers root that is a leaf 0 keys $n-1$ keys For order 4, non-root leaves hold 2–3 keys and non-root internal nodes have 2–4 children. Count child pointers, not separator labels, when checking an internal node. Lookup is interval routing At separator equality, route right into the range beginning at that boundary. Continue until a leaf, then compare actual leaf keys. An internal separator may remain as a valid boundary after the equal leaf key has been deleted; it need not be duplicated in a leaf under the lecture's retained-boundary examples. mermaid flowchart TD R["root: 13"] -- "x "x ≥ 13" G["right subtree"] G -- C{"leaf contains x?"} C -- yes P["follow record pointer"] C -- no N["not present"] Figure 1 — A separator chooses a range, not membership Read it: equality takes the right branch; only the leaf decides presence. Key takeaway: routing correctness is about ranges, not whether every separator is currently stored as a leaf key. Provenance: teaching construction from Lecture2b, PDF pp. 4–9. Range scans use linked leaves Descend once to the first leaf that can contain the lower bound, then scan right through leaf links until the upper bound is exceeded. The index preserves order; a hash index does not provide this route. Insertion: copy at leaves, promote internally 1. Route to the target leaf. 2. Insert in sorted order if capacity remains. 3. On leaf overflow, split the ordered entries. Keep all data keys in leaves and copy the first key of the new right leaf into the parent. 4. If the parent overflows, split the internal node and promote its middle separator; that separator leaves the split internal children. 5. If the root splits, create a new root. All leaves remain at the same depth. [!warning] Common confusion A leaf split and an internal split are not interchangeable. Leaf entries represent searchable keys, so the boundary is copied. Internal separators route only, so the middle separator is promoted. Deletion: remove, test, repair upward 1. Route to the leaf and remove the key if present. 2. If occupancy remains valid, update a separator only when its routing range requires it. 3. If the node underflows, apply the lecture's rule: merge with an eligible sibling when combined content fits; otherwise redistribute and adjust the parent boundary. 4. A merge deletes one parent child pointer and its separator. This may make the parent underflow, so repair can propagate upward. 5. If the root has one remaining child, replace the root with that child; height decreases by one. Sibling choice is not universally fixed when both sides satisfy the rule. State and use a consistent supported choice rather than claiming the source prescribes one. [!question] Explain it yourself Why can deleting one leaf key cause a root contraction even though most of the tree is unchanged? [!success]- Check your explanation Leaf underflow can cause a merge; deleting the corresponding parent pointer can propagate underflow upward until the root has only one child. Source: Lecture2b, PDF pp. 19–27. Height and access cost If $h$ counts edges from root to leaf, an uncached equality lookup visits $h+1$ index nodes. Fetching the data record can require another data-page read. Cache residency can reduce physical reads, so height is a structural bound under a stated cache model, not a measured latency.

entries.title: Worked example — the opening update sequence
entries.text: Initial leaves: [4,5] , [7,9] , [13,17] , [19,25,31] ; root [7,13,19] . Insert 33 The rightmost leaf becomes [19,25,31,33] and overflows. Split it into [19,25] and [31,33] ; copy boundary 31 upward. The root would have five children, so it also overflows. Promote 19 into a new root, producing two internal children whose leaf ranges remain ordered. Insert 11 Route through the left internal subtree to leaf [7,9] . Insert to obtain [7,9,11] ; this is within leaf capacity, so no split occurs. Delete 25 Route to [19,25] ; deletion leaves [19] , below the minimum of two. Under the lecture's merge-first rule, merge it with eligible sibling [31,33] to form [19,31,33] , then delete the redundant parent pointer/boundary. The right internal node now has only one child, below the minimum of two. Merge it with the left internal sibling: their 3 + 1 children fit order 4. Move the old root separator 19 down between the merged ranges. The old root then has one child, so contract it. The new root is [7,13,19] with four leaf children. The final leaves are [4,5] → [7,9,11] → [13,17] → [19,31,33] . Validation: every surviving key appears once; leaf order and links are correct; all leaves share a depth; each non-root leaf has 2–3 keys; internal ranges contain their leaf keys; the final root has four children, every leaf is one edge below it, and the temporary extra level has disappeared. Source: Lecture2b, PDF pp. 34–37; full illustrated sequence in reference notes.

entries.title: Return to the motivating question
entries.text: The tree stays balanced because each overflow or underflow is repaired locally and the repair propagates only when its parent violates capacity. The proof is invariant-based: sorted keys, correct ranges, valid occupancy, linked leaves and equal depth—not resemblance to one drawing.

entries.title: Definitions and distinctions
entries.text: Term A Term B Decisive distinction Source --- --- --- --- separator leaf key routing boundary versus searchable key entry Lecture2b, pp. 4–9 leaf split internal split copy right-leaf minimum versus promote middle separator Lecture2b, pp. 12–18 merge redistribution combine nodes and remove a parent pointer versus move entries while keeping both nodes Lecture2b, pp. 19–27 height edge count node visits a path of $h$ edges visits $h+1$ index nodes Lecture2b, pp. 10–11
