entries.title: 5-Minute Review
entries.text: - route by ranges and confirm at a leaf; - leaves are ordered and linked; - order controls maximum pointers/keys; - leaf split copies; internal split promotes; - deletion uses merge-first, otherwise redistribute; - repair may propagate and contract the root; - validate invariants after every operation.

entries.text: - order = max internal pointers - leaf max = order − 1 - root exception - equality routes right - membership at leaf - copy vs promote - merge vs redistribute - root contraction - linked-leaf range scan

entries.title: B+ tree indexing
entries.text: Course home · Notes · Exercises · Course Lab 02 — JDBC and Index B+ tree indexing Opening case — keep a changing registry searchable Synthetic teaching case using the exact tree and update sequence of Lecture 2b, PDF p. 34. A registry stores unique numerical search keys. Its index has ==order 4==: at most four child pointers in an internal node and three key entries in a leaf. Each index node occupies one block; data records are stored separately. The initial tree appears below. Treat this as a logical block model, with no DBMS selected. case-initial.svg Figure 1 — The opening registry index Read it: Start at the root; each downward arrow selects an interval. Horizontal arrows link leaves. Key takeaway: The root has four children; each leaf holds actual search keys. Given: the four leaves are [4,5] , [7,9] , [13,17] , [19,25,31] . Internal separators are 7,13,19 . All leaves have the same depth and are linked in that order. Questions 1. How do equality lookup for 17 and the inclusive range 9–25 reach their records? 2. What happens after inserting 33, then 11, then deleting 25, in that exact order? 3. What invariants prove the final tree is valid? How many index blocks does one uncached equality lookup read before and after the complete sequence? Constraints and success criteria: retain all undeleted keys exactly once in leaves; use the lecturer's leaf and internal split rules; ==merge before redistribution== when an eligible sibling pair fits; keep all leaves at one depth. Explain every separator change and distinguish index reads from data-record reads. Question Concepts needed --- --- Find 17 and 9–25 Separators, equality routing, leaf links Apply the update sequence Occupancy, split propagation, merge and root contraction Defend the result Invariants, height and block-I/O model Prerequisite: Unit 1's records, blocks, pointers, sparse and dense indexes. This chapter covers Lecture 2b, PDF pp. 2–37. All page locators below are PDF pages , which also match the displayed slide numbers in this lecture. Why an index must reorganise locally A static multilevel index can locate a block quickly, but growth can accumulate overflow blocks and require expensive reorganisation. A B+ tree changes a small number of nodes around the affected search path. Its extra space and update work buy bounded depth and continued ordered access.[^motivation] Intuitively, an internal node is a directory of key intervals; a leaf is the searchable catalogue entry. A large block can hold many directory pointers, so each step narrows the search by a large factor. This is why the tree is “short and fat”. Logical neighbours need not occupy physically adjacent disk blocks: pointers encode the relationships.[^structure] [!note] Definition and order convention A ==B+ tree== is an ordered, height-balanced index: every path from the root to a leaf has the same length. In this course, order $n$ is the maximum number of child pointers per internal node , so an internal node has at most $n-1$ separator keys. Leaf entries contain a search-key value and a record pointer or pointer to a duplicate-record bucket; a leaf also has a next-leaf pointer.[^structure] Occupancy and the root exception Node Minimum Maximum --- ---: ---: Non-root internal node $\lceil n/2\rceil$ child pointers $n$ child pointers Non-root leaf $\lceil(n-1)/2\rceil$ key entries $n-1$ key entries Root with internal children or leaf children 2 child pointers $n$ child pointers Root that is itself a leaf 0 key entries $n-1$ key entries Ceilings mean rounding upward to the next integer. For $n=4$, internal nodes need at least two children; non-root leaves need at least two keys. For $n=3$, the respective minima are two children and one key. For $n=6$, they are three children and three keys; leaves hold at most five keys, as in the source's name index on p. 6. Source wording clarification: p. 4 calls the contents of a leaf-root “children”; a leaf has no child subtrees. Here the 0 to $n-1$ bound is stated correctly in key entries . The root exception also takes precedence over the slide's blanket minimum for non-leaf nodes. These are terminology clarifications, not a change to the supplied exercises. A separator is a routing boundary For ordered separators $K_1 [!question] Check your understanding In an order-4 non-root internal node, do two separator keys mean the node is underfull? Explain using three child pointers . Lookup and ordered range access Equality lookup 1. Start at the root. At each internal node, choose the interval containing the target $V$; ==equality goes right== of the matching separator. 2. Follow that child pointer. Repeat until reaching a leaf. 3. Search the leaf for $V$. If present, follow its record or bucket pointer. Otherwise report absence. 4. If multiple records share $V$, retrieve every record referenced by its bucket. Search keys remain distinct in the course node model; duplicate records do not require repeated separator values.[^lookup][^insert] For the source tree in Figure 2, search 29 visits root [33] , internal [11,22] , then leaf [29] . It takes three index-node reads with an empty cache. Retrieving the actual record is additional work, not a fourth tree level. Range lookup Pedagogical extension of the ordered leaves shown in the source: descend once to the first leaf that can contain the lower bound, scan entries from that bound, then follow next-leaf pointers until exceeding the upper bound. A leaf skipped by equality routing may still be needed for the next range value. The linked leaves avoid restarting at the root for each result. For the opening tree and range $9\le V\le25$, read root [7,13,19] , reach leaf [7,9] , emit 9, follow to [13,17] , emit both, and follow to [19,25,31] , emit 19 and 25, then stop before 31. There are four index-node reads in this example: one root and three leaves. Five qualifying records do not imply five data-block reads; their physical placement is unspecified. Limitation: an unclustered index may point to scattered data pages. Fast index traversal does not guarantee cheap retrieval of a large fraction of a table. Why height controls search cost Let $h$ count edges from root to leaf, $K$ count distinct leaf search keys, $m=\lceil n/2\rceil$ be minimum internal fan-out, and $\ell=\lceil(n-1)/2\rceil$ be minimum keys per non-root leaf. These counts are dimensionless. For $h\ge1$: $$K\ge 2m^{h-1}\ell.$$ Derivation: the root has at least two children. Each of the next $h-1$ internal branching stages multiplies the minimum leaf count by $m$. Each resulting leaf has at least $\ell$ keys. A proposed height is impossible if the available $K$ cannot fill those leaves. The root-as-leaf case $h=0$ is handled separately. For one million distinct keys and $n=100$, $m=50$ and $\ell=50$: Proposed edge height Minimum keys --- ---: $h=3$ $2\times50^2\times50=250,000$ $h=4$ $2\times50^3\times50=12,500,000$ One million is too small for height 4. Therefore at most three edges and four index nodes are visited. This derives the slide's four-node result while stating root and leaf occupancy explicitly.[^height] [!warning] Logarithms, rounding, and measurements PDF p. 11 writes $\log_{50}(1{,}000{,}000)=4$. The logarithm is approximately 3.532 , whose ceiling is 4. Page 10's compact logarithmic bound leaves the height convention implicit; use the occupancy argument above when precision matters. A four-node bound is not a measured latency and excludes data pages. Cached nodes reduce physical reads, not logical tree depth. The source's approximately 100 pointers per 4 KB node is an illustrative scale, not a universal node format. For a synthetic internal layout with a 4096-byte block, a 16-byte header, 8-byte pointers, and 32-byte separator keys, capacity obeys $$16+8n+32(n-1)\le4096.$$ Combine terms: $40n-16\le4096$, so $n\le102.8$. Since pointers come in whole units, choose $n=102$. Check: 4064 bytes fit; $n=103$ would need 4104 bytes. Actual DBMS overhead and leaf layouts can differ. Insertion — copy at a leaf, promote internally Why split? An overflowing node cannot remain inside the block capacity, while relocating the whole tree would defeat local maintenance. Splitting creates two valid nodes and one new routing boundary.[^insert] 1. Descend to the target leaf. If the key exists, add the new record pointer to its bucket where appropriate. 2. Otherwise insert the key-pointer entry in order. If the leaf still has at most $n-1$ entries, stop. 3. On leaf overflow there are $n$ entries in a temporary memory area. Keep the first $\lceil n/2\rceil$ entries in the original leaf and put the remainder in a new right leaf. 4. Repair the leaf chain: old leaf → new leaf → old successor. Copy the new right leaf's minimum key into the parent together with the new pointer. The key remains in the leaf. 5. If the parent overflows, it contains $n$ separators and $n+1$ children. Set $c=\lceil(n+1)/2\rceil$. Keep pointers $P_1\ldots P_c$ and keys $K_1\ldots K_{c-1}$ on the left; move $K_c$ to the parent; put pointers $P_{c+1}\ldots P_{n+1}$ and keys $K_{c+1}\ldots K_n$ on the right. 6. Continue upward. Splitting a root creates a new root with two children and increases every root-to-leaf path by one edge. split-rules.svg Figure 3 — Two different split rules Read it: Read each column downward; compare where the promoted or copied key remains. Key takeaway: Leaf entries survive in leaves; an internal promoted separator leaves both children. Synthetic leaf example, source internal mechanism pp. 13–16. Worked internal split: with $n=4$, an overflowing internal node has separators [7,13,19,31] and five children. $c=\lceil5/2\rceil=3$. Promote the third separator, 19. The left node has [7,13] and three children; the right has [31] and two children. Neither internal child retains 19. Limitation: a leaf split need not increase height. It does so only if propagation reaches an overflowing root. Different valid splitting policies exist; source exercises use the precise distribution above. Deletion — repair occupancy without losing ranges Deleting one record is different from deleting an entire search-key entry. If a duplicate bucket still contains records, keep its leaf entry. Remove the key entry only when its bucket is empty, or when the indexed key itself is to be deleted.[^delete] For an underfull node, consider an adjacent sibling with the same parent . The course checks merging first: merge if the pair fits in one node; otherwise redistribute. It does not prescribe a universal left-versus-right preference when both choices are valid. State the sibling chosen. Repair What moves Parent action --- --- --- Merge leaves Combine leaf entries; reconnect leaf chain Remove separating key and redundant child pointer Redistribute leaves Move enough boundary entries to satisfy both minima Replace separator by the new right-leaf lower boundary Merge internal nodes Combine children and pull down the parent separator Remove that separator and redundant pointer Redistribute internal nodes Move boundary child pointer; rotate keys through parent Old parent separator moves down; donor boundary key moves up Leaf worked example, order 4: after a deletion, [10,20,30] and [40] contain four keys together. Maximum leaf capacity is three, so merging is impossible. Move 30 from the left leaf to the right: [10,20] , [30,40] ; replace parent separator 40 by 30. Both leaves now contain the required two keys. internal-redistribute.svg Figure 4 — Internal redistribution Read it: A–D denote ordered child subtrees. Follow C from left to right and the boundary keys through the parent. Key takeaway: Pointers and routing boundaries move together. Synthetic example of PDF p. 24. Internal worked example, order 3: the left internal node in Figure 4 has three children; the underfull right node has one. Four children exceed the three-child capacity of a merged internal node. Move left's last child C to the right. Separator 50 descends to separate C from D, while 35 rises to separate the two internal nodes. Both finish with two children. Moving only a key without its child pointer would disconnect an entire subtree. After a merge, the parent can itself become underfull; repeat at that level. If the root is left with a single child, make that child the new root and decrease the height by one. A final empty leaf-root is valid. This is local reorganisation along a search path, not a full rebuild.[^delete] Solve the opening case 1 — Lookup and range For 17, choose the root interval $13\le17 [!summary] A defensible short answer Order 4 permits at most three leaf entries. Inserting 33 splits the rightmost leaf and then the full root; promote 19. Inserting 11 fits its leaf. Deleting 25 causes a leaf merge, an internal merge, and root contraction. The final root is [7,13,19] with leaves [4,5] , [7,9,11] , [13,17] , [19,31,33] . Occupancy, routing, key preservation, and equal leaf depth all hold. For an unfamiliar problem: write the order and minima first; preserve the supplied starting tree; trace the target; make the local change; test overflow/underflow; propagate only when necessary; finally check all leaves and every child range. Count child pointers for internal occupancy and keys for leaf occupancy. This method assumes the course model and its merge-first policy, not a confirmed commercial implementation. Misconceptions and quick review Tempting claim Correct reasoning --- --- A separator proves a record exists Only a matching leaf entry establishes membership Order 4 means four keys per leaf It means up to four internal child pointers; three leaf keys A leaf merge pulls down the parent key Only an internal merge needs that separator as an internal boundary Any two neighbouring leaves are eligible siblings Local repair uses siblings with the same parent Every insert changes the root Most fit locally; only root overflow increases height One matching key means one record A duplicate bucket can reference multiple records Before looking at a solution, be able to draw a leaf split, rotate an internal child through its parent, explain an absent separator, and derive the four-node million-key example. Then attempt the original lecture tasks in Exercises. Study status remains untested. entries.title: B+ tree exercises
entries.text: Course home · Notes · Exercises B+ tree exercises Attempt each task before opening its hint. Every original lecture task and worked update appears below; A–E headings indicate retrieval, guided, independent, diagnosis, and exam practice. Original tasks retain their data. Brackets denote keys within one node, never an unordered bag of whole-tree keys. All original page references are to Lecture2b - B+Tree Indexing (1).pdf . A1 — Read the order correctly Supplementary practice · Difficulty: ★☆☆ For orders 3, 4, and 6, give minimum and maximum non-root internal child counts and leaf key counts. Explain the root exception. [!tip]- Hint Keep pointers and keys separate. [!success]- Solution Internal child ranges are 2–3 , 2–4 , and 3–6 . Leaf key ranges are 1–2 , 2–3 , and 3–5 . These follow from ceilings of $n/2$ and $(n-1)/2$, respectively. An internal root requires only two children; a leaf-root may contain zero through $n-1$ keys. Two children imply one separator, not two. B1 — Find 29, 31, and 33 Original course worked lookup and questions · PDF pp. 8–9 · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Using the source tree below, trace lookup for 29 , 31 , and 33 . State whether each exists and where the decision is made. lookup.svg Figure E1 — Original lookup starting tree Read it: Use the key intervals at each internal node. Key takeaway: An internal match is a routing instruction, not a final answer. [!tip]- Hint At separator equality choose the right child. Always finish in a leaf. [!success]- Solution Step 1 — Route 29. At 33 go left, then at [11,22] take the rightmost pointer. Leaf [29] contains 29. Follow its record pointer. Step 2 — Route 31. Take the same path as 29. Leaf [29] contains no 31, so the search is unsuccessful. Step 3 — Route 33. Equality at root 33 selects the right child. In [44] , 33 is smaller than 44, so visit [37,41] . No 33 exists there. Each search examines three index nodes in the empty-cache model. ==33 is absent== despite appearing as an internal separator. These paths match the algorithm on PDF p. 7. B2 — Insert Adams, then follow the name deletions Original course worked updates · PDF pp. 17–18 and 25–27 · Difficulty: ★★★ The source tree has ==order 4==, visible from its node capacities. Use the tree below; names are search keys ordered lexicographically. Apply these operations sequentially , drawing each state: 1. Insert Adams . 2. Delete Srinivasan . 3. Delete Singh , then Wu , showing both intermediate results. 4. Delete Gold . names-0.svg Figure E2 — Initial name index Read it: The root separates names at Mozart; each lower internal node points to its own leaves. Key takeaway: Only same-parent adjacent nodes are eligible for the immediate local repair. [!tip]- Hint Leaves hold 2–3 keys; non-root internal nodes need 2–4 children. Try merging first. Internal merging must count child pointers. [!success]- Solution Step 1 — Insert Adams. [Brandt,Califieri,Crick] overflows into [Adams,Brandt,Califieri,Crick] . Split 2+2 and copy Califieri into the left internal parent. That parent now has four children and fits. names-1.svg Figure E3 — After Adams Read it: The new boundary is Califieri. Key takeaway: The root remains Mozart. Step 2 — Delete Srinivasan. The rightmost leaf becomes [Wu] , under the two-key minimum. Merge it with [Mozart,Singh] into [Mozart,Singh,Wu] . The right internal node is left with one child. Merging the internal siblings would require $4+1=5$ child pointers, exceeding order 4, so redistribute instead: move leaf [Gold,Katz,Kim] from the left internal node to the right. The root separator changes from Mozart to Gold ; old root boundary Mozart moves down into the right internal node. names-2.svg Figure E4 — After Srinivasan Read it: Gold rises; Mozart moves down. Key takeaway: A leaf merge can trigger internal redistribution. Step 3a — Delete Singh. [Mozart,Singh,Wu] becomes [Mozart,Wu] ; two entries remain, so stop. names-3.svg Figure E5 — After Singh Read it: Only one leaf changes. Key takeaway: Minimum occupancy is still satisfied. Step 3b — Delete Wu. The leaf becomes [Mozart] . With sibling [Gold,Katz,Kim] , the total is four keys, so a three-key leaf merge cannot fit. Move Kim right and update their parent boundary from Mozart to Kim . The leaves become [Gold,Katz] and [Kim,Mozart] . names-4.svg Figure E6 — After Wu Read it: Kim becomes the new right-leaf minimum. Key takeaway: Redistribution preserves two leaves. Step 4 — Delete Gold. [Gold,Katz] becomes [Katz] ; merge with [Kim,Mozart] into [Katz,Kim,Mozart] . The right internal node has one child. Its sibling has three children, so an internal merge fits four pointers. Pull down the root separator Gold , then remove the redundant root level. names-5.svg Figure E7 — After Gold Read it: The new root is Califieri, Einstein, Gold. Key takeaway: Gold remains a valid boundary even though its data entry was deleted. Interpretation: the final leaves contain exactly the original names plus Adams, minus Srinivasan, Singh, Wu, and Gold. Gold in the root separates El Said on the left from Katz on the right; it need not be a current leaf key. This matches the source's retained-boundary convention. C1 — Construct the order-3 tree Original course exercise · PDF p. 28; source stages pp. 29–30 · Difficulty: ★★☆ Start with an empty B+ tree of ==order 3==. Insert (2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17) in that exact order . Draw the tree after each insertion. [!tip]- Hint A leaf copies its new right minimum upward; an internal split removes the promoted key from its children. [!success]- Solution Leaves hold at most two keys. On overflow, keep $\lceil3/2\rceil=2$ keys in the left leaf and put one in the right. An overflowing internal node has three separators and four children; promote separator $\lceil(3+1)/2\rceil=2$. Step 1. Insert 2 into the leaf-root. construct-1.svg Figure E8 — Construction stage 1 Read it: Read the tree from root to leaves. Key takeaway: The leaf sequence preserves all keys inserted so far. Step 2. Insert 3 into the same leaf; it now reaches capacity. construct-2.svg Figure E9 — Construction stage 2 Read it: Read the tree from root to leaves. Key takeaway: The leaf sequence preserves all keys inserted so far. Step 3. Insert 5: split [2,3,5] into [2,3] and [5]; copy 5 to a new root. construct-3.svg Figure E10 — Construction stage 3 Read it: Read the tree from root to leaves. Key takeaway: The leaf sequence preserves all keys inserted so far. Step 4. Insert 7: the right leaf becomes [5,7]. construct-4.svg Figure E11 — Construction stage 4 Read it: Read the tree from root to leaves. Key takeaway: The leaf sequence preserves all keys inserted so far. Step 5. Insert 11: split [5,7,11] into [5,7] and [11]; root becomes [5,11]. construct-5.svg Figure E12 — Construction stage 5 Read it: Read the tree from root to leaves. Key takeaway: The leaf sequence preserves all keys inserted so far. Step 6. Insert 13: the final leaf becomes [11,13]. construct-6.svg Figure E13 — Construction stage 6 Read it: Read the tree from root to leaves. Key takeaway: The leaf sequence preserves all keys inserted so far. Step 7. Insert 17: split the final leaf into [11,13] and [17]. The root temporarily has [5,11,17] and four children; promote 11 to a new root, leaving internal children [5] and [17]. construct-7.svg Figure E14 — Construction stage 7 Read it: Read the tree from root to leaves. Key takeaway: The leaf sequence preserves all keys inserted so far. The final tree has two edges to every leaf; each internal non-root node has two pointers, and every non-root leaf contains one or two keys. Sorting the input first is unnecessary here because it is already sorted, but changing the stipulated insertion order in another problem can change the shape. C2 — Two deletion paths from the same initial tree Original course exercise · PDF p. 31, parts (1)–(2); solutions pp. 32–33 · Difficulty: ★★★ Use the ==order-3== tree below. It is not the final tree of C1. 1. Delete 5, then delete 11. Draw both states. 2. Restart from the original tree below and delete 11 only. Draw the result. delete-initial.svg Figure E15 — Original deletion starting tree Read it: The left internal node has three children; the right has two. Key takeaway: The reset in part 2 is essential. [!tip]- Hint For part 1, state which sibling you choose for the empty [5] leaf. After any leaf merge, inspect the parent child count. [!success]- Solution Part 1, delete 5. Its leaf becomes empty. Choose the left sibling [2,3] ; combining two keys fits the maximum of two. Remove the old separator 5 and redundant pointer. The left internal node becomes [7] with two children. Choosing the right sibling is also a permitted source alternative, but this solution follows the displayed result on p. 32. delete5.svg Figure E16 — After deleting 5 Read it: Left internal separator is 7. Key takeaway: No height change is needed yet. Part 1, then delete 11. Its leaf becomes empty. Merge with [13,17] . The right internal node is left with one child. Merge it with the left internal sibling, which has two children: $2+1=3$ fits order 3. Bring down root separator 11 and contract the old root. The new root is [7,11] , with leaves [2,3] , [7] , [13,17] . delete5-11.svg Figure E17 — Then delete 11 Read it: The tree is one level shorter. Key takeaway: Separator 11 still partitions 7 from 13 correctly. Part 2, restart and delete 11. The same leaf merge leaves the right internal node with one child. This time its left internal sibling still has three children. $3+1=4$ exceeds order 3, so merge-first now fails at the internal level. Redistribute the rightmost left child [7] to the right internal node. Root separator 11 moves down; left boundary 7 moves up. Final root [7] ; left internal [5] over [2,3] , [5] ; right internal [11] over [7] , [13,17] . delete11.svg Figure E18 — Restart, then delete 11 only Read it: Compare the still-present leaf [5] with part 1. Key takeaway: Different prior operations change which repair fits. Both final trees satisfy the capacity and routing invariants. The source notes that leaf redistribution can also solve the original deletion, but requests merging first (p. 33); that is the policy used here. D1 — Diagnose three incorrect explanations Supplementary practice · Difficulty: ★★☆ A student says: (a) “The root contains 33, so record 33 exists”; (b) “An internal merge joins the two key lists but ignores the parent separator”; (c) “Deleting one record always removes its search key.” Correct each claim with a counterexample. [!tip]- Hint Use B1, the internal merge rule, and a bucket containing two record pointers. [!success]- Solution (a) B1 reaches leaf [37,41] and proves 33 absent; the root value is only a boundary. (b) If the left subtree covers values below 11 and the right begins above it, pulling 11 down preserves the boundary between their child-pointer groups; omitting it leaves one fewer separator than required for the combined children. (c) A leaf entry Physics → [r1,r2] remains after deleting r1 because r2 is still indexed. Remove the entry only after its bucket becomes empty. E1 — The sequential order-4 update exercise Original course exercise · PDF p. 34, operations (1)–(3); answers pp. 35–37 · Difficulty: ★★★ Draw the trees after (1) insert 33, (2) insert 11, (3) delete 25 . Each operation uses the preceding result. The source starting tree is reproduced here so that you can attempt this without returning to Notes. case-initial.svg Figure E19 — Original order-4 starting tree Read it: Use all four leaves and the supplied separators. Key takeaway: Do not rebuild a different valid tree from the same data. [!tip]- Hint For insertion 33, test both the leaf and the root. After deletion 25, count the parent pointers again. [!success]- Solution 1 — Insert 33. The rightmost leaf overflows to [19,25,31,33] ; split 2+2, copy 31 upward. The root overflows to [7,13,19,31] with five children. Promote 19, leaving internal [7,13] and [31] . case-insert33.svg Figure E20 — After operation 1 Read it: All leaves move one level farther from the new root. Key takeaway: A split cascade reaches the root. 2 — Insert 11. Descend left of 19, then between 7 and 13. Leaf [7,9] becomes [7,9,11] , which fits. case-insert11.svg Figure E21 — After operation 2 Read it: Only the second leaf changes. Key takeaway: No split is needed. 3 — Delete 25. Leaf [19,25] becomes [19] ; merge with [31,33] to get [19,31,33] . Remove parent separator 31. Its parent now has one child, so merge with the three-child left sibling, bringing separator 19 down. Contract the root. Final root [7,13,19] over [4,5] , [7,9,11] , [13,17] , [19,31,33] . case-delete25.svg Figure E22 — After operation 3 Read it: The final root again points directly to leaves. Key takeaway: Every non-root leaf has two or three entries, and all survivors appear once. E2 — Capacity and a search bound Supplementary transfer problem · Difficulty: ★★☆ An internal-node block has 4096 bytes, a 16-byte header, 8-byte child pointers, and 32-byte separator keys. Find its maximum order. Separately, for order 100 and one million distinct leaf keys, prove a bound on uncached index-node reads. Do not assume that the computed byte-layout order and the stipulated order 100 are identical. [!tip]- Hint With n pointers there are n−1 keys. For height, count minimum leaves and keys at a proposed depth. [!success]- Solution Step 1 — Capacity. $16+8n+32(n-1)\le4096$ gives $40n\le4112$ and $n\le102.8$. Floor to ==102 pointers==. At 102, bytes used are $16+816+3232=4064$; 103 would use 4104 and fail. Step 2 — Order-100 occupancy. Minimum internal fan-out and leaf occupancy are both 50. A tree with four root-to-leaf edges would require at least $2\times50^3\times50=12,500,000$ keys. One million cannot fill it; at most three edges and ==four index-node reads== are possible. Data-record retrieval and caching are separate. The argument is about an academic structural model, not measured performance.

entries.title: In 60 Seconds
entries.text: Hashing computes a bucket address from a search key. A collision means several keys share a bucket, so lookup still compares actual keys. Static hashing keeps a fixed main address set and uses overflow chains when buckets fill. Extendable hashing adds a directory: global depth says how many high-order hash bits the directory reads; each bucket's local depth says how many bits distinguish that bucket. A full bucket may split with or without directory doubling. Some collisions cannot be separated by more bits, so overflow can still be necessary. You should be able to trace fixed-width hashes, split/alias states, deletion/coalescing and workload choice without assuming hash order or constant worst-case lookup.

entries.title: Concept Preview
entries.text: [!note] Collision Plain-language meaning: different search keys can map to the same bucket address. Why it matters: the hash gives a candidate bucket, not guaranteed equality. Connects to: overflow chains and failed lookup. Source: Lecture3a - Hash Indexing.pdf , PDF pp. 2–12. [!note] Global depth Plain-language meaning: the number of high-order hash bits currently used by the directory. Why it matters: the directory has $2^i$ pointer entries. Connects to: directory doubling. Source: Lecture3a, PDF pp. 13–18. [!note] Local depth Plain-language meaning: the number of prefix bits that uniquely identify one physical bucket. Why it matters: it determines alias count and whether a split needs directory growth. Connects to: $2^{i-i_j}$ shared directory pointers. Source: Lecture3a, PDF pp. 13–21. [!note] Full-hash collision Plain-language meaning: keys share every available hash bit, so another split cannot separate them. Why it matters: overflow is then necessary under the supplied model. Connects to: the Taiyuan rollback case. Source: Lecture3a, PDF pp. 32–40.

entries.title: Before You Start
entries.text: You need modulo arithmetic, fixed-width binary and the distinction between a directory pointer and a physical bucket. [!question] Prerequisite check Write $1$ as a three-bit value. [!success]- Check your answer 001 . Leading zeros determine high-order prefix routing. Source principle: Lecture3a, PDF pp. 13–18.

entries.title: A motivating question
entries.text: Use the source's numeric state on Lecture3a, PDF p. 23. Bucket capacity is three; $h(x)=x\bmod8$ is written in exactly three bits. Global depth is 1. One bucket holds [9] ; the other holds [4,5,7] . Insert 13, then explain: 1. why the directory must double; 2. which old entries move after splitting; 3. why a later insertion may still require overflow even after several splits.

entries.title: Learn the mechanism
entries.text: Static hashing With a fixed set of $B$ buckets, a function such as $h(v)=(av+b)\bmod B$ chooses a main bucket. If it is full, add an overflow page. Lookup reads the main bucket and follows its chain until finding the key or exhausting candidates. mermaid flowchart LR K["search key"] -- H["hash function"] H -- B["main bucket"] B -- "full/collision" O1["overflow page"] O1 -- O2["next overflow page"] Figure 1 — Static hash lookup follows one address and its chain Read it: the hash selects the chain; actual key comparisons decide the result. Key takeaway: growth concentrated at one address lengthens that chain even when other buckets are empty. Provenance: teaching construction from Lecture3a, PDF pp. 7–12. Static hashing is simple, but fixed capacity creates a trade-off: too few buckets create overflow; too many waste space. If all keys collide, worst-case lookup grows with the chain. Hashing gives no sorted next-key route for range queries. Extendable hashing: directory versus buckets Let $i$ be global depth and $i_j$ a bucket's local depth. Quantity Meaning --- --- $2^i$ directory pointer entries $i_j\le i$ bits distinguishing bucket $j$ $2^{i-i_j}$ directory aliases pointing to bucket $j$ Physical buckets are at most $2^i$; equality is possible. The strict inequality printed on lecture p. 13 excludes the valid case where every directory entry reaches a distinct bucket, so Tutor Mode records the corrected bound and preserves the source discrepancy. Insertion decision 1. Compute the fixed-width hash. 2. Read the first $i$ high-order bits and follow that directory entry. 3. Insert if the bucket has room. 4. If full and $i_j [!warning] Common confusion Doubling the directory does not duplicate data buckets. It duplicates pointers first; only the overflowing bucket is split. Deletion and coalescing Remove the key from its bucket/overflow chain. Two buddy buckets can coalesce only when they share the same local depth, differ in the relevant last prefix bit, and their combined entries fit one bucket. The survivor's local depth decreases. If no bucket now needs the current global depth, the directory can contract. Hash versus ordered index Workload Hash index B+ tree --- --- --- exact equality direct candidate bucket, collision check root-to-leaf route ordered range no adjacent-key path linked leaves support scan skew/collisions chains or repeated splits depends on balanced occupancy growth overflow or directory/bucket changes splits/merges along a path This is a mechanism comparison, not a universal benchmark. [!question] Explain it yourself At global depth 3, why can a local-depth-1 bucket have four directory aliases? [!success]- Check your explanation One prefix bit is fixed and two directory bits remain free, giving $2^{3-1}=4$ combinations. Source: Lecture3a, PDF pp. 13–18.

entries.title: Worked example — insert 13
entries.text: $h(13)=13\bmod8=5=101_2$. At global depth 1, prefix 1 routes to full bucket [4,5,7] . Its local depth equals global depth, so double the directory from 2 to 4 pointers and increase global depth to 2. Split by the first two bits: - 4 hashes to 100 , prefix 10 ; - 5 hashes to 101 , prefix 10 ; - 7 hashes to 111 , prefix 11 ; - 13 hashes to 101 , prefix 10 . The resulting buckets are 10 → [4,5,13] and 11 → [7] , each with local depth 2. The old [9] bucket has hash 001 and local depth 1, so both directory entries 00 and 01 still alias it. Source: Lecture3a, PDF pp. 23–28.

entries.title: Return to the motivating question
entries.text: The directory doubled because the overflowing bucket already used all directory bits. Only that bucket split; the [9] bucket remained shared. Redistribution used fixed-width high-order prefixes. More splitting cannot solve keys that share every available hash bit, so the supplied algorithm eventually rolls back the failed split and uses overflow.

entries.title: Definitions and distinctions
entries.text: Term A Term B Decisive distinction Source --- --- --- --- hash address search key candidate location versus actual value compared in the bucket Lecture3a, pp. 2–12 directory entry physical bucket pointer slot versus storage container Lecture3a, pp. 13–18 global depth local depth bits read by directory versus bits distinguishing one bucket Lecture3a, pp. 13–21 directory doubling bucket split duplicate pointer table versus redistribute one bucket Lecture3a, pp. 19–31 collision duplicate key same address versus same search-key value Lecture3a, pp. 2–12

entries.title: Review
entries.text: Full Understanding Return to Learn the mechanism and Worked example — insert 13.

entries.title: 5-Minute Review
entries.text: - hash to a candidate bucket, then compare keys; - static hashing uses fixed main buckets and overflow; - directory size is $2^i$; - bucket aliases are $2^{i-i_j}$; - keep leading zeros and read high-order bits from the left; - split without doubling when $i_j<i$; - double then split when $i_j=i$ and bits remain; - coalesce only valid buddies that fit; - range workloads favour ordered indexes.

entries.title: 60-Second Recall
entries.text: - collision ≠ equality - main bucket + overflow - fixed-width hash - high-order prefix - global depth - local depth - alias formula - double versus split - buddy coalescing - equality versus range

entries.title: Hash indexing
entries.text: Course home · Notes · Exercises Hash indexing Opening case — an equality index that must grow Synthetic teaching case. A service repeatedly finds records by numerical ID. Start with the exact numeric structure used in Lecture 3a, PDF p. 23: one bucket holds [9] , the other [4,5,7] . Each bucket holds at most ==three entries==. The hash is $h(x)=x\bmod8$, represented in exactly three bits . The directory currently reads its first bit, from the left . Records are stored separately; entries contain IDs and record pointers. 692 Figure 1 — Opening directory Read it: Two directory entries select two buckets; both local depths are 1. Key takeaway: Read fixed-width hash prefixes from the left; source initial state p. 23. Questions 1. Insert 13, then 21. Draw the directory, bucket contents, global depth, and every local depth after each operation. 2. Insert 29. The hash-width limit is ==three bits==; when that limit prevents useful splitting, use overflow. Explain why more bucket allocation alone cannot separate some entries. 3. Find 21 and the absent key 37. How does overflow affect the lookup? Would this layout also be an efficient ordered range index for IDs 4–21? Success criteria: every entry has a valid route from its hash prefix; all main buckets respect capacity; directory aliases are correct; overflow preserves every entry; failed searches inspect all candidate entries. The first insertion is source-derived; the subsequent operations are explicitly additional teaching practice. Case question Concepts needed --- --- Insert 13 and 21 Hash representation, global/local depth, splitting and directory doubling Insert 29 Full-hash collision, split limit, overflow Find 21, reject 37, assess a range Candidate buckets, equality comparison, query workload Prerequisites: block and pointer concepts from Unit 1, and the ordered-index comparison from Unit 2. The chapter covers Lecture 3a, PDF pp. 2–43; p. 44 is its reading reference. The course DBMS, version, and dialect remain unconfirmed. Hashing replaces an ordered route with a computed address A bucket is a storage unit, typically a disk block, containing multiple entries. A hash function maps a search key into a finite address space. In hash file organisation , buckets hold the data records. In a hash index , buckets hold search keys with record pointers. The source calls the latter secondary indexing: its terminology for a primary index requires sequential file order on that key.[^basics] [!note] Collision and lookup A ==collision== occurs when different search-key values map to the same bucket. The hash identifies a candidate bucket , not a unique matching record. Search the bucket and its overflow chain, comparing actual keys. Equal hashes do not imply equal keys. What makes a useful hash function? A useful function spreads keys across addresses with little dependence on troublesome patterns in the actual dataset. “Random” here describes distribution quality; lookup must still reproduce the same address for the same key. An adversarial or skewed distribution can overload one bucket while others remain empty.[^basics] The source gives $h(v)=(av+b)\bmod N$, where $v$ is a numerical key, $a,b$ are chosen constants, and $N$ is the number of static buckets. Remainders are addresses 0 through $N-1$. The formula alone does not guarantee uniformity: with $a=2,b=0,N=8$, integer inputs reach only even residues. With $h(v)=v\bmod8$, keys 5,13,21,29 all collide. Constants and key distribution matter. Source worked calculation: on p. 5, the teaching character encoding assigns M=13, U=21, S=19, I=9, C=3, so Music hashes as $(13+21+19+9+3)\bmod8=65\bmod8=1$. This is the slide's alphabet-position example, not a specified Unicode or ASCII algorithm. The alphabet row repeats G where J would normally occur and prints X as 25; spacing and punctuation handling for department names are unspecified. Preserve the supplied Music result and the depicted department placement; do not invent missing encoding rules. Static hashing and overflow chains Static hashing fixes the main bucket address set. Insertions target the same bucket as lookup. If that bucket is full, attach an overflow page and continue the chain as necessary. Deletion first finds the matching entry; the main hash route remains the same. Overflow pages are additional storage attached to an existing address, not new values in the hash function's range.[^static] 810 Figure 2 — Static collision and overflow Read it: Trace the digit-sum calculation to bucket 5, then its linked overflow page. Key takeaway: The source bucket contents on p. 11 require key comparisons. Source worked example: the ID index on PDF p. 11 uses sum-of-digits modulo 8. For 15151, the digit sum is $1+5+1+5+1=13$ and the bucket is 5. The source's bucket 5 also contains 33456, with 58583 and 98345 in overflow. For 98345, the sum is $9+8+3+4+5=29$, and $29\bmod8=5$. A lookup may require both pages before following a record pointer. The slide's data-row label for Gold is 33465 while the index entry is 33456; both digit sums are 21, but they are different IDs. No exercise silently equates them. Cost and the growth trade-off Let $r$ be number of stored entries, $B$ main buckets, and $c$ entries per bucket. The synthetic occupancy ratio is $\alpha=r/(Bc)$; it is dimensionless and measures average main-bucket demand, not a guarantee against local overflow. With 8 buckets of capacity 2 and 12 entries, $\alpha=12/16=0.75$. A chain can still occur because four entries hash to one bucket. If a target bucket spans $q$ pages including overflow, an unsuccessful lookup scans those $q$ candidate pages in the source model. Add directory and data-record reads separately where relevant. This explains both extremes: too few buckets cause long chains as a file grows, while preallocating many buckets wastes space before growth or after shrinkage. Rehashing all entries can repair the layout but disrupts normal access.[^static] Counterexample to a universal performance promise: no hash index guarantees constant worst-case lookup. If all keys collide, a bucket chain can grow in proportion to the file. Extendable hashing — two depths, one routing invariant The lecture's spelling is extendable hashing , also commonly called extendible hashing. A fixed-width hash provides $b$ bits; the directory uses only its first $i$ high-order bits. Here $i$ is the ==global depth==. A bucket $j$ stores its ==local depth== $i_j$, the number of hash-prefix bits needed to identify that bucket.[^depth] Quantity Meaning Constraint --- --- --- $b$ Full hash width in bits Fixed for the chosen function/representation $i$ Global depth in bits $0\le i\le b$ $i_j$ Local depth of bucket $j$ $0\le i_j\le i$ $2^i$ Directory pointer entries Count, not number of physical buckets $2^{i-i_j}$ Directory aliases for bucket $j$ All aliases share its $i_j$-bit prefix Derive the alias count: once the first $i_j$ bits are fixed, each of the remaining $i-i_j$ bits has two choices. Multiplying those choices gives $2^{i-i_j}$. At global depth 3, a bucket with local depth 1 has $2^{3-1}=4$ directory pointers. A local-depth-3 bucket has one. Source correction: PDF p. 13 says the number of physical buckets is less than $2^i$. Equality is possible when every local depth equals $i$; the precise relation is at most $2^i$. Do not confuse directory duplication with creation of new physical buckets. Fixed-width binary representation matters For the opening hash, $h(9)=1$ must be written 001 , not just 1 . At global depth 1, its high-order bit is 0. By contrast, $h(5)=5=101_2$, whose high-order bit is 1. Omitting leading zeros routes 9 incorrectly. At global depth 2, 5 uses prefix 10 . The lecture query on p. 18 follows directory entry 10 to bucket [4,5] , then compares keys to find 5. Entries 00 and 01 share bucket [9] with local depth 1; 11 points to [7] with local depth 2.[^query] [!question] Check your understanding A directory has 16 pointers and one bucket's local depth is 2. How many pointers reach that bucket? Identify global depth before calculating. Insertion — separate directory growth from bucket splitting Why do two operations exist? The directory may already distinguish the next bit even when a particular bucket ignores it. Only when the directory is too shallow must it grow.[^insertion] 1. Compute the full-width hash and follow its $i$-bit prefix to bucket $j$. 2. If there is room, insert the entry and stop. 3. If full and $i_j [!warning] Supplementary technical correction — PostgreSQL Lecture 3a, PDF p. 42 says PostgreSQL does not support hashing on disk. PostgreSQL 18's official documentation explicitly describes persistent, crash-recoverable on-disk hash indexes and equality-only support. The source claim is therefore not correct for that documented version. This correction does not establish PostgreSQL as the SOE201 course DBMS.[^postgres] Exam-style answer and reusable method [!summary] A defensible answer to the opening case Fixed-width hashes route 13,21,29 to 101 . Inserting 13 doubles global depth to 2 and splits bucket 1. Inserting 21 doubles it to 3 and splits bucket 10. Inserting 29 reaches the three-bit limit and adds overflow. The final directory has eight pointers to four main buckets; duplicate prefixes share buckets according to their local depths. Lookup must compare actual keys and inspect overflow before declaring absence. For any new task: write the fixed hash width, capacity, bit direction, current global depth, local depths, and split limit; compute the target hash; distinguish alias updates from entry movement; retry insertion; enforce rollback if required; check all routes and entry counts. Do not transfer a suffix-bit algorithm into these prefix-bit exercises without explicitly changing the convention. Misconceptions and quick review - “Two directory entries imply two buckets.” They may be aliases of one bucket. - “Low average occupancy prevents overflow.” Skew concentrates local demand. - “Different IDs separate after enough splits.” They can share a complete finite hash. - “Doubling changes every local depth.” Only buckets actually split change local depth. - “The first bucket proves absence.” Overflow belongs to the same candidate route. Explain the two depths without looking, draw insertion 13, and then solve the city rollback exercise with its original data. Personal learning remains untested . [^basics]: Lecture3a - Hash Indexing.pdf , PDF pp. 3–6, 9–10. Encoding and identifier ambiguities are explicitly retained. [^static]: Lecture3a - Hash Indexing.pdf , PDF pp. 7–12. Occupancy ratio and cost examples are labelled teaching calculations. [^depth]: Lecture3a - Hash Indexing.pdf , PDF pp. 13–16; alias formula is visible on p. 15. [^query]: Lecture3a - Hash Indexing.pdf , PDF pp. 17–18. [^insertion]: Lecture3a - Hash Indexing.pdf , PDF pp. 19–21. [^numeric]: Lecture3a - Hash Indexing.pdf , PDF pp. 23–28. [^limits]: Lecture3a - Hash Indexing.pdf , PDF pp. 29–40; two-split limit specified on p. 32. [^deletion]: Lecture3a - Hash Indexing.pdf , PDF p. 22; capacity and directory-pair reasoning are explanatory consequences of the depicted structure. [^comparison]: Lecture3a - Hash Indexing.pdf , PDF pp. 41–43. Vendor statements on p. 42 are source context rather than confirmed course configuration. [^postgres]: Supplementary official clarification: [PostgreSQL 18 — Hash Indexes]( section 65.6.1, checked 2026-09-20. Supports the persistent on-disk hash-index correction only; no PostgreSQL execution was performed.

entries.title: Hash-index exercises
entries.text: Course home · Notes · Exercises Hash-index exercises All original page references below identify Lecture3a - Hash Indexing.pdf ; its (1) copy is byte-identical. Try each question before opening the adjacent hint or solution. The supplementary exercises are labelled explicitly. A1 — Directory entries and physical buckets Source-derived worked relationship · PDF pp. 15–16; supplementary numerical check · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Explain why a bucket of local depth $i_j$ receives $2^{i-i_j}$ directory pointers. For the source example $i=2$, $i_1=1$, $i_2=i_3=2$, give every bucket's pointer count. Then find the alias count for a local-depth-2 bucket when global depth is 4. [!tip]- Hint Fix the local prefix; count the remaining free directory bits. [!success]- Solution Derivation: each of the $i-i_j$ remaining bits has two choices, giving $2^{i-i_j}$ aliases. In the source example, the counts are $2^{2-1}=2$, $2^{2-2}=1$, and 1: four pointers to three physical buckets. In the supplementary case, $2^{4-2}=4$ aliases reach that bucket. Counting pointers as separate buckets would overcount storage. B1 — Reproduce the supplied hash calculations Original course worked examples · PDF pp. 5 and 11 · Difficulty: ★☆☆ 1. Using the source's letter values M=13, U=21, S=19, I=9, C=3, compute the bucket for Music with sum modulo 8. 2. Using digit-sum modulo 8, compute the bucket for ID 15151 . The source diagram shows bucket 5 with entries 15151,33456 and overflow 58583,98345 ; explain why collisions require full-key comparison. Do not replace the supplied character values with ASCII codes. The slide's inconsistent alphabet cells and Gold data-row ID are documented in Notes; they are not silently corrected inputs here. [!tip]- Hint Sum first, then take the remainder on division by 8. [!success]- Solution 1. $13+21+19+9+3=65=8\times8+1$, so Music maps to ==bucket 1==. 2. $1+5+1+5+1=13=8+5$, so ID 15151 maps to ==bucket 5==. IDs 33456, 58583, and 98345 have digit sums 21,29,29, all remainder 5. The hash narrows the candidate set; compare actual IDs to distinguish them. A search for 98345 must continue into the overflow page. The bucket entry 33456 is retained exactly; the source row elsewhere labelled 33465 is not treated as the same identifier. B2 — Follow the source lookup for 5 Original course worked lookup · PDF p. 18 · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Use $h(x)=x\bmod8$, three-bit hashes, global depth 2. Directory 00,01 points to [9] of local depth 1; 10 points to [4,5] of local depth 2; 11 points to [7] of local depth 2. Trace the source lookup for 5 . [!tip]- Hint Use the first two bits of 101, then compare entries. [!success]- Solution $h(5)=5=101_2$. Its two-bit prefix is 10 , so follow that directory entry to [4,5] . Compare the full key and find 5. The directory does not return a record merely because the prefix matches: 4 is in the same bucket. If the directory is cached, the candidate-bucket read is one block in this simplified model; fetching a separate record is additional. C1 — Insert 13 into the original two-bucket index Original course exercise · PDF p. 23; source solution pp. 24–28 · Difficulty: ★★☆ The hash is $h(x)=x\bmod8$, stored as three bits. A bucket holds ==three records==. The initial index below has global depth 1. Draw the index after inserting a record with search key 13 ; show directory growth, bucket redistribution, and local depths. 575 Figure E1 — Original numeric starting index Read it: Both buckets have local depth 1. Key takeaway: Insert into the route determined by the high-order bit. [!tip]- Hint The target is full and its local depth equals global depth. Double the directory before splitting. [!success]- Solution Step 1 — Locate. $13\bmod8=5=101_2$; prefix 1 selects [4,5,7] , already full. Step 2 — Double. Increase global depth from 1 to 2. Before redistribution, 00,01 both point to [9] and 10,11 both point to [4,5,7] . Local depths remain 1 at this intermediate step. Step 3 — Split. Split the latter bucket into prefixes 10 and 11 , each with local depth 2. Existing hashes are 4→100 , 5→101 , 7→111 ; therefore redistribute as [4,5] and [7] . Step 4 — Insert. Put 13 into the 10 bucket, producing [4,5,13] . The [9] bucket remains local depth 1 and retains two aliases. insert13.svg Figure E2 — Original insertion result Read it: Four directory entries point to three physical buckets. Key takeaway: All buckets fit capacity 3, and all original records are retained. This matches the final source figure on PDF p. 28. The algorithm changes neither the numerical hash function nor unrelated bucket contents. C2 — Another Comp.Sci. record Original course worked insertion · PDF pp. 29–30 · Difficulty: ★★☆ The source uses an index on Department , global depth 3, and two-record buckets. Its displayed buckets are: Music (local depth 1) containing (15151, Mozart, Music, 40000) ; Physics (depth 3) containing Einstein and Gold; Finance (depth 3) containing Wu; History (depth 3) containing El Said; and Comp.Sci. (depth 3) containing (10101, Srinivasan, Comp.Sci., 65000) and (45565, Katz, Comp.Sci., 75000) . Insert the exact new record (83821, Brandt, Comp.Sci., 92000) . Explain the overflow result shown on p. 30. A numerical hash function and exact trial limit are not supplied for this example ; do not invent them. [!tip]- Hint Hashing depends on Department. Ask whether another bit can distinguish equal Department values. [!success]- Solution All three Comp.Sci. records have the same search-key value and therefore the same complete hash. The existing two-record bucket is full. Splitting on more bits cannot separate identical values. Under the source's stated limit/fallback rule, retain or restore the original directory and chain an overflow bucket containing (83821, Brandt, Comp.Sci., 92000) to the existing Comp.Sci. bucket. The other four buckets stay unchanged. Equality lookup for Comp.Sci. must return all three records across the chain. We cannot reconstruct a numerical split trial without the missing hash/limit inputs; the source demonstrates the final overflow outcome directly. E1 — Taiyuan and the two-split rollback rule Original course case study · PDF pp. 32–34; supplied solution pp. 35–40 · Difficulty: ★★★ A block holds up to ==three records==. Begin with the original city-name index below. It already contains one Taiyuan record . The task is to insert a new record with Taiyuan , retaining the existing record. If insertion is still unsuccessful after ==two splits==, revert to the original index and use overflow. City name Supplied 32-bit hash --- --- Lianyungang 1101 0111 1011 0101 1110 0101 1110 1111 Nottingham 0010 0110 1101 0101 0111 0010 1100 0101 Cambridge 0110 1001 1000 0011 1100 0010 0101 0000 Venice 0011 0001 0011 0100 1101 1101 0111 0101 Kuala Lumpur 1000 0001 1100 0000 1010 0001 1100 1110 Taiyuan 0010 1001 1000 0011 1100 0010 0101 0000 Java Island 0111 1001 1000 0011 0110 1001 1000 0011 Valencia 1110 1001 1000 0011 1100 0010 0101 0000 Florence 0010 1001 1000 0011 0110 1001 1000 0011 Chiang Mai 0010 1110 0001 0001 0101 0111 1100 1100 The full table is retained from PDF p. 33. Only the stated Taiyuan insertion is required; the other city names are not extra unstated insertion tasks. 607 Figure E3 — Original city starting index Read it: Global depth is 2; prefixes 10 and 11 share the local-depth-1 bucket. Key takeaway: A duplicate city name denotes another record, not an instruction to discard it. [!tip]- Hint Taiyuan, Florence, and Nottingham share prefix 0010. Show both failed split states before the required rollback. [!success]- Solution Step 1 — Locate the full bucket. The new Taiyuan hash begins 00 , so its candidate bucket already holds Taiyuan, Florence, Nottingham. Four records do not fit three slots. Step 2 — First attempt. Local depth 2 equals global depth 2, so double the directory to global depth 3. Split 00 into 000 and 001 , both local depth 3. All three existing records and the new one begin 001 ; 000 remains empty and the new record still cannot fit. city-split1.svg Figure E4 — First failed split Read it: The main bucket at 001 still contains only the three old records. Key takeaway: The pending new Taiyuan record is not silently stored beyond capacity. Step 3 — Second attempt. Increase global depth to 4 and split 001 into 0010 and 0011 , both local depth 4. Taiyuan, Florence, and Nottingham all begin 0010 ; the new Taiyuan does too. The split again leaves the target full and an empty sibling. city-split2.svg Figure E5 — Second failed split Read it: 0000 and 0001 share the earlier empty local-depth-3 bucket. All sixteen directory entries are shown. Key takeaway: Both allowed splits have failed; continuing to bit 5 would violate this exercise. Step 4 — Roll back, then overflow. Restore global depth 2 and the original three main buckets with local depths 2,2,1 . Remove the temporary buckets and redirect directory aliases exactly as before the first attempt. Attach an overflow page to prefix 00 containing the new Taiyuan record . city-overflow.svg Figure E6 — Required final city index Read it: The main bucket retains the old Taiyuan; overflow holds the new record. Key takeaway: Rollback restores the original directory, not the deepest failed state. Check: the initial six records plus one new record give seven records: three in bucket 00 , one in its overflow, one in 01 , and two in prefix 1 . The final directory has four pointers to three main buckets. This reproduces PDF p. 40 without treating the duplicate city name as a typo. D1 — Find the routing error Supplementary error diagnosis · Difficulty: ★★☆ A student uses $h(x)=x\bmod8$ but writes $h(9)=1$ and follows directory prefix 1 at global depth 1. They then claim every physical bucket doubles when the directory doubles. Correct both errors. [!tip]- Hint The hash representation has a fixed width; pointers can alias a bucket. [!success]- Solution Write $h(9)=001_2$. Its first bit is 0 , so the correct route is prefix 0. Directory doubling creates twice as many pointer entries , initially copying routes. Existing physical buckets and local depths do not double. Only an actual split creates one additional main bucket and increases the two resulting local depths by one. E2 — Merge buddies, then assess query type Supplementary transfer problem · Difficulty: ★★☆ Start from C1's final index. Delete 13. Decide whether buckets 10 and 11 can merge and whether the directory can shrink. Then explain why this index does not provide an ordered range traversal. [!tip]- Hint Check local depths, common prefix, combined occupancy, and all directory pairs. [!success]- Solution After deletion, 10 holds [4,5] and 11 holds [7] . They are buddies of local depth 2, share prefix 1 , and their three entries fit one bucket. Merge them into local-depth-1 prefix 1 , then redirect both aliases. Prefix 0 already covers 00,01 ; every adjacent directory pair now aliases one bucket. Shrink global depth from 2 to 1. Final buckets are 0:[9] , 1:[4,5,7] . Numerical order is not directory order: 9 precedes bucket entries 4,5,7 in the directory. A B+ tree's ordered leaves support range traversal; this hash organisation would generally need to examine multiple buckets and filter actual keys.

entries.title: In 60 Seconds
entries.text: Different predicates need different structures. LSM and buffer trees batch updates; bitmap indexes compute exact sets; Bloom filters cheaply reject definite non-members but may return false positives; k-d trees, quadtrees and R-trees prune spatial regions; temporal indexes locate versions by valid interval. The right question is not “which index is fastest?” but “which mechanism preserves the predicate and workload we need?” After study, you should be able to select a mechanism, trace its intermediate state, distinguish exact results from candidates, and explain its trade-offs without turning vendor examples into universal behaviour.

entries.title: Concept Preview
entries.text: [!note] LSM tree Plain-language meaning: accumulate newer entries in memory and merge sorted batches into larger disk levels. Why it matters: converts scattered writes into batched sequential work but adds merges and multi-level reads. Source: Lecture3b - Advanced Indexing.pdf , PDF pp. 4–6. [!note] Bitmap index Plain-language meaning: one aligned bit vector represents which record positions have a value. Why it matters: Boolean operations return exact candidate positions quickly for suitable low-cardinality attributes. Source: Lecture3b, PDF pp. 8–10. [!note] Bloom filter Plain-language meaning: a compact probabilistic membership filter with no false negatives under its model, but possible false positives. Why it matters: it can avoid expensive lookups when any required bit is zero. Source: Lecture3b, PDF pp. 11–12. [!note] Spatial pruning Plain-language meaning: partition or bound regions so a query examines only plausible objects. Why it matters: a bounding-region hit may still need an exact geometry predicate. Source: Lecture3b, PDF pp. 13–20. [!note] Temporal interval Plain-language meaning: a version is valid over a time interval, possibly with an open end. Why it matters: current and historical lookups may require different access paths. Source: Lecture3b, PDF pp. 21–22.

entries.title: Before You Start
entries.text: Recall B+ tree ordered access, hash equality access, Boolean AND/OR and coordinate pairs. [!question] Prerequisite check What is the bitwise AND of 101010 and 110011 ? [!success]- Check your answer 100010 : a position is 1 only when both input bits are 1. Source principle: Lecture3b, PDF pp. 8–10.

entries.title: A motivating question
entries.text: A campus system receives frequent asset updates and supports four queries: 1. ingest updates without scattered one-record disk writes; 2. return records that are both sensor and active ; 3. reject most absent IDs before searching a disk structure; 4. find map objects inside a rectangle and the version valid at time 5. No single structure is automatically best. Match each predicate to a mechanism and state what extra work or uncertainty remains.

entries.title: Learn the mechanism
entries.text: A decision map mermaid flowchart TD Q{"What must the query/update do?"} Q -- "batch writes" L["LSM or buffer tree"] Q -- "exact Boolean categories" B["bitmap"] Q -- "cheap membership rejection" F["Bloom filter"] Q -- "spatial range/overlap" S["k-d / quadtree / R-tree"] Q -- "valid-at time" T["temporal interval index"] Figure 1 — Choose by predicate and workload Read it: start with the required operation, not a favourite data structure. Key takeaway: each branch changes the meaning of a “match” and the work still required. Provenance: teaching synthesis from Lecture3b, PDF pp. 2–22. LSM trees and buffer trees An LSM tree keeps newer ordered entries in memory ($L_0$) and merges batches into larger disk levels. With growth factor $k$, the simplified threshold relation is $T_{i+1}=kT_i$. If $T_0=100$ and $k=4$, then $T_1=400$ and $T_2=1600$ entries. Merging scans ordered inputs and produces ordered output. This reduces scattered insert work but rewrites older entries, and a lookup may search several levels. A deletion tombstone must remain until older relevant versions can no longer reappear. A buffer tree retains a search tree but stores pending updates in internal buffers. When a buffer fills, it partitions updates by child range and pushes batches downward. Queries must account for relevant buffered updates. Structure Batches where? Read consequence --- --- --- LSM across memory/disk sorted levels search/reconcile relevant levels buffer tree inside internal search-tree nodes inspect path plus pending updates Bitmap indexes are exact set algebra All bitmaps share the same record-position order. For source bitmaps m=11010 and L1=10010 , the conjunction is: text 11010 & 10010 = 10010 Positions with 1 satisfy both predicates. Bitmap space grows with record count × distinct indexed values, so very high cardinality and frequent position-changing updates can weaken the basic design. Bloom filters answer “definitely not” or “possibly” Insertion sets every bit selected by the element's hash functions. Query recomputes those positions: - any zero → definitely absent; - all ones → possibly present; verify in the real structure. False positives occur when other inserted elements set all queried bits. Under the lecture's idealised approximation, after $n$ inserted values, $k$ hashes and $m$ bits: $$p\approx\left(1-e^{-kn/m}\right)^k.$$ The lecture's 10% and 1% are rounded illustrations; the reference notes derive approximately 9.52% and 0.819% under their stated model. A Bloom filter does not itself return the record and ordinarily does not support deletion without an extended design. Spatial structures prune different shapes Structure Partition/bound Natural lesson --- --- --- k-d tree alternating coordinate splits point/range pruning by axis quadtree recursively equal spatial quadrants adapts resolution by subdividing occupied regions R-tree bounding rectangles over objects/groups handles rectangles/polygons and overlap; verify exact geometry A bounding rectangle can overlap a query even when the contained object's exact shape does not. Spatial indexes produce candidates; the final predicate may still reject false candidates. Temporal indexing The lecture separates current open-ended entries from historical closed intervals. Tutor examples use half-open intervals [start,end) because the source does not fully define endpoint inclusion. Under that declared convention, [1,5) is valid at 4 but not 5, while [5,∞) begins at 5. [!question] Explain it yourself Why is a Bloom “possibly present” result different from a bitmap AND result? [!success]- Check your explanation Bloom bits can be shared by unrelated elements, so all-one is only a candidate. Aligned bitmap AND exactly represents the indexed record positions. Source: Lecture3b, PDF pp. 8–12.

entries.title: Worked example — solve the campus questions
entries.text: 1. Writes: use an LSM or buffer tree to batch propagation. LSM inherits merge and multi-level lookup work; a buffer tree inherits pending-update visibility along the path. 2. Categories: sensor=101010 AND active=110011 gives 100010 , so record positions 0 and 4 match when the leftmost bit is position 0. 3. Absent-ID rejection: use a Bloom filter. A zero bit proves absence; all ones require the real lookup. 4. Map rectangle: use k-d/quadtree for point partitioning or an R-tree for bounded objects; always test the exact spatial predicate after pruning. 5. Time 5: under the explicit half-open convention, the old [1,5) version is excluded and the new [5,∞) version is valid.

entries.title: Return to the motivating question
entries.text: The problem is solved by composing structures, not selecting one winner. Each mechanism answers a different predicate and carries a different residual cost: merges, buffered updates, bitmap maintenance, Bloom verification, exact geometry testing or interval-boundary handling.

entries.title: Definitions and distinctions
entries.text: Term A Term B Decisive distinction Source --- --- --- --- LSM level buffer-tree node buffer sorted version level versus pending updates attached to a search-tree node Lecture3b, pp. 4–7 bitmap Bloom filter exact aligned set representation versus probabilistic membership filter Lecture3b, pp. 8–12 false positive false negative candidate returned for absent item versus missed present item; standard Bloom model permits only the former Lecture3b, pp. 11–12 k-d tree quadtree data/axis split versus recursive equal-region subdivision Lecture3b, pp. 13–17 R-tree bound exact geometry pruning rectangle versus final object predicate Lecture3b, pp. 18–20

entries.title: Review
entries.text: Full Understanding Return to Learn the mechanism and Worked example — solve the campus questions.

entries.title: 5-Minute Review
entries.text: - batch writes with LSM levels or node buffers; - bitmaps compute exact aligned sets; - Bloom zero means absent, all-one means verify; - spatial indexes prune regions but may return candidates; - k-d, quadtree and R-tree encode different spatial organisation; - temporal answers depend on interval semantics; - choose by predicate, update pattern and remaining work.
