entries.title: Lab 2 — JDBC and Index
entries.text: Course home · Index foundations · B+ tree theory · Lab 02 Lab 2 — JDBC and Index Lab goals By the end of the released work, you should be able to: - explain the role of ==JDBC== between a Java application and MySQL; - trace a query through DriverManager , ==MySQL Connector/J==, MySQL, and a ==ResultSet==; - map each stage of the JDBC lifecycle to the supplied Java sources; - explain the exact SQL assembled from searchKey = "num" and searchKeyValue = "7" ; - distinguish the baseline query from the program that first creates numIndex ; - explain why creating an index does not by itself prove that a query became faster or used that index; and - identify source inconsistencies and rerun hazards before changing an official file. Official tasks Task 1.1 — basic JDBC query Set up the environment, understand the supplied JDBC.java , and test its basic JDBC query.[^tasks] Task 1.2 — JDBC query with an index Understand and test the supplied JDBCandIndex.java , which creates an index and then runs the basic JDBC query.[^tasks] Task 2 — query execution timing Implement functionality that prints the time taken by the same query without and with an index. The measured interval must contain only rs = stmt.executeQuery(sql); ; connection, index changes, result iteration/output, setup, and cleanup remain outside the timer.[^task2] [!warning] Scope boundary Task 2 measures the single executeQuery call for the Task 1 query. The local solution additionally verifies index state, logical-result equality, and the indexed execution plan; those checks are outside the measured interval. Opening practical question — what actually changes? You receive the same imported Orf_Motif data and two programs: - JDBC.java connects and runs SELECT FROM Orf_Motif WHERE num=7 . - JDBCandIndex.java first runs CREATE INDEX numIndex ON Orf_Motif (num) , then runs the same logical SELECT . Questions: What path carries the query from Java to MySQL? What is returned to Java? What changes when the index is created, and what remains unproved? Constraints: preserve the original sources; use placeholders or environment variables rather than recorded credentials; do not access university infrastructure without current authorised connection details; and do not infer a storage-engine-specific index structure without engine evidence. Success criteria: you can trace each source line, predict the SQL text, explain the result-reading loop, distinguish logical equivalence from performance evidence, and identify the checks required before a safe rerun. Opening question Concepts needed --- --- How does Java reach MySQL? JDBC API, DriverManager , Connector/J, Connection How is the query submitted and read? Statement , executeQuery , ResultSet , rs.next() What does the second program add? CREATE INDEX , object naming, repeated-run behaviour What can the lab prove? Source behaviour versus execution plan and timing evidence Architecture JDBC is the Java API used to connect Java programs to relational data. The source presents JDBC as classes and interfaces, with database providers supplying drivers.[^jdbc-definition] This lab selects the pure-Java Type 4 MySQL driver, MySQL Connector/J.[^connector] mermaid flowchart TB A["Java application"] -- B["JDBC API"] B -- C["DriverManager"] C -- D["MySQL Connector/J Type 4 JDBC driver"] D -- E["MySQL server"] E -- F["Execute SQL"] F -- G["ResultSet for SELECT"] G -- A Figure 1 — The Lab 2 JDBC request path Read it: Follow the request downward from the Java program. For a SELECT , follow the returned ResultSet back to the application. Key takeaway: Java calls the standard JDBC interfaces; Connector/J translates that work into the MySQL protocol. The course source also shows other historical/generic driver routes, but this lab uses Connector/J.[^architecture] Environment setup Course source instructions The official slides provide two environment choices: install MySQL locally, or use the school MySQL service under current institutional access rules. They instruct students to obtain MySQL Connector/J, place the driver on the classpath or import it into the IDE, import yeast_prosite.sql , and replace the Java connection placeholders in a working file.[^mysql-setup] Component Source-supported requirement Important boundary --- --- --- Java Compile and run the supplied class in its declared package The PDF gives no JDK version MySQL Local installation or the authorized school service MySQL server version and storage engine are not stated Driver MySQL Connector/J; driver class com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver PDF p. 10 calls Connector/J 9.4.0 current; this is source-stated, not a detected installation Dataset Import yeast_prosite.sql Inspect import messages before assuming all 12,913 inserts succeeded Connection Replace database, username, and password placeholders in a working copy Never put real credentials in this vault, note, logs, or shared commands The archived originals are here: - Official Lab 2 PDF - Official released task sheet - JDBC.java - JDBCandIndex.java - yeast_prosite.sql [!warning] Work on a copy Both Java files contain literal placeholders. Copy a source into the instructor-approved IDE project before adapting its package or connection parameters. Do not modify the archived original and do not paste a real password into study notes, YAML, screenshots, terminal history, or version control. Source discrepancies to check before execution 1. PDF p. 6 gives the school MySQL host as 10.7.1.127 , whereas PDF p. 11 shows 10.7.1.36/[DATABASE_NAME] . Both supplied Java files contain jdbc:mysql://10.7.1.127/[DATABASE NAME] . On 24 September 2026, a direct TCP probe from the current machine reached 10.7.1.127:3306 , while 10.7.1.36:3306 did not respond within three seconds. That observation supports .127 for the current network but proves neither authentication nor universal availability.[^host-discrepancy] 2. PDF p. 11 names JDBCIndex.java , but the supplied originals are JDBC.java and JDBCandIndex.java . Use the actual supplied filenames for Tasks 1.1 and 1.2.[^preparation-name] 3. The source instructs students to modify a package name if needed. The current files declare package xjtlu.soe201.JDBC; , so an IDE project or javac -d output must respect that package. 4. The source contains institutional login guidance that may age. Follow current instructor/IT instructions. This pass performed reachability probes only; it did not submit credentials, log in, import data, or execute SQL on university infrastructure. Supplementary modern guidance This task's local compile check used JDK 17 and needed no Connector/J JAR because the driver name is loaded reflectively at runtime. That proves only that the Java syntax and standard-library references compile. Running the program requires both Connector/J and a reachable, authorized database. sh javac -d out Sources/JDBC.java Sources/JDBCandIndex.java This command contains no credentials and performs no network access. Runtime classpaths differ between operating systems and IDEs; follow the current lab instructions rather than copying an unverified command. Dataset — Orf_Motif The SQL source drops and recreates one table, deletes earlier rows per orf , and supplies 12,913 INSERT statements. Static parsing found 418 distinct orf values and 216 distinct acc_num values. These are source-file observations, not a claim that a remote import completed. Column Exact SQL type Role in this lab Static source observation --- --- --- --- orf varchar(12) Printed as the second output column No supplied NULL ; maximum text length 9 acc_num varchar(12) Printed as the first output column No supplied NULL ; maximum text length 7 num int(3) Search column; the programs filter on num=7 No supplied NULL ; values 1–57; not declared unique pos int(3) Motif position 285 supplied NULL values len int(3) Motif length No supplied NULL ; values 1–565 mmatch varchar(12) Matched sequence text 285 supplied NULL values; source-width conflict described below Table 1 — Compact schema for the supplied dataset Read it: Start with num , the predicate column, then follow the two printed columns acc_num and orf . The DDL contains no primary key, foreign key, NOT NULL , or engine clause. Key takeaway: num is a repeated occurrence number, not a global identifier. Static inspection finds 614 INSERT statements with num=7 , spanning 252 distinct orf values. The file also contains later per- orf deletions, so insert-statement counts are not final table counts. The controlled local import described below ended with 607 rows matching num=7 . Each result row prints only acc_num and orf even though SELECT retrieves all six columns. [!warning] Dataset import compatibility The DDL declares mmatch varchar(12) , but 771 supplied non- NULL values are longer than 12 characters; the maximum is 89. Modern MySQL strict mode treats invalid or overlong assignments as errors, while non-strict handling can adjust values and issue warnings.[^strict-mode] The SQL also begins with unconditional drop table Orf_Motif; , which can report an error if the table does not yet exist. Preserve the official SQL unchanged, inspect the import report, and ask the instructor for the intended schema rather than silently widening the archived source. JDBC lifecycle The source condenses JDBC work into six phases; the following eight-step trace separates statement creation, result acquisition, and iteration so that every supplied operation is visible.[^lifecycle] mermaid flowchart TD A["1 Import java.sql classes"] -- B["2 Load the JDBC driver"] B -- C["3 Establish Connection"] C -- D["4 Create Statement"] D -- E["5 Build and execute SQL"] E -- F["6 Obtain ResultSet"] F -- G["7 Iterate with rs.next and read columns"] G -- H["8 Close ResultSet, Statement, Connection"] Figure 2 — Lifecycle used by both supplied Java programs Read it: Each box maps to a concrete import, field, call, or cleanup line in the source table below. Key takeaway: The second program inserts one DDL operation—index creation—between statement creation and the same logical SELECT . Stage JDBC.java JDBCandIndex.java --- --- --- Import classes lines 11–15 lines 11–15 Load driver line 58, Class.forName(JDBC_DRIVER) line 67 Establish ==Connection== line 60 line 69 Create ==Statement== line 65 line 74 Build SQL line 38 lines 39 and 44 Execute / obtain ==ResultSet== line 39 index: line 40; query: line 47 Iterate and read lines 48–50 lines 57–59 Close resources lines 72–74 lines 81–83 JDBC.java — without creating the new index Configuration fields Name Exact supplied meaning --- --- DB_URL JDBC URL placeholder containing host 10.7.1.127 and [DATABASE NAME] USER [USERNAME] placeholder PASS [PASSWORD] placeholder JDBC_DRIVER com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver conn JDBC Connection , initially null stmt JDBC Statement , initially null rs JDBC ResultSet , initially null sql Current SQL string searchKey Column name num searchKeyValue Text 7 , concatenated without quotes into the numeric predicate Build and submit the query The source constructs: java sql = "SELECT FROM Orf_Motif WHERE " + searchKey + "=" + searchKeyValue; With the supplied constants, the exact SQL is: sql SELECT FROM Orf_Motif WHERE num=7 stmt.executeQuery(sql) submits a SELECT and returns a ResultSet , matching the source tutorial's distinction between executeQuery for queries and executeUpdate for data-changing statements.[^execute] Advance and read rs.next() advances the cursor to the next row and returns whether a row is available. Inside that loop: - rs.getString("acc_num") converts the current row's acc_num value to a Java String ; - rs.getString("orf") does the same for orf ; and - the program prints the two values separated by a tab.[^resultset] The loop continues until rs.next() returns false . The text labels “first col” and “second col” are only console headings; the getters select by column name. [!info] Static expectation, not a runtime observation The unchanged SQL file contains 614 inserts whose num value is 7, and neither printed field is NULL in those source rows. A controlled local MySQL 9.4.0 import finished with 607 matching rows because the script's later DELETE statements affect the final state. A different database state or failed import can still produce a different result. JDBCandIndex.java — creating the index After making the connection and Statement , the second program constructs and executes: sql CREATE INDEX numIndex ON Orf_Motif (num) It then constructs the same logical query: sql SELECT FROM Orf_Motif WHERE num=7 stmt.execute(sql) is used for the DDL statement because the program is not expecting a query row set from CREATE INDEX . stmt.executeQuery(sql) is then used for the SELECT . Conceptually, numIndex creates an access structure keyed by num . That makes an indexed access path available to the optimizer. The SQL source does not declare a storage engine, and the Java source does not inspect index metadata, so this note does not assert that the physical index is a B+ tree. Use B+ tree theory for the course's ordered-tree model and hash-index theory for the contrasting equality-oriented model; neither identifies this table's actual engine. Re-running the program On a first successful run, the named index exists afterward. A later run again requests the same index name. MySQL reports a duplicate-key-name error when an index name already exists, so the program can stop at stmt.execute(sql) before reaching the SELECT .[^duplicate-index] [!warning] Troubleshooting decision First determine whether numIndex already exists. Do not repeatedly rerun the program and do not modify the lecturer's archived file merely to hide the failure. SUPPLEMENTARY GUIDANCE — verified MySQL syntax: sql SHOW INDEX FROM Orf_Motif; This lists table indexes. If the instructor explicitly asks for a reset, MySQL's documented syntax is: sql DROP INDEX numIndex ON Orf_Motif; DROP INDEX changes schema state; use it only in the intended lab database and only after confirming the index name and reset purpose.[^show-drop-index] Without new index versus with new index Aspect JDBC.java JDBCandIndex.java --- --- --- Schema change before query None Requests CREATE INDEX numIndex ON Orf_Motif (num) Logical predicate num=7 num=7 Selected columns Printed columns acc_num , orf acc_num , orf Expected logical result if data are unchanged All rows satisfying num=7 The same rows satisfying num=7 Timing code None None Plan inspection None None Proof MySQL used numIndex None None Same logical result ≠ proven performance improvement. The supplied programs demonstrate JDBC connectivity, SQL submission, index creation, and equivalent query structure before and after the schema change. They do not measure latency, page reads, throughput, or optimizer choice. Evidence for a general performance claim would require a controlled setup and additional observations such as repeated timings, stable data/cache conditions, and an identified server version and engine. The released Task 2 run below supplies one local executeQuery timing pair plus EXPLAIN ; it does not establish a universal speedup. Statement, PreparedStatement, and CallableStatement Interface Course-source role Relation to this lab --- --- --- Statement General-purpose, simple static SQL with no bind parameters Used by both supplied programs PreparedStatement Precompiled SQL that may accept runtime input parameters; recommended by the source for repeated execution Not used in the supplied files CallableStatement Calls stored procedures/functions and may use input/output parameters Introduced in the PDF; not used in the supplied files This comparison comes from PDF p. 26.[^statement-types] The supplied code uses Statement because it assembles a complete SQL string before submission. That works for its hard-coded teaching values. If a value came from a user or another external source, a PreparedStatement would normally separate SQL structure from parameter values. That is supplementary engineering guidance, not a rewrite of Task 1.1 or 1.2. SQL-to-Java data mapping The tutorial explains that SQL values must be mapped to Java types and gives direct, convertible, and special-class cases.[^type-mapping] SQL type in the PDF JDBC/Java type shown Setter shown --- --- --- VARCHAR , CHAR java.lang.String setString() NUMERIC java.math.BigDecimal setBigDecimal() INTEGER int setInt() FLOAT float setFloat() DOUBLE double setDouble() DATE java.sql.Date setDate() TIME java.sql.Time setTime() TIMESTAMP java.sql.Timestamp setTimestamp() [!note] Internal slide wording discrepancy PDF p. 24 says SQL DATE maps to a Java Date object “defined in java.Date ,” while the table on p. 25 specifies java.sql.Date . The table's fully qualified JDBC type is retained here; the inconsistency is not silently merged. Cleanup and failure limits Both programs explicitly close ResultSet , Statement , and Connection in that order, matching PDF p. 23.[^cleanup] This cleanup is reached only if earlier operations complete. Because the source uses throws and has no finally block or try-with-resources, an exception during connection, index creation, query execution, or row processing can bypass those final close calls. That limitation does not invalidate the teaching sequence, but it matters when interpreting failures. A compile pass is not a runtime pass, and a runtime exception is not evidence about query performance. Supplementary engineering notes These notes support safe interpretation; they are not lecturer-required modifications. Keep credentials out of source control The official examples use string constants for clarity. In a real project, secrets should come from an approved runtime configuration or secret store rather than committed Java or Markdown. This lab note intentionally contains placeholders only. Prefer bounded resource lifetime Modern Java often uses try-with-resources so each JDBC object closes even when an exception occurs. Do not replace the official source during Task 1.1/1.2; first understand the explicit lifecycle the lecturer supplied. Use parameters for external values For an externally supplied numeric value, use a parameter marker and PreparedStatement rather than concatenating raw input. The current fixed 7 is a teaching constant, not an invitation to concatenate untrusted text. Treat import warnings as evidence After importing the SQL in an authorized environment, inspect errors and warnings, confirm the table definition actually created, and verify row counts before attributing a missing or shortened value to JDBC. The mmatch width conflict makes this especially important. Released-task procedure and checkpoints Task 1.1 procedure 1. Preserve the archived JDBC.java ; place a working copy in the instructor-approved project. 2. Confirm the package path and that Connector/J is on the runtime classpath. 3. Import the SQL only into the intended authorized lab database; inspect the import report. 4. Replace placeholders in the working copy without recording real credentials in this vault or logs. 5. Before execution, predict the exact SQL and explain each lifecycle line. 6. Run only in the authorized environment. Record observed output separately from this source-derived expectation. 7. Close or terminate the client cleanly and remove any insecure working credential copy according to instructor policy. Task 1.2 procedure 1. Confirm whether numIndex already exists before running. 2. Trace the DDL and the subsequent SELECT in JDBCandIndex.java . 3. Run in the authorized lab environment only. 4. Check that the logical rows correspond to the Task 1.1 predicate; do not infer a speedup from similar output. 5. Use the released Task 2 procedure below for the timing comparison. Task 2 procedure 1. Remove numIndex outside the timer, then verify that no index exists on Orf_Motif(num) . 2. Start System.nanoTime() , call stmt.executeQuery(sql) , and stop the timer immediately after the call returns. 3. Iterate the first ResultSet only after its timer has stopped. 4. Create numIndex outside the timer and verify that it exists. 5. Time only the same stmt.executeQuery(sql) call again, then iterate afterward. 6. Compare the two logical result multisets and require them to match. 7. Run EXPLAIN after the indexed timer has stopped and require key=numIndex . java long startNanos = System.nanoTime(); ResultSet resultSet = statement.executeQuery(SELECT_SQL); long elapsedNanos = System.nanoTime() - startNanos; Connection establishment, statement creation, index removal/creation, result iteration/output, comparison, plan inspection, and cleanup are all outside this interval.[^task2] Completed reference solution for Tasks 1.1, 1.2, and 2 The runnable solution is Lab2Solution.java, with exact commands in Solution README. The five files under Sources/ remain byte-for-byte unchanged. The solution keeps the source SQL statements, reads connection details from environment variables, closes JDBC resources with try-with-resources, measures only executeQuery , compares both result sets without assuming row order, and verifies the indexed query plan. Run it safely Compile with JDK 17 and MySQL Connector/J. Set the three environment variables only in the shell used for the lab; do not paste a real password into this note or commit it to source control. bash export LAB_DB_URL='jdbc:mysql://HOST:3306/DATABASE' export LAB_DB_USER='USERNAME' read -s LAB_DB_PASSWORD && export LAB_DB_PASSWORD CONNECTOR_JAR='Solution/lib/mysql-connector-j-9.4.0.jar' BUILD_DIR="$(mktemp -d)" javac -Xlint:all -cp "$CONNECTOR_JAR" -d "$BUILD_DIR" \ 'Solution/Lab2Solution.java' java -cp "$BUILD_DIR:$CONNECTOR_JAR" \ xjtlu.soe201.jdbc.Lab2Solution baseline java -cp "$BUILD_DIR:$CONNECTOR_JAR" \ xjtlu.soe201.jdbc.Lab2Solution indexed java -cp "$BUILD_DIR:$CONNECTOR_JAR" \ xjtlu.soe201.jdbc.Lab2Solution timing unset LAB_DB_PASSWORD Use baseline before the index exists for Task 1.1. Use indexed for Task 1.2; it creates numIndex only when metadata shows that it is absent. On a fresh isolated lab database, mode both runs the controlled before/after sequence and refuses to proceed if numIndex already exists. The timing mode implements Task 2; it deliberately removes and recreates numIndex , so run it only in the intended lab database. Observed local result — 24 September 2026 The reference solution was compiled with JDK 17.0.18 and Connector/J 9.4.0. It was first validated against an ephemeral local MySQL 9.4.0 server, then independently revalidated against an isolated local MySQL 8.0.46 server. Both runs imported the exact archived yeast_prosite.sql bytes with non-strict SQL mode so its declared varchar(12) width did not abort the overlong supplied values, and both produced the results below. This is local validation, not evidence about the school server. Check Observed result --- --- Import messages Expected first-line error: DROP TABLE Orf_Motif found no table in the fresh database; import continued Final table rows 12,791 Task 1.1 query 607 rows for SELECT FROM Orf_Motif WHERE num=7 Task 1.2 query 607 rows; same (acc_num, orf) multiset as Task 1.1 Created index numIndex on num ; MySQL reported index method BTREE in this local environment Indexed plan type=ref , possible_keys=numIndex , key=numIndex , estimated rows=607 Task 2 time without index 8.723 ms (8,723,125 ns) Task 2 time with index 2.083 ms (2,083,375 ns) Task 2 logical comparison 607 rows in each run; equal order-independent (acc_num, orf) multisets [!success]- Interpretation Task 1.1: the program connects through Connector/J, submits the source query, iterates its ResultSet , and reads acc_num and orf . The controlled local run observed 607 final matches. Task 1.2: the solution created numIndex , submitted the same logical query, and observed the same 607 logical rows. The local EXPLAIN row named numIndex in both isolated validations, so index use is observed for those local MySQL runs. Task 2: the timer surrounded only executeQuery . The observed local run measured 8.723 ms without an index and 2.083 ms with numIndex ; both returned the same 607 logical rows, and EXPLAIN selected numIndex . Limit: one local observation does not establish a universal speedup or the behaviour of the university server. Cache state, server load, data size, engine, statistics, and repeated-trial methodology can change timings. The local server used non-strict mode, and the school's authenticated import outcome and plan remain untested. Supplementary practice Exercise 1 — reconstruct the two SQL statements Without looking back, write the exact query produced by both programs and the additional DDL produced by JDBCandIndex.java . [!tip]- Hint Substitute searchKey and searchKeyValue into the concatenated strings. [!success]- Solution Both programs produce SELECT FROM Orf_Motif WHERE num=7 . The second also produces CREATE INDEX numIndex ON Orf_Motif (num) before that query. The first changes no schema; the second requests a persistent named index. Exercise 2 — classify four claims Classify each claim as supported , unsupported , or requires runtime evidence : 1. The supplied query filters on num . 2. MySQL used numIndex for the second program. 3. Both programs print acc_num and orf . 4. The indexed query is faster by a specific percentage. [!tip]- Hint Separate source-code facts from optimizer and timing observations. [!success]- Solution 1 is supported by both Java sources. 2 requires runtime plan evidence ; the completed local Task 2 run supplied that evidence with key=numIndex . 3 is supported by the two getString calls. 4 requires an explicit local timing observation and must not be generalized beyond its test conditions. Exercise 3 — diagnose the second run The first run creates numIndex ; the second run stops before printing rows. Give the most direct source-grounded hypothesis and a safe first check. [!tip]- Hint Identify the first schema-changing statement and remember that the index remains after the program exits. [!success]- Solution The second CREATE INDEX numIndex ... can fail because that index name already exists. First inspect indexes with SHOW INDEX FROM Orf_Motif; . Do not drop anything until the instructor's reset intent and the target database are confirmed. Resolve the opening practical question Decision: both programs use the same JDBC request path and the same logical SELECT ; the second program adds one persistent schema operation before the query. Justification: Class.forName selects Connector/J, DriverManager.getConnection produces the Connection , createStatement produces the Statement , and executeQuery returns a ResultSet . The row loop advances with rs.next() and prints acc_num plus orf . Operation: the baseline assembles SELECT FROM Orf_Motif WHERE num=7 . The second assembles CREATE INDEX numIndex ON Orf_Motif (num) , executes it, and then assembles the same SELECT . Result: if both runs use the same successfully imported data, their logical result sets should match. The controlled local run observed 607 final rows in each mode and an order-independent match. The source contains 614 candidate inserts with num=7 , but later deletions reduce the local final table result; another database state still requires its own observation. Interpretation: index creation makes a new access path available. The supplied Task 1 programs contain no plan inspection or timing, while the completed Task 2 solution measures only executeQuery and separately verifies key=numIndex . Its observed local difference is evidence for that run, not a universal performance guarantee. Quick review - Can you draw Java → JDBC → Connector/J → MySQL → ResultSet from memory? - Can you identify the exact lines that create Connection , Statement , and ResultSet ? - Can you explain why num=7 can return many rows? - Can you separate a compile check, JDBC runtime check, database connectivity check, and performance experiment? - Can you explain the duplicate-index rerun failure and the mmatch import risk? - Can you identify the exact three Task 2 timing lines and explain why iteration is excluded? Study status: untested. Source review, compilation, and successful local execution validate the implementation, not your personal mastery or remote university-server behaviour. entries.title: In 60 Seconds
entries.text: Run the same Task 1 query with and without an index and print the time spent in only rs = stmt.executeQuery(sql); . Connection setup, creating an index and consuming results belong outside the timed interval. Compare logical results and inspect the index state separately. Source: tasks PDF pp.1–3 and the updated reference lab's Released Task 2 section.

entries.title: Before You Start
entries.text: Complete the preceding JDBC setup practical. Use an isolated, intended lab database with valid configuration. These web activities explain the task and do not connect to the university database or execute Java. Required university server and JDK versions remain unconfirmed by the task sheet.

entries.title: 1. Keep the query fixed
entries.text: Both Task 1 source programs select SELECT FROM Orf_Motif WHERE num=7 . The indexed version makes an index on num available before submitting that query. Do not compare different predicates, tables, or result interpretations and call that an index experiment. Source: tasks PDF pp.1–2; official JDBC.java and JDBCandIndex.java .

entries.title: 2. Place the timer around exactly one call
entries.text: The updated reference solution uses: java long startNanos = System.nanoTime(); ResultSet resultSet = statement.executeQuery(SELECT_SQL); long elapsedNanos = System.nanoTime() - startNanos; Convert nanoseconds to milliseconds by dividing by 1_000_000.0 . Keep the while (resultSet.next()) loop after the timer. The task defines its interval as the API call; The driver can retrieve and buffer rows during executeQuery; moving the iteration loop afterward does not isolate server execution from transfer time. Supplementary technical reference: [Connector/J implementation notes]( ResultSet section, checked 2026-10-07. Streaming configurations can change that boundary. Source: tasks PDF p.3; reference 03 Lab.md , Released Task 2 timing lines.

entries.title: 3. Record index state and the chosen plan
entries.text: An index existing, an optimiser choosing it, and an elapsed time are three different observations. Record the intended before/after index state and inspect a plan separately. The local reference solution records numIndex ; do not recreate a named index blindly on every rerun. A duplicate-index error can stop the intended experiment before the SELECT. Source: official JDBCandIndex.java , index creation; updated reference lab's execution procedure.

entries.title: 4. Establish equal results
entries.text: Consume both result sets outside the timer and compare them without assuming row order. Keep duplicates when comparing multisets rather than changing query semantics. The reference run compared (acc_num, orf) multisets with 607 rows in each run. This is recorded local evidence, not a promised row count for every import. Source: updated reference lab's Task 2 logical comparison.

entries.title: 5. Explain a measurement honestly
entries.text: The existing reference records one local pair, 8.723 ms and 2.083 ms. It supports a difference in that controlled run. Cache state, load, statistics, data size and configuration can change the result. These values are not newly measured by this web import and do not establish a universal speedup or university-server behaviour. Source: updated reference lab's observed local execution and limits.

entries.title: Review
entries.text: Point to the exact three timer lines. Identify the operations excluded from the interval. Explain how you would show equal logical results and actual plan selection, then name one condition that could change the timings. Use the local cost activity to separate a theoretical estimate from an actual JDBC interval.

entries.title: What is the blocking factor for unspanned fixed records?
entries.text: $\lfloor\text{block size}/\text{record size}\rfloor$: the number of complete records that fit in one block.

entries.title: Why is the final block count rounded upward?
entries.text: Any remaining record needs a real block even when that block is not full.

entries.title: What makes an index primary in this course?
entries.text: Its search-key order matches the physical sequential order of the data file.

entries.title: What does a dense index represent, and how are duplicate search-key values handled?
entries.text: Every search-key value in the data file has an index entry. Duplicate values must lead to all their matching records, for example via a run or pointer list. One entry per record is a particular layout, not the only dense layout.

entries.title: What invariant makes a sparse primary index usable?
entries.text: Ordered data lets a representative entry select the block/range containing the target.

entries.title: What is an index entry's basic size here?
entries.text: Search-key bytes plus pointer bytes, unless the source explicitly supplies additional overhead.

entries.title: What are the HDD read-time phases?
entries.text: Seek time, rotational waiting and transfer time.

entries.title: Why can one page fetch serve several rows?
entries.text: Several rows may share the fetched page, which remains available while buffered.

entries.title: One 300-byte student and its five 200-byte module records must stay together. What group size must the block-capacity calculation use, and why?
entries.text: One 300-byte student record together with its five 200-byte module records: a 1300-byte group.

entries.title: Why does a small index not prove a cheap query?
entries.text: Qualifying records may still occupy many scattered data pages; cache and clustering are unspecified.

entries.title: What does B+ tree order mean in this course?
entries.text: The maximum number of child pointers in an internal node.

entries.title: How many keys can an order-$n$ leaf hold at most?
entries.text: $n-1$ search-key entries.

entries.title: In a B+ tree lookup, where is key membership confirmed?
entries.text: At the reached leaf, not at an internal separator.

entries.title: In this course’s B+ tree convention, which child range is chosen when the search key equals a separator?
entries.text: Route to the right-hand range beginning at that separator.

entries.title: After splitting a B+ tree leaf, which key is copied into the parent?
entries.text: The first key of the new right leaf is copied into the parent.

entries.title: After splitting a B+ tree internal node, which separator is promoted?
entries.text: The middle separator moves to the parent and is removed from the split children.

entries.title: What repair preference does the lecture use after underflow?
entries.text: Merge first when an eligible sibling combination fits; otherwise redistribute.

entries.title: When does deletion reduce the height of a B+ tree?
entries.text: When an internal root is left with one child and that child replaces it.

entries.title: Why are leaves linked?
entries.text: To continue ordered range scans without returning to the root for each next key.

entries.title: What must every root-to-leaf path share?
entries.text: The same depth; this is the tree's height-balance invariant.

entries.title: What does a hash function return for lookup?
entries.text: A candidate bucket address; actual keys must still be compared.

entries.title: What handles a full static bucket?
entries.text: One or more linked overflow pages under the source model.

entries.title: In this course’s extendable hashing, what does global depth measure?
entries.text: The number of high-order hash bits currently read by the directory.

entries.title: What does a bucket’s local depth measure in extendable hashing?
entries.text: The number of prefix bits that distinguish one physical bucket.

entries.title: How many directory entries exist at global depth $i$?
entries.text: $2^i$ pointer entries.

entries.title: At global depth $i$, how many directory entries point to one bucket of local depth $i_j$?
entries.text: $2^{i-i_j}$ directory pointers.

entries.title: When can a full extendable-hash bucket split without doubling the directory?
entries.text: When its local depth is less than the global depth.

entries.title: Why preserve leading zeros?
entries.text: High-order prefix routing depends on the fixed-width bit positions.

entries.title: When can buddy buckets coalesce?
entries.text: Equal local depth, correct buddy prefixes, and combined entries fitting one bucket.

entries.title: Why is hashing poor for ordered range scans?
entries.text: Bucket addresses do not preserve adjacent search-key order.

entries.title: What does an LSM tree batch?
entries.text: Ordered updates, merging memory batches into larger sorted disk levels.

entries.title: What must an LSM lookup reconcile?
entries.text: Relevant versions and tombstones across every searched level.

entries.title: What does a buffer-tree internal buffer hold?
entries.text: Pending updates waiting to be partitioned and pushed toward child ranges.

entries.title: What record-position invariant must hold before combining two bitmap indexes?
entries.text: The same record-position order.

entries.title: If any queried Bloom-filter bit is zero, what can you conclude under the standard insertion-only model?
entries.text: The queried element is definitely absent under the filter model.

entries.title: If all queried Bloom-filter bits are one, what can you conclude and what must happen next?
entries.text: Only possible membership; the real structure must verify it.

entries.title: How does a k-d tree divide space?
entries.text: By recursive coordinate splits, typically alternating dimensions.

entries.title: How does a quadtree divide two-dimensional space?
entries.text: Recursively into four equal spatial quadrants.

entries.title: What does an R-tree internal entry bound?
entries.text: A minimum bounding rectangle covering objects or child regions.

entries.title: Why can temporal endpoint assumptions change an answer?
entries.text: A version at the boundary may be included or excluded depending on interval convention.

entries.title: What does selection change?
entries.text: Selection keeps tuples satisfying a predicate; it preserves the attribute schema.

entries.title: What does projection change?
entries.text: Projection keeps named attributes. In set relational algebra identical result tuples collapse to one.

entries.title: What is union compatibility?
entries.text: Equal arity and compatible corresponding attribute domains; align names/order before a set operation.

entries.title: Is difference commutative?
entries.text: No. r−s keeps tuples in r absent from s; s−r asks the opposite question.

entries.title: How large is a Cartesian product?
entries.text: Every left tuple pairs with every right tuple: r×s = r · s . Rename ambiguous attribute names.

entries.title: What does natural join match?
entries.text: Equality of all attributes with common names, then one copy of each common attribute remains.

entries.title: Why rename a relation?
entries.text: To name an intermediate result or distinguish copies of the same relation and their attributes.

entries.title: For relations r(X,Y) and s(Y), what does division r ÷ s return, and where do candidate X values come from?
entries.text: Return X tuples from πX(r) that occur in r paired with every Y tuple in s. Extra Y pairings are allowed; if s is empty, every candidate in πX(r) qualifies.

entries.title: For r(X,Y) and s(Y), how does candidates minus failures implement division?
entries.text: Start T=πX(r). Missing pairs are (T×s)−r. Project their X values and subtract those failed candidates from T.

entries.title: How can difference find a maximum?
entries.text: Rename a second copy, find values smaller than some other value, and subtract those nonmaximum values from all values. Ties remain.

entries.title: How do borrower and depositor answer both versus either?
entries.text: Intersect projected customer names for both; union them for either.

entries.title: Does algebra projection equal ordinary SQL SELECT?
entries.text: Not necessarily: this lecture uses sets; SQL without DISTINCT can preserve duplicates and has additional NULL behavior.

entries.title: What are the three query-processing stages, and which stage runs the chosen plan?
entries.text: Parsing/translation, optimization, and evaluation. Evaluation executes the chosen plan.

entries.title: Does equivalent algebra imply equal cost?
entries.text: No. Equivalent results can be computed by different algorithms and access paths with different costs.

entries.title: What does a query plan add?
entries.text: Concrete algorithms and evaluation choices for algebra operations.

entries.title: What information helps cost estimates?
entries.text: Catalog statistics such as relation size, tuple size and distinct values; estimates may differ from measured execution.

entries.title: State the lecture’s estimated disk-time formula and define its counts and time units.
entries.text: b·tT+s·tS, where b counts transferred blocks and s counts seeks; both time parameters must use compatible units.

entries.title: Why can fewer transferred blocks still be slower?
entries.text: A plan may save transfers while adding expensive seeks. Compare both terms.

entries.title: What is omitted from the simplified comparison?
entries.text: The lecture focuses on disk access and typically ignores CPU and network in the model. Real elapsed time has additional factors.

entries.title: What is 1 millisecond in microseconds?
entries.text: 1000 microseconds. Convert units before adding time terms.

entries.title: What does JDBC stand for?
entries.text: Java Database Connectivity.

entries.title: Which driver class does the source use?
entries.text: com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver .

entries.title: Which method executes a query returning rows?
entries.text: executeQuery , returning a ResultSet .

entries.title: Which method is suitable for CREATE INDEX ?
entries.text: executeUpdate , because the statement changes schema state rather than returning query rows.

entries.title: What does ResultSet.next() do?
entries.text: Advances the cursor to the next row and reports whether one exists.

entries.title: What proves index selection?
entries.text: An observed execution plan or equivalent server evidence, not index creation alone.

entries.title: What proves a speedup?
entries.text: Controlled measurements under comparable data, cache, server and timing conditions.

entries.title: What exact Java call does released Lab 02 Task 2 ask you to time?
entries.text: The newer task sheet releases timing only rs = stmt.executeQuery(sql); before and after indexing. See the Released Query Timing segment.

entries.title: What disagreement between the two JDBC setup documents needs confirmation?
entries.text: The privilege handout requires manual database creation, while Lab2 says provisioning is automatic.

entries.title: Does the static count of 614 parsed source records establish the number returned by MySQL for num=7?
entries.text: No. It is a static count from parsing supplied SQL, not an observed SELECT result. The recorded local run returned 607 rows for num=7; that historical count is also environment-specific, not a promised result for a future import.

entries.title: Which operation does released Task 2 time?
entries.text: Only rs = stmt.executeQuery(sql); with timestamps immediately before and after that call.

entries.title: Where must the result-iteration loop be placed, and does that exclude all row transfer from executeQuery timing?
entries.text: Place the application’s ResultSet.next() loop and printing after the ending timestamp. The driver may already retrieve and buffer rows inside executeQuery, so this does not exclude all data transfer from the measured call.

entries.title: How are nanoseconds converted to milliseconds?
entries.text: Subtract nanoTime timestamps and divide by 1_000_000.0.

entries.title: Which query stays constant?
entries.text: SELECT FROM Orf_Motif WHERE num=7, for both index states.

entries.title: Why compare multisets rather than row order?
entries.text: Without ORDER BY row order is not guaranteed; repeated keys/rows still require counts, so plain set equality can hide duplicates.

entries.title: Do historical faster timings prove indexing always wins?
entries.text: No. The recorded local result is a single environment observation with its own plan/data/cache/driver boundary.

entries.text: Course sources and scope Course index Confirmed identity and boundaries SOE203 — Software Engineering I is established by Week1-Module-Overview.pdf , PDF p. 1, and Week1-Lecture-Introduction.pdf , PDF p. 1. Lab sheets use “Software Engineering 1”. The destination retains that folder name. All original files remain unmodified in /Users/muxnoz/Documents/Software Engineering 1 . The supplied teaching sequence supports four units: introduction and professional responsibility; software processes; empirical development and Scrum; requirements engineering and SRS. These combine related lectures, readings and activities rather than treating every file as a unit. No later unit is inferred from the textbook. The module overview describes three lecture hours, one supervised tutorial/lab hour and six hours of independent study each week (p. 8). It refers to two coursework tasks using the same group, preferably six students (pp. 11–12), and a consolidation week (p. 7). The subsequently supplied CW1 specification confirms a 15% module weight, release on 8 October 2026 and deadline on 8 November 2026. Its required work is requirements analysis, four use-case models and activity diagrams, an EARS SRS, and one software-process model analysis. The precise submission time/timezone and live Learning Mall configuration remain unverified. The complete syllabus, handbook and CW2 requirements remain UNCONFIRMED. Screenshot text is historical evidence. Tools and conventions Learning Mall and an AI tutor are shown in the overview. Java is an example mention in the introduction, not confirmation of a required programming stack. Required language, framework, IDE and runtime versions are UNCONFIRMED . Scrum terminology and planning-poker conventions are reconciled in Unit 03. EARS, FURPS and UML use cases are source-supported; their required versions remain UNCONFIRMED. The UML check used 2.5.1 as a labelled supplementary reference. TLS 1.3, AES-256, Java/.tsx filenames and REST examples in the SRS case do not establish a required implementation stack. entries.title: Software Engineering I — Tutor Mode
entries.text: Software Engineering I — Tutor Mode SOE203 · Companion edition. The standard notes remain your reference. How to use this companion Orient with In 60 Seconds and Concept Preview → learn the mechanism → close references and attempt recall/practice → open a hint if needed → compare reasoning → record a demonstrated gap → revisit the explanation → try transfer. Preview cards orient you; recall cards test retrieval. Reading a solution is not evidence of mastery, and no fixed review interval is claimed optimal. Six complete historical question sections are available inside ExamsSoftware1.pdf : five coded CPT203 papers and one XJTLU-branded set with no visible code/date. XJTLU's catalogue identifies CPT203 as Software Engineering I, but the local material says SOE203; the code equivalence is unconfirmed. Use the corpus as adjacent-code historical evidence, not proof of the current format. No official marking scheme is supplied. All study status starts untested. Optional chat conventions include /teach , /quiz , /grade , /weak , /cram ; they do not run automatically. Resume from the tutor state, preserving prior attempts and source versions. Standard course index · Source scope and unresolved issues Unit 01 — Introduction and Professional Responsibility - Tutor Notes - Recall and Practice - Standard reference Unit 02 — Software Processes - Tutor Notes - Recall and Practice - Standard reference Unit 03 — Empirical Development and Scrum - Tutor Notes - Recall and Practice - Standard reference - Original practical lab Unit 04 — Requirements Engineering and SRS - Tutor Notes - Recall and Practice - Standard reference - Original practical lab If You Are Short on Time [!warning] Evidence boundary The six question sections are fully visible, but cover pages are missing, one set is undated, the local course code differs, and no marking scheme is present. This is a study-priority guide based on the supplied historical assessment sample, not a forecast of the next exam. Open the complete paper inventory, marks and limitations Priority 1 — High Exam Relevance Follow prerequisites first, then use the observed history: 1. Process models and justified selection — observed in 6/6 question sections, 112 known marks across process/agile allocations. Learn the decision method in Unit 02 · 5-Minute Review, then attempt Unit 02 · Problem T1. 2. Requirements engineering and specification — observed in 6/6 , 68 known marks , plus use-case modelling in 2/6 for 30 marks . Review Unit 04 · Definitions and distinctions, then attempt Unit 04 · Problem E1. 3. Agile decision reasoning — observed in 5/6 , 55 shared marks ; only one set directly tests Scrum mechanics. Review Unit 03 · 5-Minute Review, then attempt Unit 03 · Problem E1. The mark groups above are not additive: agile allocations overlap the broad process total. Priority 2 — Medium Exam Relevance - Fundamental lifecycle activities — observed once for 8 marks , shared with Unit 02. Use Unit 01 · 5-Minute Review and Card 11. - Specific Scrum mechanics — directly observed once for 6 marks even though broader agile reasoning recurs. Keep acceptance criteria, accountabilities and evidence loops precise; do not turn general agile frequency into a claim about velocity, poker or every Scrum event. Priority 3 — Remaining Source-Supported Material Do not drop the rest of the course. Professional responsibility, specification ownership, the four introductory quality attributes, change/evolution, detailed Scrum roles/events, estimation/forecast limits, EARS, interaction analysis, traceability and controlled change remain source-supported even where they were not observed—or were observed less often—in this historical sample. The papers also repeatedly contain design principles, testing/JUnit, risk/quality management, and UML class/state/activity/sequence diagrams. These are recorded as NOT IN MATERIALS for the currently supplied corpus. They are gaps, not permission to invent unsupported Tutor units. If You Have Only 30 Minutes This is a suggested schedule, not a measured learning guarantee: - 5 minutes — foundation: retrieve the four lifecycle activities and the difference between a process and a model from Unit 01 Card 11 and Unit 02 Card 01. - 8 minutes — process choice: read Unit 02 review and outline Problem T1 before opening its hint. - 7 minutes — agile reasoning: distinguish empirical learning from a model name, then outline Unit 03 Problem E1. - 8 minutes — requirements: review user/system and functional/quality distinctions, then outline Unit 04 Problem E1. - 2 minutes — closed-book recall: speak one justification, one limitation and one missing-evidence question for each of the previous two answers. Sacrifices: this route omits most worked examples, full exercise navigation, detailed Scrum events/forecasting, use-case drawing practice, EARS variants, traceability/change-control practice, professional ethics and all unsupported historical-paper gaps. It is not full coverage. Production and study status All four companion units are ready for self-study: eight primary notes, 53 recall cards and 23 local practice problems. The navigation covers all 68 original tasks and their subparts through the unchanged reference exercises/labs. All study status remains untested . Source and structural review passed for the original Tutor edition; the assessment update was separately checked against all 29 page images and the affected Markdown. Native Obsidian viewing and A4 export remain untested. The preserved source disagreements matter when interpreting examples; Unit 03 locally corrects the standard reference's chart panel count. Historical CPT203 question evidence is available with the code/cover/scheme limitations above; the current SOE203 format and official marking criteria remain unconfirmed. entries.text: Past-paper intelligence Tutor start · Coverage and validation Evidence base and limits Evidence base: six distinct, completely inspected question sections in one 29-page image-only compilation: five coded XJTLU CPT203 papers and one XJTLU-branded paper set whose code/date are not visible. The missing first/cover pages make every document administratively partial, but the supplied question sequences begin with Question A/A1, total 100 marks, and end with the paper. Thus positive observations, question marks and question-section absences are usable; duration, choice rules, allowed materials and cover-page instructions remain unknown. ExamsSoftware1.pdf is a user-assembled image PDF, not an original digital paper bundle. XJTLU branding, academic-use watermarks and visible paper codes support the embedded pages' institutional origin. No answer key, rubric or official marking scheme is present. Marks below are question allocations, not inferred marking points. The current teaching sources say SOE203 — Software Engineering I . The [XJTLU module catalogue]( identifies CPT203 — Software Engineering I and describes closely matching outcomes, but no supplied official source states that SOE203 and CPT203 are equivalent codes. The corpus is therefore treated as historical adjacent-code evidence . It supports bounded study priorities for source-supported overlapping topics; it does not establish the current SOE203 format or make questions outside the supplied teaching material part of the current course. entries.title: In 60 Seconds
entries.text: Software engineering begins when other people must depend on software over time. A working program is one part of that commitment. You need to identify the whole product, establish who controls its requirements, judge four different quality attributes, manage change, and communicate honestly about evidence and risk. These ideas connect: ownership determines whose needs matter; quality makes those needs discussable; lifecycle work produces evidence; professional responsibility governs the claims you make. After studying, you should be able to explain why a demonstration is insufficient, distinguish generic from customized products, diagnose a quality weakness, and justify a release decision within practical constraints. No programming background is required. Source: S15 PDF pp.4–8,17–28,35–41 (full filenames in the cards and references below).

entries.title: Concept Preview
entries.text: [!info] The professional product Concept: The professional product. Plain-language meaning: People need configuration and understandable documentation as well as executable behavior. Why it matters: A program can work for its author yet fail the people receiving it. Connects to: quality and lifecycle evidence. Source: Week1-Lecture-Introduction.pdf , PDF pp.4–8,14–15. [!info] Specification ownership Concept: Specification ownership. Plain-language meaning: The person paying or using a product does not always control its future requirements. Why it matters: Ownership changes how scope decisions are negotiated. Connects to: generic and customized products. Source: Week 1-Lab-Introduction-ExampleAnswers.pdf , PDF p.2, Q3. [!info] Four quality lenses Concept: Four quality lenses. Plain-language meaning: Changeability, trust, resource use and user fit answer different questions. Why it matters: One good attribute cannot establish the others. Connects to: maintainability; dependability/security; efficiency; acceptability. Source: Week1-Lecture-Introduction.pdf , PDF p.17, source table. [!info] Change and responsibility Concept: Change and responsibility. Plain-language meaning: Software does not physically wear out; changed logic and assumptions can introduce faults. Why it matters: Engineering must support useful evolution while making honest claims about its risks. Connects to: modularity, validation and professional duties. Source: Week1-Lecture-Introduction.pdf , PDF pp.21–23,35–38.

entries.title: Before You Start
entries.text: A requirement says what is needed from a system; a constraint limits acceptable solutions, such as a budget. A stakeholder is someone with a relevant interest in the system. Here these are working meanings needed to understand the lecture's requirements/customer discussion; Unit 04 develops the requirements methods. A program expresses instructions, while configuration supplies environment-specific information needed to operate it. [^product] [!question] Quick prerequisite check Does a demonstration establish that somebody else can install and maintain the program? [!success]- Answer No. It shows behavior in the demonstrated environment, while installation, configuration and maintainable knowledge require their own evidence. Source: S15 PDF pp.6,14–15.

entries.title: The motivating question — A release under pressure
entries.text: Synthetic case. A university commissions a room-display service. It runs quickly on its author's laptop. Only that author knows the configuration. Staff cannot correct a room without asking the author. No one checked unauthorized changes. Management says the demonstration looks good and the budget is nearly spent. A room-allocation policy may change after release. Your task: Explain what is missing, who decides scope, what the demonstration proves, how to handle future change, and what to say about release. A successful answer covers the complete product and all four qualities, identifies missing evidence, and proposes a feasible next decision without inventing a numerical target or promising zero defects. Question Knowledge needed --- --- What is being delivered? Program versus professional system Who decides a scope change? Specification ownership What evidence is missing? Four quality attributes Why can tomorrow's change break today's behavior? Dependencies and deterioration What may the team honestly promise? Constraints and responsibility

entries.title: 1. Why does a working program still need engineering?
entries.text: [!note] Supplementary historical example — operating conditions matter A 1992 U.S. GAO report describes a Patriot tracking calculation whose time inaccuracy increased with continuous operation; its Appendix II lists approximately 0.34 seconds of inaccuracy after 100 hours. The teaching connection is that a short successful demonstration cannot establish behavior over a much longer operating period. This case does not prove that every failure has the same cause or that one design method prevents all failures. Primary source: [GAO/IMTEC-92-26]( Appendix II, printed p.15. Supplementary context, outside the course lecture. Intuition. A recipe that only its author can follow is not yet a dependable service for a kitchen. Similarly, a program that runs for its author is not the whole product another person needs. The analogy concerns supporting knowledge, not a claim that software follows physical wear mechanisms. Precise idea. The source describes a software system as software components plus configuration, system documentation and user documentation. Software engineering concerns all aspects of software production , including supporting management, within organizational and financial constraints. Computer science emphasizes theory and fundamentals; software engineering emphasizes practical development and delivery. Neither distinction makes theory irrelevant to engineering. [^product] Work through the release claim. First identify the users' task: staff must display and correct rooms. Then identify what has been delivered: one successful execution. Next identify what someone else needs: usable configuration, instructions and system knowledge, plus evidence about intended behavior. The gap between those lists explains why documentation, estimation and relevant discussion are engineering work, even when they add no executable feature. The lecture's Java screenshot includes this output statement: java System.out.print("Hello World!"); This snippet illustrates an output statement; it does not install or validate a complete system. The lecture's Java screenshot illustrates a program; it does not establish a required language/version. Its System.out.print("Hello World!") call is explained in the standard reference. No code is executed in this companion. [^product] Question Evidence from a successful demonstration Evidence still needed for delivery --- --- --- Does the behavior work? The demonstrated input and environment Agreed behavior under relevant conditions and failure cases Can others operate it? The author can run this setup Reproducible configuration and instructions, checked by intended users Can it change? The current version runs Understandable system knowledge and checks when requirements change Can a team support it? One author knows the implementation Shared information and an achievable agreement about responsibility and effort A program can already have excellent structure and tests. The distinction here is the scope of the evidence , not a claim that individual programming is necessarily fragile or unprofessional. Source principles: S15 PDF pp.6–9,14–15; the comparison is supplementary teaching reasoning. Worked decision. Reserve effort for documented configuration and a user check before calling the service ready. The justification is not “documentation is always good”; it is that the next user cannot reproduce the demonstrated behavior without the author's private knowledge. If the budget cannot cover the agreed delivery, negotiate scope or schedule instead of redefining an incomplete demonstration as completion. [!question] Explain it yourself Why can estimating work and writing user instructions count as engineering, although neither changes the program’s output? [!success]- Check your explanation Engineering covers all aspects of production under constraints. Estimation supports an achievable commitment; instructions help intended users operate the delivered system. Source: S15 PDF pp.7–9.

entries.title: 2. Who owns the specification?
entries.text: Problem first. The university pays a supplier, but can it insist on any future feature? Payment alone does not answer the question. For a generic product , the developer controls the specification for a wider market. For a customized product , a particular customer commissions the system and controls its specification through agreement with the developer. This is a distinction about product boundary and authority, not free versus paid software. [^ownership] Visible worked comparison. Suppose the university buys a general image editor. Its users can request an interface change, but an individual customer normally cannot dictate the supplier's roadmap. Now suppose the university commissions its own room service. Its agreed requirements determine the custom product, and later changes must be negotiated with the supplier because they may affect effort and schedule. A generic component can sit inside that customized service; classify the level you are discussing. Return to the case: “commissions” makes customized development the supported interpretation. The university decides desired scope through agreement; the developer must explain implementation consequences. Neither party can make an added feature consume no resources by calling it a small change.

entries.title: 3. How do the four quality attributes guide action?
entries.text: Problem first. The screen responds quickly. Is the product therefore good? The source's four attributes make this question precise. [^quality] Attribute Ask this question Case evidence and limit --- --- --- Maintainability Can it evolve as needs change? Knowledge held by one author makes future changes difficult Dependability and security Can users trust behavior and protection against damage or misuse? Unauthorized changes were not checked; do not claim protection passed Efficiency Does it use time, memory and processing resources appropriately? A quick demonstration is limited evidence for that demonstrated workload Acceptability Can intended users understand and use it in their environment? Staff need the author's help for their normal task How to reason step by step: name the observed fact; connect it to an attribute's meaning; state what the fact does and does not prove; choose evidence addressing the gap. A fast but wrong room display can be responsive and still undependable. An accurate display that staff cannot operate can be unacceptable. These are pedagogical counterexamples to the inference “one strength means total quality.” Worked plan. Have a second person reproduce the setup and explain a change, check permitted and unauthorized operations, agree a representative workload before measuring performance, and ask intended staff to complete their task. These are proposed evidence-gathering actions, not reported successful tests. The source supplies no performance target for this invented service, so do not silently invent one. The lecturer groups dependability and security together as one of four attributes. Lab Q1 asks for four additional attributes but lists five suggestions; any appropriate four should be explained. Usability, for example, overlaps with acceptability rather than becoming a fifth essential row. [^quality]

entries.title: 4. Why does software deteriorate if it does not wear out?
entries.text: Intuition. Changing a shared assumption can disturb code that still looks untouched. Logical relationships matter even when there is no physical material to erode. The source's curves show an idealized fall in failure rate as faults are fixed, then a schematic “actual” curve with spikes after changes. They illustrate possible new errors and interacting changes, not measured probabilities or a law that every change must fail. [^change] change-and-failure.svg Figure 1 — Following change into possible failure risk Read it: Follow the changed need through modification and possible side effects, then the controls used to reduce them. An arrow is a possible causal link, not a guaranteed failure. Key takeaway: Control dependencies and evidence around change; waiting alone does not wear out code. Provenance: Reused unchanged teaching SVG from the standard edition, based on S15 PDF pp.21–23; informal causal diagram, not UML. Worked change. A new allocation rule alters which room is displayed. First clarify the actual rule with stakeholders to avoid implementing the wrong change. Next identify the responsible part of the software and affected interactions. Make the change in a maintainable structure; then recheck the new behavior and behavior that used to work. Keep supporting information current so later engineers can understand the result. This operationalizes the source's requirements work, modularity, maintainability and comprehensive testing. [^change] Limit. Refusing all changes may preserve old behavior while making the product useless. Testing reduces uncertainty; it cannot establish the absence of every possible fault. Likewise, maintaining an existing system often preserves valuable knowledge, but the lab's strong preference for maintenance does not prove replacement is never justified. [^challenges]

entries.title: 5. How do lifecycle and responsibility change the release decision?
entries.text: Problem first. Management counts visible code as progress and asks the team to say “ready.” What work and obligations does that claim hide? The four fundamental activities are specification, design and implementation, validation, and evolution. They establish needs, construct a solution, check it against needs, and change it over time. They are activities, not a rule that each happens only once. Estimation, coordination and documentation support them. [^process] The long delivery time and high cost discussed in Lab Q2 follow from skilled work across these activities and the rework caused by dependencies. Rare inputs and environments help explain why not every fault is found before delivery. Embedded institutional knowledge helps explain maintenance effort. Intangibility and incomplete integration make “90% done” harder to verify than a count of physical objects. Each explanation connects a mechanism to a consequence instead of merely calling software complex. [^challenges] Application context changes the balance: stand-alone applications, interactive transaction systems, embedded control, batch processing, entertainment, simulation and data collection do not have identical constraints. The lecture's aircraft versus e-commerce contrast emphasizes criticality versus evolving requirements. Its web discussion emphasizes reuse, browser constraints and learning through increments for diverse users. AJAX and cloud-pricing remarks are historical source examples, not required technologies or current market claims. [^process] Professional responsibility extends to the effects of requirements, plans, tests and manuals as well as programs. The source names confidentiality, competence, intellectual property rights and computer misuse. In the case, competence includes representing what was checked honestly; confidentiality means entrusted information is not a convenient public debugging artifact. Client satisfaction does not cancel these obligations. [^ethics] Visible worked argument. “The client likes it, therefore release is responsible” has an unsupported step: satisfaction does not show that unauthorized modification was checked. A defensible response reports the successful demonstration and its limits, identifies the unfinished checks, and negotiates a release decision that respects scope, budget and affected users. Certification can support evidence of a minimum professional standard, but it cannot substitute for this product-specific reasoning. [^ethics]

entries.title: Return to the motivating question
entries.text: 1. Deliver the whole system: make configuration, instructions and maintainable knowledge part of the deliverable, because other people must operate it. 2. Agree scope with the commissioning university: treat the service as customized; discuss the costs of later policy changes. 3. Separate four quality conclusions: maintainability and acceptability show concrete weaknesses; efficiency has narrow demonstration evidence; dependability/security still lacks the stated check. 4. Prepare for evolution: clarify the room rule, contain side effects through maintainable responsibilities, and test changes and affected existing behavior. 5. Communicate the release boundary: report evidence and unknowns, then negotiate scope or schedule within budget. Do not claim unperformed validation passed. This closes every case question without prescribing an unsupported architecture, performance threshold or zero-defect guarantee.

entries.title: Definitions and distinctions
entries.text: Pair Decisive distinction Source --- --- --- Program / software system Instructions versus the wider delivered components and supporting information S15 pp.5–6 Generic / customized Developer versus commissioning customer specification control S12 p.2 Q3 Efficiency / acceptability Resource use versus fit for intended users S15 p.17 Deterioration / physical wear Change-induced logical risk versus material degradation S15 pp.21–23 Certification / product evidence Minimum professional standard versus behavior of this particular system S12 p.3 Q5

entries.title: Review
entries.text: Full Understanding Return to sections 1–5 and the case decisions. The standard reference expands application examples, the Java illustration and all original questions; use it when a distinction remains unclear. 5-Minute Review Identify the complete product and intended users. Establish who controls the specification. Use all four quality attributes separately. Explain change-induced risk through dependencies, then connect requirements work, maintainability and testing to risk reduction. Choose lifecycle emphasis for the actual application. State evidence, unknowns, constraints and consequences before recommending release. 60-Second Recall - Program versus system - Specification owner - Four quality attributes - One strength versus whole quality - Change without physical wear - Four lifecycle activities - Honest release evidence [^product]: Week1-Lecture-Introduction.pdf, PDF pp.4–9,14–15,43; Java screenshot at p.14 is illustrative and was not executed.
