entries.title: Introduction and Professional Responsibility
entries.text: Introduction and Professional Responsibility Course index · Notes · Exercises Learning goals Explain why a working program is only part of a professional system; distinguish generic and customized products by who controls their specification; use the four quality attributes to diagnose a proposal; and justify responses to change and professional dilemmas. No programming framework is required for this unit. Opening case — A program becomes a service Synthetic teaching case. A student wrote a timetable viewer for personal use. A university now wants staff and students to depend on it. The existing program runs on its author's laptop; its configuration is undocumented, only the author understands it, and nobody has checked it on other devices. The university may change room-allocation rules after release. The team has a fixed budget and must explain what it will deliver before promising a date. Questions: What is missing from the product? Who should control changes if this is commissioned solely for the university? Which qualities matter? Why can a later change break a previously working feature? What responsibilities remain if management wants to release immediately? Success criteria: Propose a defensible delivery approach covering the whole product, specification ownership, all four quality attributes, change risk, and honest communication within the budget. Do not invent a particular architecture or claim that all bugs can be eliminated. What We Need to Learn Case question Required concepts --- --- What must be delivered? Program, software system, professional production Who controls changes? Generic versus customized products What counts as good software? Maintainability, dependability/security, efficiency, acceptability Why can changes cause trouble? Intangibility, complexity, deterioration, lifecycle activities How should the team act? Constraints, stakeholder needs, professional responsibility 1. From instructions to a professional product A program describes computations, but users depend on more than instructions. A software system also includes the configuration needed to make the software work in its environment and the documentation needed to operate, understand and change it. A successful run on one laptop establishes very little about whether another person can install, use or maintain it.[^system] [!note] Software engineering An engineering discipline concerned with all aspects of software production , including the technical work and the management needed to deliver within organizational and financial constraints.[^engineering] “Engineering” means selecting methods that fit the actual problem. A team must reconcile useful behavior, cost, schedule and dependability. Computer science supplies theories and fundamentals; software engineering is concerned with the practical development and delivery of professional systems. These areas support one another.[^engineering] Worked example — Delivery evidence. “The viewer displays a timetable” is evidence of one behavior. A professional delivery also needs a known configuration, understandable user instructions, evidence that intended behavior has been checked, and enough system knowledge for someone else to make a safe change. Writing documentation and discussing needs are therefore part of production, even though neither adds a line of executable code. Professional software is commonly used by people other than its author, developed by teams and maintained throughout its life. These are motivating characteristics, not a rule that an individual can never create professional software. The source contrasts this with personal spreadsheets, experimental-data programs and hobby projects.[^professional] The Java illustration in the lecture The screenshot on PDF p. 14 contains this small example, transcribed without modernizing its syntax: java package com.example.helloworld; public class HelloWorld { public static void main(String args[]) { System.out.print("Hello World!"); } } HelloWorld is the class; execution of its main method calls System.out.print with the literal text Hello World! . The shown code does not use args or contain branching. Its expected effect is to print that text without adding a newline. It was not executed here. The screenshot is an illustration of programming, not an assigned project or evidence of a required Java version.[^professional] 2. Product ownership determines who can change the specification A specification describes what the product is required to do. For a ==generic product== sold to a market, the developer owns and controls its specification. For a ==customized product== commissioned by a particular customer, the customer controls it, and changes must be negotiated with the developer. The crucial distinction is control, not whether the user pays money.[^products] Product Who decides the specification? Practical consequence --- --- --- Generic Product developer Individual customers can influence requests but normally cannot dictate the evolution Customized Commissioning customer, through agreement with the supplier Scope changes need negotiation and may change cost or schedule Worked example. A general image editor serves many customers; one university cannot require the supplier to preserve its preferred interface. A commissioned university logistics system must follow the university's agreed needs. Generic components can still be used inside a customized system. The categories can overlap at different product boundaries, which explains the lecture's warning that the distinction is becoming blurred. Trade-off. A generic product spreads development cost across a market but may require the customer to adapt its workflow or train staff after a supplier update. Customization gives greater specification control but also makes the customer's decisions and change negotiations central to delivery. “No control” in the lab answer is best read as no individual authority over the supplier's specification, not no possibility of giving feedback. 3. Four attributes make quality discussable Saying “high quality” is too vague to guide a decision. The four essential attributes identify different reasons a functioning program may still be inadequate. The source table groups dependability and security as one attribute .[^quality] Attribute Meaning and mechanism Viewer example — synthetic --- --- --- Maintainability The software can evolve as needs change; understandable structure makes modifications feasible Another engineer can change the room rule without guessing what unrelated code does Dependability and security Reliability, safety and security support justified trust; failures and malicious access should not cause damage Check that users see correct information and cannot make unauthorized changes Efficiency Avoid wasting resources; includes response time, processing time and memory Measure whether the viewer responds adequately under its agreed workload Acceptability Intended users can understand and use it, and it fits the systems they use Staff can complete their normal task on supported devices Worked diagnosis. A fast viewer with the wrong room is efficient in one sense but undependable. A correct viewer with an incomprehensible interface may fail acceptability. A correct, usable viewer that only its author can change is still weak in maintainability. Quality cannot be inferred from a single attractive screen. Trade-off. More detailed checking takes effort now but may prevent costly failure later. More flexible structure can make change easier but also costs design time. State the user need and constraint before choosing the balance; no source gives a universal percentage of budget for each attribute. Other attributes in the lab suggestions include correctness, reusability, portability, usability and interoperability. These are not necessarily independent: usability contributes to acceptability, for example. When asked for four additional attributes, choose four and explain them rather than mistakenly presenting all five as the requested count.[^lab] 4. Software does not physically wear out, but it can deteriorate Software is intangible: its logical structure does not erode like a moving mechanical part. That makes copying and changing it possible without manufacturing a new physical mechanism, but it does not make complexity free. Interactions, assumptions and changes can make a system difficult to understand and expensive to modify.[^change] The lecture's idealized failure-rate curve falls as existing defects are corrected. Its “actual” curve has spikes after changes: a modification can introduce errors, correction reduces some of them, and another modification may arrive before the earlier baseline is recovered. These are schematic explanations , not measured data or a mathematical law. Unchanged software can also encounter a new environment or input that exposes an existing defect.[^change] change-and-failure.svg Figure 1 — How changes can create new failure risk Read it: Follow the possible causal chain from a changed need to a modification, possible defects, and controls for the next change. An arrow does not mean every change must fail. Key takeaway: The risk comes from changed logic, interactions or operating conditions; elapsed time alone does not physically wear down code. Provenance: Original teaching diagram based on Week1-Lecture-Introduction.pdf , PDF pp. 21–23; informal explanation, not UML. Two complementary ways to limit deterioration First, reduce avoidable change by understanding stakeholder needs and checking requirements early. Second, make necessary change safer through modularity, maintainability and comprehensive testing. A module is a part with a manageable responsibility; changing one part should disturb as few other parts as practicable. Testing seeks evidence about behavior after the change.[^change] Counterexample. Refusing all new requirements preserves old code but may make the system useless as the university changes. “Prevent deterioration” therefore means control the side effects and cost of change, not freeze a living product forever. Similarly, testing cannot prove the absence of every possible defect. Why the five development challenges persist Long delivery times come from understanding needs, designing, building, checking and reworking interconnected parts. Costs reflect skilled effort across that lifecycle. Some faults appear only with unusual data or production conditions. Existing systems embed knowledge and workflows, so replacement can be riskier than maintenance. Finally, progress is hard to observe in an intangible product: code quantity or a partly finished screen does not establish tested usefulness.[^lab] The lab answer strongly favors maintaining established systems. Treat this as a reasoned tendency under its assumptions, not proof that replacement is never justified. This limitation matters when the existing system no longer meets needs or cannot be changed economically. 5. Four activities, with methods chosen for the situation Every software process includes specification , design and implementation , validation , and evolution . Specification establishes needs and constraints; design and implementation construct a solution; validation checks that it meets requirements and user needs; evolution changes it after needs or circumstances change. These names identify activities, not a requirement to complete them once in that order.[^process] Worked example. Discussing whether students need the viewer on mobile devices supports specification. Deciding how responsibilities are divided supports design. Writing the implementation develops it. Checking real user tasks supports validation. Adapting room rules later is evolution. Estimation, team coordination and documentation support these activities. The lecture distinguishes stand-alone applications, interactive transaction-based applications, embedded control systems, batch processing systems, entertainment systems, modeling/simulation systems and data-collection systems. A personal image editor, an interactive booking service and an aircraft controller face different constraints; a process must match the product, organization and people.[^types] The aircraft/e-commerce contrast on p. 27 emphasizes careful early specification for critical control systems and feedback while web requirements evolve. It is a course illustration of different emphases; it does not establish that every aircraft project literally freezes every detail before any development. Why web-based development emphasizes feedback and reuse The lecture presents the web as an application platform, web services as ways to access functionality remotely, and cloud computing as remotely supplied computing services. Web systems can assemble existing components, but assembly still needs engineering. Browser capabilities constrain the interface, and diverse users make requirements difficult to predict. Delivering useful increments lets developers learn from real feedback.[^web] Source context. The lecture mentions AJAX and usage-based cloud payment. These are source examples, not a verified current ranking of interface techniques, a universal cloud-pricing rule, or a prescribed stack. The learning point is to consider platform constraints, reuse and feedback. Across systems, the lecture identifies heterogeneity, business/social change and security/trust as recurring challenges. A viewer working on one machine does not yet address different devices, changing institutional rules or justified user trust.[^types] 6. Professional responsibility changes technical decisions The source emphasizes that decisions affect people through programs and requirements, plans, specifications, designs, tests, manuals and training materials. Professional responsibility extends beyond merely avoiding unlawful behavior.[^ethics] Responsibility Engineering interpretation Synthetic failure to avoid --- --- --- Confidentiality Handle information entrusted to the team responsibly Publishing private configuration or user information as a debugging shortcut Competence Represent capabilities and limits honestly Claiming a safety review was completed when nobody qualified performed it Intellectual property rights Respect others' rights in software and materials Treating any available component as unrestricted material to copy Computer misuse Do not use technical ability dishonestly or abusively Using access granted for maintenance for unrelated unauthorized activity These are course-level ethical principles, not jurisdiction-specific legal advice. Certification is a discussion question : the supplied lab favors it for competence, accountability and public trust, while also acknowledging that certification is not a guarantee of continuing competence. A defensible answer distinguishes evidence of a minimum standard from proof that a particular product is safe.[^lab] The lecture names schedule, budget, operational, technical/external, security, coding, staffing and compromised-design risks in the p. 39 infographic. The useful mechanism is to connect a risk to a consequence: lateness can delay benefits; an overrun can consume funds needed elsewhere; faulty behavior can interrupt work or harm users. Understanding and validating requirements reduces the chance of efficiently building the wrong product.[^risk] [!warning] Satisfaction is not a complete release test PDF p. 40 calls client satisfaction the primary measure of project success. Read this alongside pp. 35–38 and the quality attributes: a satisfied client does not erase obligations concerning honest evidence, security or the effects on other users. Solve the opening case 1 — Deliver a system. Add a documented configuration, user instructions, checked behavior and maintainable system knowledge to the existing code. This follows the distinction between a program and a product other people must depend on. The result is a delivery scope the team can estimate, rather than an unsupported promise based on a laptop demonstration. 2 — Establish ownership. Because the case says the university alone commissions the product, treat it as customized development. Agree requirements and negotiate later changes with the university. This gives the customer scope control while exposing the cost and schedule consequences of requested additions. 3 — Define quality evidence. Use the four attributes: show another engineer can understand a rule change; check intended behavior and unauthorized changes; agree and measure an appropriate workload; and ask representative staff/students to attempt their tasks on supported devices. The case supplies no numerical performance threshold, so negotiating one is necessary before claiming success. 4 — Prepare for change. Organize room-rule responsibility so a later change has limited side effects, keep documentation current, and recheck affected and previously working behavior. The purpose is to lower avoidable rework and new defects, while retaining the ability to evolve. 5 — Respond to release pressure. State what is checked, what is unknown and what remains in the agreed scope. If the budget cannot cover the proposed scope and evidence, negotiate scope or schedule with the customer. Do not claim that unperformed checks passed. This is both an engineering constraint decision and a professional-responsibility decision. Success check: The response covers all five questions and every quality attribute. It uses the fixed budget as a constraint, preserves room for later change, makes no unsupported architecture choice, and offers no impossible guarantee of zero bugs. Exam-style answer and reusable method Example answer: Software engineering is needed when others depend on a system over time. It coordinates specification, development, validation and evolution under practical constraints. Quality includes maintainability, dependability/security, efficiency and acceptability. Appropriate methods depend on the application and organization, while professional responsibility requires honest claims and attention to the effects of decisions. For a new case: identify users and product boundary; establish specification ownership; identify constraints and quality evidence; connect risks to their mechanisms; choose a proportionate process; and explain the decision's consequences and limits. This framework organizes an argument, but cannot replace missing stakeholder information or determine detailed design by itself. Common mistakes and quick review - “It runs, so it is ready.” A successful execution is only one piece of evidence about a complete system. - “Generic means free.” The distinction concerns the target market and specification ownership. - “Changing software is cheap because copying is cheap.” Logical dependencies make modifications costly even without manufacturing costs. - “Certification guarantees safe software.” A credential and product evidence answer different questions. - “One process is best everywhere.” Product criticality, change, people and constraints affect the choice. [!summary] Review checkpoint Explain the difference between a program and a maintained product. Name all four attributes without splitting dependability/security into two. Explain a change-induced failure without physical wear. Then justify a delivery decision using evidence and constraints. Practice these in the linked Exercises; reading a solution is not evidence of mastery. [^system]: Week1-Lecture-Introduction.pdf , PDF pp. 4–6. [^engineering]: Week1-Lecture-Introduction.pdf , PDF pp. 7–8, 24 and 43. [^professional]: Week1-Lecture-Introduction.pdf , PDF pp. 14–15; code read from the page-14 screenshot. [^change]: Week1-Lecture-Introduction.pdf , PDF pp. 4 and 20–23; Week 1-Lab-Introduction-ExampleAnswers.pdf , PDF pp. 1–3, Q2 and Q4. [^process]: Week1-Lecture-Introduction.pdf , PDF pp. 26–28. entries.title: Introduction and Professional Responsibility — Exercises
entries.text: Introduction and Professional Responsibility — Exercises Course index · Notes · Exercises Attempt each statement first. Hints and complete solutions sit immediately below it. Original prompts are retained, including prompts embedded in the lecture. Solutions to opinion questions are reasoned interpretations unless an instructor answer is supplied. Exercise L1 — Attributes of professional software ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Week 1-Lab-Introduction-ExampleAnswers.pdf, PDF p. 1, Q1. What are the four important attributes that all professional software should have? Suggest four other attributes that may sometimes be significant. [!tip]- Hint Recall the source table; one of its four rows combines two related terms. [!success]- Solution Step 1 — Essential attributes. Maintainability; dependability and security; efficiency; acceptability. They address evolution, trust, resource use, and fit for intended users respectively. Step 2 — Four additional attributes. Correctness: fulfills the specified behavior. Reusability: useful in another system. Portability: adaptable to another environment. Interoperability: works with other systems. Interpretation. The supplied answer also lists usability, giving five possible suggestions despite asking for four. Any defensible selection of four can meet the question; attributes can overlap. Exercise L2 — Five persistent development challenges ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★★☆ Source: Week 1-Lab-Introduction-ExampleAnswers.pdf, PDF pp. 1–2, Q2; also S15 PDF p. 20. Develop your own answers and discuss with classmates: 1. Why does it take so long to get software finished? 2. Why are development costs so high? 3. Why can’t we find all errors before delivery? 4. Why do we spend so much time maintaining existing programs? 5. Why is progress difficult to measure? [!tip]- Hint For each answer, connect a property of the work to its consequence rather than repeating “software is complex”. [!success]- Solution 1 — Time. Needs must be understood, designs implemented, and behavior checked. Requirements changes can disturb other parts and require rework. 2 — Cost. Skilled people perform those activities across the lifecycle; cost includes understanding, design, validation and maintenance, not only coding. 3 — Errors. The possible inputs and situations exceed what normal evaluation can cover. Some faults need unusual production conditions or changed hardware to become visible. Testing reduces uncertainty; it does not prove universal correctness. 4 — Maintenance. Established software embodies business rules, edge cases and working routines. Preserving those while changing the existing system can be less disruptive than replacement. The source favors maintenance; this is not a proof that replacement is always worse. 5 — Progress. Intangible work and incomplete integration make percentage claims difficult to verify. A feature can appear nearly complete yet conceal an unknown amount of defect correction. Discuss evidence of useful checked behavior, rather than code volume alone. Discussion step. Compare which mechanism dominates in each classmate’s example. No class discussion is claimed to have occurred. Exercise L3 — Who owns the specification ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Week 1-Lab-Introduction-ExampleAnswers.pdf, PDF p. 2, Q3. What is the most important difference between generic and custom software product development? What does it mean in practice for users of generic products? [!tip]- Hint Distinguish influence through feedback from authority to decide the specification. [!success]- Solution Step 1 — Distinction. The generic-product developer controls its specification; the commissioning customer controls the customized product’s specification through agreement with the developer. Step 2 — Consequence. Generic-product users normally cannot dictate individual feature or interface decisions. Supplier updates may require training or workflow changes, and users may need to adapt business processes to available functionality. Limit. Users can still give feedback or choose another product. The issue is lack of individual specification authority, not lack of any influence. Exercise L4 — Limit deterioration under change ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Week 1-Lab-Introduction-ExampleAnswers.pdf, PDF pp. 2–3, Q4. Modern applications need frequent modification before and after first release. Suggest ways to build software to stop deterioration due to changes. [!tip]- Hint Address both unnecessary change and the side effects of necessary change. [!success]- Solution Step 1 — Reduce avoidable rework. Work with stakeholders and improve requirements study so the team understands intended needs before committing to the wrong behavior. Step 2 — Contain necessary changes. Use modular structure and maintainable code/documentation so a modification affects fewer other parts and can be understood. Step 3 — Detect side effects. Test comprehensively after modification, including behavior that used to work. Conclusion. These measures reduce deterioration risk. They cannot guarantee that no change will introduce a defect; freezing the product would also prevent needed evolution. Exercise L5 — Should engineers be certified ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★★☆ Source: Week 1-Lab-Introduction-ExampleAnswers.pdf, PDF p. 3, Q5. Discuss whether professional software engineers should be certified in the same way as doctors or lawyers. [!tip]- Hint Separate the public-interest argument, evidence of competence, and the limits of a credential. [!success]- Solution Step 1 — Source position. The suggested answer favors certification because software failures can cause economic damage or endanger people, and a recognized minimum standard supports competence, accountability and trust. Employers also gain a benchmark for assessing candidates. Step 2 — Evaluate the inference. Demonstrating a minimum standard at certification does not establish that every later decision or product is correct. Continuing competence and product-specific checks still matter. Step 3 — Reasoned discussion. One defensible position supports certification where the consequences of failure justify it, while requiring an appropriate scope and current evidence. A critical answer can discuss the limits of one credential across varied software work. The source supplies an argument, not a uniquely provable answer or a statement that a particular licensing law applies. Exercise P4 — Intangible software ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Week1-Lecture-Introduction.pdf, PDF p. 4, implications prompt. What benefits and drawbacks follow from software being abstract and intangible, without the material/manufacturing constraints described in the lecture? [!tip]- Hint Think about the freedom to change logical structures and the cost of understanding the resulting interactions. [!success]- Solution The benefit is flexibility: software can implement and change logical behavior without fabricating a new physical mechanism for each change. The drawback is that weak natural constraints permit very complex structures and interactions, making understanding and modification expensive. This does not mean running software escapes limits on processor time, memory, money or people. Exercise P5 — Is Java code software ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Week1-Lecture-Introduction.pdf, PDF p. 5, “Your JAVA code?”. Relate your Java code to the lecture’s definition of computer software. [!tip]- Hint Distinguish a program from the larger system delivered to users. [!success]- Solution Java source code is a program representation and therefore part of computer software. A professional system may additionally require configuration, documentation and other components. The question does not establish Java as the course’s mandatory language or any version requirement. Exercise P9 — Which activities belong ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Week1-Lecture-Introduction.pdf, PDF p. 9. Which are activities when developing a software system? Test the program; write source code; estimate completion time; write user documentation; discuss with classmates. [!tip]- Hint Use the “all aspects of production” definition. [!success]- Solution All five can contribute: testing checks behavior; coding implements it; estimation supports planning; user documentation supports use; and relevant discussion helps clarify needs or coordinate decisions. Discussion counts when it concerns the work, not merely because classmates are present. Exercise P12 — Potential causes of failure ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Week1-Lecture-Introduction.pdf, PDF p. 12. Assess each proposed cause: changing requirements; adding budget; starting development immediately to save time; software bugs. [!tip]- Hint Ask what mechanism would cause harm; do not treat every change as intrinsically harmful. [!success]- Solution Unmanaged requirements changes can cause rework and scope/schedule problems. Adding budget is not inherently a failure cause; it may fund necessary work, although poor management can still waste it. Starting implementation before understanding needs risks building the wrong product; starting promptly after suitable clarification is different. Bugs can cause incorrect behavior and rework. Thus the likely intended selections are requirements change, premature development and bugs, with these qualifications; no official key is supplied for this prompt. Exercise P16 — Engineering boundaries ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Week1-Lecture-Introduction.pdf, PDF p. 16. Discuss whether software engineering includes team forming, specification, software selection, validation, and software sales. [!tip]- Hint Distinguish core technical activities, supporting management and related commercial work. [!success]- Solution Specification and validation are core technical activities. Team formation supports project management. Selecting software can be engineering when evaluating components or systems to satisfy needs. Sales is a commercial activity rather than one of the four fundamental engineering activities, although engineers may provide technical evidence during it. The broad wording admits context-dependent answers; it is not safe to declare selection unrelated when the course also teaches reuse. Exercise P18 — Examples of product types ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Week1-Lecture-Introduction.pdf, PDF p. 18, both “Any example?” prompts. Give an example of a generic software product and of a customized software product. Explain the distinction. [!tip]- Hint State the product boundary and who controls its requirements. [!success]- Solution A general-market image editor is generic: its developer sets the specification for many customers. A university-commissioned logistics application is customized: the university controls its agreed requirements. These source-compatible examples are about market and ownership; using a generic component does not make the entire commissioned product generic. Exercise P19 — Classify the four examples ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Week1-Lecture-Introduction.pdf, PDF p. 19. Which can be considered generic software? A. Adobe Photoshop; B. logistics software for the XJTLU library; C. a language-translation mobile app in the Apple Store; D. ChatGPT. [!tip]- Hint Use the descriptions as classroom examples, not a claim about any product’s current features or pricing. [!success]- Solution Under the lecture’s intended descriptions, A, C and D are offered to broad user populations and are generic. B is treated as a system commissioned for the library and therefore customized. If B instead meant an off-the-shelf library package, classification would depend on that missing fact; the source wording alone should not erase the assumption. Exercise P33 — Why incremental web delivery ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Week1-Lecture-Introduction.pdf, PDF p. 33. Which reasons support incremental web development? It runs in a browser; users are diverse and requirements unpredictable; developers learn from feedback while building; the web is too large. [!tip]- Hint Choose reasons that connect increments to reduced uncertainty. [!success]- Solution The strongest reasons are diverse/unpredictable requirements and learning from feedback. Each increment exposes behavior that users can evaluate, helping the team revise the next work. Browser execution alone does not force incremental delivery, and “the web is too large” does not identify a relevant development mechanism. Exercise P41 — Consequences of project trouble ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Week1-Lecture-Introduction.pdf, PDF p. 41. What can happen if software development is late, over budget, or produces a system that does not work or is full of bugs? [!tip]- Hint Give a consequence and explain why it follows; avoid treating every project as equally critical. [!success]- Solution Late: intended benefits arrive later; dependent work may be delayed. Over budget: the organization may lose funds needed for other commitments, and severe overruns can threaten viability. Faulty: users may be unable to do their work or may act on wrong results; consequences depend on the system and can include economic or human harm. These mechanisms explain the lecture’s bankruptcy warning without asserting that every defect bankrupts a company. Exercise S1 — A fast but fragile release SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Provenance: Synthetic practice using the concepts taught in Notes. A team says its product is ready because a demonstration is fast. Only one person understands it, and users cannot complete their normal task without that person. Identify the weak quality attributes and justify the next action. [!tip]- Hint A positive result for one attribute does not establish all four. [!success]- Solution Maintainability is weak because system knowledge is concentrated in one person. Acceptability is weak because intended users cannot independently complete their work. A fast demonstration offers limited efficiency evidence for that workload and gives no assurance of dependability/security. Clarify the required tasks, improve support and maintainable knowledge, and validate with intended users before asserting readiness.

entries.title: In 60 Seconds
entries.text: A process model is a simplified picture of how development work is organized. This unit teaches three mechanisms: Waterfall makes phase outputs and agreements explicit; incremental development creates opportunities to learn from working versions; reuse-oriented development reconciles needs with available software. All three still require specification, design/implementation, validation and evolution. You should be able to choose a process basis from project conditions, explain its benefit and limitation, trace a change through dependent work, and distinguish planning tests from running them. The important question is not which model is universally best, but which mechanism addresses the uncertainty and consequences in front of you. Source: S17 PDF pp.3–13,15–49,52–67.

entries.title: Concept Preview
entries.text: [!info] Process versus model Concept: Process versus model. Plain-language meaning: Real teams do activities; a model abstracts how those activities are organized. Why it matters: A model name cannot prove the team performed the necessary work. Connects to: roles, artifacts and evidence. Source: Week2-Lecture-Software Processes-r.pdf , PDF pp.3–4,10–13. [!info] Phase commitments Concept: Phase commitments. Plain-language meaning: Waterfall uses distinct stages and reviewed outputs to coordinate work. Why it matters: Changing an agreed input can require changes and approval in downstream work. Connects to: requirements stability and change cost. Source: Week2-Lecture-Software Processes-r.pdf , PDF pp.15–21. [!info] Useful increments Concept: Useful increments. Plain-language meaning: Build a useful part, check it with the existing system and learn before choosing more work. Why it matters: Early feedback can correct assumptions before every feature is built. Connects to: uncertainty, dependencies and integration. Source: Week2-Lecture-Software Processes-r.pdf , PDF pp.28–37. [!info] Fit through reuse Concept: Fit through reuse. Plain-language meaning: Understand needs, examine candidate capabilities, then negotiate fit before integration. Why it matters: Less new code does not automatically mean the right system. Connects to: two requirements activities and supplier control. Source: Week2-Lecture-Software Processes-r.pdf , PDF pp.46–49.

entries.title: Before You Start
entries.text: Recall Unit 01: requirements describe needs and constraints; validation checks the product against requirements and user needs; evolution keeps it useful as circumstances change. A component is a part of the system; integration combines parts so their interactions can be checked. The source develops component/interface design and integration on pp.59–65. No framework is required. Review Unit 01 if these meanings are unclear [!question] Prerequisite retrieval Why does a correct component not establish that the whole system works? [!success]- Answer Components can disagree at interfaces or interact unexpectedly. Integration and system-level checks examine relationships that isolated component tests do not establish. Source: S17 PDF p.65.

entries.title: The motivating question — Four projects, one proposed method
entries.text: Source-based problem: Lab Q1 presents an anti-lock braking controller, a novel virtual-reality maintenance-research system, a replacement university accounting system, and an interactive journey planner for low environmental impact. A manager proposes using one identical method for all four. Explain a more defensible choice for each. The source gives no budget, mandatory tool, complete architecture or assurance standard. Success means connecting a project condition to a process mechanism, identifying a trade-off and stating what needs confirmation. A model recommendation is not a safety certification or a completed design. [^lab] Decision question Knowledge needed --- --- What is the team choosing? Model versus real process What needs early agreement? Phase outputs and rework What must be learned from users? Increments and feedback What can existing software provide? Component analysis and fit Which checks remain necessary? Validation levels and test planning

entries.title: 1. What does a process model leave out?
entries.text: Intuition. A route map can show major stops without specifying who drives, whether the vehicle works, or how a disruption is handled. A process model similarly simplifies real work. Its usefulness is coordination and reasoning, not a guarantee of execution quality. A software process is the actual related activities, methods and practices used to develop and maintain software. A process model represents selected activities and their organization. A real process must supply local roles, outputs, reviews, tools and constraints. The source's broad claim that a model “ensures” good practice should be understood as its intended support, not proof of an outcome. [^model] Worked inference. “We follow Waterfall” tells you something about intended phase organization. It does not tell you whether the requirements were correct or the test results were inspected. Ask what artifact was produced, who reviewed it and what evidence supports the claim. The same challenge applies to “we are agile.” The lecture names other model families for orientation, but fully develops the three below. Naming a Spiral or V-Model here is not a substitute for source-supported instruction in that method.

entries.title: 2. When are phase outputs useful—and expensive to change?
entries.text: Problem first. If design was approved using a requirement that later changes, why does the correction cost more than editing one sentence? Waterfall represents principal work as stages: requirements analysis/definition; system/software design; implementation and unit testing; integration and system testing; operation and maintenance. Each stage produces an output that informs later work. A deliverable is an output to supply; a milestone is a significant point in the plan. The phase structure makes commitments and progress artifacts visible. [^waterfall] waterfall-phases.svg Figure 1 — Read the outputs between stages Read it: Follow the main progression downward. Implementation already includes unit testing. The source allows overlap and feedback; this simplified sequence does not prohibit rework. Key takeaway: A downstream stage relies on decisions made earlier, which is why changing them has consequences. Provenance: Unchanged standard teaching SVG based on S17 PDF pp.15–21; informal process diagram. Visible worked trace: A requirement says a report covers one term. After design approval it changes to compare several terms. First identify affected design/data decisions. Then identify code and expected test results based on the old scope. Update those artifacts and repeat appropriate reviews. The propagated work plus reapproval—not merely the size of the edited requirement—explains the schedule and budget cost in Lab Q4. Reducing avoidable revisits is sensible; preserving a known serious mistake to protect a schedule is not the implication. [^waterfall] When it helps. Stable, understood requirements and explicit review obligations can make phase agreements valuable. Documentation preserves reasoning and supports planning. Limit: document approval cannot reveal every problem users would notice in the working whole. If assumptions are highly uncertain, late feedback can invalidate much completed work. [^tradeoffs] [!warning] Source reconciliation: testing and risk SOURCE A: S17 p.25 says testing is late and risk management is not inherent. SOURCE B: pp.16–17 include unit testing; pp.62–63 include reviews and early test plans; p.24 praises controlled change. CONFLICT: an absolute reading makes these incompatible. SAFEST INTERPRETATION: whole-system execution may arrive late, but early reviews, unit checks and planning remain possible; change control supports risk work without replacing explicit risk analysis. CONFIRMATION STATUS: interpretation, not an instructor-confirmed correction. Exact assessment wording remains unconfirmed.

entries.title: 3. What does an increment let the team learn?
entries.text: Problem first. An online flower shop cannot yet take payment. Can showing its listing and registration functions still be useful? An increment adds functionality to a previous version. Incremental development interleaves specification, development and validation: evidence from building or checking one part can change what is specified next. Interleaving is about information flowing during the work, not an excuse for undefined requirements. [^increments] Work through the source case: begin with an outline of the shop's needs; select listing and registration; specify, design and build those functions; unit-test and integrate them; expose the version to users; use feedback to plan cart/checkout, followed by later payment, tracking and reviews. Listing alone cannot deliver the final purchase workflow, but it can expose misunderstandings about navigation and product presentation earlier. Be explicit about that partial value. [^increments] Why it helps. The team commits less work before seeing selected user evidence. Feedback can redirect later effort. A useful early release may deliver value while the rest is built. These benefits require actual feedback and a meaningful decomposition. Dependency counterexample. Suppose feedback changes the meaning of a product variant. The current cart and an earlier listing may both depend on it. S17 p.32's claim that only the current increment changes is therefore a favorable local-change case; pp.36–37 explicitly warn about dependencies across increments. Earlier work may need revision and regression checks. Supporting an old increment while building a new one also consumes resources. Incremental delivery is not identical to agile. A team can plan increments in detail long in advance. The source's agile introduction adds an emphasis on adaptation, customer collaboration and short feedback cycles; Scrum is taught next. [^increments] [!question] Explain it yourself Why can three numbered releases still fail to provide the learning benefit of incremental development? [!success]- Check your explanation If no useful feedback influences later decisions, the releases may merely divide delivery dates. Dependencies, integration and validation still need management. Source: S17 PDF pp.29,32–37,74.

entries.title: 4. Why does reuse require requirements work twice?
entries.text: Problem first. A replacement package is attractive, but cannot perform one essential university workflow. Should the team simply remove that requirement? Intuition. Shopping for a ready-made part requires knowing both what you need and what is actually available. Reuse-oriented engineering makes that reconciliation explicit. It can use web services, packaged components or configured stand-alone systems; framework names in the lecture are examples, not selected course tools. [^reuse] reuse-and-requirements.svg Figure 2 — The information changes between requirements activities Read it: Requirements specification → component analysis → requirements modification → system design with reuse → development/integration → system validation. Key takeaway: You learn candidate capabilities after setting broad needs, so the second requirements activity has different information. Provenance: Unchanged standard teaching SVG, checked against S17 PDF p.47; informal flow, not UML. Worked negotiation: state the required accounting services and integration constraints first. Evaluate candidate packages against those needs. Then separate acceptable adaptations from essential gaps: negotiate a changed workflow when it preserves the real need; plan additions when feasible; reject a candidate when an essential need cannot reasonably be met. Design and integrate the chosen combination, then validate the whole. This is the source's two requirements activities made operational. [^reuse] Reuse can reduce new development, cost and time, but may introduce requirement compromises and dependency on supplier evolution. “Already exists” is evidence of availability, not suitability. A generic supplier's update does not automatically respect the commissioned system's promises.

entries.title: 5. Which work remains in every process?
entries.text: Question. If a team chooses a model, can it omit work not drawn in the diagram? No: a simplified representation does not remove the underlying obligations. [^activities] Activity Mechanism and useful output --- --- Specification Check feasibility; elicit/analyze needs; record user/system requirements; validate the agreed document Design and implementation Define architecture, interfaces, components and data; implement, review, build and integrate Validation Inspect artifacts and execute suitable checks; compare evidence with requirements and customer needs Evolution Correct faults, adapt to environments, improve qualities and prevent future problems Architecture concerns main components and their relationships. Interfaces specify interactions; ambiguity can make separately correct components fail together. Component design specifies internal operation or changes to a reused part. Data/database design is in this course's source, but no particular DBMS is selected. Supporting work includes planning and risk management, version/change/build control, deployment and training, documentation and process improvement. [^activities] Testing is not one undifferentiated event. Component tests check parts, system tests check the integrated whole, and acceptance tests examine operational suitability with customer data/needs. Test planning specifies what evidence will be needed; execution produces actual observations. Requirements and system specifications can inform an acceptance-test plan before an executable system exists. System specification/design inform integration planning; execution later checks the built product. The p.63 diagram shows these relationships. [^validation] Visible worked example: for a journey planner, component evidence can check a cost calculation for controlled input; system evidence checks that the displayed route matches the selected result; acceptance evidence checks intended users' journey cases. Passing the first does not establish the other two. Regression tests recheck previously tested behavior after changes. Source language about “free of defects” is a goal, not a universal guarantee from sampled executions. [^validation]

entries.title: Return to the motivating question
entries.text: - Braking controller: the source favors a plan-driven/Waterfall basis because failure consequences demand careful upfront analysis and evidence. Confirm timing, hardware and assurance needs. The process name alone does not establish safety. - Novel research VR: use increments and possibly UI prototypes to discover needs. Confirm the intended users and evaluation purpose; a prototype is feedback evidence, not proof of final quality. - Accounting replacement: evaluate reuse because established needs and integration with existing systems may fit available software. Confirm actual candidates before treating this as feasible. - Journey planner: use meaningful increments and user feedback to refine interaction needs. Confirm whether partial versions are useful and what environmental-impact assumptions mean. These reproduce the lab's recommendations while exposing their conditions. A project can combine mechanisms. Criticality and uncertainty are independent dimensions: internal learning may be needed even when deploying incomplete operational behavior is unacceptable. [^lab]

entries.title: Definitions and distinctions
entries.text: Pair Decisive distinction Source --- --- --- Process / model Real activities versus an abstraction of their organization S17 pp.3–13 Deliverable / milestone Output versus significant plan point S17 pp.17,24 Incremental / agile Functional growth versus a wider adaptive philosophy S17 p.74 Test plan / test execution Intended evidence versus observed behavior S17 pp.63,71 Component / system test Part versus integrated relationships S17 p.65

entries.title: Review
entries.text: Full Understanding Revisit the three mechanism sections and their worked examples, then the four project decisions. Consult the standard reference for the expanded comparison dimensions and support-activity catalog. 5-Minute Review Begin with stability, uncertainty and failure consequences. Ask whether useful partial functionality and stakeholder feedback are possible. Examine reusable capabilities without surrendering essential needs. Select the mechanisms that fit; state their trade-offs. Plan evidence early, execute it when the relevant artifact exists, and keep all four lifecycle activities and supporting work visible. 60-Second Recall - Process versus model - Phase outputs and reapproval - Useful increment and feedback - Cross-increment dependencies - Two reuse requirements activities - Plan versus execute a test - Model choice versus quality evidence [^model]: Week2-Lecture-Software Processes-r.pdf, PDF pp.3–13. [^waterfall]: Week2-Lecture-Software Processes-r.pdf, PDF pp.15–21; Week 2-Lab- Software Process-Example-Answer.pdf, PDF p.2 Q4. [^tradeoffs]: Week2-Lecture-Software Processes-r.pdf, PDF pp.23–26,38–45. [^increments]: Week2-Lecture-Software Processes-r.pdf, PDF pp.28–37,74; flower-shop case p.33. [^reuse]: Week2-Lecture-Software Processes-r.pdf, PDF pp.46–49; Week 2-Lab- Software Process-Example-Answer.pdf, PDF p.2 Q3. [^activities]: Week2-Lecture-Software Processes-r.pdf, PDF pp.52–61,67,70–73. [^validation]: Week2-Lecture-Software Processes-r.pdf, PDF pp.62–66,71; p.63 diagram visually inspected. [^lab]: Week 2-Lab- Software Process-Example-Answer.pdf, PDF pp.1–2 Q1–Q5.

entries.title: Software Processes
entries.text: Software Processes Course index · Notes · Exercises Learning goals Choose and justify a process using requirement stability, failure consequences, feedback opportunities and reusable components. Explain how the same four fundamental activities appear in different models. Interpret process diagrams and distinguish evidence of progress from a model's promises. Prerequisite: Unit 01's product, quality and lifecycle concepts. Opening case — Choose a process before choosing a slogan Source-based case: Lab Q1 asks about four systems: an anti-lock braking controller; a virtual-reality system for studying software maintenance; a replacement university accounting system; and an interactive journey planner seeking the lowest environmental impact. The source provides no budgets, technologies or detailed requirements. Task: Recommend a process basis for each, explain the decisive condition, and state what you would need to confirm before applying the recommendation. Do not assume one process fits all four. Success criteria: Each recommendation connects a property of the system to a process mechanism, states a trade-off and avoids claiming a model alone guarantees quality. Detailed designs of braking or accounting systems are outside this unit. What We Need to Learn Decision Concepts needed --- --- What exactly are we selecting? Actual process versus simplified model When is early agreement valuable? Waterfall, deliverables, review and rework When is early user feedback valuable? Incremental development and interleaved activities When can existing software shape requirements? Reuse and two requirements activities What work remains in every model? Specification, design/implementation, validation, evolution and supporting work 1. A process is work; a model is an abstraction A software process is the actual related activities, methods and practices used to develop and maintain a product. It can involve new code, changes to existing systems, or configuring and integrating existing software. A software process model is a simplified representation of that process. It helps explain the overall organization without describing every local task.[^model] [!note] Model selection is a reasoned approximation The model tells us how work is organized; the actual process must still specify people, products, reviews, tools and local constraints. A model's name cannot establish that the work was done well. A ==critical system== is one whose failure can produce significant human, economic or environmental loss. Safety-critical is an important case, but criticality is broader than physical safety. Novelty and change are different dimensions: a system can be highly critical and also poorly understood. This is why models can be combined rather than selected by a single industry label.[^model] The source lists wider families—linear/sequential, iterative/incremental, agile, prototyping, component-based, formal methods, hybrid, RAD and lean—on p. 8. Names such as V-Model, Spiral, Kanban, XP, CBD, DSDM and DevOps are orientation examples there, not fully taught methods. The detailed comparison in this unit covers the three models actually developed in the lecture.[^model] 2. Waterfall — make phase commitments visible The waterfall model represents principal activities as distinct phases with outputs and approval points. A phase produces an artifact that the next phase uses: requirements guide design, design guides implementation, and the integrated implementation is checked before operational use. A deliverable is an output to be supplied; a milestone marks a significant point in the plan.[^waterfall] waterfall-phases.svg Figure 1 — Principal waterfall phases Read it: Move down the main progression. Unit testing is already present during implementation. Rework can return to earlier phases, as the original diagram's feedback arrows and pp. 19–21 explain. Key takeaway: The model emphasizes stage outputs and review, not a factual claim that real projects never revisit earlier decisions. Provenance: Teaching redraw of the principal sequence in Week2-Lecture-Software Processes-r.pdf , PDF pp. 15–21; informal process diagram. What flows between the phases Phase Work and output Why the next phase needs it --- --- --- Requirements Elicit services and constraints; agree a requirements document Designers need to know the problem to solve Design Specify architecture, interfaces and component and data design Implementers need a coherent solution structure Implementation and unit testing Produce code, documentation and unit checks Integration needs functioning parts with understood behavior Integration and system testing Combine parts, execute tests, record results Operational acceptance needs evidence about the whole Operation and maintenance Deploy, configure, train, support, correct and improve The product must remain useful after delivery Source: PDF pp. 16–17. The table explains purpose; it is not a complete mandated document template. Why revisiting an earlier phase is costly Suppose a requirement changes after design approval. The change may invalidate design decisions, implementation and test expectations. The team must update affected artifacts and repeat their review/approval. The cost is therefore change propagation plus reapproval , not merely editing a sentence. Lab Q4 asks why revisits should be limited.[^waterfall] Trade-off. Documentation gives managers visible evidence of completed work, preserves decisions, supports traceability and allows resource planning by phase. These benefits depend on the documents being accurate and on early assumptions being sufficiently stable. Prematurely freezing a mistaken requirement can produce a well-documented system that disappoints users. The lecture's strengths include structure, planning, documentation, control, resource allocation, milestones and controlled change. Its limitations include rigidity, delayed whole-system feedback, uncertain risks remaining unresolved, limited working-product feedback, administrative effort, uneven resource use and delayed benefits. A signed document is evidence of an agreement; it is not automatically evidence of a useful working system.[^comparison] [!warning] Reconcile the lecture's “late testing” wording PDF p. 25 says testing occurs late, but pp. 16–17 include unit testing during implementation and pp. 62–63 show reviews and early test planning. The usable interpretation is that major integration/acceptance evidence can arrive late in a simple sequential delivery. It is incorrect to infer that every check must wait until all code is finished. Likewise, p. 24 praises controlled-change risk management while p. 25 says the model does not inherently include risk-management activities. Review gates may help control changes, but an explicit risk-identification and mitigation process still has to be supplied. These claims describe different things and should not be memorized as “waterfall has no risks”. 3. Incremental development — learn through working versions An increment adds useful functionality to the existing product. Incremental development builds an initial version, exposes it to user comment and evolves it through further versions. Specification, development and validation are ==interleaved==: discovering a problem while implementing or checking can change what should be specified next.[^incremental] Mechanism. Begin with an outline of overall needs. Choose a useful subset, clarify it sufficiently, build and validate it with the current system, and obtain feedback. Use what was learned to decide the next subset. This bounds some commitments and brings selected evidence forward. It does not remove the need for architecture, planning, documentation or checking. Worked example — the source's flower shop PDF p. 33 proposes basic product listing and user registration first. The team designs, builds, unit-tests, integrates and deploys that increment, then gathers feedback. It next plans shopping-cart and checkout functionality; later versions add payment, order tracking and reviews. Interpretation. A first increment need not deliver the complete eventual business benefit. Product listing can be evaluated early, but it does not yet allow a complete purchase. This limitation should be explicit to stakeholders. If feedback reveals that product selection needs a different organization, the team can adapt before every later feature is built. Counterexample. A change to a shared definition of “product” may affect both the old listing and the new cart. PDF p. 32's statement that “only the current increment” needs changing is therefore an optimistic local-change case, not a universal property. PDF pp. 36–37 themselves warn about dependencies and cross-increment effects. Benefits need enabling conditions Earlier useful functionality provides earlier feedback and possibly earlier value. Smaller planning horizons may improve estimates. Frequent integration can reveal problems earlier. Teams may work in parallel when dependencies and coordination permit it . None of these benefits follows just by naming a release “increment 1”.[^incremental] Costs include integrating new and old work, coordinating dependencies, supporting released increments while creating new ones, allocating varied skills, controlling scope changes, maintaining stakeholder involvement, and managing the incomplete functionality of early versions. Quality needs continuous effort across versions; smaller batches do not make faulty work correct by themselves. Incremental is not identical to agile. Incremental describes how functionality grows. The course's Appendix 3 describes agile as a broader emphasis on adaptation, collaboration, short cycles and frequent feedback. A team can pre-plan increments extensively. Scrum, introduced next, adds a particular empirical framework.[^appendix] 4. Reuse — negotiate fit before integration Reuse-oriented engineering centers development on available components and systems. The source distinguishes remotely invoked web services , packaged collections of objects integrated with a framework, and configurable stand-alone systems . Its .NET and J2EE mentions are examples of frameworks, not selected tools or confirmed versions for this course.[^reuse] reuse-and-requirements.svg Figure 2 — Why requirements are revisited during reuse Read it: Broad requirements guide component analysis; candidate capabilities then inform requirements modification. Continue through design with reuse, development/integration and validation. Key takeaway: Requirements work occurs twice because the information available changes after candidate components are examined. Provenance: Teaching redraw of Week2-Lecture-Software Processes-r.pdf , PDF p. 47, preserving stage order and terminology; informal process flow. Worked example — replacing a university system Before evaluating a reusable accounting package, identify the services needed and its relationships with existing university systems. Without those needs, “this package looks impressive” is not a reason to select it. After evaluating candidates, compare their actual capabilities with the needs. Negotiate acceptable adjustments and identify required additions before designing integration. This is why Lab Q3 requires two separate requirements activities , rather than choosing components once and forcing users to accept all their limitations.[^lab] Trade-off. Reuse can reduce new development effort, cost and risk, and accelerate delivery. It can also force compromises that undermine users' real needs and place component evolution under another supplier's control. Reusing a part does not prove it fits the new whole; system validation remains necessary. 5. Compare mechanisms, not slogans The lecture develops fifteen comparison dimensions on pp. 38–40. They can be applied as three sets of questions rather than memorized as an unconditional ranking: Dimension What to ask before deciding --- --- Requirement stability; adaptability; user-centered work; market change How much is known, and how will feedback alter priorities? Early functionality; time to market; maintenance/enhancement Can a partial delivery be useful, and how often must the product evolve? Size/complexity; risk; integration Can work be decomposed safely, and when do we need evidence about the whole? Stakeholder involvement; documentation/audits; regulatory constraints Who can review work, what evidence is needed, and how stable are the constraints? Resource availability; parallel work Which skills are available and which dependencies prevent independent work? Under the lecture's assumptions, stable and well-understood requirements favor early agreement and phase planning; uncertain interactive behavior favors increments and feedback. Reusable capabilities introduce an additional selection-and-fit problem. The models are not mutually exclusive.[^comparison] The lecture illustrates these tendencies with avionics, medical devices, banking, government and infrastructure on the planning/documentation side, and e-commerce, social/mobile apps, healthcare management and educational software on the evolving-requirements side. These are classroom examples of rationale , not verified descriptions of named companies' internal processes or rules prescribing one method to an entire industry. Size alone is insufficient: a small uncertain project can need feedback, and a large project can need both formal agreements and incremental work. 6. The activities inside every model Specification — decide what should be built Requirements engineering identifies required services and constraints. The lecture's workflow includes a feasibility study , elicitation and analysis , specification , and validation . Feasibility asks whether a proposed system is practicable; elicitation discovers needs; analysis clarifies and reconciles them; specification records them; validation checks that they represent stakeholder needs. The source diagram associates these with a feasibility report, system models, user/system requirements and an agreed requirements document. Feedback means this is not one irreversible pass.[^activities] Customers and end users need understandable high-level requirements; developers need more detailed system requirements. A wrong early requirement can misdirect both design and implementation, so detecting it only after coding can mean rebuilding the wrong solution rather than repairing a small programming defect. Design and implementation — turn requirements into an executable system Design defines structure, data, interfaces and sometimes algorithms. PDF p. 57 shows platform information, requirements specification and data description as inputs, with architecture, interface, component and database specifications as outputs. Designers add detail iteratively and revise earlier decisions.[^activities] Architectural design chooses the principal components and relationships. Interface design specifies how components interact; ambiguity here can make independently correct parts fail together. Component design describes operation, which may be a functional description, changes to reused software or a detailed model. Database design specifies relevant data structures and representations. This last activity is independently present in this course source; no particular DBMS, indexing topic or other course's examples are imported. Implementation includes coding, reviews, unit tests, integration and build management. A build assembles the executable product from its parts. The level and representation of design detail varies: critical work may need explicit precise documents; model-driven work may use diagrams; an agile team's design knowledge may also be expressed in code. Less separate paperwork does not mean no design. Validation — obtain evidence at the right level The lecture treats verification and validation broadly as showing conformity to specification and alignment with customer expectations. Testing executes the system with selected data; inspections and reviews examine artifacts without needing that execution. They can occur throughout development.[^validation] Source testing stage Purpose Synthetic example --- --- --- Development/component testing Check parts during development A journey-cost component calculates an expected result for controlled input System testing Check the integrated whole and component interactions The route displayed uses the same cost that the selection component ranked Acceptance testing Check operational suitability using customer-supplied data and needs Intended users evaluate their real journey-planning cases PDF p. 65 describes development testing in the narrow component-testing sense. Do not infer that all testing performed by developers must be isolated: Appendix 1 also includes integration. A source diagram on p. 63 links requirements to acceptance-test plans, system specification to system-integration plans, and system design to subsystem-integration plans. Planning a test and executing it are different events. A test case specifies inputs, expected results and conditions. Execution records actual results. Defect tracking preserves findings. Regression testing reruns prior tests after changes to look for newly introduced failures. Acceptance criteria state the conditions expected by stakeholders. None of these activities justifies a claim that every possible defect has been excluded. Appendix p. 71's phrase “free of defects” is treated as an objective, not something ordinary testing guarantees.[^appendix] Evolution — maintain usefulness after delivery The source distinguishes corrective maintenance (fix defects), adaptive maintenance (respond to environment changes), perfective maintenance (improve performance, usability or maintainability), and preventive maintenance (reduce future problems). Release coordination and user support accompany those changes. Evolution continues engineering work rather than constituting a separate, intellectually trivial activity.[^appendix] Supporting activities — make the work repeatable and visible Project management plans, schedules, manages risk, and monitors/control progress. Configuration management keeps track of artifact versions, coordinates changes and builds. Deployment includes release, installation/configuration and user support/training. Documentation supports both users and maintainers. Process improvement assesses how the team works and introduces changes to improve it. These responsibilities support every model; they should not disappear because a diagram omits them.[^appendix] Solve the opening case System Decision and source rationale Consequence, limitation and confirmation needed --- --- --- Anti-lock braking The lab recommends a plan-driven/waterfall basis with careful upfront analysis because failure can endanger people Requires precise needs and rigorous evidence. Confirm constraints and required assurance; choosing waterfall alone does not establish safety Virtual reality for maintenance research Incremental development, perhaps with UI prototyping, because the system is novel and needs will emerge Early versions support learning; confirm users and evaluation goals. Prototype feedback does not establish final-product quality Replacement university accounting Reuse-oriented development because many needs are established and integration with existing systems matters Evaluate candidates against real needs, then renegotiate fit. Confirm that suitable reusable software exists Low-impact journey planner Incremental development because the interface and requirements benefit from real user experience Evaluate useful behavior early and revise priorities. Confirm environmental-impact assumptions and whether partial releases are useful These reproduce the supplied suggestions while exposing assumptions. The accounting answer is not proved simply by the word “university”; it depends on component availability and fit. Likewise, hard real-time or safety constraints do not make every incremental development activity impossible; they can make partial deployment and late architectural change inappropriate. The distinction between developing in parts and releasing an operationally incomplete system is crucial.[^lab] Success check: All four recommendations connect a source property to a process mechanism, state a limitation and identify missing information. None substitutes a product label for assurance or a detailed design. Exam-style answer and reusable method Example answer: Incremental development is useful when business requirements evolve because early versions expose assumptions to users and reduce the amount of work committed before feedback. Its benefits depend on useful decomposition and continued integration; dependencies and scope growth can still cause overruns. Plan-driven agreements may be preferable for stable interfaces and evidence obligations, while reuse requires requirements to be reconciled with available capabilities. For any process-choice answer: identify what is known and uncertain; identify failure consequences; test whether useful increments are possible; examine reuse; select a model or combination; explain one mechanism, one consequence and one limitation. Then state how the four activities and supporting work will be performed. This is a decision procedure, not a scoring formula that can replace missing project information. Common mistakes and quick review - “Waterfall never revisits a stage”: pp. 19–21 explicitly describe feedback and rework. - “Incremental means no planning”: increment selection, dependencies and integration require planning. - “A reusable component removes requirements work”: it creates a second fit/negotiation activity. - “Testing happens only at the end”: distinguish unit work, early test planning and later whole-system execution. - “All real-time systems are safety-critical”: the source lab's explanation is a common scenario, not a definition of real-time behavior. [!summary] Review checkpoint Name the three studied models and the mechanism behind each. Explain why a requirements change can require reapproval. Give one condition that defeats the benefit of early increments. Explain why tests at component, system and customer levels answer different questions.
