entries.title: Software Processes — Exercises
entries.text: Software Processes — Exercises Course index · Notes · Exercises Original Lab 2 tasks have local solutions. A process suggestion must be justified from the problem, and alternatives require explicit assumptions. Exercise L1 — Choose a model for four systems ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★★☆ Source: Week 2-Lab- Software Process-Example-Answer.pdf, PDF p. 1, Q1(a–d). Suggest and justify a process model for each: a. Anti-lock braking control in a car. b. A virtual-reality system to study software maintenance. c. A university accounting system replacing an existing system. d. An interactive travel planner helping users find journeys with the lowest environmental impact. [!tip]- Hint Use criticality, uncertainty, feedback and reusable capabilities as distinct decision dimensions. [!success]- Solution a — Braking. The suggested answer chooses plan-driven/waterfall development with careful upfront requirements analysis, possibly formal transformations, because incorrect behavior can threaten safety. This is a process basis, not sufficient safety evidence. b — Research VR. Choose incremental development, perhaps with UI prototyping: novelty and user interaction make evolving requirements likely, so early feedback can change what is built next. c — Accounting replacement. Choose reuse-oriented development under the source assumption that established needs can be met by available software and integrated with systems such as research-grant management. Confirm component fit; a familiar domain does not prove a particular package meets every need. d — Journey planning. Choose incremental development because user experience with the interactive interface will refine requirements. Deliver meaningful functionality and use feedback without ignoring cross-increment dependencies. Interpretation. Each answer is conditional. A justified hybrid can be defensible, but must explain how it preserves necessary evidence and manages the named uncertainty. Exercise L2 — Business change and real-time constraints ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★★☆ Source: Week 2-Lab- Software Process-Example-Answer.pdf, PDF p. 1, Q2. Explain why incremental development is the most effective approach for business software systems. Why is it less appropriate for real-time systems engineering? [!tip]- Hint Explain the source’s assumed business environment; distinguish hardware constraints, criticality, development and deployment. [!success]- Solution Step 1 — Business rationale. Business goals and processes change; early useful increments let users clarify needs before the whole system is committed. Interleaved specification/development/validation can reduce rework. Step 2 — Real-time case in the source. Hardware coupling, whole-system timing constraints and costly physical changes can make it difficult to deploy an incomplete increment. Where failures are safety-critical, additional upfront analysis and planned evidence are needed. Step 3 — Limit the generalization. “Real-time” concerns timing constraints and does not by itself imply safety-criticality. Internal iterative development may remain possible even when incomplete operational deployment is unacceptable. Thus incremental development is a strong business-system choice under change/feedback assumptions, not a theorem that excludes every other process. Exercise L3 — Two requirements activities in reuse ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Week 2-Lab- Software Process-Example-Answer.pdf, PDF p. 2, Q3. Why is it essential to have two separate requirements-engineering activities in the reuse-based process? [!tip]- Hint What can you know before component analysis, and what do you learn only after it? [!success]- Solution Before selection: understand the needed functions and broad constraints well enough to evaluate candidate systems/components. After selection: compare actual capabilities with business needs; identify needed changes/additions and negotiate acceptable requirements modifications. Reason: available software constrains the feasible solution. Skipping the first activity makes selection directionless; skipping the second risks pretending the selected component meets needs it does not meet. The source p. 47 sequence places component analysis between specification and modification. Exercise L4 — Why waterfall revisits are costly ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Week 2-Lab- Software Process-Example-Answer.pdf, PDF p. 2, Q4. A waterfall engineer may revisit the previous stage for refinement. Explain in your own words why the number of revisits should be limited. [!tip]- Hint Trace a modified requirement through approved artifacts rather than simply saying iteration is slow. [!success]- Solution Each completed stage has documented outputs that have been reviewed and approved. Revisiting changes those outputs and can invalidate dependent design, implementation and test work, requiring further updates and reapproval. Repeated cycles consume time and budget. Therefore the team should reduce avoidable revisits through careful work and controlled decisions. This is not a reason to knowingly preserve a critical defect: compare the cost of correcting it with the consequence of leaving it unresolved. Exercise L5 — Why requirements matter early ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Week 2-Lab- Software Process-Example-Answer.pdf, PDF p. 2, Q5. Explain why requirements engineering is a critical stage in the software process. [!tip]- Hint Distinguish building the wrong thing from coding the intended thing incorrectly. [!success]- Solution Requirements guide design and implementation. If a requirement misstates the needed service or constraint, later work may correctly implement the wrong solution. Repair then needs reconsideration of the requirement and its dependent artifacts. Early elicitation, analysis and validation reduce this risk. The source’s “inevitably” emphasizes propagation risk; a later review can still catch a mistake before it reaches operational software. Exercise P11 — What a process model includes ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Week2-Lecture-Software Processes-r.pdf, PDF p. 11, embedded question. What will be included in software process models? [!tip]- Hint Think at the framework level: what activities, relationships and outputs help explain the process? [!success]- Solution A model represents principal activities/phases and their organization, including sequence, overlap and feedback where relevant. It can show the outputs or deliverables connecting activities, such as requirements feeding design. The actual process adds local roles, detailed practices and constraints. The three lecture diagrams illustrate different organizations rather than every detail of a project. Exercise P75 — What is agile ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Week2-Lecture-Software Processes-r.pdf, PDF p. 75, introductory prompt; context p. 74. Give the brief, informal meaning of agile introduced at the end of the lecture. [!tip]- Hint Use Appendix 3; do not assume that merely delivering numbered releases defines the whole approach. [!success]- Solution In the lecture’s introduction, agile emphasizes adapting to change, close customer collaboration and frequent feedback while delivering small functional increments in short cycles. Incremental development is one important feature, but by itself does not establish the broader philosophy or a specific framework. Scrum is developed in the next supplied teaching materials; the linked video was not viewed. Exercise S1 — Read the test-planning evidence SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Provenance: Synthetic practice using the concepts taught in Notes. A manager says: “The model places system testing after implementation, so we should wait until then to plan acceptance tests.” Use the source diagram on PDF p. 63 to identify the error. [!tip]- Hint Distinguish the information used to define a test from the executable product needed to run it. [!success]- Solution Requirements can inform the acceptance-test plan before code exists; system specification can inform system-integration plans, and system design can inform subsystem-integration plans. Execution must wait for the relevant product, but planning expected evidence need not. The manager confuses ordering of test execution with ordering of test design. Exercise S2 — Diagnose a reuse shortcut SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Provenance: Synthetic practice using the concepts taught in Notes. A team chooses a component first, then deletes every requirement the component cannot satisfy. Explain why this is not an adequate reuse-oriented process. [!tip]- Hint Use both requirements activities and the need to preserve real business value. [!success]- Solution Candidate analysis is useful only relative to broad needs. After selection, requirements may be negotiated, but deleting every mismatch can produce a system that fails essential business needs. Identify which requirements are negotiable, which require additions and which make the candidate unsuitable; then validate the integrated whole. Reuse reduces new code but does not erase responsibility for fit.

entries.title: In 60 Seconds
entries.text: When requirements and technical assumptions are uncertain, progress depends on learning from evidence. Scrum connects three pillars—transparency, inspection and adaptation—to accountabilities, events and artifacts. Acceptance criteria describe what an item must do; Definition of Done establishes the shared quality threshold. Relative estimates support discussion, and observed Done work supports a conditional forecast. You should be able to locate who owns a decision, explain why “almost done” cannot count as Done, resolve divergent estimates by uncovering assumptions, and calculate a forecast with units and limitations. The Campus Express activity is a UI-refinement exercise; its proposed estimates are not measured team performance. Source: S07 pp.4–46, S09 pp.1–15, S03 pp.1–4 and S14 Q1–Q7.

entries.title: Concept Preview
entries.text: [!info] Empirical learning Concept: Empirical learning. Plain-language meaning: Make the work visible, compare it with a goal, and adjust using what you learn. Why it matters: A plan based on uncertain assumptions needs an evidence-driven way to change. Connects to: defined control and the cone of uncertainty. Source: SE Methodologies Scrum - Reading Material.pdf , PDF pp.1–3,6. [!info] Scrum decisions Concept: Scrum decisions. Plain-language meaning: Product value, implementation and team effectiveness have distinct accountabilities. Why it matters: Meetings help only when evidence reaches someone able to act. Connects to: Product Owner, Developers and Scrum Master. Source: SE Methodologies Scrum - Reading Material.pdf , PDF pp.7–10. [!info] Acceptance and Done Concept: Acceptance and Done. Plain-language meaning: An item’s behavior and the product’s shared quality threshold answer different questions. Why it matters: A correct-looking screen may still lack review or usable integration. Connects to: acceptance criteria, Increment and velocity. Source: Product Backlog Refinement Activity Task Sheet.pdf , PDF p.1, Definition of Done. [!info] Sizing and forecasting Concept: Sizing and forecasting. Plain-language meaning: Compare work to a shared baseline; forecast using comparable completed work. Why it matters: Numbers do not remove unknown scope, and points are not hours. Connects to: planning poker, mean velocity and conditional forecasts. Source: SE Methodologies Scrum - Reading Material.pdf , PDF pp.12–14.

entries.title: Before You Start
entries.text: An increment adds functionality; integration makes parts work together; a process model describes organization, not actual quality. Recall these from Tutor Unit 02. A Product Backlog Item (PBI) is a unit of work described in the ordered Product Backlog. A Sprint is the bounded interval containing the Scrum work and feedback events. Precise scope and quality still need clarification. [^scrum] [!question] Prerequisite retrieval Why does assembling completed screens not automatically produce a usable increment? [!success]- Answer Navigation, shared state and other interactions may fail even when individual screens look complete. The combined result needs integration and quality evidence. Source: S03 p.1 DoD; S09 pp.10–11.

entries.title: The motivating question — How much is actually known?
entries.text: Source-based setting: Campus Express has six Developers and an instructor acting as PO. Checkout needs delivery-location and payment-method selection, but the sheet explicitly asks whether real payment integration or mockups are intended. In the tutorial, votes of 2, 3, 3 and 13 disagree. A separate tutorial dataset records 18, 22 and 20 Done points in three two-week Sprints , with 100 points remaining . These are separate teaching inputs, not measured Campus Express results. [^activity] Questions: Who resolves the checkout scope? What do the different votes mean? Can an item missing peer review count as Done? What forecast follows from the tutorial data? What would invalidate it? Success requires a justified decision for each question, all four activity DoD conditions, correct units, and explicit assumptions. No real PO decision, workshop, implemented wireframe or test result has been produced here. Case question Knowledge needed --- --- Why not trust the first plan completely? Uncertainty and empirical control Who decides and adapts? Accountabilities, events and artifacts What does completed mean? Acceptance criteria and DoD How do votes become useful? Shared scope and relative sizing What can the data predict? Velocity, units and forecast limits

entries.title: 1. Why is learning part of the process?
entries.text: Intuition. If the team learns that “payment” means a live gateway rather than a static selector, it is now estimating a different problem. Ignoring that discovery preserves the old number, not the old validity. A defined process assumes a sufficiently understood and repeatable transformation under controlled conditions. An empirical process uses observation and adaptation when significant aspects are uncertain. Software development can reveal needs through use and constraints through implementation. A repeatable build may still be a defined activity within an empirical product effort; these are not labels dividing all work into predictable physical systems and unpredictable software. [^foundations] Read the uncertainty mechanism. The source cone shows an illustrative range of 0.25×–4× at concept stage, narrowing toward 1× at release. An initial reference of 100 would illustrate 25–400, not a guaranteed confidence interval. The diagram's “variance” is estimation spread, not a computed statistical variance. Clarifying scope and testing technical assumptions can improve knowledge; elapsed time alone cannot. [^foundations] Worked risk trace. Two components implement different meanings of “paid.” If the mismatch is found only after many dependent features exist, correction affects design, code, tests and documents. Short integrated increments can expose it earlier. This is a conditional risk-reduction mechanism, not proof that agile eliminates risk or that Waterfall lacks early test planning. Agile values prefer interaction, working results, collaboration and adaptation when these compete with administrative mechanisms; processes/tools, documentation, contracts and plans still matter. The twelve source principles reinforce the same logic: early valuable delivery, welcoming change, frequent delivery, business–developer cooperation, supported motivated people, direct communication, working-software evidence, sustainable pace, technical excellence, simplicity, self-organization and regular reflection. A useful explanation connects them: feedback only helps if people can communicate and act, while sound design and sustainable work make continuing adaptation feasible. [^agile]

entries.title: 2. What turns meetings into empirical control?
entries.text: Problem first. A team holds every scheduled meeting but hides broken integration behind “90% complete.” Why does the meeting schedule fail to make its forecast trustworthy? Transparency makes relevant work and quality understandable. Inspection compares that evidence with goals and standards. Adaptation changes the work or process when the comparison reveals a meaningful issue. Misleading completion data undermines inspection; inspection without an actionable change does not realize adaptation. [^pillars] empirical-learning.svg Figure 1 — The evidence must survive the whole loop Read it: Start with understandable work, inspect it against a goal and adjust. Repeat with the changed work made visible. These are linked responsibilities, not one-time Waterfall phases. Key takeaway: A meeting is useful when it improves evidence or a decision, not merely because it occurred. Provenance: Unchanged standard teaching SVG based on S07 p.17 and S09 p.6; informal empirical-learning diagram. Locate the decision Accountability What it contributes Case consequence --- --- --- Product Owner Product value and understandable, ordered backlog Clarify whether checkout requires real processing or mock selection Developers Plan and perform work toward a usable Increment, maintaining quality Explain implementation assumptions, dependencies and estimates Scrum Master Effective Scrum through coaching, facilitation and impediment removal Help the team resolve blocked communication; do not assign every task as a taskmaster Cross-functional means the team collectively has the required skills, not that every member has every skill. Shared accountability does not erase personal responsibility. A PO who dictates implementation and a Scrum Master who becomes a status clerk each blur a useful distinction. [^scrum] Match event to evidence Sprint Planning establishes the Sprint's purpose, selected work and delivery plan. The Daily Scrum helps Developers inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt their plan. Review examines the product outcome and changed context with stakeholders. Retrospective examines how the team worked and chooses useful improvements. For a one-month Sprint, the source maxima are 8 hours, 15 minutes, 4 hours and 3 hours respectively; the longer events are usually shorter for shorter Sprints. The Daily remains 15 minutes. [^scrum] Visible worked distinction. If customers now need another delivery location, discuss its product implications in ongoing PO collaboration and product review. If broken screen transitions repeatedly escape review, use team reflection to change the checking process—for example, explicitly checking upstream/downstream navigation before sign-off. “Communicate better” lacks an observable action. The Product Backlog is ordered, evolving product work. Refinement adds understanding, size and order. The Sprint Backlog holds selected work and the practical plan toward the Sprint Goal. An Increment must be usable and integrated with earlier work, not merely a collection of disconnected finished parts. [^scrum] [!warning] Version reconciliation — SUPPLEMENTARY TECHNICAL CLARIFICATION SOURCE A: S09 pp.8–10 uses 3–9 Development Team members and four ceremonies; S07 pp.23,25–27,34 includes older wording. SOURCE B: the [2020 Scrum Guide]( CONFLICT: team boundary, event counting and timing conventions differ. SAFEST INTERPRETATION: the Guide has one Scrum Team, typically ten or fewer including PO/SM; Developers remain individually accountable. The Sprint contains four other events. Its Goal is finalized during Planning. Daily questions are optional; refinement is ongoing; Done value can be released before Review. Product Goal, Sprint Goal and DoD are artifact commitments. Points/poker are optional techniques. CONFIRMATION STATUS: official 2020 clarification, not an instructor-confirmed marking convention. Preserve the course's terminology when identifying its questions.

entries.title: 3. What counts as Done in this practical?
entries.text: Problem first. The cart displays the correct total, but Checkout navigation is broken and no peer has reviewed it. Does the visible total settle completion? Acceptance criteria are item-specific conditions on behavior. Definition of Done is a shared quality standard for completed work. For this particular activity, all four conditions are required: an interactive UI wireframe; fulfilled AC; review by at least one other Developer; verified upstream/downstream screen integration. A static drawing alone does not satisfy interactive flow. The source reading's illustrative code-coverage threshold is not an added Campus Express requirement. [^done] Worked decision: identify the missing evidence—navigation and review. Compare it with the activity DoD. Do not count the item as Done or include partial points in velocity. Repair, review and integrate it, then reassess. Unfinished work returns to the Product Backlog for future consideration; it is not automatically guaranteed the next Sprint. If the screen already satisfies one AC, preserve that fact without confusing it with overall completion. [!question] Explain it yourself Can an item pass the shared quality checks while implementing the wrong behavior? [!success]- Check your explanation Yes. Review and integration do not establish that the item satisfies its intended acceptance criteria. Check both the specific behavior and shared quality conditions. Source: S03 p.1; S09 p.11.

entries.title: 4. How should the team handle 2 versus 13?
entries.text: Intuition. The votes may represent different hidden assumptions, not simply different confidence levels. Averaging different scopes produces a number with no shared meaning. The activity's points compare complexity, effort and risk/uncertainty against a reference such as US-01 or US-03 at 2 or 3 points. The required scale is 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 20, 40, 100 . Points are not fixed hours and are not comparable across unrelated teams. [^sizing] Worked poker sequence: explain the item; clarify AC and DoD; each estimator selects privately; reveal together; ask the high and low voters what they included; clarify with the PO; re-vote. The 13 voter may include a real gateway while the 2 voter assumes mock selection. Neither a mean of 5.25 nor rounding it to a legal card resolves that disagreement. No unique final estimate follows from the votes alone. If the clarified story remains large, split it into meaningful smaller outcomes. The activity requires four fields for every US-01–US-10: PO questions, initial estimate, refined estimate/splits and suggested priority. Order must respect dependencies such as Menu Selection before Cart Summary; recommend value trade-offs to the PO rather than claiming your proposed order is official. The complete original practice is linked in this unit's navigation. [^activity] [!warning] Local activity rule, not universal Scrum SOURCE A: S03 p.1 says typically 13 points. SOURCE B: p.4 Step 3 says 13 or higher. CONFLICT: a 13-point story falls on different sides of the threshold. SAFEST INTERPRETATION: apply the explicit operational step, ≥13, in this activity and record any instructor direction. CONFIRMATION STATUS: not instructor-confirmed. S02's printable deck contains extra cards beyond the required scale; do not silently substitute those for required numerical estimates. No real PO answers, final votes, wireframes or peer checks are supplied by a worked example. If scope changes from mock UI to live integration, revisit estimates and split definitions; do not preserve their numbers as measured facts.

entries.title: 5. What does velocity allow you to conclude?
entries.text: Problem first. The tutorial records 18, 22 and 20 points across three Sprints. Can these numbers fix the release date of another team? A Sprint's velocity is the sum of points for items actually meeting DoD in that Sprint. An unfinished 8-point item contributes zero in this convention; count it once when Done. For N observed Sprints, mean velocity is total Done points divided by N. Remaining points divided by this rate gives a conditional forecast in Sprints . [^forecast] Work the tutorial dataset: 1. Total observed delivery: 18 + 22 + 20 = 60 points. 2. Mean rate: 60 points ÷ 3 Sprints = 20 points/Sprint . 3. Remaining duration: 100 points ÷ 20 points/Sprint = 5 additional Sprints . 4. Calendar conversion: 5 × 2 weeks = 10 weeks , under the supplied Sprint length. The arithmetic is exact for these inputs; the forecast is uncertain because future capacity, scope, sizing and quality conditions may change. It is not measured Campus Express velocity. The reading's 150 ÷ 25 = 6 example supplies no Sprint length, so it does not independently establish weeks. [^forecast] If division produces a fraction and planning requires complete Sprint slots, round upward and say why. If mean velocity is zero, the division gives no usable completion estimate. A three-to-five-Sprint history is the source heuristic, not proof of stability. A team can inflate point values without delivering more value; velocity is not employee productivity or a valid cross-team league table. Read the chart’s units before its story S07 p.46 has one chart with two vertical axes : remaining effort in hours on the left, and remaining/completed tasks on the right. The remaining-effort curve, remaining-task curve and completed-task bars must use their own axes. No plotted series supplies Done story-point velocity. The ideal line is a reference trajectory, not a guarantee of uniform work. A line above it calls for investigation; its shape alone does not distinguish scope growth from impediments. [^chart] [!warning] Standard-reference correction preserved locally SOURCE A: S07 p.46, actual image: one combined chart with two vertical axes. SOURCE B: standard Unit 03 Notes, “Read a burndown before diagnosing it,” calls them two charts. CONFLICT: panel count is misstated in the reference edition. SAFEST INTERPRETATION: read one dual-axis chart; retain the hours-versus-tasks distinction. CONFIRMATION STATUS: verified from the original slide image. The protected standard file is unchanged; this companion records the correction.

entries.title: Return to the motivating question
entries.text: Ask the PO about checkout's intended scope while Developers explain feasibility and effort. Resolve the 2/13 assumptions before estimating; split clarified large work using the activity's ≥13 instruction. An item missing peer review fails this activity's DoD, so do not count it as Done. The separate tutorial data support five Sprints/ten weeks under comparable future conditions. Revise that forecast when scope, capacity, sizing or DoD changes. This answers every case question without inventing actual workshop outcomes or a promised release date.

entries.title: Definitions and distinctions
entries.text: Pair Decisive distinction Source --- --- --- Defined / empirical Predictable transformation versus observation-led adaptation under uncertainty S09 pp.1–3 Review / Retrospective Product outcome/context versus quality and effectiveness of the way of working S09 p.9 Acceptance criteria / DoD Item behavior versus shared quality standard S09 p.11; S03 p.1 Points / hours Relative work size versus time S09 pp.12–14 Forecast / guarantee Conditional projection versus an unsupported certainty claim S09 p.14; assumptions made explicit here

entries.title: Review
entries.text: Full Understanding Revisit the mechanism sections and complete calculation, then attempt the linked original tutorials and all ten lab stories. Use the standard reference for expanded event/role examples, keeping the chart correction above in mind. 5-Minute Review Expose uncertainty rather than hiding it in fixed numbers. Make work transparent, inspect evidence and adapt. Locate the decision in the correct accountability and event. Test AC and DoD separately. Compare points against shared scope and a baseline; uncover high/low vote assumptions. Count Done work once, compute the mean with units, and state forecast conditions. Read axes before interpreting curves. 60-Second Recall - Defined versus empirical - Three pillars - Who decides value, delivery and effectiveness? - Review versus Retrospective - AC versus DoD - 2, 3, 3, 13 - Done-only velocity - Forecast conditions - One chart, two axes [^foundations]: SE Methodologies Scrum - Reading Material.pdf, PDF pp.1–3; SE Methodologies Scrum - Lecture Slides.pdf, pp.4–9; cone p.8 image inspected. [^agile]: SE Methodologies Scrum - Reading Material.pdf, PDF pp.3–5; lecture pp.11–15. Course preferences and principles are paraphrased, not assessment predictions. [^pillars]: SE Methodologies Scrum - Reading Material.pdf, PDF p.6; lecture p.17. [^scrum]: SE Methodologies Scrum - Reading Material.pdf, PDF pp.7–10; lecture pp.20–34. Version correction is separately linked to the 2020 Guide above. [^done]: Product Backlog Refinement Activity Task Sheet.pdf, PDF p.1; SE Methodologies Scrum - Reading Material.pdf, p.11; lecture p.33. [^sizing]: Product Backlog Refinement Activity Task Sheet.pdf, PDF pp.1,4; SE Methodologies Scrum - Reading Material.pdf, pp.12–13; Week 3 - Tutorial Questions.docx, Q6. [^activity]: Product Backlog Refinement Activity Task Sheet.pdf, PDF pp.1–4; Week 3 - Tutorial Questions.docx, Q6–Q7; Printable Scrum Planning Poker Deck (A4 Size).pdf, pp.1–4 (unchanged prior source inspection). [^forecast]: Week 3 - Tutorial Questions.docx, Q7; SE Methodologies Scrum - Reading Material.pdf, pp.13–14; lecture pp.43–44. Arithmetic recomputed; reading p.14 formula image inspected. [^chart]: SE Methodologies Scrum - Lecture Slides.pdf, PDF pp.45–46; p.46 actual image checked for axes, curves and bars. SE Methodologies Scrum - Reading Material.pdf, pp.14–15.

entries.title: Empirical Development and Scrum
entries.text: Empirical Development and Scrum Course index · Notes · Exercises · Lab Learning goals Explain why uncertain product development benefits from feedback. Use the Scrum accountabilities, events and artifacts to locate a decision. Distinguish quality from percentage complete; estimate relatively without turning points into hours; calculate a conditional forecast and explain its limits. Prerequisite: Unit 02's process models and incremental development. Opening case — A campus app with uncertain scope Source-based context: The Campus Express practical asks six developers to refine ten food-delivery interface stories with the instructor as Product Owner. Checkout mentions delivery location and payment choices but leaves gateway integration unclear. A group votes 2, 3, 3 and 13 on an item (the tutorial's disagreement example). A separate tutorial team completed 18, 22 and 20 points in three two-week Sprints and has 100 points remaining.[^case] Constraints: Use the practical's scale and Definition of Done. Do not assume that a wireframe task includes production payments, or that the two classroom teams have interchangeable velocities. The voting example and velocity dataset are separate teaching inputs, not measured Campus Express results. Questions: Who resolves product scope? How should divergent estimates be handled? Can a 90%-finished item count as Done? What forecast does the tutorial dataset support? What evidence might change it? Success criteria: Give a decision, its justification, its consequence and its uncertainty for each question. The Lab then applies the method to all ten original stories. What We Need to Learn Case question Required concepts --- --- Why is early certainty unreliable? Defined versus empirical control; uncertainty and risk Who decides and who implements? Product Owner, Scrum Master and Developers How does feedback alter work? Transparency, inspection, adaptation; events and artifacts What counts as finished? Acceptance criteria and Definition of Done How do we resolve 2 versus 13? Relative sizing, assumptions and planning poker When might the remaining work finish? Done-only velocity, mean, forecast and limitations 1. Why empirical development exists A defined process relies on a sufficiently understood, repeatable transformation: stable inputs and controlled conditions make outputs predictable. An empirical process uses observations to guide work when important details cannot be specified reliably in advance. Software is intangible and often discovers requirements and technical constraints through implementation. A stakeholder may change their mind after using an interface; an integration may reveal an undocumented constraint; the market may change during development.[^foundations] This does not make all physical engineering deterministic or all software unpredictable. It identifies a decision condition: when the product and solution contain substantial uncertainty, a fixed initial plan needs opportunities to learn. Empirical work still plans, documents and applies technical discipline. Its plan changes because evidence changes. Uncertainty is not the same as elapsed time The lecture's Cone of Uncertainty illustrates a wide early estimation range that narrows as knowledge improves. Its graphic labels initial concept at 0.25×–4×, requirements complete at approximately 0.67×–1.5×, detailed specification at 0.90×–1.1×, and release at 1×.[^cone] If an initial reference estimate is 100 units, the first range illustrates 25–400 units, not a promise that every project falls in that interval. The mechanism is resolved uncertainty : clarified scope, tested technical assumptions and observed delivery. Merely waiting does not narrow the range. The source/tutorial word “variance” describes estimation spread informally; the diagram does not provide a statistical variance, probability distribution or calibrated confidence interval. [!warning] A fixed commitment can hide rather than remove risk Fixing scope, budget and date before resolving uncertainty transfers the uncertainty into the delivery promise. Record assumptions and revisit forecasts when evidence changes. The cone is an explanatory model, not a formula that automatically makes a project predictable. Why late integration can be expensive A mistaken interface assumption discovered late can require redesign, code changes, retesting and document revision across several components. Costs propagate through dependencies. Short integrated increments can expose such assumptions sooner and limit the affected work. This is a mechanism for reducing some risks, not proof that agile projects are low-risk in every context. Architecture, security, supplier and operational risks still need deliberate attention. Unit 02 also showed that waterfall can plan testing early; late execution of integrated tests is the particular concern here.[^risk] 2. Agile values guide trade-offs The course presents four preferences: emphasize people and interaction; prioritize useful working software; collaborate with customers; and respond to change. The corresponding processes/tools, documentation, contracts and plans still have value. The preference matters when these compete, not as permission to discard the latter entirely.[^agile] The twelve principles make those values operational: Principle in the course Mechanism and practical interpretation --- --- Early, continuous valuable delivery Obtain feedback before the entire investment is committed Welcome changing requirements Use new knowledge, including late knowledge, to improve value Deliver frequently Shorten the feedback delay; choose a practical cadence Business and developers work together Resolve meaning and priority close to implementation Support motivated people Provide resources, trust and an environment for responsible work Direct conversation Reduce clarification delay; retain important decisions when needed Working software measures progress Seek usable evidence beyond completed documents Sustainable pace Avoid relying on permanent overtime to make a plan appear feasible Technical excellence and good design Keep future adaptation affordable Simplicity Avoid work that does not contribute necessary value Self-organizing teams Let those doing the work organize how to achieve it Regular reflection and adjustment Improve the process using observed outcomes The lecture's comparison table contrasts stable, predictive, milestone-led development with dynamic, adaptive, increment-led development. Use it to identify tendencies: frequent feedback can reveal market mismatch earlier; modular design and refactoring can reduce change cost. Neither column guarantees its outcome. Required documentation and a need for prediction can coexist with iterative delivery.[^agile] 3. Scrum makes feedback opportunities explicit [!definition] Empirical control Transparency makes the relevant state understandable. Inspection compares evidence with a goal or standard. Adaptation changes the work or process when inspection finds a meaningful deviation. Missing one weakens the others: inspecting misleading “90% complete” reports cannot reliably guide release decisions.[^pillars] empirical-learning.svg Figure 1 — Empirical learning loop (informal process diagram) Read it: Follow the vertical arrows, then repeat with the consequences of the adaptation made visible. These are linked responsibilities, not separate project phases. Key takeaway: Inspection only helps if the information is trustworthy and someone can act on it. Accountabilities: value, delivery and effective use of Scrum Accountability Main decision/work Common failure and its consequence --- --- --- Product Owner (PO) Maximize product value; make the Product Backlog understandable and ordered A proxy who only forwards messages delays decisions; a technical dictator undermines Developers' implementation decisions; an absent PO leaves ambiguity unresolved Developers (source also says Development Team) Plan and perform the work needed for a usable Increment; maintain quality and adapt their plan Hand-offs between isolated specialties can leave an integrated item unfinished even when each local task seems complete Scrum Master (SM) Help establish Scrum and improve the team's effectiveness through coaching, facilitation and removing impediments A meeting clerk adds ceremony without improvement; a taskmaster assigns all work; a dogmatist enforces form without purpose Cross-functional means the team collectively has the skills needed for the work; it does not mean every member is equally skilled at everything. Shared delivery responsibility does not erase an individual's responsibility to colleagues. “No titles” in the lecture is about internal Scrum hierarchies, not a ban on expertise or employment titles.[^roles] Events: distinct purposes, connected learning The source teaches four recurring events within the Sprint. A Sprint is the bounded container in which the team works toward a Sprint Goal and creates usable results. Avoid treating the following as unrelated meetings.[^events] Event What it resolves People and evidence Source maximum for a one-month Sprint --- --- --- --- Sprint Planning Why this Sprint matters, what can be selected and how work will proceed Scrum Team; backlog, recent results and capacity 8 hours Daily Scrum How Developers adapt their plan toward the Sprint Goal Developers; current progress and impediments 15 minutes Sprint Review What was achieved and what product adaptation follows Scrum Team and stakeholders; actual product and changed context 4 hours Sprint Retrospective How the team's quality and effectiveness can improve Scrum Team; interactions, practices, tools and quality problems 3 hours For shorter Sprints, Planning, Review and Retrospective are usually shorter. Daily Scrum remains a 15-minute event. The lecture's yesterday/today/impediments questions can help a team focus; a recital to a manager that produces no adapted plan misses the purpose. Review is product feedback with stakeholders; Retrospective improves how the team works. An actionable retrospective outcome might be “pair-review navigation transitions before peer sign-off,” rather than the untestable “communicate better.” Artifacts expose work and quality The Product Backlog is the ordered, evolving work needed to improve the product. Ordering involves value, dependencies and risk, not just selecting the smallest item. Refinement clarifies and sizes items so upcoming decisions are better informed. The Sprint Backlog contains the Sprint Goal, selected items and an actionable delivery plan. An Increment is usable, integrated work meeting the quality standard; cumulative integration matters because disconnected completed screens are not necessarily a usable flow.[^artifacts] [!warning] Source/version reconciliation — SUPPLEMENTARY TECHNICAL CLARIFICATION The course reading p.8 says 3–9 Development Team members; the [2020 Scrum Guide]( describes one Scrum Team, typically ten or fewer people including PO and SM. Its terms are PO, SM and Developers. It includes the Sprint itself among five events. Developers hold each other accountable; shared responsibility does not replace personal accountability. The Sprint Goal is finalized during Planning, rather than necessarily arriving complete as an input. The artifact commitments are Product Goal, Sprint Goal and Definition of Done. Daily Scrum format is flexible; the three questions are optional. Refinement is ongoing, not confined to a “pre-Sprint” stage; usable Done increments can be released before the Sprint ends. Sprint Review is not a release gate. Story points and planning poker are classroom techniques, not mandatory Scrum rules. Use lecturer terminology when discussing the supplied questions while stating these distinctions. Instructor confirmation is needed if marking expects an older convention. This clarification addresses S07 pp.23, 25–26, 31 and 34 and S09 pp.8–10. It does not silently rewrite their diagrams. 4. Acceptance criteria and Done answer different questions Acceptance criteria (AC) are item-specific conditions: for example, selecting a dish updates the cart's quantity and displayed total. Definition of Done (DoD) is the shared quality standard an Increment must satisfy: the practical requires an interactive wireframe, fulfilled AC, peer review by at least one other developer, and verified integration with upstream/downstream screens.[^quality] An item can satisfy a happy-path criterion while failing integration or review. Conversely, well-reviewed code may implement the wrong behavior. You need both appropriate item behavior and the shared quality threshold. The reading's unit-test coverage above 80% is an illustrative DoD clause; it is not the Campus Express requirement or a proven guarantee of correctness. [!example] Worked decision — A nearly finished cart A cart wireframe displays the right total, but its Checkout transition is broken and no peer has reviewed it. The item's required behavior is only partly supported and the practical's DoD is unmet. Decision: do not count it as Done. Consequence: repair and review it, then assess it again. “90%” does not create a usable Increment or 90% of its velocity points. The unfinished item returns to the Product Backlog for future consideration. Do not count it as part of the Done Increment or present it as a completed deliverable at the Review. Its future selection and forecast need reconsideration; it is not automatically a promise for the next Sprint.[^quality] 5. Relative sizing exposes assumptions Absolute duration depends on people, context, interruptions and unknowns. Story points compare work against a shared reference using complexity, effort and risk/uncertainty. A 5-point item is not inherently five hours or five days. Nor does one team's 5 equal another team's 5. The reading's developer-speed comparisons illustrate why naive hour estimates vary; they are not measurements of this class.[^sizing] The practical's scale is 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 20, 40, 100 . Gaps grow to discourage false precision for larger, less understood work. Use US-01 or US-03 as a 2- or 3-point baseline, clarify what Done includes, then compare other stories against it. A larger estimate can reflect uncertainty; clarification or splitting may change it. Planning poker procedure 1. PO presents an item; Developers ask questions and discuss technical assumptions. 2. Each estimator chooses privately so the first speaker does not anchor everyone. 3. Reveal simultaneously. 4. Ask the high and low voters to explain what work and risks they included. 5. Clarify assumptions, update the item if necessary, and re-vote. 6. Agree a shared estimate, or record unresolved questions and revisit. Do not force arithmetic consensus over unresolved scope. For votes 2, 3, 3, 13 , an average of 5.25 hides disagreement and is not on the task's scale. A 13 voter might include real payment integration while a 2 voter assumes a static selector. Ask the PO which outcome is intended. Then estimate the clarified work or split it into meaningful smaller outcomes. No final point value follows uniquely from the four votes.[^poker] [!warning] Split threshold differs within the task sheet S03 p.1 says “typically 13”; its explicit step on p.4 says 13 or higher . For this classroom activity, use the operational instruction ≥13 , and record the discrepancy. This is a task heuristic, not a universal Scrum threshold. After splitting, estimate the children separately; their sum need not equal the parent's old uncertain estimate. The printable deck includes extra cards such as 0, ½, ?, coffee and infinity. For this task, use only the stated numeric scale; special cards can flag confusion or a break if the instructor permits, not replace the required estimate.[^deck] 6. Velocity supports a conditional forecast For Sprint i, velocity Vᵢ is the sum of points for items actually meeting the DoD during that Sprint. A planned 8-point item that is 90% finished contributes zero points that Sprint. Count it once when Done; counting fractions now and the full item later double-counts work.[^forecast] For N observed Sprints: $$\bar V = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} V_i}{N}, \qquad \text{forecast Sprints} = \frac{\text{remaining points}}{\bar V}.$$ Use an upward whole-Sprint rounding when scheduling whole Sprint slots and the division is non-integer. If mean velocity is zero, this division gives no usable completion forecast. The source's suggested 3–5-Sprint baseline is a heuristic, not a guarantee of stable evidence. [!example] Worked source example The reading gives 150 remaining points and mean velocity 25 points/Sprint. Units cancel: 150 points ÷ 25 points/Sprint = 6 Sprints . This says nothing about calendar weeks until Sprint length is supplied. It assumes comparable sizing, team conditions and scope. Velocity measures delivery in the team's own sizing system, not product value, employee effort or a valid league table across teams. Inflating point values can increase the number without delivering anything sooner. A forecast must be revised when scope, capacity, DoD, technical risk or the team's estimating scale changes. Read a burndown before diagnosing it A burndown plots remaining work vertically against time horizontally. An ideal line is a reference trajectory, not proof of uniform work. If the actual line stays above it, progress in the chosen measure is slower than that reference; inspect unfinished work, impediments and scope changes before diagnosing the cause. A jump can be newly discovered work, not “negative productivity.”[^burndown] Source figure reading: S07 p.46 contains two charts: the left measures remaining effort hours ; the right measures remaining tasks . The preceding slide discusses story points too, but these axes are not interchangeable. The yellow completed-task markers on the right are a different series, not a second remaining-points curve. Never derive point velocity from an hours axis. A line below ideal is also not automatic permission to change the Sprint Goal. 7. Return to the opening case Decision Justification Consequence and interpretation --- --- --- Ask the PO to clarify checkout scope; Developers assess implementation Product value and technical feasibility need different accountabilities Record whether payment is a mock selection or real integration; unresolved scope remains visible Hear high/low explanations, then re-vote 2, 3, 3, 13 may encode different assumptions No unique estimate can be inferred from votes alone; split large clarified work Do not count a 90%-finished item failing DoD Done is the shared quality threshold No partial velocity; unfinished work needs future consideration Forecast five additional Sprints for the tutorial team Mean = (18 + 22 + 20)/3 = 20; 100/20 = 5 At two weeks per Sprint, approximately ten weeks, conditional on stable assumptions Revisit the forecast as evidence changes Refinement, actual Done work and scope changes alter inputs The answer is a planning forecast, not a fixed release commitment The Campus Express lab contains no observed Sprint velocity; the tutorial calculation must not be used as its measured delivery rate. A reusable reasoning procedure First identify the decision and uncertainty. Locate the accountable person/team and the relevant artifact. Ask what evidence an event should inspect. Apply item-specific AC and the shared DoD before counting progress. Clarify and size relative to a reference, then expose dependencies and split large work. Forecast using comparable observations with units and assumptions. Finally explain what evidence would change your answer. [!question] Check your understanding A team holds every event but hides unfinished integration behind “almost done.” Which empirical pillar fails first, and how does that affect inspection? Answer: transparency; inspection sees misleading completion evidence, so adaptation and forecasts are unreliable. [!summary] Compact review Uncertainty motivates feedback. Agile preferences retain the value of planning and documentation. Scrum connects accountabilities, events and artifacts to transparency, inspection and adaptation. AC specify an item's behavior; DoD governs usable quality. Points are relative; velocity counts Done work; forecasts are conditional. A diagram's labels and units control its interpretation. [^case]: Product Backlog Refinement Activity Task Sheet.pdf, pp.1–4; Week 3 - Tutorial Questions.docx, questions 6–7 (unpaginated document). [^foundations]: SE Methodologies Scrum - Lecture Slides.pdf, pp.4–7; matching PPTX slides 4–7; SE Methodologies Scrum - Reading Material.pdf, pp.1–2. [^cone]: SE Methodologies Scrum - Lecture Slides.pdf, p.8 (actual diagram inspected); reading pp.2–3. Multipliers are the course illustration, not a calibrated statistical model. [^risk]: SE Methodologies Scrum - Lecture Slides.pdf, p.9; reading p.3. Late integration is the causal concern; universal exponential cost is not established. [^agile]: SE Methodologies Scrum - Lecture Slides.pdf, pp.11–15; matching PPTX slides 11–15; reading pp.3–5. Values/principles also checked against the primary [Agile Manifesto]( and its [principles]( these verify rather than expand scope. [^pillars]: SE Methodologies Scrum - Lecture Slides.pdf, p.17; reading p.6. [^roles]: SE Methodologies Scrum - Lecture Slides.pdf, pp.20–24; reading pp.6–8. Source “individual accountability is replaced” is qualified in the reconciliation callout. [^events]: SE Methodologies Scrum - Lecture Slides.pdf, pp.25–29; reading pp.8–9. The 2020 clarification distinguishes the Sprint container, Planning goal and optional Daily questions. [^artifacts]: SE Methodologies Scrum - Lecture Slides.pdf, pp.31–34; reading pp.9–11. Original overview diagram inspected; its stage-like layout is qualified above. [^quality]: SE Methodologies Scrum - Lecture Slides.pdf, p.33; reading pp.10–11; Product Backlog Refinement Activity Task Sheet.pdf, p.1. [^sizing]: SE Methodologies Scrum - Lecture Slides.pdf, pp.36–38; reading pp.11–12; task sheet pp.1,4. [^poker]: SE Methodologies Scrum - Lecture Slides.pdf, pp.39–41; reading pp.12–13; tutorial question 6. The slide's illustrated consensus is an example, not a computed rule. [^deck]: Printable Scrum Planning Poker Deck (A4 Size).pdf, pp.1–4; task sheet p.4 restricts the activity scale. [^forecast]: SE Methodologies Scrum - Lecture Slides.pdf, pp.43–44; reading pp.13–14; equation and worked fraction on p.14 inspected as images. [^burndown]: SE Methodologies Scrum - Lecture Slides.pdf, pp.45–46 (both chart axes inspected); reading pp.14–15.

entries.title: Scrum — Exercises and Worked Solutions
entries.text: Scrum — Exercises and Worked Solutions Course index · Notes · Exercises · Lab Work through the original tutorial in order. Questions are identified by their order in the unpaginated DOCX. Show reasoning and assumptions before revealing each solution. The practical's ten stories are in Lab. Exercise T1 — Defined and empirical control ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Week 3 - Tutorial Questions.docx, question 1. Explain the difference between defined process control and empirical process control. Why does software development align more effectively with empirical process control? [!tip]- Hint Ask whether inputs, transformation and expected outputs are sufficiently understood and repeatable. [!success]- Solution A defined process specifies a repeatable transformation whose outputs can be predicted under controlled conditions. An empirical process inspects observations and adapts when the work or context is uncertain. Software commonly discovers needs through use and technical limits through implementation, so feedback changes the plan. This makes empirical control useful in uncertain development; it does not imply that all software work lacks repeatable processes. A stable automated build can be defined within an empirical product-development effort. Exercise T2 — The cone and early commitments ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Week 3 - Tutorial Questions.docx, question 2. According to Boehm’s Cone of Uncertainty, how does estimation variance change from initial concept to release? Why is committing to fixed budgets and delivery dates at initiation risky in plan-driven models? [!tip]- Hint Distinguish narrowing knowledge from a calendar effect. Read the range as a teaching illustration, not a statistical guarantee. [!success]- Solution The course picture begins with a wide spread (0.25×–4×) and narrows toward 1× at release as requirements and technical understanding improve. Its word variance means spread, not a computed statistical variance. At initiation, scope and effort assumptions may be wrong; fixing budget and date before learning makes overruns or scope cuts more likely if those assumptions fail. Refinement, technical investigation and delivered increments provide evidence for revised estimates. Time passing alone does not guarantee a narrower range. Exercise T3 — Risk and late integration ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Week 3 - Tutorial Questions.docx, question 3. Contrast the risk accumulation profile of traditional Waterfall with Agile frameworks. Why can late integration and testing lead to budget overruns? [!tip]- Hint Trace one mistaken interface assumption through design, code, testing and documents. [!success]- Solution In the course comparison, sequential delivery can defer integrated feedback while decisions accumulate, so an interface mismatch discovered late affects many dependent artifacts. Rework can include redesign, recoding, retesting and documentation, causing schedule and cost overruns. Frequent integrated increments expose some mismatches earlier, when less dependent work has accumulated, and stakeholder feedback can reveal value risks. This is a conditional advantage, not a guarantee that agile eliminates risks or that waterfall performs no early testing: unit tests and early test planning can exist in a waterfall process. Exercise T4 — Accountability without command and control ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Week 3 - Tutorial Questions.docx, question 4. Define the primary accountabilities of the Product Owner, Scrum Master and Development Team. Give a Scrum Master anti-pattern. [!tip]- Hint Separate product value, effectiveness of Scrum, and creation of usable work. [!success]- Solution PO: maximize product value and manage an understandable, ordered Product Backlog. Developers (the source’s Development Team): plan and perform the work to produce a usable Increment meeting the DoD. Scrum Master: help establish Scrum and improve team effectiveness through coaching, facilitation and impediment removal. A taskmaster who assigns every task and turns Daily Scrum into a status report prevents Developers from adapting their own plan. A meeting clerk who never helps improvement is another valid anti-pattern. Shared accountability does not abolish individual responsibility. Exercise T5 — Acceptance and Done ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Week 3 - Tutorial Questions.docx, question 5. Distinguish Acceptance Criteria from Definition of Done. What happens to a Product Backlog Item that is 90% finished at Sprint end but does not satisfy DoD? [!tip]- Hint Use two different questions: does this item do the required thing, and is it usable at the shared quality threshold? [!success]- Solution AC describe an item’s required behavior; DoD describes the common quality conditions for completed work. A cart may show the required total but still lack peer review or working integration. If DoD is unmet, the item contributes no Done Increment and no partial story-point velocity. It returns to the Product Backlog for future consideration, rather than being counted as completed or automatically guaranteed a slot next Sprint. The percentage does not override quality. Exercise T6 — Resolve 2, 3, 3, 13 ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Week 3 - Tutorial Questions.docx, question 6. How should a team resolve significantly divergent estimates, for example votes of 2, 3, 3 and 13? [!tip]- Hint The low and high voters may be estimating different scopes. [!success]- Solution Ask the lowest and highest voters to explain their technical assumptions, effort and uncertainty. Suppose one assumes a static payment selector and another includes a live gateway: take this scope question to the PO, clarify AC and DoD, and then vote again privately and reveal together. Split a clarified large story if appropriate. Repeat toward agreement; record unresolved assumptions if more information is needed. Do not simply average to 5.25, which hides the disagreement and is not a task-scale value. There is no uniquely inferable final estimate from these votes. Exercise T7 — Forecast from observed delivery ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Week 3 - Tutorial Questions.docx, question 7. A Scrum team completed 18, 22 and 20 story points across three 2-week Sprints . (a) Calculate mean velocity Ṽ. (b) With 100 remaining Product Backlog points, forecast the additional Sprints required to release. [!tip]- Hint Add completed points, divide by observed Sprints, then divide remaining points by that rate. Keep units. [!success]- Solution (a) Ṽ = (18 + 22 + 20)/3 = 60/3 = 20 points/Sprint . (b) 100 points ÷ 20 points/Sprint = 5 additional Sprints , equivalent to 10 weeks at two weeks each. No rounding is needed. This forecast assumes comparable team capacity, sizing, scope and DoD and that the observed points really were Done. It is not a guaranteed release date, and it cannot be transferred to Campus Express as a measured velocity. Exercise S1 — Read the axis before the trend SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Provenance: Synthetic practice using the concepts taught in Notes. A remaining-effort chart falls from 40 to 24 hours in one Sprint. Can you report a velocity of 16 story points? What should you report instead? [!tip]- Hint The plotted unit determines what subtraction measures. [!success]- Solution No. The decrease is 16 hours of remaining estimated effort, not 16 Done story points. Hours can be revised and unfinished items may still have less work remaining. Report the change in the plotted quantity and inspect scope changes; calculate point velocity separately from points of items meeting DoD.

entries.title: Campus Express — Backlog Refinement Lab
entries.text: Campus Express — Backlog Refinement Lab Course index · Notes · Exercises · Lab Objective and setup Refine the complete Campus Express backlog by clarifying needs, estimating relative effort, splitting large items and advising the PO on order. Original course practical: Product Backlog Refinement Activity Task Sheet.pdf, all four pages. Allow 30–45 minutes; form a group of six Developers (software engineers/UI designers); the instructor acts as Product Owner. The app serves students and staff ordering meals for delivery to dormitories, libraries or lecture halls. No framework, wireframing application or software version is prescribed. Use paper or a chosen wireframing tool and the supplied Printable Scrum Planning Poker Deck (A4 Size).pdf. The original sources remain in the source folder listed in the course source guide. Use this activity's cards 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 20, 40, 100 , even though the printable deck contains extra values and special cards. Notes teaches all concepts needed here. Required Definition of Done - UI wireframe sketched with interactive navigation flow. - Acceptance criteria fully satisfied. - Peer-reviewed by at least one other developer. - Integration with upstream/downstream screens verified. The source provides this standard but does not provide full AC or actual PO answers for every story. Clarify those during the activity. A submitted table alone does not prove the wireframes meet DoD. Original sequence and required output 1. Read and question — 10 minutes: Review every story and ask specific business or technical questions. Raise your hand to ask the instructor/PO. 2. Relative sizing — 10 minutes: Pick US-01 or US-03 as baseline, for example 2 or 3 points. Vote privately; reveal together; high/low voters explain; clarify and re-vote toward consensus. 3. Decompose — 10 minutes: Split stories estimated 13 or higher into two or more smaller PBIs. The p.1 wording “typically 13” differs; use p.4's explicit step ≥13 for this activity. 4. Priority and delivery — 5 minutes: Reorder the refined table around technical dependencies and effort/value; communicate recommended priority changes to the PO. The source explicitly places Menu Selection before Cart Summary. For each US-01–US-10, record: questions for PO; initial points; refined estimate or split PBIs; suggested priority. Keep unresolved questions visible. The ten exercises below preserve all original stories and provide local worked examples. Their answer keys assume a mock-data interactive UI exercise , with no real authentication, payment gateway, delivery backend or live tracking. These are illustrative assumptions for reasoning, not confirmed PO decisions . If the instructor requires live integration, re-estimate and reconsider splits. Expected output: Completed, ordered backlog table plus clearly defined split items and recorded scope assumptions. Wireframes/navigation, AC checks, peer review and screen-integration evidence are needed to demonstrate the stated DoD. Actual output: No workshop, PO interview, wireframe implementation or peer review was executed here; no team estimates or successful tests are claimed. Exercise US-01 — User Authentication ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★★☆ Source: Product Backlog Refinement Activity Task Sheet.pdf, pp.2–3, backlog US-01; instructions p.4. As a student, I want to view a login/register screen with email and password fields so that I can access my campus account. Complete all four table fields: (a) questions for PO; (b) initial points; (c) refined estimate or split PBIs; (d) suggested priority. Apply the activity DoD. [!tip]- Hint Compare against a clarified 3-point baseline. Identify unresolved behavior and screen dependencies before sizing. Check whether ≥13 requires splitting. [!success]- Solution Illustrative solution; mock UI assumptions require PO confirmation. Questions: Does campus access require institutional sign-on or a mock email/password flow? Are login and registration separate screens? What invalid-input states are required? Initial estimate: 3 points, a plausible discussion input rather than an observed vote or uniquely correct value. Refinement: Use as the agreed 3-point baseline only after clarifying scope. Keep one item if the small mock navigation and validation fit; split login and registration if the required flows make it too large. Suggested priority: 1 among the original story groups. Establish the access flow before screens that require an account; browsing anonymously is a PO decision. Verification: Check the specified behavior and interactive navigation, have another developer review it, and check upstream/downstream screen integration before marking Done. Do not claim that drawing email/password fields implements secure authentication. Exercise US-02 — Restaurant Browsing ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★★☆ Source: Product Backlog Refinement Activity Task Sheet.pdf, pp.2–3, backlog US-02; instructions p.4. As a hungry student, I want to see a scrollable list/grid of open campus eateries with ratings and delivery times so that I can pick a place to eat. Complete all four table fields: (a) questions for PO; (b) initial points; (c) refined estimate or split PBIs; (d) suggested priority. Apply the activity DoD. [!tip]- Hint Compare against a clarified 3-point baseline. Identify unresolved behavior and screen dependencies before sizing. Check whether ≥13 requires splitting. [!success]- Solution Illustrative solution; mock UI assumptions require PO confirmation. Questions: Who supplies open/closed status, ratings and delivery times? How should an empty list appear? Is list or grid sufficient? Initial estimate: 5 points, a plausible discussion input rather than an observed vote or uniquely correct value. Refinement: Retain 5 under mock-data scope: repeated cards, scroll behavior, and links to menus add work relative to US-01. Clarify empty-state AC before finalizing. Suggested priority: 2 among the original story groups. Browsing provides the entry point to menu selection. It can use representative ratings without implementing the detailed reviews screen first. Verification: Check the specified behavior and interactive navigation, have another developer review it, and check upstream/downstream screen integration before marking Done. A displayed delivery-time label is not an implemented prediction service. Exercise US-03 — Menu Selection ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★★☆ Source: Product Backlog Refinement Activity Task Sheet.pdf, pp.2–3, backlog US-03; instructions p.4. As a user, I want to view a restaurant’s menu with item descriptions and price tags so that I can select my food items. Complete all four table fields: (a) questions for PO; (b) initial points; (c) refined estimate or split PBIs; (d) suggested priority. Apply the activity DoD. [!tip]- Hint Compare against a clarified 3-point baseline. Identify unresolved behavior and screen dependencies before sizing. Check whether ≥13 requires splitting. [!success]- Solution Illustrative solution; mock UI assumptions require PO confirmation. Questions: Are price changes or unavailable dishes in scope? Must each item include an image? How does selection lead to customization or the cart? Initial estimate: 3 points, a plausible discussion input rather than an observed vote or uniquely correct value. Refinement: Retain 3 for a simple mock menu; it could instead be the chosen baseline allowed by the sheet. Preserve descriptions, prices and selectable items. Suggested priority: 3 among the original story groups. The source requires Menu Selection before Cart Summary; agree its selected-item output with US-04 and US-05. Verification: Check the specified behavior and interactive navigation, have another developer review it, and check upstream/downstream screen integration before marking Done. A static menu screenshot alone does not satisfy interactive navigation. Exercise US-04 — Customization Modal ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★★☆ Source: Product Backlog Refinement Activity Task Sheet.pdf, pp.2–3, backlog US-04; instructions p.4. As a user, I want a pop-up modal when tapping a dish to select portion size and add special instructions (e.g., "no onions"). Complete all four table fields: (a) questions for PO; (b) initial points; (c) refined estimate or split PBIs; (d) suggested priority. Apply the activity DoD. [!tip]- Hint Compare against a clarified 3-point baseline. Identify unresolved behavior and screen dependencies before sizing. Check whether ≥13 requires splitting. [!success]- Solution Illustrative solution; mock UI assumptions require PO confirmation. Questions: Does portion size change price? Which options are required? Is there a length limit for special instructions? What does cancel preserve? Initial estimate: 5 points, a plausible discussion input rather than an observed vote or uniquely correct value. Refinement: Retain 5 if options and text-entry behavior are small. Define confirm/cancel and carry the chosen size/instructions into the cart. Suggested priority: 4 among the original story groups. Depends on a selected dish; its result feeds cart review. Verification: Check the specified behavior and interactive navigation, have another developer review it, and check upstream/downstream screen integration before marking Done. Treat proposed size-price rules and text limits as questions, not invented official requirements. Exercise US-05 — Cart Summary ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★★☆ Source: Product Backlog Refinement Activity Task Sheet.pdf, pp.2–3, backlog US-05; instructions p.4. As a user, I want a shopping cart view displaying selected items, subtotal, delivery fee, and total price so that I can review my order. Complete all four table fields: (a) questions for PO; (b) initial points; (c) refined estimate or split PBIs; (d) suggested priority. Apply the activity DoD. [!tip]- Hint Compare against a clarified 3-point baseline. Identify unresolved behavior and screen dependencies before sizing. Check whether ≥13 requires splitting. [!success]- Solution Illustrative solution; mock UI assumptions require PO confirmation. Questions: How is the delivery fee calculated? What rounding and currency rules apply? Are quantity edits/removals required? What appears for an empty cart? Initial estimate: 8 points, a plausible discussion input rather than an observed vote or uniquely correct value. Refinement: Retain 8 for the mock flow because totals and screen-state integration are more involved than displaying a menu. Specify a representative fee rule with the PO before checking total = subtotal + delivery fee. Suggested priority: 5 among the original story groups. Menu Selection precedes Cart Summary; customization choices must be reflected if included. Verification: Check the specified behavior and interactive navigation, have another developer review it, and check upstream/downstream screen integration before marking Done. Do not invent discounts, taxes or production pricing rules as mandatory scope. Exercise US-06 — Checkout & Payment ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★★☆ Source: Product Backlog Refinement Activity Task Sheet.pdf, pp.2–3, backlog US-06; instructions p.4. As a user, I want a checkout screen with delivery location selection (e.g., Library, Dorm A) and payment method selection (e.g., Campus Card, Credit Card). Complete all four table fields: (a) questions for PO; (b) initial points; (c) refined estimate or split PBIs; (d) suggested priority. Apply the activity DoD. [!tip]- Hint Compare against a clarified 3-point baseline. Identify unresolved behavior and screen dependencies before sizing. Check whether ≥13 requires splitting. [!success]- Solution Illustrative solution; mock UI assumptions require PO confirmation. Questions: Is payment a mock selection or real-time gateway integration? Which campus locations are valid? What validation and failure paths are needed? Initial estimate: 13 points, a plausible discussion input rather than an observed vote or uniquely correct value. Refinement: Split at ≥13: US-06a Delivery location selection (5) lets a user choose the intended campus destination and continue. US-06b Payment method selection (5 under mock-only scope) lets a user choose Campus Card/Credit Card and reach a confirmation state. Clarify real processing before sizing it. The sheet gives Payment Gateway Processing as an example split, not an answer that resolves the mock-versus-live question. Suggested priority: 6 among the original story groups. Checkout follows cart review. Keep location and payment state connected; prioritizing a selection screen does not deliver real payment. Verification: Check the specified behavior and interactive navigation, have another developer review it, and check upstream/downstream screen integration before marking Done. The new 5 + 5 need not preserve the old 13; clarified scope changed the uncertainty. Exercise US-07 — Live Order Tracking ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★★☆ Source: Product Backlog Refinement Activity Task Sheet.pdf, pp.2–3, backlog US-07; instructions p.4. As a customer, I want a progress screen showing order stages (Received Preparing Out for Delivery Arrived) so that I know when to collect my food. Complete all four table fields: (a) questions for PO; (b) initial points; (c) refined estimate or split PBIs; (d) suggested priority. Apply the activity DoD. [!tip]- Hint Compare against a clarified 3-point baseline. Identify unresolved behavior and screen dependencies before sizing. Check whether ≥13 requires splitting. [!success]- Solution Illustrative solution; mock UI assumptions require PO confirmation. Questions: Are transitions simulated or live? Who supplies status and update frequency? How is stale information shown? Is collection guidance specified? Initial estimate: 13 points, a plausible discussion input rather than an observed vote or uniquely correct value. Refinement: Split for the UI exercise: US-07a View current order stage (5) displays any of the four specified states; US-07b Observe stage transitions (5) connects simulated transitions through Received → Preparing → Out for Delivery → Arrived. Each has a testable user outcome. Obtain PO confirmation that simulated transitions meet activity scope; real tracking would require new analysis. Suggested priority: 7 among the original story groups. A placed order provides the context. Do not drop any of the four official stages when splitting. Verification: Check the specified behavior and interactive navigation, have another developer review it, and check upstream/downstream screen integration before marking Done. The name Live Order Tracking makes the mock assumption particularly important to confirm. Exercise US-08 — Search & Filter ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★★☆ Source: Product Backlog Refinement Activity Task Sheet.pdf, pp.2–3, backlog US-08; instructions p.4. As a user, I want a top search bar with filter tags (e.g., "Vegetarian", "Under $10", "Fastest") so that I can quickly find specific foods. Complete all four table fields: (a) questions for PO; (b) initial points; (c) refined estimate or split PBIs; (d) suggested priority. Apply the activity DoD. [!tip]- Hint Compare against a clarified 3-point baseline. Identify unresolved behavior and screen dependencies before sizing. Check whether ≥13 requires splitting. [!success]- Solution Illustrative solution; mock UI assumptions require PO confirmation. Questions: Does search match restaurants, dishes or both? Can filters combine? Does Under $10 include fees? Is Fastest a sort order or a filter? Initial estimate: 8 points, a plausible discussion input rather than an observed vote or uniquely correct value. Refinement: Retain 8 for agreed mock-data matching and filter states; search plus multiple tags raises behavior combinations. Explicitly define what each tag means before final estimation. Suggested priority: 8 among the original story groups. Useful after the browsable/menu dataset and labels exist; PO may raise its value priority while respecting dependencies. Verification: Check the specified behavior and interactive navigation, have another developer review it, and check upstream/downstream screen integration before marking Done. Do not silently decide the meaning of Fastest or whether price includes fees. Exercise US-09 — Ratings & Reviews ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★★☆ Source: Product Backlog Refinement Activity Task Sheet.pdf, pp.2–3, backlog US-09; instructions p.4. As a user, I want to view customer star ratings and text reviews on a restaurant’s detail page so that I can judge food quality. Complete all four table fields: (a) questions for PO; (b) initial points; (c) refined estimate or split PBIs; (d) suggested priority. Apply the activity DoD. [!tip]- Hint Compare against a clarified 3-point baseline. Identify unresolved behavior and screen dependencies before sizing. Check whether ≥13 requires splitting. [!success]- Solution Illustrative solution; mock UI assumptions require PO confirmation. Questions: Are reviews read-only? How many are shown and in what order? What appears when there are no reviews? Where does the aggregate rating come from? Initial estimate: 5 points, a plausible discussion input rather than an observed vote or uniquely correct value. Refinement: Retain 5 for a read-only mock detail page with ratings and text. Writing reviews or moderation is outside the stated story unless the PO adds it. Suggested priority: 9 among the original story groups. Connect from restaurant browsing/detail navigation. Existing sample rating summaries can support US-02 first. Verification: Check the specified behavior and interactive navigation, have another developer review it, and check upstream/downstream screen integration before marking Done. Displaying sample stars does not establish the credibility or freshness of real customer feedback. Exercise US-10 — Order History ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★★☆ Source: Product Backlog Refinement Activity Task Sheet.pdf, pp.2–3, backlog US-10; instructions p.4. As a returning user, I want a profile tab showing past orders with a "Reorder" button so that I can quickly repurchase frequent meals. Complete all four table fields: (a) questions for PO; (b) initial points; (c) refined estimate or split PBIs; (d) suggested priority. Apply the activity DoD. [!tip]- Hint Compare against a clarified 3-point baseline. Identify unresolved behavior and screen dependencies before sizing. Check whether ≥13 requires splitting. [!success]- Solution Illustrative solution; mock UI assumptions require PO confirmation. Questions: What if prices or availability changed? Does Reorder populate a cart or immediately place an order? How much history is shown? Is authentication required? Initial estimate: 13 points, a plausible discussion input rather than an observed vote or uniquely correct value. Refinement: Split at ≥13: US-10a View past orders in profile (5) shows representative order history; US-10b Reorder from history (8) sends a chosen past order into the agreed review/cart flow, with changed/unavailable items handled according to clarified AC. Do not assume immediate purchase without PO agreement. Suggested priority: 10 among the original story groups. History needs prior-order representation; reorder reuses a defined menu/cart/checkout flow.
