Verification: Check the specified behavior and interactive navigation, have another developer review it, and check upstream/downstream screen integration before marking Done. A Reorder button without a defined destination and changed-item behavior leaves the story ambiguous. Exercise SESSION — Deliver the refined backlog ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★★☆ Source: Product Backlog Refinement Activity Task Sheet.pdf, p.4 steps 1–4. Run the four timed steps as a group of six: ask the PO questions, choose a baseline, use the required planning-poker scale and reconcile differing votes, split every item estimated ≥13, then order and communicate the refined table. Preserve the stated DoD. Explain what evidence supports the resulting scope and priorities. [!tip]- Hint Assemble the ten local rows. Look for undefined interfaces between screens, and separate a proposed answer from one actually confirmed by the PO. [!success]- Solution One defensible hypothetical result is the order shown by priorities 1–10 above, with US-06a/b, US-07a/b and US-10a/b replacing their parent stories. US-03 precedes US-05 as required. Each child carries a local user outcome, AC to confirm, an estimate and the same DoD. This is a partial order constrained by dependencies made into one proposed sequence; it is not the only valid product order. Use US-01 = 3 as the chosen reference; preserve all four fields for every story. Present unresolved questions about authentication, payment, live status, search semantics, fees and reorder behavior to the PO. If real integrations are required, revise affected points/splits rather than reusing the mock estimates. Explain to the PO which proposed ordering decisions are technical dependencies and which are value judgments. Expected evidence includes the completed table, recorded PO answers, final team votes, child-story definitions and proposed priorities. To claim DoD, add wireframes/navigation, AC checks, named peer review and integration checks. None of those workshop observations was produced by this worked example. There is no defensible delivery-date calculation until comparable team velocity and Sprint length are available. Troubleshooting and limitations If votes remain far apart, identify the conflicting assumption instead of choosing a mean. If all stories seem large, revisit the baseline and DoD; if one story is ≥13, split by a meaningful user outcome rather than isolated technical chores that never produce usable behavior. If a wireframe has dead ends, check screen contracts and navigation before calling it Done. If the timing runs out, preserve unanswered questions and report incomplete refinement honestly. The worked sequence demonstrates reasoning; it does not provide instructor-approved AC, a production architecture, secure payment processing or measured team performance. Different estimates and priorities can be valid when their scope assumptions and justifications are explicit.

entries.title: In 60 Seconds
entries.text: Requirements Engineering (RE) turns evidence about people's needs into commitments that developers can implement and reviewers can check. This unit connects six ideas: elicitation, analysis, precise specification, validation, traceability and controlled change. The SRS holds the agreed description; its baseline identifies the authorized version. After studying, you should be able to preserve a stakeholder's intent, separate behavior from quality, choose an EARS pattern, expose an unresolved policy, derive a test, and follow a change through an RTM. The running room-swap case shows why a sentence can sound reasonable while leaving the system's most important decision undefined.

entries.title: Concept Preview
entries.text: [!info] Evidence before commitment Concept: Evidence before commitment. Plain-language meaning: Record what was said or observed before deciding how the system should respond. Keep interpretation linked to its source. Why it matters: A plausible solution can otherwise erase the original need. Connects to: elicitation, viewpoints and user requirements. Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx , §§4.4.1–4.4.5, 4.5.2. [!info] Conditions and observable responses Concept: Conditions and observable responses. Plain-language meaning: A precise requirement tells you when an obligation applies and what result to expect. Quality targets also need a measurement rule. Why it matters: This makes missing decisions visible before implementation. Connects to: EARS, FR/NFR and test design. Source: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides.pdf , PDF pp.35–42,52–53. [!info] Requirements interact Concept: Requirements interact. Plain-language meaning: Two individually reasonable rules can disagree when they govern the same situation. Why it matters: A queue, an urgent request and an approval policy need a joint interpretation. Connects to: interaction grids and validation. Source: Step-by-step SRS Example.pdf , PDF pp.14–15. [!info] SRS and baseline Concept: SRS and baseline. Plain-language meaning: The SRS organizes the specification. A baseline is its approved version, maintained through recorded decisions. Why it matters: A filename or blank signature block cannot establish approval. Connects to: governance and change control. Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx , §§4.6.1–4.6.2, 4.8.2. [!info] Traceability Concept: Traceability. Plain-language meaning: Follow a need into its detailed rules, design and tests; follow an artifact back to its justification. Why it matters: A change can affect more than the sentence being edited. Connects to: RTM, impact analysis and evidence status. Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx , §§4.8.1–4.8.2.

entries.title: Exam Evidence Snapshot
entries.text: Requirements concepts appear in every historical adjacent-code question section; source-supported use-case modelling appears in two. Cover pages, current-code equivalence and official schemes remain unconfirmed; see past-paper intelligence. Topic Observed papers Known marks Typical depth Priority --- ---: ---: --- --- Requirements levels, types, elicitation, specification and validation 6/6 68 Define, compare, classify, analyse HIGH EXAM RELEVANCE Use-case modelling 2/6 30 Identify, analyse, construct HIGH EXAM RELEVANCE EARS, interaction analysis, traceability and change control 0/6 directly None observed Not observed NOT OBSERVED IN THE AVAILABLE PAST-PAPER SAMPLE The sample does not define the syllabus. Preserve EARS, traceability and controlled change because the supplied materials support them.

entries.title: Before You Start
entries.text: From Unit 02, a lifecycle model organizes activities and feedback. From Unit 03, acceptance criteria describe item-specific behavior while DoD sets shared quality conditions. Here, requirements validation checks the description before treating it as an authorized basis for downstream work; a planned acceptance test is not an executed result. Revisit process models · Revisit acceptance criteria and Done [!question] Explain it yourself Does an upfront requirements phase mean a draft may be examined only once? [!success]- Check your explanation No. Upfront locates RE before downstream design; the internal RE spiral repeatedly refines business, user and system understanding before baselining. Later authorized revisions use change control. Source: S06 §§4.1,4.2.2,4.8.2.

entries.title: A motivating question
entries.text: Official case: Dr. Li wants urgent room swaps (E-002); Ms. Lee requires her sign-off (E-003). The initial use case creates a pending request and queues a notification. The supplement adds a FIFO waitlist, approved urgent precedence, a 48-hour rule for recurring class-time changes, study-room bookings and maintenance exclusions. [^case] Reasoning task: What must be preserved so “fast swapping” does not bypass approval? Can a capacity check alone satisfy the whole request? What happens if a later change introduces encryption? Case question Knowledge needed --- --- Whose rule are we implementing? Evidence, viewpoints and user/system levels What happens before approval? EARS, use-case conditions and observable state Can both policies hold? Interaction analysis and validation What changes after sign-off? Traceability and ECR/CCB governance Success means an explicit, testable interpretation plus visible unresolved decisions. It does not mean inventing a deadline, claiming real stakeholder approval or treating fictional Passed labels as our results.

entries.title: 1. How do we avoid specifying the wrong solution?
entries.text: Intuition. Preserve the problem long enough for the people affected to recognize it. A detailed API for an unnecessary operation is still the wrong system. The course teaches five phases: 0 Feasibility → 1 Elicitation → 2 Analysis & Classification → 3 Specification → 4 Validation . Feasibility asks whether the proposal is viable; proceed, scope down or cancel are distinct outcomes. Elicitation captures raw needs; analysis organizes and evaluates them; specification assembles precise commitments; validation checks them and sends unresolved findings back. Authorized sign-off establishes a baseline. Management continues as requirements change. [^process] The internal spiral deepens Business → User → System understanding, revisiting elicitation, specification and validation. Analysis is part of the accompanying five-phase account, although the spiral image names three sectors. This iteration can occur within an upfront RE phase. A late misunderstanding may require revising design, code, tests and procedures because those artifacts inherited it; the source does not establish a universal numerical cost multiplier. Choose evidence that can answer the missing question Missing knowledge Technique and durable output --- --- One person's goals or exceptions Interview; attributed dated notes and open questions Several conflicting perspectives Workshop/JAD; speaker-attributed minutes and actions Unspoken habitual work Observation/shadowing; field notes and current-workflow sketch Input from a wider population Survey; responses organized by question and sample Existing formal rule Document analysis; exact policy reference and extracted statement Reaction to a possible interaction Low-fidelity prototype; annotated screens and feedback The Elicitation Register holds raw ID, wording, source/technique, date and status. Supporting outputs include draft use-case diagrams/descriptions, stakeholder/viewpoint list, glossary and the records above. Draft material is useful evidence but not yet a finalized authorized requirement. Domain jargon calls for a glossary; tacit work calls for observation; competing departmental interests call for facilitated discussion. [^elicit] Worked chain: E-002 records an urgent-swap problem. Organize it as UR-2 , an accessible statement of the lecturer's need. Attach E-003's approval constraint; do not discard it because it lacks a separate UR. Refine detailed system rules such as SR-2.1 capacity rejection. That one rule covers only one part of the larger user need. A User Requirement (UR) communicates stakeholder intent; a System Requirement (SR) specifies detailed behavior or constraints for development and testing. Viewpoint-Oriented Analysis asks a different question: Interactor (direct user), Indirect (affected consumer of outputs), or Domain (environment/policy/technical constraint). Abstraction is detail; viewpoint is perspective. A policy communicated by a person can still be a domain constraint. [^analysis]

entries.title: 2. Can a diagram establish who may approve?
entries.text: Problem first. A Student-to-swap line appears in the broad diagram. Does it authorize every student to use every lecturer-only precondition? timetabling-use-cases.svg Figure 1 — Timetabling actors and use cases Read it: Roles stand outside the system boundary; use cases are ellipses inside. Student and Lecturer each associate with schedule viewing and requesting a swap. Facility Administrator associates with review/approval, allocations and reports. The seven plain associations show participation, not execution order or permission inheritance. Crossing lines are not junctions. Key takeaway: Scope is visible, but authorization and exceptional behavior need descriptions. This existing figure is reused unchanged from the standard edition; source: S04 PDF p.22, actual image rechecked; S11 p.23 repeats the broad view. UC-04's description adds the primary actor, preconditions, success postconditions, main path and exceptions. Its lecturer is authenticated and has an assigned session within the next 48 hours. The path selects a session/room, records a mandatory reason, submits, checks capacity/equipment and returns a tracking ID. The postcondition is PENDING_ADMIN_REVIEW , notification queued and room flagged SWAP_REQUESTED . Pending is not approved; queued is not delivered. [^uc] Worked state reasoning: before submission, no request exists. After a valid submission, a pending request and its tracking record exist. The sources do not justify concluding that allocation has already changed. To enforce E-003, a proposed derived rule would prevent the allocation change until the authorized sign-off is recorded. That proposal needs validation alongside eligibility and exception rules; it is not a claim that the source excerpt already implements it. The initial elicitation description can emphasize the main path; the specification version must make conditions, alternatives and links precise. Reusing UC-04 for student study-room bookings requires revising or specializing its lecturer-specific conditions. The broad association alone cannot perform that refinement. [!question] Explain it yourself Why is an administrator alert insufficient evidence that no swap bypasses approval? [!success]- Check your explanation Notification describes communication, not the condition that permits allocation to change. Specify and test that the change is blocked without authorized approval, including exceptional paths. Source: S04 pp.21,24–25,53; S11 pp.15,20.

entries.title: 3. How do we turn “quickly, with approval” into a checkable rule?
entries.text: Intuition. Separate the event, the continuing state, the exception and the promised response. Then ask which words still admit competing interpretations. EARS means Easy Approach to Requirements Syntax. Its five basic course patterns structure obligations: [^ears] Pattern Form and appropriate condition --- --- Ubiquitous The system shall respond; no trigger or condition Event-driven WHEN an event occurs, the system shall respond State-driven WHILE a state holds, the system shall respond Option-driven WHERE a feature/configuration is included, the system shall respond Unwanted behavior IF an unwanted condition holds, THEN the system shall respond Worked decomposition, proposed for the main case: 1. Preserve E-003 as the reason; preserve Ms. Lee's role. 2. Use an event-driven rule for submission creating a pending request and alerting the administrator. 3. Use an unwanted-behavior rule to prevent allocation change if authorized approval is absent. 4. Define what eligible approval permits and which request it applies to; do not assume approval bypasses capacity, equipment or availability checks. 5. Separate “quickly” into a performance target with agreed timing endpoints, threshold and conditions. Until those are supplied, label the target UNCONFIRMED . An EARS sentence such as “WHEN submitted, the system shall respond quickly” remains ambiguous. Grammar helps expose the missing decision; it cannot supply policy or a number. WHERE in the course templates denotes an option/configuration, whereas S11 p.15 uses it for runtime urgent precedence; preserve that source variant while explaining its intended condition. Behavior, quality and category are separate questions An FR specifies behavior, input, output or action. An NFR specifies quality or constraints on behavior. FURPS+ is the classification checklist: Functionality, Usability, Reliability, Performance, Supportability, plus design/implementation/interface/physical constraints. Category names are not themselves testable commitments. [^quality] Worked sentence: “reset a password securely within 10 seconds” contains password-reset behavior, a performance limit and an undefined security promise. Keep the original 10 seconds; clarify start/end, workload and whether human/email delays count. Elicit the actual security controls. Do not invent them or treat “securely” as an acceptance procedure. For a measurable quality target, supply metric + threshold with unit + conditions . The case's “fetch and render within 3.0 seconds over 4G” provides more than “quickly,” but still needs an operational measurement procedure: start/end events, data volume, workload and repeat policy. A usability proposal can measure completion of a specified task by representative first-time users without help; any proposed success proportion remains non-official. Some constraints are categorical: the goal is objective evaluation, not merely attaching a number.

entries.title: 4. What if reasonable requirements compete?
entries.text: Problem first. A routine request arrived first, then an urgent request targets the same room. FIFO and urgent precedence cannot both determine first position without a qualification. An interaction grid compares pairs: +1 compatible, 0 neutral, −1 potential conflict in this classroom scheme. It is symmetric; leave the diagonal unscored. A negative score identifies a question requiring evidence and a decision, not a probability or proof of impossibility. [^conflict] Worked policy resolution: put UR-2 and UR-4 before the relevant stakeholders; walk through this same-room case; log the inconsistent ordering; revise the rule to allow urgent precedence subject to Ms. Lee's sign-off , as S11 p.15 does. Recheck cancellation, ties, urgency authority and permissions. The supplement resolves one ambiguity, not all possible queue behavior. The source also flags encryption versus a short response-time budget. Identify the data path and mandatory controls, evaluate representative overhead and compare feasible designs. If both commitments cannot be met, present scope/resource/target alternatives to the authorized decision-makers. Do not quietly weaken security. In this story encryption starts as an anticipated risk and becomes NFR2 only through the later ECR.

entries.title: 5. What makes the SRS ready for a baseline?
entries.text: Intuition. A governed specification needs a readable organization and evidence that its commitments make sense together. Merely collecting every sentence into a file achieves neither. The course's five top sections are 1 Introduction; 2 Overall Description; 3 Specific Requirements; 4 Appendices; 5 Approval/Sign-off . Under 3, place FRs by feature/module (3.1), external interfaces (3.2), NFRs by quality/constraint category (3.3), and finalized use cases/models (3.4). The RTM, dictionary, interaction grid and revision history belong in appendices. Stable IDs and cross-references connect the groups. [^srs] The SRS is the specification; its baseline is an authorized version. The Joint Steering Committee considers technical feasibility/completeness, client intent and project budget/schedule. The case uses a contractual scenario; an SRS filename does not universally establish legal enforceability. Choose the property, then the evidence-gathering technique Validation check Question in the room-swap case --- --- Validity Does the workflow preserve Ms. Lee's actual authority? Consistency Can FIFO, urgency and approval rules hold together? Completeness Are reason, cancellation and exceptions covered? Realism Can staff keep maintenance flags sufficiently current? Verifiability Can an objective test decide whether the timing rule holds? A check names the property; a technique gathers evidence. Reviews/inspections compare the written commitments; prototypes expose interaction gaps; test-case generation exposes missing expected outcomes; walkthroughs examine a scenario with stakeholders; model consistency checks compare diagrams/text; traceability analysis finds missing links. Combining techniques reduces different blind spots, without proving absence of every defect. [^validation] Visible worked test design: SR-2.1 says reject if capacity is below enrollment. With capacity 30 and enrollment 45, 30 < 45 is true, so submission must be rejected with the specified capacity response. At capacity 45 the inequality is false: this rule alone does not reject, but other checks can still prevent approval. A test at equality therefore does not establish “always approve.” This is a derived test, not an executed result; the capacity-override variant below must be resolved for a final baseline.

entries.title: 6. What changes when a new rule arrives after sign-off?
entries.text: requirement-lineage.svg Figure 2 — Requirement lineage (informal traceability diagram) Read it: Follow linked evidence, user need, detailed requirement, realization and test. Downward links indicate derivation/realization, not runtime sequence. Follow the relationships upward to recover the justification. Key takeaway: A local edit can have nonlocal consequences. Existing standard figure reused unchanged; source principles: S06 §4.8.1 and ID glossary; S04 pp.62–64. The RTM cross-references requirements, design/code, tests and status. Forward tracing finds missing realization; backward tracing challenges artifacts with no authorized purpose, including unrequested features (“gold plating”). Necessary infrastructure may have a derived architectural justification; missing linkage is a finding to investigate. [^trace] Worked impact sequence: an ECR records request ID, submitter, description and reason. Locate affected requirements and versions in the RTM; follow modules, interfaces and tests; inspect shared dependencies; estimate implementation, data changes, retesting and milestone impact. The CCB weighs business, schedule/resource, technical and QA evidence. An approved request changes the baseline and dependent artifacts; rejection preserves the baseline and records why. [^change] In the fictional example, the later ECR adds NFR2 , affects SR-1.1 and TC-API-204, and produces v1.1. Code/API names in the reading are trace references, not executable files supplied here. “Passed” in the source's RTM is a story status, not test evidence from this production task. The displayed sign-off block remains blank v1.0, so it cannot prove actual v1.1 signatures.

entries.title: Source precision and unresolved variants
entries.text: Keep the two claims visible, state the safest usable interpretation, and retain confirmation status. The following items are source disagreements or demonstrable gaps, not student mistakes. The unchanged standard reference expands them; the tutor state preserves the ordinary issue register. Sources and conflict Safest interpretation and confirmation --- --- S04 p.4: no formal reversal; pp.65–68: CCB revision Use the later authorized-change mechanism; simplified early wording is not a prohibition. Intended wording unconfirmed. S04 p.21: E-002 workshop, 5 Feb; S11 pp.3,6: interview, 4 Feb Preserve both provenance records; actual intended event unconfirmed. S04 pp.44–46: FR versus cross-cutting “F”; S06 §4.5.3: FRs receive F tags Separate category, statement and cross-cutting scope; lecturer's preferred assessment convention unconfirmed. S04 p.25: capacity override; p.53: reject insufficient capacity State the variant used; final exception policy unconfirmed. S04 p.25: concurrency rejection; S11 pp.12,15: waitlist and approved urgent priority Treat supplement as a documented refinement; remaining queue/cancellation rules need confirmation. S04 pp.24–25: lecturer-specific UC-04; S11 pp.13,20: student workflow reuse Specify student permissions/preconditions; do not inherit an assigned lecturer session automatically. S04 p.52: login, fetch/render ≤3.0s; p.63 and S11 p.24: tab, JSON fetch <2.0s Different triggers, endpoints and thresholds. A nested API budget is only a hypothesis; authoritative baseline unconfirmed. S04 p.47 and S06 Q23: <3s; p.52: within 3.0s Preserve wording; equality boundary unconfirmed. S11 p.13: FR7 rejects and shows earliest date; p.20 drops the display Retain fuller p.13/SR-3.1 meaning as a visible interpretation; final catalog wording unconfirmed. S11 p.13 calls automatic cross-checking NFR3; S06 §4.5.3 defines action as FR Keep source ID, explain functional behavior; separate measurable quality target still needs agreement. S04 p.21 requires sign-off; S04 p.59/S11 p.20 emphasize FR2 alert Notification does not establish enforcement. Approval transition and tests remain underspecified. S11 pp.24–25 show example Passed rows; p.27 has blank v1.0 sign-off; S04 p.68 narrates v1.1 Distinguish illustrative trace status, baseline story and actual signatures. No execution or approval established here. Further boundaries: EARS syntax does not guarantee semantic precision (S04 pp.35,39 versus its own vague examples); the recurring class-time notice rule is not automatically a ban on urgent room changes (S11 pp.4,13,15). The RTM excerpt does not list every NFR or approval constraint despite completeness language (S06 §4.8.1; S11 pp.24–25). The exact 30-day legal attribution (S04 p.18/S06 §4.4.2) and “end-to-end” encryption wording (S04 p.68) require the separately labelled authoritative clarifications in the standard Notes; they are not confirmed applicable university obligations or interchangeable security properties.

entries.title: Return to the motivating question
entries.text: Preserve E-002's goal and E-003's authority; separate request, pending state, authorization and allocation effect. Capacity rejection is one derived behavior, not the whole UR-2. Reconcile queue rules with approved urgent precedence, distinguish recurring time changes from room changes, and resolve the documented capacity/role/timing variants before authoritative acceptance tests. The later encryption ECR requires impact analysis and a recorded baseline decision, with trace and test updates. This answers the opening problem while leaving genuinely unspecified policy visible. For full case coverage, also trace E-001 → UR-1/SR-1.1 mobile viewing; E-004 → UR-3/SR-3.1/FR7 notice; E-005 → UR-4/SR-4.1 waitlist; E-006 → UR-5/SR-5.1/FR6 study rooms; E-007 → source NFR3 automatic checking; and E-008 → UR-6/SR-6.1 maintenance exclusions. The standard reference contains the full FR1–FR7/NFR1–NFR3 catalog and six UR/SR trace rows. [^case]

entries.title: Review
entries.text: Full Understanding Return to the case, mechanisms, figures and worked derivations above. Attempt the linked original questions and the five-row RTM/headings-only SRS lab. The source-variant table should travel with any use of the standard catalog. 5-Minute Review Capture attributed evidence and missing perspectives. Refine business/user intent before detailed system commitments. Split behavior, quality and approval conditions; choose EARS by condition type and measure quality under explicit circumstances. Compare interacting rules, organize the SRS and validate with complementary techniques. Trace every obligation and justified artifact, then route later changes through ECR, impact analysis and CCB decision. Keep assumptions, source versions and evidence status visible. 60-Second Recall - Five RE phases; three depths - Evidence and interpretation - Viewpoint versus abstraction - Pending versus approved - Five EARS conditions - Metric, threshold, conditions - Interaction and validation - SRS and baseline - Bidirectional trace and ECR [^case]: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides.pdf, PDF pp.15,21,52–54; Step-by-step SRS Example.pdf, pp.3–15,20–25. entries.title: Requirements Engineering and SRS
entries.text: Requirements Engineering and SRS Course index · Notes · Exercises · Lab Learning goals Turn stakeholder evidence into an analyzable requirement set and a reviewable SRS. Distinguish purpose, behavior, quality and implementation constraints; use EARS without mistaking grammar for correctness; analyze conflicts; derive tests; and trace an approved change through affected artifacts. Read the course's use-case diagram and identify what it does not specify. Prerequisites: process models from Unit 02 and the contrasting agile approach in Unit 03. Opening case — Three reasonable requests can hide a broken system Official running case: Sarah wants her weekly timetable on her phone. Dr. Li needs urgent room swaps. Ms. Lee says swaps must never bypass her sign-off. The supplement adds a 48-hour policy for recurring class-time changes, a FIFO waitlist, student study-room bookings, slow manual timetable checking, and an unofficial list of rooms with broken equipment.[^case] Known information: Feasibility in the case is judged positive: a web/mobile system is considered viable within the stated two-semester development budget and can integrate with existing university records. This is a fictional worked decision, not a feasibility assessment performed here. The main requirement target is a timetable rendered within 3.0 seconds over 4G. The supplied sources contain some inconsistent detail, explicitly reconciled below. Questions: What should be captured before designing APIs? How can a fast swap preserve approval? What happens when urgency meets a FIFO queue or the 48-hour rule? How can testers distinguish a correct requirement from a vague promise? What changes when encryption is introduced after a baseline? Success criteria: Preserve stakeholder provenance, write testable behavior without inventing unapproved policy, identify unresolved conflicts, map requirements to evidence, and distinguish a proposed specification from an approved or executed result. What We Need to Learn Decision Concepts needed --- --- Is the project worth pursuing? Feasibility and proceed/scope-down/cancel outcomes What do people actually need? Elicitation techniques, register, viewpoints and use cases What does each statement commit us to? User/system levels, EARS, FR/NFR and FURPS+ Can the commitments coexist? Interaction analysis and negotiated conflict resolution What document can people approve? SRS organization, governance and baselines How do we detect missing or wrong behavior? Five validation checks and complementary techniques How do we preserve meaning after change? Stable IDs, RTM and formal change control 1. Process context: upfront does not mean one pass The lecturer explicitly returns to a Waterfall teaching context in Chapter 4. The source's sequence is Requirements → System Design → Implementation → Testing, with a baselined SRS, design specification, working modules and verified system as respective deliverables. Detailed future units are not supplied. In this context, requirements are reviewed and baselined before downstream design; agile requirements are refined throughout development.[^process] The reason for rigorous early RE is dependency: a misunderstood policy can become design, code, tests and training before users discover it. Correcting only one sentence late may therefore require changing several artifacts. Formal documentation and gates provide a review trail and stable hand-offs; their cost is effort upfront and slower authorized change. Fixed plans do not themselves make uncertain outcomes predictable. [!warning] The course's Waterfall descriptions conflict S04 p.4 says there is “no formal mechanism” to revisit a signed-off phase, but pp.65–68 explicitly define formal change control; Unit 02 also describes feedback/rework. Read the early slide as a simplified one-way default, not a prohibition on authorized revision. The later CCB process is the usable mechanism. Nor does documentation literally replace all stakeholder conversation: the chapter itself requires interviews and walkthroughs. Five activities and three depths Course phase Work and decision Result --- --- --- 0 — Feasibility Assess organizational value, technology, integration, budget and schedule Feasibility Report: proceed, reduce scope or cancel 1 — Elicitation Capture needs, observations and constraints with provenance Raw Elicitation Register and supporting artifacts 2 — Analysis & Classification Organize meaning, viewpoints and levels; clarify and compare commitments Organized, classified requirements and recorded conflicts 3 — Specification Refine precise system requirements and assemble the governed document Draft SRS 4 — Validation Check whether the specification is suitable, consistent and testable; resolve findings SRS ready for authorized sign-off and baselining The source's spiral image repeats requirements work at Business → User → System depth. The inner loop asks whether the initiative meets business needs; the next specifies user needs; the outer loop details system behavior and constraints. Elicitation, analysis, specification and validation recur as understanding improves. The actual image names three sectors—elicitation, specification and validation—with feasibility, prototyping and reviews as validation-side examples; analysis is discussed in the accompanying five-phase model. The spiral is internal refinement of requirements, not a claim that this course's entire project lifecycle is agile.[^roadmap] A feasibility study uses business mandates, high-level expectations, legacy documentation and market/technology information. “Scope down” is different from pretending an infeasible requirement was never requested: document what is removed and why. Feasibility can be revisited if later evidence invalidates its assumptions. 2. Elicit evidence before turning it into a solution Elicitation discovers and captures stakeholder needs and domain constraints. Analysis interprets, organizes and evaluates that material. The course separates them to prevent premature filtering: preserve an inconvenient request even if it later conflicts with another. In practice, learning a conflict may trigger another interview; the boundaries distinguish purposes, not a ban on thinking during a conversation.[^elicitation] Choose a technique for what is missing Technique Useful when Record --- --- --- Interview An individual's goals, exceptions or reasons need depth Attributed notes, date, raw wording and open questions Workshop / JAD Several perspectives must be heard together Minutes, speaker-attributed requests and actions Observation / shadowing Experts omit habitual steps or unofficial workarounds Time-stamped field notes and current-workflow sketches Survey / questionnaire A larger population must contribute Responses tabulated by question, with relevant sample context Document analysis Existing rules are already written Extracted statements with exact policy/document provenance Low-fidelity prototype Users need something concrete to react to Annotated wireframes and feedback for each screen The Elicitation Register records informal ID, raw statement, source/technique, date and status. Entries initially remain Draft. It is not yet a list of authorized features. Keep the source statement alongside its interpretation so future reviewers can challenge a mistaken derivation. Sources include operational managers (reports, resource use), corporate policies (approval rules), physical environment (hardware/network/temperature limits) and applicable external rules. A stakeholder list alone misses constraints not represented by the interviewees. Typical problems and responses are tacit knowledge → observation; jargon → shared glossary; unrealistic wishes → feasibility/cost-value discussion; political conflict → facilitated multi-perspective workshop.[^elicitation] [!warning] Source legal example — SUPPLEMENTARY TECHNICAL CLARIFICATION S04 p.18 and S06 §4.4.2 attribute an exact 30-day post-termination purge to GDPR Article 17. [Article 17's official text]( provides conditional erasure without undue delay and exceptions, not that universal rule. Treat “30 days” as an illustrative policy needing authoritative confirmation, not a legal fact. These course examples also mix regulations and standards; they do not establish which obligations apply to the fictional university. Worked evidence: the supplement adds what interviews miss The supplement's interview notes identify missing approval confirmation; its workshop records the Registrar's notice policy, Dr. Li's waitlist request and the student representative's study-room idea. Observation finds 14 pending emails, requests up to three days old, 10–15 minutes of manual checking, a broken-projector spreadsheet and approvals without system records. Those are observations in the teaching scenario, not measured results from our work.[^supplement] Raw ID Evidence and source meaning Organized destination in the course --- --- --- E-001 Sarah wants mobile schedule access UR-1 → SR-1.1 E-002 Dr. Li depends on email for urgent swaps UR-2 → SR-2.1; UC-04 E-003 Ms. Lee requires sign-off Constraint attached to UR-2 and approval workflow E-004 Registrar requires 48-hour notice for recurring time changes UR-3 → SR-3.1 → FR7 E-005 Dr. Li requests first-come allocation plus a waitlist UR-4 → SR-4.1, subsequently refined for urgency E-006 Students want study-room bookings to use the same workflow UR-5 → SR-5.1 → FR6 E-007 Observation finds slow manual timetable cross-checking Source's NFR3 (classification problem discussed below) E-008 Observation finds unofficial “problem rooms” list UR-6 → SR-6.1 S04 p.21 records E-002 as a 5 Feb workshop ; S11 pp.3,6 records a 4 Feb interview . Preserve both as source variants; the actual provenance needs instructor confirmation. E-007 being inferred from observation does not by itself make the resulting requirement non-functional. Confirm inferred needs with the stakeholder. Elicitation outputs also include draft use-case diagrams/descriptions, a stakeholder/viewpoint list, draft domain glossary, interview/workshop/field records and prototype feedback. Drafts help confirm understanding; they have not earned a baseline merely by being written down. 3. Use cases describe interaction, not implementation A use-case diagram scopes actor–system interactions. The source shows Student and Lecturer linked to both View Weekly Schedule and Request Room / Time Swap . Facility Administrator links to Review & Approve Swap Requests , Manage Room Allocations , and View Utilization Reports . The actor links are associations, not flow arrows; their crossing does not create a junction. The system boundary separates external roles from the subject's use cases.[^usecase] timetabling-use-cases.svg Figure 1 — Timetabling actors and use cases Read it: An actor denotes a role, not one named person. Ellipses inside the rectangle denote use cases of the Timetabling System. A plain line means participation/communication; it does not specify execution order, data flow or automatic approval. This redraw preserves the source's seven associations using conventional actor symbols. Key takeaway: A map of who interacts with which function cannot specify the detailed success, failure or authorization rules by itself. No multiplicities, include/extend relationships or timing constraints are asserted here. The source's broad Student-to-swap link is later explained partly by study-room workflow reuse; precise permissions still belong in the descriptions. SUPPLEMENTARY TECHNICAL CLARIFICATION: The role, subject boundary, ellipse and association meanings are checked against [OMG UML 2.5.1, §18]( This does not establish the lecturer's required UML version. Other diagram families are named in the reading—class for domain structure, sequence for interactions, state for state-dependent behavior—but their full notations are not taught in these supplied sources, so no invented advanced UML unit is added. UC-04: Request Urgent Timetable Room Swap A use-case description supplies ID/name, primary actor, preconditions, success postconditions, main success scenario and alternate/exception flows. The initial elicitation version can focus on a happy path; specification finalizes conditions, exceptions and terminology.[^usecase] UC-04 field Source content and interpretation --- --- Primary actor University Lecturer Preconditions Authenticated lecturer; assigned session within the next 48 hours Success postconditions Request created as PENDING_ADMIN_REVIEW ; administrator notification queued; room slot flagged SWAP_REQUESTED Main interaction Open My Schedule and select session; inspect details/alternative rooms; select target and give mandatory reason; submit; validate capacity/equipment; log and return REQ-XXXX tracking ID Capacity exception Source example: capacity 30 versus enrollment 45; warn and ask for another room or a capacity override Concurrency exception Source draft rejects a concurrently requested room and refreshes the available list Creating a pending request is not approving or executing the swap. Notification queued is not proof it was delivered. Preconditions should be true before the interaction starts; input validation is behavior performed during it. [!warning] Do not merge incompatible UC-04 versions silently S04 p.25 allows a capacity-override request; p.53's SR-2.1 simply rejects insufficient capacity. S11 later introduces waitlisting where the earlier concurrency flow rejects. Student study-room bookings reuse UC-04 even though its stated actor/preconditions assume an assigned lecturer session. These require explicit revised rules or specialized descriptions. The supplied SRS excerpt does not resolve every permission and transition. Use the question's stated rule and disclose the variant; seek instructor clarification for the intended final baseline. 4. Analyze meaning along separate dimensions User level and system level A User Requirement (UR) describes stakeholder need in understandable language; a System Requirement (SR) refines exact behavior and constraints sufficiently for development and testing. “Students can view their weekly timetable on mobile” does not yet specify rendering time, operating conditions or failures. SR-1.1 adds the event, current-week calendar display and 3.0-second/4G condition. This is a refinement, not a different user goal.[^analysis] Avoid the rabbit-hole trap : selecting schemas, protocols or caching before understanding the user's problem can optimize the wrong solution. System requirements are not automatically implementation design. Include a technology or interface constraint when it is justified by an external dependency or agreed need; do not prescribe arbitrary internal tables merely to sound precise. Viewpoints and abstraction are independent Viewpoint-Oriented Analysis (VOA) checks Interactor (direct user), Indirect (affected stakeholder using outputs) and Domain (environmental, policy or technical constraints) perspectives. The abstraction question is “how detailed is this statement?”; the viewpoint question is “whose perspective or constraint must it represent?” A Registrar's policy can be a domain constraint even though a person communicates it. An observation about work can lead to either functional or quality requirements. Classifying all three viewpoints is a coverage aid, not proof no stakeholder is missing. EARS separates the condition from the response Easy Approach to Requirements Syntax (EARS) makes triggers, states, options and responses explicit. Preserve original stakeholder language in the register, then create the structured derivative with a stable link.[^ears] Pattern Template Source example/interpretation --- --- --- Ubiquitous The shall . Display weekly class schedules in calendar view; unconditional obligation Event-driven WHEN , the shall . A submitted room change triggers an administrator alert State-driven WHILE , the shall . Show a loading indicator while database synchronization is active Option-driven WHERE , the shall . Read room details when the text-to-speech feature is enabled Unwanted behavior IF , THEN the shall . An invalid university ID triggers an error response Mechanism: identify the system, the condition and the observable response; decide whether the condition is an event, a continuing state, a configured option or an error; write the appropriate sentence; then define ambiguous nouns and thresholds. Compare related conditions to find overlaps or gaps. [!example] A grammatical statement can remain untestable “WHEN a request is submitted, the system shall respond quickly” has an EARS shape but still leaves “quickly” undefined. A repair needs an agreed measured response and threshold under stated conditions. EARS exposes missing information; it does not invent the answer. SUPPLEMENTARY TECHNICAL CLARIFICATION: The EARS originator's [notation overview]( pp.10–12, also permits combined patterns. The course's five basic patterns are a teaching subset, not proof that all requirements fit one simple clause. WHERE denotes a feature/configuration option. S11 p.15 uses it for an incoming urgent request; an event/condition formulation better expresses that runtime decision. This is a labelled correction, not a silent change to SR-4.1. FR, NFR and FURPS+ answer different questions A Functional Requirement (FR) specifies behavior: updating data, deactivating an account, generating a report or synchronizing course codes with an ERP. A Non-Functional Requirement (NFR) specifies quality or constraints on behavior: performance, usability, reliability or implementation/interface limits. One stakeholder sentence may combine both: invoice printing is behavior; a two-second completion target constrains it.[^furps] FURPS+ is a classification checklist: Functionality (features/capabilities/security behavior), Usability (human factors/documentation), Reliability (availability/accuracy/recovery), Performance (speed/throughput/resource efficiency), Supportability (testability/maintainability/configurability), and + constraints (design, implementation, interface, physical). The category label is not itself a testable requirement. [!warning] FURPS+ source disagreement S04 pp.44–46 treats cross-cutting security/audit rules as “F” rather than “true FR.” S06 §4.5.3 instead explains that individual FR statements can receive the Functionality tag. Use the reading's distinction: classification label versus individual statement , with cross-cutting versus feature-local as another dimension. An audit-logging rule still specifies behavior even if it affects many features. Preserve the lecture's special convention when explaining its examples, but do not treat “F” and “FR” as universally exclusive. Instructor confirmation is needed if an assessment expects that split. Make quality observable The course's measurable-NFR checklist asks for metric + threshold with unit + condition . A test also needs an operational measurement procedure: start/end events, workload, environment and applicable population.[^nfr] Source target What it supplies What to pin down before a real test --- --- --- Search within 2 seconds for 95% of queries, ≤100 concurrent users Response time, percentile, threshold and load Dataset, query mix, timing endpoints and observation interval First-time user completes swap in [!example] From SR-2.1 to TC-UNIT-402 Given capacity 30 and enrollment 45, when the lecturer submits the request, then reject it and show the capacity warning. The inequality explains the expected decision. Additional boundary checks at equality and just below enrollment clarify the rule; equality alone does not guarantee approval because equipment, availability and sign-off may still constrain it. This is a derived test design, not an executed test. The source prototype reveals a missing mandatory reason field; the review replaces “quickly” with a number/condition. The supplement's walkthrough compares FIFO with urgency and revises SR-4.1 to let urgent requests precede the queue subject to Ms. Lee's sign-off . That resolves one priority ambiguity but still requires cancellation, tie-handling, permissions and timing rules. Source claims that the excerpt is fully validated should not hide these remaining questions. 8. Keep the reason connected to implementation and tests requirement-lineage.svg Figure 2 — Requirement lineage (informal traceability diagram) Read it: Downward links mean derives from or realizes; they are not execution order. Trace upward to explain why a module or test exists. A single UR usually needs more than the one illustrative SR shown here. Key takeaway: Preserving IDs and links lets a change propagate deliberately instead of becoming a disconnected edit. Forward traceability follows requirements into design, code and tests to detect omitted scope. Backward traceability asks which authorized need or constraint justifies an artifact, exposing unrequested features (“gold plating”). Bidirectional traceability supports both. Infrastructure can be justified through architectural or derived constraints; the slide's “no requirement ID means code should not exist” is a review prompt, not permission to delete unexplained code.[^trace] The course uses E-xxx for raw evidence, UC-xx for interaction, UR-x for user need, SR-x.x for detailed derivation, FRx/NFRx for catalog items and TC-xxx for tests. The dot in SR-2.1 expresses its UR-2 parent in this local scheme . FR6 and NFR3 are sequential IDs; their parents must be explicit in links. Do not infer a universal notation rule for all projects. The complete supplied UR/SR trace skeleton User need → system rule Design references Test references in S11 pp.24–25 --- --- --- UR-1 mobile timetable → SR-1.1 fetch/display behavior TimetableUI / ScheduleCtrl TC-UI-101 / TC-API-204 UR-2 urgent swap → SR-2.1 capacity rejection SwapModule / CapacityChk TC-UI-105 / TC-UNIT-402 UR-3 notice policy → SR-3.1 reject [!warning] SR-1.1 has incompatible representations S04 p.52 specifies login-triggered fetch and render in 3.0 seconds over 4G. Its p.63 RTM, S06 §4.8.1 and S11 p.24 instead say schedule-tab-triggered JSON fetch [!question] Check your understanding “We notified the administrator” is offered as proof of “no swap bypasses approval.” What is missing? An alert is not an authorization condition: specify and test that the allocation cannot change before the authorized approval, including exceptional and concurrent paths. [!summary] Remember the distinctions Raw evidence ≠ approved requirement. UR/SR is abstraction; FR/NFR is the kind of commitment; FURPS+ is classification; viewpoint is perspective. EARS grammar ≠ semantic precision. A use-case association ≠ workflow. A test link ≠ executed evidence. A baseline can change through an authorized revision; a source excerpt labelled complete can still contain gaps.
