entries.title: Requirements Engineering — Exercises and Worked Solutions
entries.text: Requirements Engineering — Exercises and Worked Solutions Course index · Notes · Exercises · Lab These are the original End-of-Chapter Review Questions from Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, in their original order. Q27–Q28 form the practical in Lab; Q29 preserves the additional E-003 question in the reading's “Apply What You've Learned” box. Repeated in-chapter questions remain explicitly mapped. All solutions are reasoned model answers; proposed policies/thresholds are labelled. Exercise Q1 — Process timing ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q1. What distinguishes the timing of Requirements Engineering in a Waterfall model compared to an Agile model? [!tip]- Hint Compare where the baseline is created and how later detail changes. [!success]- Solution In the course’s Waterfall model, RE is concentrated upfront and a validated SRS is baselined before system design. In Agile, backlog items and acceptance criteria are refined continuously, with feedback informing later work. Both need stakeholders and validation; cadence and governance differ. Internal iterations during the upfront RE phase do not turn the whole lifecycle into Agile. Exercise Q2 — Cost of late correction ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q2. Why is an omitted or ambiguous requirement in Waterfall significantly more expensive to fix during testing than during upfront specification? [!tip]- Hint Follow a mistaken requirement through downstream artifacts. [!success]- Solution An omitted or ambiguous statement can shape architecture, code, interfaces, test expectations and user procedures. Discovering the error in testing may require revising and rechecking all of those dependencies. During specification, fewer downstream commitments exist, so clarification often costs less. This explains the risk without assuming every late correction has an identical or exponential cost. Exercise Q3 — Elicitation versus analysis ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q3. What is Requirements Elicitation, and how does it differ from Requirements Analysis & Classification? [!tip]- Hint Separate raw evidence from the interpretation of that evidence. [!success]- Solution Elicitation discovers and records stakeholder needs, domain constraints and observations with attribution. Analysis organizes levels and viewpoints, clarifies statements, classifies them and detects conflicts. An interview quote remains raw evidence even when it sounds like a requirement. When analysis discovers a missing fact, return to elicitation; preserve the quote rather than silently replacing it with the analyst’s interpretation. Exercise Q4 — Technique and evidence ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q4. Name three Elicitation techniques and, for each, describe how its findings should be documented. [!tip]- Hint Match the evidence to a durable artifact. [!success]- Solution Three valid choices: Interview: capture dated notes attributed to the stakeholder, preserving wording and unresolved questions. Workshop/JAD: keep minutes, speaker-attributed raw requests and actions. Observation/shadowing: record time-stamped field notes and the current workflow, distinguishing observed facts from inferred needs. Add each relevant statement to the Elicitation Register with source/date/status. Surveys with tabulated results, document analysis with citations and prototypes with annotated feedback are also source-supported alternatives. Exercise Q5 — Elicitation deliverables ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q5. List the deliverables that come out of the Elicitation phase. Why is none of them yet a finalized User or System Requirement? [!tip]- Hint Include supporting evidence and models, not just the register. [!success]- Solution The outputs are the Elicitation Register, draft use-case diagram, draft use-case descriptions, stakeholder/viewpoint list, draft domain glossary and supporting interview notes, workshop minutes, observations, prototypes/feedback. They preserve a broad initial understanding. They have not yet been fully organized, classified, conflict-checked, refined and validated, so they are not finalized authorized UR/SR statements. “Draft” does not mean useless: it makes uncertain content reviewable. Exercise Q6 — Use-case maturity ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q6. Explain why a Use Case Description can reasonably be written in both Stage 1 (Elicitation) and Stage 3 (Specification). What changes between the two versions? [!tip]- Hint A document can keep its identity while increasing precision. [!success]- Solution In Stage 1, the description captures the stakeholder’s interaction in accessible language, often emphasizing the main success path so the user can correct misunderstandings. In Stage 3, the same use case is refined after analysis: actor, pre/postconditions, alternate and error flows, terms and requirement links become precise. It is incorporated into the SRS and validated before sign-off. The stage changes its maturity and purpose, not necessarily its identifier. Exercise Q7 — Approval before a quick swap ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★★☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q7. Rewrite the raw statement "the system should let students swap rooms quickly, but only if a lecturer approves it first" as one or more EARS-pattern requirements. Which pattern(s) did you use, and why? [!tip]- Hint Preserve this question’s student requester and lecturer approver: they differ from the main lecturer/admin case. Do not invent the meaning of quickly. [!success]- Solution First clarify whether swap means room-allocation change or only request submission, who the lecturer approver is, and which measurable deadline applies. Preserve the question’s roles. One proposed decomposition is: WHEN a student submits a room-swap request, the system shall record it as pending lecturer approval (event-driven); IF lecturer approval has not been recorded, THEN the system shall prevent the requested allocation change (unwanted behavior); WHEN the authorized lecturer approves an eligible request, the system shall apply the approved room change (event-driven). These separate request, authorization and effect. “Quickly” still requires a performance requirement with agreed timing endpoints, threshold and conditions; no number is given, so mark that target UNCONFIRMED and do not baseline it. These are proposed clarifications, not permission to replace the main case’s Ms. Lee sign-off rule. Exercise Q8 — User versus system ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q8. Explain the difference between a User Requirement and a System Requirement. Why must User Requirements be organized before System Requirements are written? [!tip]- Hint Ask who must understand the statement and what precision they need. [!success]- Solution A UR explains a stakeholder’s service/goal in accessible terms; an SR refines exact behavior and constraints for developers/testers. UR-1 allows mobile weekly timetable viewing; the source SR-1.1 specifies a triggering event, calendar display and a 3.0-second/4G target. Organizing the user need first lets stakeholders validate the problem before engineers optimize a technical solution. Otherwise precise APIs or schemas can implement the wrong goal. SRs need precision, not arbitrary implementation prescriptions. Exercise Q9 — Viewpoints versus levels ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q9. What is Viewpoint-Oriented Analysis (VOA), and how does it differ from sorting requirements by abstraction level? [!tip]- Hint Viewpoint and abstraction are separate axes. [!success]- Solution VOA checks Interactor, Indirect and Domain perspectives so direct interviewees do not crowd out other needs or constraints. Sorting by abstraction instead separates high-level user intent from detailed system commitments. A domain policy can generate both a user-level constraint and a precise system rule. The same requirement can therefore have a viewpoint tag and an abstraction-level tag; neither classification substitutes for the other. Exercise Q10 — Reset password securely ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★★☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q10. Using FURPS+, classify the following statement into its Functional and Non-Functional parts: "The system shall let a user reset their password securely within 10 seconds." [!tip]- Hint Separate the operation, its time budget and the vague security promise. [!success]- Solution Functional part: let a user reset a password, tagged Functionality. Performance part: finish the defined reset operation within 10 seconds , tagged Performance; specify when timing starts/stops and under what load/network, including whether human/email delays count. Security part: “securely” is not testable; elicit identity-verification, authorization and other applicable controls rather than guessing them. Security behavior can be tagged Functionality/security and/or constraints as appropriate to the course catalog. Do not mistake the FURPS+ label F for a different kind of statement that excludes FRs: the slides and reading differ on that convention. The original sentence must be split and clarified before acceptance tests are authoritative. Exercise Q11 — Interaction grid ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★★☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q11. Build a small Matrix-Based Interaction Analysis grid for three requirements of your choosing, and explain how you would resolve any conflict you find. [!tip]- Hint Select three explicit commitments; score each unordered pair once and explain every nonzero score. [!success]- Solution Example choices (proposed): A — an authenticated student can view a weekly timetable; B — the full timetable renders within 3.0 seconds over the agreed 4G test conditions; C — schedule traffic uses the agreed encryption control. Pair grid A B C --- ---: ---: ---: A — +1 0 B +1 — −1 C 0 −1 — A/B is marked compatible because usable schedule viewing is supported by responsiveness. A/C is neutral for this narrow interaction assessment. B/C is a potential resource conflict, following the source’s example: extra processing/handshake work may consume part of the time budget. It is not proof both cannot be met. Establish a representative workload, estimate or prototype timing, and consider a design that satisfies both. If commitments are incompatible, have authorized stakeholders revise a target, scope or budget and record the rationale; do not silently weaken mandatory security. The values are qualitative judgments, not probabilities or arithmetic utilities. Exercise Q12 — Measurable usability ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q12. Rewrite the following as a measurable Non-Functional Requirement: "The system shall have a friendly interface." [!tip]- Hint Replace friendly with an observable user task, a threshold and conditions. [!success]- Solution One proposed NFR: In a usability test with ten representative first-time lecturers, at least nine shall complete the specified room-swap request workflow in under three minutes without external help. Metric: task completion time and success count; thresholds: [!tip]- Hint A number alone is not enough if its unit or environment is missing. [!success]- Solution The three ingredients are the metric , a threshold with unit , and the conditions under which it applies. “Respond quickly” does not define how to measure the response, how quick is acceptable or the workload/environment. A tester cannot reproducibly decide pass/fail. Clarify the response endpoints, agree a threshold such as the case’s 3.0 seconds only where that case applies, and specify conditions rather than guessing a universal value. Exercise Q14 — SRS organization ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q14. Name the standard sections of an SRS document. Where would a use case diagram belong, and where would the Requirements Traceability Matrix belong? [!tip]- Hint Follow the course’s five major SRS sections and its subdivisions of section 3. [!success]- Solution The standard taught here is: 1 Introduction ; 2 Overall Description ; 3 Specific Requirements , divided into 3.1 FRs, 3.2 External Interfaces, 3.3 NFRs, 3.4 Use Cases/Models; 4 Appendices ; 5 Approval/Sign-off . A use-case diagram belongs in 3.4 , connected to finalized descriptions. The RTM belongs in 4 Appendices . Glossary, assumptions, dictionary and revision history support interpretation and control. This is the course template, not a claim every organization must use the same headings. Exercise Q15 — Group the catalog ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q15. Explain how Functional Requirements should be grouped within an SRS, and how Non-Functional Requirements should be grouped. Why not just list all requirements in one flat table? [!tip]- Hint Think about how a reviewer searches for behavior and how cross-cutting qualities interact. [!success]- Solution Group FRs by feature/module, such as scheduling, room swaps and notifications. Group NFRs by quality/constraint category, such as performance, usability, reliability or supportability. Use stable IDs and cross-references so an NFR can constrain several FRs without being duplicated inconsistently. A flat undifferentiated table makes feature coverage, related quality constraints and ownership harder to review as the catalog grows. Keep the RTM as the connecting view across groups. Exercise Q16 — Check versus technique ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q16. Distinguish a validation check (Section 4.7.1) from a validation technique (Section 4.7.2). Give one example of each. [!tip]- Hint One names a property; the other names an activity that gathers evidence about it. [!success]- Solution A validation check asks whether a property holds—for example, consistency asks whether FIFO priority and urgent precedence contradict. A technique is how we investigate—for example, a walkthrough places both requirements before Dr. Li and Ms. Lee and explores the same-room scenario. Reviews, prototypes and test-case generation are techniques; validity, consistency, completeness, realism and verifiability are checks. One technique can support several checks. Exercise Q17 — Derive a test ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q17. Which validation technique would you use to check whether a requirement is Verifiable? Walk through how you would apply it to a requirement of your choice. [!tip]- Hint Try to derive a reproducible test from the wording alone. [!success]- Solution Use test-case generation . Choose SR-2.1: if room capacity is below enrollment, reject the swap. Set capacity 30 and enrollment 45; submit as a lecturer meeting the use case’s preconditions; expect rejection and the specified warning. Add an equality case to ensure the capacity rule itself does not reject when capacity = enrollment, while retaining other applicable checks. If the requirement only said “a suitably sized room,” the input relation and expected decision would be undefined, revealing a verifiability defect. Designing this test does not mean it has been run. Exercise Q18 — Combine techniques ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q18. Explain why combining multiple validation techniques (e.g., a review and test-case generation) catches more defects than relying on just one. [!tip]- Hint Different techniques expose different classes of missing evidence. [!success]- Solution A review can notice contradictory approval policies or missing stakeholder scope even if each statement has a test. Test-case generation exposes ambiguous timing, inputs and expected outcomes. A UI prototype can reveal that a mandatory reason field or practical workflow is missing despite a plausible written description. Combining them therefore tests complementary assumptions and reduces blind spots. It costs more effort and still cannot prove absence of every defect; use the findings to revise the SRS and recheck affected areas. Exercise Q19 — Forward and backward tracing ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q19. Differentiate between Forward Traceability and Backward Traceability. How does backward traceability prevent "Gold Plating"? [!tip]- Hint Trace forward to find omissions; trace backward to find unsupported additions. [!success]- Solution Forward traceability follows a requirement into design, implementation and tests so an approved need is not omitted. Backward traceability starts with a module/code/test artifact and asks which approved requirement or justified derived constraint requires it. An extra feature with no justification is a gold-plating candidate: remove it from scope or take it through authorization rather than quietly expanding delivery. Necessary infrastructure can be justified through architecture/derived constraints; an unexplained row is a review finding, not an automatic deletion order. Exercise Q20 — Informal changes ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q20. Why is it dangerous to accept requirement changes informally via email or verbal communication during late-stage Waterfall implementation? [!tip]- Hint A message may record a request without authorizing a changed baseline. [!success]- Solution An informal acceptance can leave the SRS, code, tests and budget describing different products. Dependencies, regression work and schedule impact may be missed, producing scope creep and disputes about what was agreed. Capture the email or conversation as ECR input, assess impacts through the RTM, obtain the authorized decision and update the baseline plus affected artifacts. The communication medium is not inherently wrong; bypassing the agreed decision and version-control process is the problem. Exercise Q21 — RTM impact analysis ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★★☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q21. Explain, step by step, the role of the RTM during an Impact Analysis triggered by a new Engineering Change Request (ECR). [!tip]- Hint Start with changed requirements; follow every outgoing relationship and then check shared dependencies. [!success]- Solution 1. Record the ECR and identify the requirement IDs/versions it would change. 2. Query the RTM for dependent UR/SR/catalog entries, modules, code/API references and tests. 3. Inspect connected interfaces and shared constraints to find effects beyond the first row; the RTM is an index, not a substitute for engineering analysis. 4. Estimate implementation, data/interface changes, retesting, effort, cost and milestone impact. 5. Give this evidence to the CCB. 6. If approved, revise the SRS baseline, RTM, implementation/test plans and schedule/budget; retain history. If rejected, log the rationale and keep the baseline. In the case, NFR2 affects SR-1.1, GetScheduleService.java and TC-API-204; encryption evidence and timing checks must be updated, not merely the catalog sentence. Exercise Q22 — Already-booked room ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q22. Write an Unwanted Behavior EARS requirement for the case study: a lecturer attempts to request a room that is already booked at that time. [!tip]- Hint State an unwanted condition and an observable response; keep the earlier rejection variant distinct from the later waitlist revision. [!success]- Solution Following the main chapter’s rejection variant : IF a lecturer requests a room already booked for the requested time, THEN the system shall reject the swap request and refresh the available-room list. This uses Unwanted Behavior (IF/THEN), identifies the conflicting time and defines the response. It is a proposed formulation of the original rule. The supplement later replaces flat rejection with a waitlist and approved urgent precedence; a final combined specification must resolve that change explicitly rather than implementing both without conditions. Exercise Q23 — Performance and encryption ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★★☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q23. Given the conflict between NFR1 (loading time [!tip]- Hint A conflict score identifies a negotiation and evidence task, not permission to weaken a control. [!success]- Solution Mark the potential conflict symmetrically: NFR1 load --- ---: ---: NFR1 load High-security encryption −1 — Clarify the exact encryption obligation, data path and performance measurement. Measure or prototype a representative workload to establish whether overhead actually threatens the budget. Explore an implementation that meets both; if not feasible, assess scope, resources or an authorized target change and record the decision/owner. Do not silently reduce a mandatory security level. At original v1.0 in this source story, encryption was a future risk , not a committed NFR2; the later ECR makes it binding in the scenario. Document that status difference. The main text also alternates “ [!tip]- Hint Preserve E-003 as a condition even though it has no independent UR number. [!success]- Solution Feasibility: the case is allowed to proceed on its technology/budget/integration assumptions. Elicitation: Dr. Li’s E-002 records the urgent-swap problem; E-003 records Ms. Lee’s sign-off; UC-04 captures the interaction. Analysis: E-002 becomes UR-2, tagged Functionality with performance expectations; E-003 is attached as a constraint. Specification: SR-2.1 refines capacity rejection, and UC-04 supplies the pending-review workflow; FR2 triggers an administrator alert. SR-2.1 alone does not fully implement every part of UR-2. Validation: TC-UNIT-402 is derived for the capacity rule; prototype/walkthrough checks expose missing reason and approval/queue issues. RTM: UR-2 → SwapModule → TC-UI-105; SR-2.1 → CapacityChk (CapacityChecker/RoomValidationUtil.java in fuller reading) → TC-UNIT-402. Changes use ECR/CCB control. The source’s Passed labels are example statuses, not results from this task. Exercise Q25 — Transfer to an everyday app ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q25. Pick any everyday app on your phone. Write one User Requirement and derive one corresponding System Requirement from it, using EARS syntax. [!tip]- Hint Choose one familiar user outcome, then derive one observable system behavior. [!success]- Solution Chosen everyday app type: an alarm app (illustrative example, no actual phone inspection). UR-A1: A user can set an alarm to be alerted at a chosen time. Proposed SR-A1.1: WHEN the device clock reaches the enabled alarm’s saved trigger time, the alarm application shall present the configured alert. This is event-driven EARS. It refines a trigger and observable response without prescribing an internal scheduler. Clarify time zones, missed alarms, device power/permission conditions and timing tolerance before treating it as complete. Many other apps are valid if the derived SR preserves the user goal. Exercise Q26 — Spiral versus upfront ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q26. Explain, in your own words, why the Spiral View (progressive refinement) does not contradict the idea that Waterfall RE happens 'upfront.' [!tip]- Hint Distinguish the lifecycle phase boundary from activities inside that phase. [!success]- Solution “Upfront” describes the placement of RE before the course’s downstream design/implementation stages. The spiral describes repeated learning within RE: business needs are elicited/specified/validated, then user needs, then detailed system requirements. Validation can send a draft back for clarification before a baseline is approved. Internal iterations are compatible with an upfront phase gate; they do not mean the team has completed separate agile product Sprints. Later baseline changes still use the course’s change-control process. Practical review questions Q27 and Q28 are preserved with adjacent hints and full solutions in Library Book Reservation — SRS Lab. Exercise Q29 — Where E-003 goes ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★★☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, §4.9, Apply What You've Learned, third prompt. E-003 (“room swaps should never bypass my sign-off”) never receives its own UR or SR ID anywhere in this chapter. Using the ID legend in the Glossary, explain where its content actually ends up in the SRS instead, and why it does not need an ID of its own. [!tip]- Hint No separate UR does not mean no traceable constraint. Ask whether alerting someone actually enforces their approval. [!success]- Solution The course attaches E-003 as a business constraint on UR-2 and the UC-04 approval workflow rather than creating a separate user goal. E-003 already has a raw-evidence ID, so preserve that reference in the parent requirement, description and test coverage. Its intended content is that allocation changes remain subject to Ms. Lee’s approval; FR2’s notification supports the workflow but alone does not enforce it. A separate UR/SR ID is not required by the source’s chosen organization if the condition is precise, independently checkable and traceable through the parent. Supplementary engineering note: giving an approval constraint its own stable ID may improve reviewability in a real catalog; neither choice permits omitting it. The supplied excerpt’s enforcement details remain incomplete.

entries.title: Library Book Reservation — SRS Lab
entries.text: Library Book Reservation — SRS Lab Course index · Notes · Exercises · Lab Objective and setup Produce a small requirements traceability matrix and a one-page SRS outline using the course's own applied review tasks. Original source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions Q27–Q28; method from §§4.6.1 and 4.8.1. These are document-design tasks; no implementation or particular tool/version is required. Use Notes and a Markdown editor. Keep this exercise's Library Book Reservation scope separate from the university timetable and Campus Express examples. The source specifies no reservation policies, users, database or API. State assumptions before designing a trace: assumptions below are illustrative proposals, not lecturer requirements. No code, running library system or test results were provided. Expected output: Exactly five RTM requirement rows with meaningful links and honest status, plus an SRS outline containing headings only. The outline should fit one A4 page under normal document settings; native A4 pagination is not verified here. An implementation, actual executed tests and stakeholder approval are outside this document task. Actual execution: Document examples authored and structurally checked; no software behavior was executed. Exercise Q27 — Five-row library reservation RTM ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★★☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q27. Design a 5-row Requirements Traceability Matrix for a simple 'Library Book Reservation' feature. [!tip]- Hint Choose a small set of explicit, compatible requirements. Give each a stable ID, justified design responsibility and a test with an observable outcome. Planned tests must not be labelled Passed. [!success]- Solution Proposed scope/assumptions: An authenticated library member may reserve an available copy, review their active reservations and cancel a reservation. Concurrent attempts must not allocate the same copy twice. The timing target below is a proposal needing approval; borrowing, fines, waitlists and expiry are outside this small example. Requirement definitions (proposed, not official policy): - FR-L1: WHEN an authenticated member requests an available copy, the reservation system shall create an active reservation for that member and mark that copy reserved. - FR-L2: IF the requested copy has become unavailable before reservation commitment, THEN the system shall reject the attempt without creating a reservation and inform the requester. - FR-L3: WHEN a member opens My Reservations, the system shall display that member’s active reservations. - FR-L4: WHEN a member cancels their active reservation before collection, the system shall cancel it and return the copy to availability. - NFR-L1: Under an agreed test workload of up to 50 concurrent members, at least 95% of reservation-create responses shall be returned within 2 seconds of request receipt during a 10-minute measurement window. The dataset and arrival pattern must be agreed before execution. Exactly five RTM rows. The requirement/purpose column records justification; design components and test IDs are proposed artifacts, not existing code. All five requirements are at System level. FR-L1–FR-L4 are draft requirements with planned tests; NFR-L1 is a proposed target and has not been run. Requirement and purpose Design Test and evidence --- --- --- FR-L1: Reserve an available copy Reservation service TC-L1: one valid request creates the linked reservation and changes copy state FR-L2: Exclusive allocation; constrains FR-L1 Reservation commit TC-L2: concurrent requests for one copy yield at most one committed reservation; loser is informed FR-L3: Review own reservations Member reservations view TC-L3: fixture with two members displays only requester’s active reservations FR-L4: Cancel an uncollected reservation Cancellation service TC-L4: valid cancellation changes reservation and copy availability consistently NFR-L1: Timely response; constrains FR-L1 and FR-L2 Reservation request path TC-L5: record latency distribution under agreed workload; ≥95% ≤2s Why this is traceable: Start at a requirement to find the design/test obligation, or start at a component/test to find its purpose. FR-L2 supplies the concurrency condition that “available” in FR-L1 alone fails to settle. A test ID is useful only with its procedure/results and version; the table provides planned outcomes without fabricating execution. Other coherent five-row catalogs are valid if assumptions and coverage are explicit. Exercise Q28 — One-page library SRS outline ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★★☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q28. Draft a one-page SRS outline (section headings only) for the 'Library Book Reservation' feature, following the structure in Section 4.6.1. [!tip]- Hint Use the course’s five major sections, keeping specific requirements in 3.1–3.4 and the RTM in an appendix. Submit headings only, not a second full catalog. [!success]- Solution The following is the headings-only proposed outline . It retains the course template and groups the small feature catalog coherently. Printed one-page fit depends on native export settings; no export is claimed. 1. Introduction - 1.1 Purpose - 1.2 Scope of Library Book Reservation - 1.3 Definitions, Acronyms and Glossary - 1.4 References and Document Overview 2. Overall Description - 2.1 Product Perspective - 2.2 Product Functions - 2.3 User Characteristics - 2.4 Constraints - 2.5 Assumptions and Dependencies 3. Specific Requirements - 3.1 Functional Requirements - 3.1.1 Create and Protect Reservations - 3.1.2 View and Cancel Reservations - 3.2 External Interface Requirements - 3.3 Non-Functional Requirements by Quality/Constraint Category - 3.4 Use Case Specifications and Supporting Models 4. Appendices - 4.1 Data Dictionary - 4.2 Requirements Traceability Matrix - 4.3 Interaction Analysis Grid - 4.4 Revision History 5. Approval and Sign-off Review and troubleshooting Check that the RTM has five requirement rows, every test has an expected outcome, and every status reflects actual evidence. If a requirement cannot produce a clear test, refine the condition rather than marking it verified. If your outline becomes several pages, remove explanatory paragraphs—the original question asks for headings only. Keep proposed design responsibilities free of unsupported framework/version assumptions. A five-row matrix is a learning example, not a complete real library specification. Missing institutional policies remain questions for elicitation. No external stakeholder interview, approval, implementation or test execution took place.

entries.title: In 60 seconds
entries.text: A model deliberately hides detail to answer a particular question. Context shows the boundary; use cases show external roles and their goals; sequence diagrams show ordered messages for one scenario. First decide who needs the model and what decision it supports. Source: lecture PDF pp. 4–7.

entries.title: Before you start
entries.text: Recall functional requirements from Unit 04. You need to distinguish an external actor from an internal object, a goal from an implementation step, and a condition from a sequence. This unit develops context/use-case/sequence topics only. Class, activity and state-machine diagrams appear in the agenda but have no teaching section in this supplied deck; they remain pending.

entries.title: 1. Choose a perspective and precision
entries.text: Perspective Question Model --- --- --- External What lies outside? Context Interaction Who interacts, or in what order? Use case / sequence Structural What data structure exists? Class (pending here) Behavioural How does behavior evolve? Activity / state machine (pending here) An existing-system model clarifies current behavior for requirements discussions. A planned-system model communicates a proposed design. Model-driven tooling needs correct, complete specifications for what it generates; a discussion sketch can omit more detail. Accuracy expectations depend on purpose. Source: lecture PDF pp. 5–7.

entries.title: 2. Context is a boundary decision
entries.text: A context diagram shows surrounding systems and connections, not internal design or message order. Choosing the boundary affects responsibility and stakeholder interests. Supplementary boundary sketch derived from the courier tutorial: mermaid flowchart LR Customer -- Delivery[Parcel Delivery Management System] Delivery -- PayLink[External PayLink] Delivery -- SMS[External SMS gateway] Finance[Corporate invoicing software: outside scope] The Finance system is outside this project; the prompt does not require an integration to it. A box in this context sketch is not a UML use-case oval. Source: lecture PDF p. 9; Week 5 Tutorial.docx, Question 2.

entries.title: 3. Actors and goals
entries.text: A use-case diagram gives a high-level functional view: named system rectangle, actors outside, goal ovals inside, plain actor associations. An actor is a role , not a particular person; it can be a person, external system, device or timer. Primary actors pursue goals, supporting actors provide services, and offstage stakeholders have interests without directly using the system. Source: lecture PDF pp. 11–12. For the hotel exercise: Guest associates with Search Available Rooms, Book a Room, View Booking Details, Make Payment and Cancel Reservation. Hotel Receptionist associates with Check In Guest, Check Out Guest and Generate Occupancy Reports. The statement does not establish mandatory include links between these goals. Do not add policy because a booking app usually has it. Source: Week 5 - UML Lecture Exercise.docx, Hotel Reservation System.

entries.title: 4. Include, extend and generalization
entries.text: Include points from the base task to required reused behavior. Extend points from conditional additional behavior to its base use case, with its condition stated. Generalization points from specialized actor/use case to its general parent. Source: lecture PDF pp. 13–14; courier tutorial. Airline examples: Book Flight includes Make Payment; Apply Promo Code extends Book Flight [code supplied]; Request Special Assistance extends Check-In Online [assistance requested]. The exercise describes authentication as a prerequisite for every other passenger goal. Its wording can be represented as a precondition; if the teaching exercise expects an included authentication use case, state that abstraction rather than assuming a fresh login occurs within each action. The visually reviewed airline diagram in ANSWER.docx omits authentication despite that prerequisite in the worksheet. Keep the prerequisite visible in your explanation; this discrepancy does not prove that authentication is unnecessary. The diagram confirms the payment/include and promo/assistance/extend directions. [!question]- Predict the arrow A returned library book is overdue. Which use case extends which, and does every return require login? [!success]- Check Charge Overdue Fine extends Return Book [past due date], with the arrow toward Return Book. The prompt explicitly says return does not require login. Source: Week 5 Tutorial.docx, Question 1.

entries.title: 5. Requirements become scenarios
entries.text: The lecture traces banking requirements OBS-01…OBS-20 to goals and numbered flows. Its supplied excerpt gives login, transfer selection, insufficient funds, and cancel-at-confirmation requirements. Do not fabricate the full separate requirements PDF, which is referenced but absent. A full description names the use case and primary actor; preconditions; numbered main flow; alternates/exceptions branching from numbered steps; and postconditions. In Transfer Funds: choose accounts/amount, validate, show confirmation, confirm, post debit/credit/reference, then receipt/log. Insufficient funds and invalid account stop validation; cancellation discards; a posting fault rolls back. Source: lecture PDF pp. 15–22.

entries.title: 6. Read a sequence diagram
entries.text: Time runs downward on participants' lifelines. A synchronous message calls and waits; a dashed return carries its response. Activation bars show executing/waiting periods. Keep abstraction levels consistent. alt chooses guarded alternatives, opt performs one guarded optional block, loop repeats. Source: lecture PDF pp. 24–28. Supplementary textual reconstruction of the supplied login scenario (PDF pp. 29–30; lecture exercise Login): mermaid sequenceDiagram actor User participant Browser participant Auth as Authentication server User- Browser: Submit credentials Browser- Auth: Verify credentials activate Auth Auth- Auth: Check stored records Auth-- Browser: Authentication result deactivate Auth alt valid Browser-- User: Welcome else invalid Browser-- User: Error end Both branches are outcomes, not two messages that always run. The diagram is explanatory, not a prescribed implementation protocol.

entries.title: 7. Compose guarded interactions
entries.text: Checkout uses an opt [payment succeeded] for inventory update and order confirmation in the deck. The supplied ANSWER.docx checkout image uses alt [PaymentSuccessful] / [PaymentFailed] instead: the success branch updates stock and confirms the order; the failure branch sends Order Failed to the customer. These are two source variants. Neither supplies a refund or retry policy. Transfer Funds nests an outer alt for invalid/valid inputs, an opt for confirmation within valid, then an alt for posting success/fault. Sources: lecture PDF pp. 31–35; ANSWER.docx checkout image. For the vehicle-renewal tutorial, a missing record or unpaid fines must terminate before payment. For QuickMed, each failed check terminates the request; stock checks repeat for each medication; home delivery is optional. A declined payment is explicitly out of scope. These are fictional software scenarios, not clinical advice. Full adjacent worked reasoning is in Recall & practice.

entries.title: Review and source boundary
entries.text: Explain why a context diagram cannot substitute for a sequence diagram. Draw arrows for mandatory payment and optional insurance. Trace an early rejection without later successful messages. Then attempt all eight supplied Week 5 exercise/tutorial tasks in Recall & practice. The original source documents remain available from Source library. All five answer images were visually inspected and remain preserved in the original DOCX. Differences between worksheet, deck and answer image are stated above. The new local reasoning and Mermaid reconstructions are independently derived teaching aids; they are not claimed as lecturer-issued solutions. No class/activity/state teaching chapter or missing banking-description PDF is invented.

entries.title: Your route through this tutorial
entries.text: Work through all fourteen tasks in Recall & practice. Each has an adjacent hint and complete explanation. First attempt from memory, then compare the scope, unresolved criteria and reasoning. Original DOCX files are preserved in Source library.

entries.title: 1. Classical Waterfall and evolving requirements
entries.text: The worksheet compares an upfront approved requirements baseline with incremental Agile elaboration. Waterfall aims to reduce expensive downstream misunderstandings. Agile still performs requirements work and validation repeatedly. Avoid the absolute claim that Agile has no upfront work or Waterfall can never revisit a decision. Source: Tutorial Q1; Unit 04 notes.

entries.title: 2. Feasibility needs several kinds of evidence
entries.text: The parking budget addresses only one aspect. Check technical feasibility, operational fit, time/staff capacity and relevant constraints. When answering elicitation questions, connect the challenge to a concrete technique: observation for tacit practice, prototypes for unclear interaction needs, or workshops for conflicts. Source: Tutorial Q2–3.

entries.title: 3. Convert a wish into testable behavior
entries.text: Flight alerts, unusual withdrawals, approaching drivers and unlocked doors each need a trigger, defined conditions, response and acceptance criteria. User requirements express stakeholder goals; system requirements elaborate behavior. Terms such as instantly, exactly and unusual remain unresolved until criteria are agreed. Suggested criteria in solutions are proposals, not supplied instructor values. Source: Tutorial Q4; Additional Q1–3.

entries.title: 4. Separate functions and quality expectations
entries.text: Search, filtering, workout sync and offline downloading describe functions. Timing expectations constrain them under agreed conditions. FURPS Performance covers those timing concerns; security is grouped under Functionality in the supplied course framework; concurrent-save integrity concerns Reliability. FURPS categories do not replace functional/quality analysis. Source: Tutorial Q5; Additional Q4–8.

entries.title: 5. Reason about interactions
entries.text: The 500 ms signed-answer problem is a possible resource/latency conflict. Mark the interaction, explain a concrete mechanism, propose a design and identify what needs testing. Deferring signing changes what acceptance means and requires agreed semantics; it cannot silently weaken the original requirement. Source: Tutorial Q6.

entries.title: Review
entries.text: Explain one requirement without using vague speed or accuracy language. Identify at least one criterion still requiring stakeholder agreement. Compare your complete fourteen attempts with the local worked reasoning, then revisit the cards marked for review. No official thresholds or exam predictions are supplied here.

entries.title: What makes a software system broader than a program?
entries.text: It includes software components, configuration, system documentation and user documentation, not only executable instructions.

entries.title: What is the scope of software engineering?
entries.text: All aspects of software production, including supporting management, within organizational and financial constraints.

entries.title: Who controls a generic product’s specification?
entries.text: The product developer controls it for a wider market.

entries.title: Who controls a customized product’s specification?
entries.text: The commissioning customer controls it through agreement with the developer.

entries.title: Which software quality attribute concerns adapting a system when requirements change?
entries.text: Maintainability: the software can evolve as customer and business needs change.

entries.title: Which grouped quality attribute concerns reliability, safety and protection from misuse?
entries.text: Dependability and security cover reliability, safety and protection against malicious access or damage.

entries.title: Which quality attribute concerns response time, processing time and memory use?
entries.text: Efficiency concerns appropriate response time, processing time, memory and other resource use.

entries.title: Which quality concerns fit for intended users?
entries.text: Acceptability concerns understandability, usability and compatibility with the systems intended users employ.

entries.title: Why can changing software raise failure risk?
entries.text: A modification can introduce faults or disturb interactions, even when the software does not physically wear out.

entries.title: Why can a code-complete claim misrepresent progress?
entries.text: Integration and defect correction may remain, with an uncertain amount of work before useful checked behavior exists.

entries.title: What are the four fundamental lifecycle activities?
entries.text: Specification; design and implementation; validation; evolution.

entries.title: What can professional certification indicate, and what does it fail to guarantee about a particular software product?
entries.text: It can provide evidence of meeting a defined professional standard. It does not guarantee continuing competence or the correctness of every product; product-specific evidence remains necessary.

entries.title: What is a software process model?
entries.text: A simplified representation of a software process and the organization of its activities.

entries.title: What makes a system critical?
entries.text: Failure can cause significant human, economic or environmental loss.

entries.title: Why can an approved requirement be costly to change?
entries.text: Its dependent design, implementation, tests and documents may need revision and reapproval.

entries.title: Which checks occur during Waterfall implementation?
entries.text: Unit testing, alongside coding and code reviews; not every check waits for the final integrated system.

entries.title: What does an increment add?
entries.text: Useful functionality to an existing version; it need not provide the complete final workflow.

entries.title: In incremental development, what does interleaving specification, development and validation mean?
entries.text: Specification, development and validation inform each other during work instead of being entirely separate one-time phases.

entries.title: What can undermine independent increments?
entries.text: Shared dependencies can make a change affect earlier increments and require coordination and integration checks.

entries.title: Why are requirements revisited after component analysis?
entries.text: Candidate capabilities reveal mismatches requiring negotiated changes or additions to meet real needs.

entries.title: How can choosing a reused component reduce a development team’s control over future changes?
entries.text: Control over component evolution, because the supplier decides new component versions.

entries.title: What is system testing concerned with?
entries.text: The integrated system, including unexpected interactions and interface problems between components.

entries.title: What is regression testing?
entries.text: Rerunning earlier tests after changes to look for newly introduced failures.

entries.title: What distinguishes test planning from execution?
entries.text: Planning specifies intended inputs, conditions and expected evidence; execution runs checks and records actual results.

entries.title: What does empirical control use to guide decisions?
entries.text: Observed evidence and adaptation when important aspects of the work or context remain uncertain.

entries.title: What does transparency enable?
entries.text: A shared understanding of actual work and quality so inspection uses trustworthy evidence.

entries.title: What does inspection compare?
entries.text: Artifacts and progress against goals or standards to detect meaningful deviations.

entries.title: What does adaptation do?
entries.text: Changes the work or process in response to what inspection reveals.

entries.title: What is the Product Owner accountable for?
entries.text: Maximizing product value and effective, understandable, ordered backlog management.

entries.title: What is the Developers’ delivery responsibility?
entries.text: Plan and perform the work needed for a usable Increment meeting the Definition of Done.

entries.title: How can a Scrum Master become a taskmaster?
entries.text: By assigning every task and replacing Developers’ self-management with status reporting.

entries.title: What separates Review from Retrospective?
entries.text: Review inspects product outcomes and context with stakeholders; Retrospective improves how the team works.

entries.title: What do acceptance criteria describe?
entries.text: The particular behavior or conditions required of an individual backlog item.

entries.title: What does a 90%-finished item contribute if DoD is unmet?
entries.text: Zero Done story points for that Sprint; it returns to the Product Backlog for future consideration.

entries.title: Why ask high and low poker voters to explain?
entries.text: Their estimates may include different scope, effort, risks or assumptions that must be clarified before agreement.

entries.title: When does this activity require splitting a large item?
entries.text: At 13 points or higher under the explicit Step 3 instruction; page 1’s 13 wording differs.

entries.title: How is mean velocity calculated?
entries.text: Add comparable Done points across observed Sprints and divide by the number of Sprints.

entries.title: In the course’s Scrum chart (slide 46), what does each vertical axis measure, and can either be read as story-point velocity?
entries.text: Remaining effort in hours on the left; remaining and completed task counts on the right. Neither axis measures Done story points, so neither directly gives story-point velocity.

entries.title: What separates elicitation from analysis?
entries.text: Elicitation preserves attributed needs and constraints; analysis interprets, organizes, classifies and compares them.

entries.title: Why organize user needs before detailed system rules?
entries.text: Stakeholders must confirm the intended outcome before developers optimize or specify a technical solution.

entries.title: What question does viewpoint analysis ask?
entries.text: Whose direct, indirect or domain perspective must this requirement represent?

entries.title: When is the ubiquitous EARS pattern appropriate?
entries.text: When the obligation has no trigger or condition: the system shall perform the stated response.

entries.title: In an event-driven EARS requirement, what does WHEN introduce?
entries.text: An event that triggers the specified system response.

entries.title: In a state-driven EARS requirement, what does WHILE introduce?
entries.text: A continuing state during which the specified obligation applies.

entries.title: In the course’s option-driven EARS template, what does WHERE introduce?
entries.text: An included feature or configuration option, rather than merely an incoming runtime event.

entries.title: What does IF…THEN express in unwanted-behavior EARS?
entries.text: The unwanted condition and the required response when it occurs.

entries.title: What separates an FR from a FURPS+ category label?
entries.text: An FR states a behavior; a category classifies requirements and is not itself a testable statement.

entries.title: Which three ingredients make a quality target measurable?
entries.text: A defined metric, a threshold with unit, and the conditions under which it applies.

entries.title: In the course’s requirements interaction matrix, what does a score of −1 establish?
entries.text: A potential conflict needing explanation and evidence; it does not prove the requirements are jointly impossible.

entries.title: What separates a validation check from a technique?
entries.text: A check names the property examined; a technique gathers evidence about that property.

entries.title: What makes an SRS version a baseline?
entries.text: Authorized approval of that version, after which revisions follow the agreed change-control process.

entries.title: What does backward traceability investigate?
entries.text: Which authorized requirement or justified derived constraint explains a design, code or test artifact.

entries.title: How does a Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM) help evaluate a proposed change?
entries.text: Locate affected requirements, design/code and tests so impact analysis can inform the authorized change decision.

entries.title: Why omit detail in a model?
entries.text: To make one aspect discussable and support a defined audience and decision.

entries.title: What does a context diagram establish?
entries.text: The system boundary and external systems; not internal design, use-case order or a scenario timeline.

entries.title: What is an actor?
entries.text: An external role interacting at the boundary, potentially a person, system, device or timer.

entries.title: In a UML use-case diagram, which way does an «include» arrow point?
entries.text: From the base use case to the mandatory included behavior.

entries.title: In a UML use-case diagram, which way does an «extend» arrow point?
entries.text: From conditional additional behavior to the base use case, with its extension condition stated.

entries.title: What does a sequence diagram describe?
entries.text: Participants exchanging ordered messages for one scenario; time runs downward.

entries.title: What distinguishes alt and opt?
entries.text: alt has guarded alternatives; opt has a single guarded optional block without an explicit else.

entries.title: What does a loop fragment represent in a UML sequence diagram?
entries.text: A guarded repetition of enclosed messages.

entries.title: What does a complete use-case description include?
entries.text: Actor/goal, preconditions, main flow, numbered alternates/exceptions and postconditions.

entries.title: Why stop messages after an early rejection?
entries.text: Later success actions require preconditions that the rejected branch did not establish.

entries.title: Why does a user requirement need elaboration?
entries.text: Stakeholder goals must be translated into observable behavior, triggers, conditions and agreed acceptance criteria.

entries.title: Is a budget alone a feasibility argument?
entries.text: No. Technical capability, operational fit, schedule and constraints must also be assessed.

entries.title: Does Agile avoid requirements work?
entries.text: No. It revisits requirements incrementally; classical Waterfall invests earlier to reduce costly downstream misunderstanding.

entries.title: Is an unmeasured quality adjective testable?
entries.text: No. Define an agreed measure, conditions and threshold; do not silently invent official values.

entries.title: What do interactor, indirect and domain viewpoints mean?
entries.text: Interactor uses/interfaces directly; indirect has interests without direct use; domain contributes rules or constraints from the application domain.

entries.title: How do functional and FURPS classifications differ?
entries.text: Functional versus quality separates behavior from its constraints; FURPS categories group concerns and are not a one-to-one synonym for that separation.
